docs.text: GlitchyGames is a wrapper around Pygame that aims to support 20-25FPS minimum games on Raspberry Pi and other low powered Linux systems. The engine is written to provide: Readability as a first principle Scene primitives Advanced event handling Human readable/editable sprite file formats Example Game # Let's make a new game called Bitrot Adventures. The goal of our game will be to draw a pixel on the screen and handle key events to move the pixel around. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Bitrot Adventures""" import argparse import pygame from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine from glitchygames.scenes import Scene class BitrotAdventures ( Scene ): """Draws a pixel to the screen""" NAME = 'Bitrot Adventures' VERSION = '0.0.0' def __init__ ( self , options ): super () . __init__ ( options = options , groups = None ) def main (): # Pass the Scene class uninitialized; the engine creates it GameEngine ( game = BitrotAdventures ) . start () if __name__ == "__main__" : main ()

docs.text: Galimore (1998–2001): what it is and how its tools work # A survey of the Galimore project (1998–2001), the author's earlier game and its tools, made on 2026-10-18 to inform GlitchyGames' level tools ( plans/2026-10-18-level-tools.md ). Conventions: SRC/ = the original files ( galimore_files/ , kept outside this repository); X/ = where the survey extracted each archive (one directory per archive). [read] = read directly in a file; [inferred] = concluded from sizes, layouts or context. R/ = PNG renders the survey decoded from the original data with a small read-only decoder, used to confirm the binary layouts below (the decoder and renders are not in this repository). Nothing from the archives was executed. TL;DR # Not a Mac game. Galimore is a top-down tile RPG ("similar to Final Fantasy 3 (English) or Zelda", Galimore Clean Up/Old Galimore Folder/Galimore Archive/public_html copy/index.html ) [read] for MS-DOS , developed on an iMac (Photoshop 5.02 for art, Virtual PC for code: "Yeah, I'm using a Mac to write a PC game", public_html copy/development.html ) [read]. Hence the resource forks, MacBinary .bin , CR line endings and ƒ folder names. Two engine generations: 1999, Borland C++ 16-bit DOS : BGI SVGA256.BGI , 256 colours, XMS. A playable GALIMORE.EXE plus tools GEDIT, GMAP, GATTRIB, MAKEDAT, GTORAW/RAWTOG ( X/CU_galisource072399/ ) [read]. Aug 1999 – Aug 2000, DJGPP (gcc 2.8.1) + Allegro 3.9.32 WIP , 640×480 at 16/15-bit colour. Only the toolchain exists: Galibmap (bitmap/sprite editor), Mapedit (map editor), Galimake (data packer) and a fire-effect demo. The new game was "Not yet started, but should use most of the mapeditor engine" ( development.html ) [read]. Successor: in Aug 2000 the code was relicensed (LGPL) as "RPG Tools" / "Phosphor" , a SourceForge map editor ( Galimore/Old Galimore Folder/RPG Tools Code/ ) [read]; only headers and a Makefile exist (no rendering code; graphics were Allegro 2D, with no OpenGL anywhere). Formats: every file is a raw fwrite dump of a C++ object: no header, no version, little-endian, compiler-specific padding. File type is detected purely by size (2332 / 49152 / 3072 / 4608 bytes). All are fully decoded in §2. 1. Source chronology: 1999-07 BGI ( galisource072399 ) → 1999-10 102599 → 2000-04 gbe/gme_4_17_00 → 2000-05-31 May archive → 2000-06-04/05 codebackup → June daily zips → 2000-07-12 Source 7:12:00 / COMPLETE.ZIP / Archive July 12 (= 08-00 ) → 2000-07-31/08-01 Galimore Source as of 7_31_00 (newest Galimore code) → 2000-08-03 RPG Tools/ (LGPL) → 2000-08-07 RPG Tools Code/ (Phosphor) → 2000-09-05 mapedit (Binary) built → 2001-04-16 Galimore.zip . 7_12 → 7_31: flat directory split into src/ include/ bg/ fg/ get/ raw/ Backup/ ; "cross-platform" exists / file_size in g_io.cpp (later commented out); a GALIMAKE_STUB hack in gmore_raw.cpp ; small fixes in galibmap, g_data and mapedit. 1.3 File counts (2,301 originals) # Art: 845 .raw , 203 .fg , 192 .bg , 46 .gif , 26 .psp , 19 .psd , 14 .get , 3 .spr , 4 .big . Code: 297 .h , 293 .cpp , 75 .o , 25 .gpr + 25 .gdt (RHIDE), 14 .exe . Other: 34 .zip , 11 .map , 10 .dat , 19 .html , 8 .log , ~21 extension-less Mac sound files. .raw sizes: 675 × 3072 (32×32 RGB), 44 × 4608 (32×48 RGB), 118 × 768 (16×16 RGB), 4 × 6144, 4 × 4170. 1.4 Not extracted / unreadable / skipped # Zip members inside ƒ folders failed ("Illegal byte sequence"); their unpacked copies were read. 060400.zip member test<non-ASCII> (a 49,152 B sprite). Nested gbe_4_17_00.zip , gme_4_17_00.zip , gali.zip (May 2000 archive). No unar / lsar ; no StuffIt/BinHex archives found in scope. Sounds: data forks are 0 bytes; audio is only in resource forks ( sfil , System 7 sound). ClarisWorks design docs read via strings only (fragmentary). .psd / .psp / .big identified, not viewed. Skipped as personal: a personal page in public_html copy/ and an e-mail contacts file in RPG Tools Code/ . 2. Tools and file formats # All written with ofstream::write((char*)&obj, sizeof(obj)) , little-endian x86. 2.1 Galibmap: bitmap and sprite editor (2000) # Sources src/galibmap.cpp , src/bmap_gui.cpp , src/gmore_raw.cpp , src/g_object.cpp , src/g_sprite.cpp ; binary X/bitmap_Binary/galibmap.exe . - Space toggles object mode (8 frames of 32×32) and sprite mode (16 frames of 32×48). - 6× zoomed canvas: left-drag paints, right-drag eyedropper; drag frames in the strip to copy or reorder. - R/G/B sliders, three colour wells (C cycles, R replaces colour 2 with colour 1); New / Save / Load / Quit; keys 1–8, N, L, S, Esc. - Load branches purely on file_size : 2332 → object, 49152 → sprite, 3072 → raw tile, 4608 → raw sprite frame (the file browser filters by the same sizes). GALIMORE_OBJECT (tile/object), 2332 bytes ( .bg , .fg , .get ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 2048 | INT16 array[32][32] , [x][y] (offset (x·32+y)·2), RGB565 ; 0xF81F = transparent | | 2048 | 21 | objectName | | 2069 | 1 | objectType | | 2070 | 1 | objectState | | 2071 | 1 | objectSpecial | | 2072 | 2 | objectIsUsableBy (UINT16) | | 2074 | 1 | objectWeight | | 2075 | 256 | objectDescription | | 2331 | 1 | pad | The attribute block is all zeros in every shipped .dat (never authored). GALIMORE_SPRITE, 49,152 bytes ( .spr ): 16 × short array[32][48] , [x][y] RGB565. Frame plan ( spriteguide.html ): front / away / side × still / walk-R / walk-L, side mirrored → 9 used. pockets.spr uses 6 (rest grey). RAW, 3072 / 4608 bytes ( .raw ): headerless 8-bit RGB, row-major , 32×32 or 32×48 (Photoshop Raw export). Pipeline: Photoshop → .raw → Galibmap → .bg/.fg/.get/.spr . 2.2 Galimake: data packer # .dat = 2332-byte records back to back (58,300 = 25×2332, 67,628 = 29×2332, 4,664 = 2×2332). Stable tile IDs: maps store 1-based indices; on update Galimake loads the existing .dat , zeros (doesn't delete) records whose pixels no longer match a file , refreshes matches, and puts new tiles in the first blank slot, so map indices never shift. 2.3 Mapedit: map editor # Sources src/mapedit.cpp , src/mapeditor_gui.cpp , src/g_map.cpp , include/g_map.h . - 14×14 map view with scroll bars; 4×6 tile palette; layer tabs Fgnd / Bgnd / Obj / Spr / Mask ; floor radios 1F / 2F with show-layer checkboxes; "Make a Mask" and "Eraser" (tile 0). - Brush sizes 1–4; s / l save / load; Esc quits. - Mask tab: drag to stamp, right-click to pick up; magenta = no mask, purple = current, black = other. - Mask bits: 0 LAYER_SWITCH, 1 UNPASSABLE_GOOD, 2 UNPASSABLE_BAD, 3 UNPASSABLE_NEUTRAL, 4 DEEP, 5 BRIDGE, 6 CHASM, 7 PUSHABLE, 8 TRANSPARENT. An older plan ( g_mask.h , Dec 1999) added exits, burnable/bombable/freezable, hot/cold, anti-magic, death, door, soil, farmed, layer 2; "Mask Cases" planned a replacement tile in the upper 16 bits (e.g. burnt version) — never implemented. GALIMORE_MAP, 114,692 bytes (arrays [floor][x][y] ; verified by decoding house.map ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 1 | landscape (always 0) | | 1 | 8192 | UINT8 fgLayer[2][64][64] (N → record N-1 of fg.dat ; 0 = empty) | | 8193 | 8192 | UINT8 bgLayer → bg.dat | | 16385 | 1 | pad | | 16386 | 16384 | UINT16 objectLayer → get.dat | | 32770 | 16384 | UINT16 spriteLayer (unimplemented) | | 49154 | 2 | pad | | 49156 | 65536 | UINT64 maskLayer | 64×64 cells per floor, 2 floors. Samples: house.map (cottage on grass, 14 fg tiles, 1 object, 40 fully-impassable mask cells), map.map (lattice test), test.map (18 cells of tile 1). 2.4 The 1999 tools # GEDIT (32×32, 256 colours, rotate/mirror/replace/transparent colour, 8-frame sprites); GMAP (15×15 maps, layer toggles, exits); GATTRIB (attributes); GTORAW / RAWTOG (bitmap ↔ RGB raw, palette as a switch ). The two DOCs are swapped ( GMAP.DOC documents GEDIT). - Bitmap, 1312 B: bitmapSize, transparentImage, transparencyColor (default 15); byte array[32][32] palette indices [x][y] ; attribs (name[21], 3 type bytes, misc, weight, description[256]). BKG.DAT 19,680 = 15×1312. - Sprite, 9262 B: 8 frames (DOWN½, UP½, LEFT½, RIGHT½) + speed, dimensions, direction, X, Y + temp array + struct time . - Map: 1458 B = unsigned char Map[6][15][15] + 6 exits (old: 2808 B with int ). Exit = name[13] + pad + int X, Y. Layers: background, wall, object, scenery, door. 3. Assets # Asset Where Format 2000 tile art 7_31_00/raw/ , Galimore Archive/Galimore Tiles/ , Galimore Specs/Galimore Tiles/ 32×32 / 16×16 RGB raw 2000 game tiles 7_31_00/bg (25), fg (29), get (2); X/mapedit_Binary/*.dat 2332 B objects ( R/bg.png , R/fg.png , R/get.png ) Maps X/mapedit_Binary/{house,map,test}.map 114,692 B ( R/house_crop.png , R/map_crop.png ) Sprites pockets.spr , Sprite Testing/pockets_*.raw , Galimore Sprites/* .spr , raw, .psd , .gif ( R/pockets.png ) Objects / icons Galimore Objects/* , The 5 Points/* .psd / .psp World design Continent*.psd , Experiment Town.psd , House Example.jpg Photoshop 1999 art X/CU_galisource072399/ (70 bitmaps; sprites JABBA/MONK/MONST/PIMP/DOUG/MAN) 1312 B bitmaps, 9262 B sprites Sound Sound Effects/Stephen King/ (21) Mac resource forks only 4. Code quality and notable points # Good ideas: stable tile IDs (blank instead of delete); size-based type sniffing; Allegro driver trimming; reusable ID-dispatched widget toolkit with a "GUI Shell" starter template; per-function debug gating; Photoshop RAW interop; two-floor maps with a 64-bit per-cell property mask and layer-switch bit; palette-gradient fire for animated tiles; the editor doubles as the renderer. Bugs spotted (reported, not changed): 1. g_map.cpp saveMap() / loadMap() : char *fileName; strcpy(fileName, …) (uninitialized pointer). 2. g_map.cpp drawATile() : uninitialized theTileVector , no default: case. 3. mapeditor_gui.cpp : visibleLayers bit layouts disagree, and init uses && for & . 4. "Transparent" mask checkbox has no handler. 5. GALIMORE_OBJECT::getBitmap() has no return . 6. convertTo15() is identical to convertTo16() . 7. Sprite-frame copy constructor copies only 32×32 of 32×48; displayFrame() size mismatch. 8. Attribute copy/assignment skip objectWeight . 9. ~GALIMORE_BITMAP_OBJECT destroys bitmaps shared by vector copies. 10. g_mask.h constants are unsigned short but shift up to bit 25 (bits ≥ 16 are zero). 11. loadDataFile dedups by pixels, so identical tiles would collapse [inferred risk]. 12. do{}while(infile) processes the failed final read once more. 13. .dat order depends on directory order; memory-dump formats are compiler/endian-specific. Unfinished: no 2000-era game runtime; sprite layer; object attributes; mask replacement tiles; Linux port; script editor, character generation, NPC AI, OpenPlay networking. RPG Tools / Phosphor (Aug 2000): rpg_map.h (map class renamed C_RPGMap ), rpg_raw.h (LGPL), gcc Makefile, a CodeWarrior project (the only real classic-Mac toolchain artefact), CVS at cvs.rpgtools.sourceforge.net , naming style in Text Docs/CODING_STYLE.txt ( C_ classes, S_ structs, g globals, k / gk constants). 5. Relevance to GlitchyGames # Roadmap #11 "Level/room data format (and tilemaps)" is open; each game rolls its own ScreenData / FloorData / LevelManager ( plans/engine-audit.md ). 5.1 Worth porting # Map model for #11: Galimore's ordered layers (bg → fg → objects → actors), per-cell properties kept separate from the art, and named exits with entry points. The GlitchyGames design built from these ideas, adjusted for today's games and constraints (object layers, a typed property vocabulary, exit regions with named spawn points), is plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-a-tilemap-format.md . Stable tile IDs: explicit IDs or tombstones, never list position. Collision on the map cell, separate from the art. Editor features: Mapedit's brush sizes, property-paint mode with pick-up/stamp, layer and floor visibility, tileset palette, eraser = 0; Galibmap's colour wells, frame drag-reorder, and the 9-frame walk-cycle convention. Animated tiles via animation frames, or a procedural fire buffer. 5.2 Converting Galimore data # The survey's read-only decoder (not in this repository) decodes everything below to PNG; sub-plan E ( plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-e-galimore-import.md ) plans a reviewed converter. - Tiles: <1024H , transpose from [x][y] , RGB565 → RGB888, 0xF81F → magenta; write TOML pixels + [colors] (10–60 colours per tile); keep the 1-based .dat index as the tile ID. - Sprites: 16 × 32×48 frames ( <1536H , [x][y] ); drop all-grey frames; walk_down (0–2), walk_up (3–5), walk_side (6–8, mirrored). - Raw: RGB888 row-major → PNG for Bitmappy. - Maps: offsets in §2.3; layers per floor; mask bits → named properties. - 1999 data: 1312 B indexed bitmaps (palette from GTORAW or GALIMORE PALLETE.GIF ; honour transparencyColor ), 9262 B 8-frame sprites, 1458 / 2808 B maps with exits — the best test case for a room/exit design. - Caveats: tiles may be RGB555 if saved in 15-bit mode; attribute blocks are empty; sounds need resource-fork extraction first (e.g. DeRez ).

docs.text: Sources src/galibmap.cpp , src/bmap_gui.cpp , src/gmore_raw.cpp , src/g_object.cpp , src/g_sprite.cpp ; binary X/bitmap_Binary/galibmap.exe . - Space toggles object mode (8 frames of 32×32) and sprite mode (16 frames of 32×48). - 6× zoomed canvas: left-drag paints, right-drag eyedropper; drag frames in the strip to copy or reorder. - R/G/B sliders, three colour wells (C cycles, R replaces colour 2 with colour 1); New / Save / Load / Quit; keys 1–8, N, L, S, Esc. - Load branches purely on file_size : 2332 → object, 49152 → sprite, 3072 → raw tile, 4608 → raw sprite frame (the file browser filters by the same sizes). GALIMORE_OBJECT (tile/object), 2332 bytes ( .bg , .fg , .get ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 2048 | INT16 array[32][32] , [x][y] (offset (x·32+y)·2), RGB565 ; 0xF81F = transparent | | 2048 | 21 | objectName | | 2069 | 1 | objectType | | 2070 | 1 | objectState | | 2071 | 1 | objectSpecial | | 2072 | 2 | objectIsUsableBy (UINT16) | | 2074 | 1 | objectWeight | | 2075 | 256 | objectDescription | | 2331 | 1 | pad | The attribute block is all zeros in every shipped .dat (never authored). GALIMORE_SPRITE, 49,152 bytes ( .spr ): 16 × short array[32][48] , [x][y] RGB565. Frame plan ( spriteguide.html ): front / away / side × still / walk-R / walk-L, side mirrored → 9 used. pockets.spr uses 6 (rest grey). RAW, 3072 / 4608 bytes ( .raw ): headerless 8-bit RGB, row-major , 32×32 or 32×48 (Photoshop Raw export). Pipeline: Photoshop → .raw → Galibmap → .bg/.fg/.get/.spr .

docs.text: .dat = 2332-byte records back to back (58,300 = 25×2332, 67,628 = 29×2332, 4,664 = 2×2332). Stable tile IDs: maps store 1-based indices; on update Galimake loads the existing .dat , zeros (doesn't delete) records whose pixels no longer match a file , refreshes matches, and puts new tiles in the first blank slot, so map indices never shift.

docs.text: Sources src/mapedit.cpp , src/mapeditor_gui.cpp , src/g_map.cpp , include/g_map.h . - 14×14 map view with scroll bars; 4×6 tile palette; layer tabs Fgnd / Bgnd / Obj / Spr / Mask ; floor radios 1F / 2F with show-layer checkboxes; "Make a Mask" and "Eraser" (tile 0). - Brush sizes 1–4; s / l save / load; Esc quits. - Mask tab: drag to stamp, right-click to pick up; magenta = no mask, purple = current, black = other. - Mask bits: 0 LAYER_SWITCH, 1 UNPASSABLE_GOOD, 2 UNPASSABLE_BAD, 3 UNPASSABLE_NEUTRAL, 4 DEEP, 5 BRIDGE, 6 CHASM, 7 PUSHABLE, 8 TRANSPARENT. An older plan ( g_mask.h , Dec 1999) added exits, burnable/bombable/freezable, hot/cold, anti-magic, death, door, soil, farmed, layer 2; "Mask Cases" planned a replacement tile in the upper 16 bits (e.g. burnt version) — never implemented. GALIMORE_MAP, 114,692 bytes (arrays [floor][x][y] ; verified by decoding house.map ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 1 | landscape (always 0) | | 1 | 8192 | UINT8 fgLayer[2][64][64] (N → record N-1 of fg.dat ; 0 = empty) | | 8193 | 8192 | UINT8 bgLayer → bg.dat | | 16385 | 1 | pad | | 16386 | 16384 | UINT16 objectLayer → get.dat | | 32770 | 16384 | UINT16 spriteLayer (unimplemented) | | 49154 | 2 | pad | | 49156 | 65536 | UINT64 maskLayer | 64×64 cells per floor, 2 floors. Samples: house.map (cottage on grass, 14 fg tiles, 1 object, 40 fully-impassable mask cells), map.map (lattice test), test.map (18 cells of tile 1).

docs.text: Good ideas: stable tile IDs (blank instead of delete); size-based type sniffing; Allegro driver trimming; reusable ID-dispatched widget toolkit with a "GUI Shell" starter template; per-function debug gating; Photoshop RAW interop; two-floor maps with a 64-bit per-cell property mask and layer-switch bit; palette-gradient fire for animated tiles; the editor doubles as the renderer. Bugs spotted (reported, not changed): 1. g_map.cpp saveMap() / loadMap() : char *fileName; strcpy(fileName, …) (uninitialized pointer). 2. g_map.cpp drawATile() : uninitialized theTileVector , no default: case. 3. mapeditor_gui.cpp : visibleLayers bit layouts disagree, and init uses && for & . 4. "Transparent" mask checkbox has no handler. 5. GALIMORE_OBJECT::getBitmap() has no return . 6. convertTo15() is identical to convertTo16() . 7. Sprite-frame copy constructor copies only 32×32 of 32×48; displayFrame() size mismatch. 8. Attribute copy/assignment skip objectWeight . 9. ~GALIMORE_BITMAP_OBJECT destroys bitmaps shared by vector copies. 10. g_mask.h constants are unsigned short but shift up to bit 25 (bits ≥ 16 are zero). 11. loadDataFile dedups by pixels, so identical tiles would collapse [inferred risk]. 12. do{}while(infile) processes the failed final read once more. 13. .dat order depends on directory order; memory-dump formats are compiler/endian-specific. Unfinished: no 2000-era game runtime; sprite layer; object attributes; mask replacement tiles; Linux port; script editor, character generation, NPC AI, OpenPlay networking. RPG Tools / Phosphor (Aug 2000): rpg_map.h (map class renamed C_RPGMap ), rpg_raw.h (LGPL), gcc Makefile, a CodeWarrior project (the only real classic-Mac toolchain artefact), CVS at cvs.rpgtools.sourceforge.net , naming style in Text Docs/CODING_STYLE.txt ( C_ classes, S_ structs, g globals, k / gk constants).

docs.title: 5. Relevance to GlitchyGames

docs.text: Map model for #11: Galimore's ordered layers (bg → fg → objects → actors), per-cell properties kept separate from the art, and named exits with entry points. The GlitchyGames design built from these ideas, adjusted for today's games and constraints (object layers, a typed property vocabulary, exit regions with named spawn points), is plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-a-tilemap-format.md . Stable tile IDs: explicit IDs or tombstones, never list position. Collision on the map cell, separate from the art. Editor features: Mapedit's brush sizes, property-paint mode with pick-up/stamp, layer and floor visibility, tileset palette, eraser = 0; Galibmap's colour wells, frame drag-reorder, and the 9-frame walk-cycle convention. Animated tiles via animation frames, or a procedural fire buffer.
docs.title: 5.1 Worth porting

docs.text: The survey's read-only decoder (not in this repository) decodes everything below to PNG; sub-plan E ( plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-e-galimore-import.md ) plans a reviewed converter. - Tiles: <1024H , transpose from [x][y] , RGB565 → RGB888, 0xF81F → magenta; write TOML pixels + [colors] (10–60 colours per tile); keep the 1-based .dat index as the tile ID. - Sprites: 16 × 32×48 frames ( <1536H , [x][y] ); drop all-grey frames; walk_down (0–2), walk_up (3–5), walk_side (6–8, mirrored). - Raw: RGB888 row-major → PNG for Bitmappy. - Maps: offsets in §2.3; layers per floor; mask bits → named properties. - 1999 data: 1312 B indexed bitmaps (palette from GTORAW or GALIMORE PALLETE.GIF ; honour transparencyColor ), 9262 B 8-frame sprites, 1458 / 2808 B maps with exits — the best test case for a room/exit design. - Caveats: tiles may be RGB555 if saved in 15-bit mode; attribute blocks are empty; sounds need resource-fork extraction first (e.g. DeRez ).

docs.text: Multi-Controller System Documentation # Overview # The Multi-Controller System enables up to 4 simultaneous controllers to navigate and interact with the bitmappy tool independently. Each controller has its own visual indicator, navigation state, and can operate simultaneously without conflicts. Features # Multi-Controller Support : Up to 4 simultaneous controllers Independent Navigation : Each controller navigates film strips and frames independently Visual Distinction : A unique color for each controller (Red, Green, Blue, Yellow): triangles on the film strips, squares on the canvas, circles on the sliders Smart Positioning : Automatic collision avoidance when multiple controllers select the same spot State Preservation : Controllers maintain their selection state when switching between them Hotplug Support : Controllers can be connected/disconnected during operation Architecture # Core Components # MultiControllerManager ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/manager.py ) - Central singleton managing all controllers ControllerSelection ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/selection.py ) - Individual controller state management VisualCollisionManager ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/indicators/collision.py ) - Smart positioning and collision avoidance ModeSwitcher ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/modes.py ) - Each controller's mode (film strip, canvas, R/G/B slider), switched with the L2/R2 triggers Integration with Bitmappy - ControllerEventHandler ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/event_handler.py ) and the per-mode button strategies ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/strategies.py ) The button and trigger bindings are listed in CONTROLLER_CONTROLS_README.md at the repository root. Controller Color Scheme # MultiControllerManager.CONTROLLER_COLORS , indexed by controller ID. In Bitmappy, activating a controller (Start) gives it the next color in activation order ( assign_color_to_controller ), so the first controller activated is red: Controller 0 : Red (255, 0, 0) Controller 1 : Green (0, 255, 0) Controller 2 : Blue (0, 0, 255) Controller 3 : Yellow (255, 255, 0) Usage Examples # Basic Setup # from bitmappy.controllers import ControllerSelection , MultiControllerManager from bitmappy.indicators import VisualCollisionManager # Initialize the system (MultiControllerManager is a singleton) manager = MultiControllerManager () visual_manager = VisualCollisionManager () controller_selections = {} # Find the connected controllers (through the engine's devices door; at most once a second) connected_instance_ids = manager . scan_for_controllers () # Set up a controller: only a connected controller can be assigned (None otherwise) instance_id = connected_instance_ids [ 0 ] controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) Controller Activation # # Activate a controller controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () manager . activate_controller ( instance_id ) # Set initial selection controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "animation_name" , 0 ) # Add visual indicator visual_manager . add_controller_indicator ( controller_id = controller_id , instance_id = instance_id , color = manager . CONTROLLER_COLORS [ controller_id ], position = ( 100 , 100 ) ) Navigation # # Navigate to different animation/frame controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "new_animation" , 5 ) # Get current selection animation , frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () print ( f "Controller { controller_id } is at { animation } , frame { frame } " ) # Get navigation history (an entry is added when the animation changes) history = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_navigation_history () for entry in history : print ( f "Previous: { entry [ 'animation' ] } , frame { entry [ 'frame' ] } " ) Multi-Controller Navigation # # Set up multiple controllers for i , instance_id in enumerate ( manager . scan_for_controllers ()): controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () # Each controller can navigate independently controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( f "animation_ { i } " , i ) # Add visual indicators visual_manager . add_controller_indicator ( controller_id = controller_id , instance_id = instance_id , color = manager . CONTROLLER_COLORS [ controller_id ], position = ( 100 + i * 50 , 100 ) ) # All controllers can navigate independently controller_selections [ 0 ] . set_selection ( "animation_A" , 0 ) controller_selections [ 1 ] . set_selection ( "animation_B" , 1 ) controller_selections [ 2 ] . set_selection ( "animation_C" , 2 ) controller_selections [ 3 ] . set_selection ( "animation_D" , 3 ) Visual Collision Avoidance # # Multiple controllers at same position for i in range ( 3 ): visual_manager . add_controller_indicator ( controller_id = i , instance_id = i , color = ( 255 , 0 , 0 ), position = ( 100 , 100 ) # Same position ) # System automatically applies offsets (VisualCollisionManager.POSITION_PATTERNS) to prevent overlap visual_manager . get_final_position ( 0 ) # (100, 100) - no offset visual_manager . get_final_position ( 1 ) # (85, 85) - (-15, -15) offset visual_manager . get_final_position ( 2 ) # (115, 85) - (15, -15) offset Controller State Management # # Check controller status if manager . is_controller_active ( instance_id ): print ( f "Controller { instance_id } is active" ) # Get controller information info = manager . get_controller_info ( instance_id ) if info : print ( f "Controller { info . controller_id } : { info . status . value } " ) # Deactivate controller (the manager has no deactivate; cleanup_inactive_controllers() # unassigns controllers idle for more than ASSIGNMENT_TIMEOUT seconds) controller_selections [ controller_id ] . deactivate () Hotplug Support # # Handle controller connection def on_controller_connected ( instance_id ): controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) if controller_id is not None : controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) print ( f "Controller { controller_id } connected" ) # Handle controller disconnection def on_controller_disconnected ( instance_id ): if instance_id in manager . assigned_controllers : controller_id = manager . assigned_controllers [ instance_id ] if controller_id in controller_selections : del controller_selections [ controller_id ] print ( f "Controller { controller_id } disconnected" ) Integration with Bitmappy # Event Handling # Bitmappy's ControllerEventHandler.on_controller_button_down_event scans for controllers, assigns the controller on its first button press, and passes the button to its current mode's strategy ( FilmStripModeStrategy , CanvasModeStrategy or SliderModeStrategy ). A simplified version of the film strip navigation: def on_controller_button_down_event ( event ): """Handle controller button presses in bitmappy.""" controller_id = manager . get_controller_id ( event . instance_id ) if controller_id is not None : if event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_START : # Start button - activate the controller on the first frame of the first animation if controller_id in controller_selections : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "first_animation" , 0 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_LEFT : # D-pad left - previous frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () if current_frame > 0 : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame - 1 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_RIGHT : # D-pad right - next frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame + 1 ) Film Strip Integration # def update_film_strip_indicators (): """Update visual indicators on film strips.""" for controller_id , selection in controller_selections . items (): if selection . is_active (): animation , frame = selection . get_selection () # Update visual indicator position if animation in film_strips : # frame_layouts maps (animation, frame) to the frame's rect on the strip frame_rect = film_strips [ animation ] . frame_layouts [ animation , frame ] visual_manager . update_controller_position ( controller_id , frame_rect . midtop ) Advanced Features # State Cloning # # Clone controller state to another controller source_controller = controller_selections [ 0 ] target_controller = controller_selections [ 1 ] source_controller . set_selection ( "animation_A" , 5 ) source_controller . clone_state_to ( target_controller ) # Target controller now has same state animation , frame = target_controller . get_selection () assert animation == "animation_A" assert frame == 5 Navigation History # # Track navigation history controller = controller_selections [ 0 ] controller . set_selection ( "animation1" , 0 ) controller . set_selection ( "animation2" , 1 ) controller . set_selection ( "animation3" , 2 ) # Get history history = controller . get_navigation_history () print ( f "Navigation history: { len ( history ) } entries" ) for entry in history : print ( f " { entry [ 'animation' ] } , frame { entry [ 'frame' ] } " ) Performance Optimization # # Clean up inactive controllers manager . cleanup_inactive_controllers () # Optimize visual positioning visual_manager . optimize_positioning () # Clear all indicators visual_manager . clear_all_indicators () Error Handling # Invalid Operations # # Handle invalid controller IDs gracefully if not manager . is_controller_active ( 999 ): print ( "Controller 999 not found" ) # Handle missing controller selections if controller_id not in controller_selections : print ( f "Controller { controller_id } not initialized" ) System Resilience # # System handles rapid controller switching for cycle in range ( 1000 ): for i in range ( 4 ): if i in controller_selections : controller_selections [ i ] . set_selection ( f "animation_ { i } " , cycle % 50 ) # System handles controller disconnection/reconnection for i in range ( 10 ): manager . _handle_controller_connect ( i ) # ... use controller ... manager . _handle_controller_disconnect ( i ) Best Practices # 1. Controller Lifecycle Management # def setup_controller ( instance_id ): """Properly set up a new controller.""" controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) if controller_id is not None : controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () manager . activate_controller ( instance_id ) return controller_id return None def cleanup_controller ( instance_id ): """Properly clean up a controller.""" if instance_id in manager . assigned_controllers : controller_id = manager . assigned_controllers [ instance_id ] if controller_id in controller_selections : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . deactivate () del controller_selections [ controller_id ] 2. Visual Indicator Management # def update_controller_visuals (): """Update all controller visual indicators.""" for controller_id , selection in controller_selections . items (): if selection . is_active (): animation , frame = selection . get_selection () position = get_frame_position ( animation , frame ) visual_manager . update_controller_position ( controller_id , position ) 3. State Synchronization # def sync_controller_states (): """Synchronize controller states with UI.""" for controller_id , selection in controller_selections . items (): if selection . is_active (): animation , frame = selection . get_selection () # Update UI elements update_film_strip_selection ( controller_id , animation , frame ) update_visual_indicator ( controller_id , animation , frame ) Troubleshooting # Common Issues # Controller not responding Check if controller is assigned: manager.assigned_controllers Verify controller is active: manager.is_controller_active(instance_id) Visual indicators overlapping System automatically handles collision avoidance Check collision groups: visual_manager.film_strip_collision_groups , canvas_collision_groups or slider_collision_groups State not preserved Ensure controller selection is activated: selection.activate() Check navigation history: selection.get_navigation_history() Debug Information # # Get system status print ( f "Active controllers: { manager . get_active_controllers () } " ) print ( f "Visual indicators: { len ( visual_manager . indicators ) } " ) print ( f "Collision summary: { visual_manager . get_collision_summary () } " ) # Get controller details for instance_id , info in manager . controllers . items (): print ( f "Controller { info . controller_id } : { info . status . value } , color { info . color } " ) Future Extensions # The multi-controller system provides a foundation for: Collaborative Editing : Multiple users editing simultaneously Advanced Visual Management : Custom indicators and positioning Session Management : Save/load controller configurations Permission Systems : Master/slave controller relationships API Reference # MultiControllerManager # scan_for_controllers() - Scan for connected controllers (at most once per scan_interval , 1 s) and return their instance IDs assign_controller(instance_id) - Assign a controller ID to a connected controller activate_controller(instance_id) - Activate an assigned controller assign_color_to_controller(controller_id) - Give a controller the next color in activation order get_controller_id(instance_id) / get_controller_color(instance_id) - Look up an assigned controller is_controller_active(instance_id) - Check if controller is active get_controller_info(instance_id) - Get controller information get_active_controllers() - Get list of active controllers cleanup_inactive_controllers() - Unassign controllers idle for more than ASSIGNMENT_TIMEOUT (5 s) ControllerSelection # activate() - Activate the controller deactivate() - Deactivate the controller set_selection(animation, frame) - Set animation and frame get_selection() - Get current animation and frame get_navigation_history() - Get navigation history clone_state_to(other) - Clone state to another controller VisualCollisionManager # add_controller_indicator(controller_id, instance_id, color, position, location_type=LocationType.FILM_STRIP) - Add visual indicator (a triangle on the film strip, a square on the canvas, a circle on a slider) remove_controller_indicator(controller_id) - Remove visual indicator update_controller_position(controller_id, position) - Update indicator position get_final_position(controller_id) - Get final position with offsets optimize_positioning() - Optimize all indicator positions clear_all_indicators() - Remove every indicator

CONTROLLER_BUTTON_START : # Start button - activate the controller on the first frame of the first animation if controller_id in controller_selections : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "first_animation" , 0 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_LEFT : # D-pad left - previous frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () if current_frame > 0 : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame - 1 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_RIGHT : # D-pad right - next frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame + 1 )

Command-Line Argument System # GlitchyGames uses a composable argparse architecture where the engine, event managers, font system, and individual games each contribute argument groups to a single parser. Every game built on the engine automatically inherits all engine-level flags, and can extend the parser with its own game-specific options. How Arguments Are Assembled # GameEngine.initialize_arguments() , called from GameEngine.__init__() , builds one parser from three layers. Here is what happens when you run Bitmappy ( uv run bitmappy ): the Engine box adds layers 1 and 2, the Bitmappy box layer 3, and argparse's ArgumentParser is outside both. sequenceDiagram participant PARSER as ArgumentParser box rgb(232,238,255) Engine participant INIT as initialize_arguments participant ENGINE as GameEngine.args participant MANAGERS as the 12 event managers end box rgb(255,243,224) Bitmappy participant GAME as BitmapEditorScene.args end INIT->>PARSER: ArgumentParser("Bitmappy version 1.0") INIT->>ENGINE: GameEngine.args(parser) Note over ENGINE: Layer 1
Graphics Options (15)
Diagnostics Options (15, 2 hidden) loop for each of the 12 ENGINE->>MANAGERS: manager.args(parser) end Note over MANAGERS: Layer 2, in this order
App, Audio, Controller (1), Drop,
Font (7), Game (3), Joystick, Keyboard,
Midi, Mouse, Touch, Window
(the 9 without a count add empty groups) INIT->>PARSER: add_argument_group("Bitmappy v1.0 Options") INIT->>GAME: BitmapEditorScene.args(group) Note over GAME: Layer 3
-v, -s INIT->>PARSER: parse_args() PARSER-->>INIT: the parsed options Note over INIT: GameEngine.OPTIONS = the options
target_fps resolved
game.options = OPTIONS Every option each layer adds is listed in the Complete Flag Reference . The Argument Group Hierarchy # Each layer adds its own add_argument_group() , so --help shows clearly separated sections, in the order of the layers. The layers mirror the engine's architecture. %%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 500}}}%% flowchart TB subgraph ENGINE_ARGUMENT_LAYERS["Engine"] L1["Layer 1: the engine (GameEngine.args)
Graphics Options, Diagnostics Options"] L2["Layer 2: event managers and fonts (each one's args)
Controller Options, Font Options, Game Options,
and 9 reserved groups with no options yet"] end subgraph GAME_ARGUMENT_LAYERS["Your game"] L3["Layer 3: your game (its scene's args)
GameName vX.Y Options"] end L1 --> L2 --> L3 In --help (Bitmappy's or Paddle Slap's) the groups hold 15 Graphics, 15 Diagnostics (2 more hidden), 1 Controller, 7 Font and 3 Game options, then the game's own; the nine empty groups are left out. The Complete Flag Reference lists them all. How Games Add Arguments # A game adds arguments by defining a @classmethod called args() on its scene class. The engine discovers this method via getattr(game, 'args', None) and calls it with a dedicated argument group. If the game does not define args() , the engine logs an informational message (INFO, once the command line has set the level, so --log-level info shows it; the default warning does not) and continues. flowchart TD subgraph Engine["Engine: GameEngine.initialize_arguments()"] CHECK{"getattr(game, 'args', None)"} CHECK -->|"method exists"| GROUP["parser.add_argument_group( GameName vX.Y Options)"] GROUP --> CALL["game.args(group)"] CHECK -->|"None"| LOG["log.info: Game does not implement arguments"] end subgraph GameCode["Your game: its scene class"] ARGS["@classmethod def args(cls, parser): parser.add_argument(...)"] end CALL --> ARGS Pattern: Minimal Game # class MyGame ( Scene ): NAME = 'My Game' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) Pattern: Game with Custom Options # class TimedDemo ( Scene ): NAME = 'Timed Demo' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): parser . add_argument ( '--time' , type = int , default = 10 , help = 'time in seconds to wait before quitting' , ) parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) Note that the game receives an argument group , not the root parser. This means game arguments appear under their own heading in --help output. OPTIONS Dictionary Flow # After parsing, the Namespace is converted to a plain dict and propagated to every component that needs it. flowchart TD PARSE["parser.parse_args()"] --> VARS["vars(args) Namespace -> dict"] VARS --> OPT["GameEngine.OPTIONS (class var)"] OPT --> FPS["OPTIONS['target_fps'] resolved (--target-fps, else the game's TARGET_FPS, else 60.01)"] FPS --> BACKPROP["game.options = OPTIONS"] BACKPROP --> SM_OPT["SceneManager.OPTIONS = OPTIONS"] SM_OPT --> SCENE_INIT["Scene.__init__(options=OPTIONS)"] SCENE_INIT --> SELF_OPT["self.options = OPTIONS"] subgraph Access["Runtime Access"] A1["self.options['target_fps']"] A2["self.options['font_name']"] A3["self.options['log_level']"] A4["self.options['debug_events']"] A5["GameEngine.OPTIONS['resolution']"] end SELF_OPT --> Access Logging level and the startup options block # A game logs at WARNING unless --log-level says otherwise (the owner, 2026-10-28: games default to WARNING, as the replay tools do), so a plain run prints only warnings and worse: the exit code it ended with, whether its seed was rolled or given, and the end-of-run performance reports are INFO, shown with --log-level info . Nothing else sets a level (the logger guards: no level set at import). Each failure a player sees (a crash, exit 70; a failed teardown; a playback that failed) logs one more line after its traceback, exit_codes.BUG_REPORT_HINT : "To report this, run the game again with --log-level info and include the output." The glitchygames command has no --log-level , so its own tool crashes do not say it. Every engine start ( start() or start_async() ) logs the run's whole options dictionary once, at CRITICAL, so it shows at every level ("for now": plans/future-work.md): game.engine - CRITICAL - Options for Paddle Slap (secrets redacted): allow_dirty = False ... log_level = 'warning' ... replay_trace = 'src/games/paddleslap/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz' Names are sorted, one name = value per line, aligned, with values as Python writes them; a nested mapping is indented below its name. Path options (the tools' and the engine's, the set a recording's header stores) are shown relative to the project root when inside it and absolute otherwise. An option whose name holds key, token, secret, password or credential, in any case, shows . The environment is never read. A replay's options are the recorded run's. random_seed is the seed the run uses, rolled or given (the owner, 2026-10-28: "The seed should definitely be in the options"), never None, so --random-seed with it plays the run again. Complete Flag Reference # Every option, by the layer that adds it and grouped as uv run bitmappy --help prints it: each with its type and default, then its help text. Layer 1: the engine # Graphics Options # Added by GameEngine.args() in src/glitchygames/engine/game_engine.py . -f, --target-fps TARGET_FPS ( float ): cap the framerate (default: the game's TARGET_FPS, else 60.01; 0 = uncapped) --fps-log-interval-ms FPS_LOG_INTERVAL_MS ( float ): how often to log the FPS counter in ms (default: 1000) -w, --windowed, --no-windowed ( bool ): run in a window; --no-windowed runs fullscreen (default: windowed) -r, --resolution RESOLUTION ( str ): the resolution to use (default: 800x480) --use-gfxdraw ( store_true , default False ): not used yet: stored, but nothing draws with pygame.gfxdraw because of it --update-type {update,flip} ( choice ): update or flip (default: update) --timer-backend {auto,fast,pygame} ( choice ): timer backend for draw loop pacing (default: auto, the fast backend with this machine's sleep delay measured, so each sleep wakes in time; fast assumes sleeps wake on time; pygame is the legacy backend) --sleep-granularity-ns SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS ( int , default 1000000 ): how long before each frame deadline the fast backend is to wake from its sleep and spin (ns); 0 spins only --windows-timer-1ms ( store_true , default False ): on Windows, request 1ms system timer resolution --random-seed RANDOM_SEED ( int ): master seed for every engine random stream (default: a random 64-bit seed, logged in recordings) --screen-shake-intensity SCREEN_SHAKE_INTENSITY ( float ): screen shake strength from 0.0 (off) to 1.0 (default: 1.0) --rumble-intensity RUMBLE_INTENSITY ( float ): controller rumble strength from 0.0 (off) to 1.0 (default: 1.0) --live-voice-pool LIVE_VOICE_POOL ( int ): mixer channels reserved for real-time synth voices (default: 4) --crt-power-on {auto,on,off} ( choice , default auto ): show the game's canvas switching on like a CRT before the game starts: auto (default: when someone can see it, so not on SDL's dummy driver or before a replay, audit, rebaseline or recording), on (always; refused with a replay or a recording) or off --default-background {test-pattern,channel-3} ( choice ): the background of a scene that sets none: the TV test pattern or the channel 3 blue screen (default: test-pattern) --video-driver {cocoa,offscreen,dummy} ( choice , default None ): not applied yet: stored, but SDL picks its video driver from SDL_VIDEODRIVER (or --headless) instead --video-driver choices by platform (SDL 2's video driver names, by platform.system() ; --help above is macOS's): Platform Choices macOS ( Darwin ) cocoa , offscreen , dummy Windows windows , offscreen , dummy Linux x11 , wayland , kmsdrm , offscreen , dummy any other offscreen , dummy Diagnostics Options # Added by GameEngine.args() right after the Graphics Options: how any run is watched, recorded, replayed or diagnosed, whatever the game; they change no game settings. Recording and replay are described in Gameplay Recording and Replay . Two more are hidden from --help : the watched replay's restart internals. --log-timer-jitter ( store_true , default False ): log frame pacing jitter statistics periodically --perf-trim-percent PERF_TRIM_PERCENT ( float , default 5.0 ): percent of frames to trim from top and bottom in global FPS report --fps-histogram {equal-range,target-relative} ( choice , default equal-range ): FPS histogram buckets in the shutdown report: equal-range (10 equal buckets spanning the analyzed min to max, default) or target-relative (10% steps of the target FPS) --debug-overlay, --no-debug-overlay ( bool , default False ): show the debug overlay at startup (F3 toggles, F4 cycles panels) --debug-events ( store_true , default False ): log a warning the first time each unhandled event type arrives (--no-unhandled-events raises on one instead) --record-trace PATH ( PATH ): record the session (sprites, frame times, input events, random seed) to a gzip JSON Lines trace for inspection and later replay (default: off) --replay-trace PATH ( PATH ): replay a --record-trace recording exactly through the engine, comparing every frame with it and reporting the first divergence (default: off) --replay-fps {recorded,real} ( choice , default None (read as recorded )): with --replay-trace: post FPS events from the recorded frame times (recorded, the default: exact, and compared with the recording) or from this machine's measured frame times (real: what this machine achieves; FPS events are then not compared, and sprites that draw the FPS value may diverge) --audit, --no-audit ( bool , default False ): with --replay-trace: instead of replaying, replay the recording twice in fresh headless processes with different hash seeds and compare every frame with the recording and between the runs; exits 0 when both match, 3 otherwise, 70 if a run could not finish --compare-processing ( store_true , default False ): with --replay-trace --headless: measure each frame's processing time (its work, without presenting or pacing) and report how it compares with the recording's (only meaningful on the machine that recorded) --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT ( PERCENT , default None ): with --replay-trace --headless (implies --compare-processing): a replay that matched but took more than PERCENT longer than the recording's processing time exits 8; a recording without processing times exits 65 --replay-pause-at-frame N ( N (non-negative int), default None ): with --replay-trace, watched: skip the start screen, run frames 0 to N - 1 without showing them, then pause with frame N next (what step back restarts with; ignored with --headless) --rebaseline NEW ( NEW , default None ): with --replay-trace OLD and --headless: replay OLD on the current code without stopping at divergences, write the run's recording (OLD's inputs, the current sprites) to NEW, print a summary of the frames and sprites that changed and exit 0 --replay-digest PATH ( PATH , default None ): with --replay-trace: write a SHA-256 of every replayed frame, then the divergence, to PATH as JSON lines (used by --audit) --list-input-devices ( store_true , default False ): print every joystick and game controller the game would see (index, instance id, name, GUID, whether SDL maps it as a game controller, its axes, buttons, hats and balls; how many SDL counted before its queue was pumped and each device added or removed while listening, with when), then exit 0 without running the game. At a terminal, when none is found it asks you to plug one in and waits for it (Ctrl-C stops). Refused with --replay-trace or --record-trace --headless ( store_true , default False ): run on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers: no window, no sound. With --replay-trace the replay also runs unpaced and prints its report to stdout (exit 0 when it matches, 1 when it diverges, 65 for a truncated recording) Layer 2: event managers and fonts # Controller Options # Added by ControllerEventManager.args() in src/glitchygames/events/controller.py (see Event System ). --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} ( choice ): Which gamepads the game sees (default: auto, every device; a mapped pad sends controller events, any other device joystick events; joystick: every device sends joystick events; controller: mapped pads only) Font Options # Added by FontManager.args() in src/glitchygames/fonts/font_manager.py . --font-name FONT_NAME ( str ): Font to use (default: the bundled Vera; the bundled variants are Vera, VeraBd, VeraIt and VeraBI; any other name is looked up among the system's fonts) --font-size FONT_SIZE ( int ): size of the default font, used by text that asks for no font of its own (default: 14) --font-bold ( store_true , default False ): not used yet: stored, but no text is drawn bold because of it --font-italic ( store_true , default False ): not used yet: stored, but no text is drawn italic because of it --font-antialias ( store_true , default False ): not used yet: stored, but each text widget chooses its own antialiasing --font-dpi FONT_DPI ( int ): the resolution, in dots per inch, freetype font sizes are scaled at (sets pygame.freetype's default resolution); the pygame font system ignores it (default: 72) --font-system {pygame,freetype} ( choice , default freetype ): Font system to use: freetype (enhanced, default) or pygame (built-in) Game Options # Added by GameEventManager.args() in src/glitchygames/events/game.py . -l, --log-level {debug,info,warning,error,critical} ( choice , default warning ): set the logging level (default: warning; a bug report asks for info) --no-unhandled-events ( store_true , default False ): fail on unhandled events -p, --profile ( store_true , default False ): enable profiling Reserved groups (empty, no arguments yet) # These event managers create their group as an extension point but add no options, so --help leaves them out. Group Name Source File Manager Class App Options events/app.py AppEventManager Sound Mixer Options events/audio.py AudioEventManager Drop Options events/drop.py DropEventManager Joystick Options events/joystick.py JoystickEventManager Keyboard Options events/keyboard.py KeyboardEventManager Midi Options events/midi.py MidiEventManager Mouse Options events/mouse.py MouseEventManager Touch Options events/touch.py TouchEventManager Window Options events/window.py WindowEventManager Layer 3: the game # Bitmappy v1.0 Options # Added by BitmapEditorScene.args() in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/editor.py ; the heading is v Options . -v, --version ( store_true , default False ): print the game version and exit -s, --size SIZE ( str ): the canvas size in pixels, WIDTHxHEIGHT (default: 32x32) Other games # The other games add their own options the same way: Game File Arguments Paddle Slap src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py -v, --version , -b, --balls (int, default 1), --ball-spawn-mode (choice, default paddle_only ) DT Demo src/demos/dt-demo/src/dt_demo/__init__.py -v, --version , -b, --balls (int, default 1) Clockwork Keep src/games/clockwork-keep/src/clockwork_keep/game.py --floor (int, default 0) Brave Adventurer (both editions) src/games/brave-adventurer/src/brave_adventurer/game.py , src/games/brave-adventurer/src/brave_adventurer_papyrus/game.py -v, --version Brave Adventurer's launcher src/games/brave-adventurer/src/brave_adventurer_modes/launcher.py (read before the engine's parser, which never sees it), title.py ( TitleScene.args() lists it in -h ) --game {classic,papyrus} , -v, --version Joystick Demo src/demos/joystick-demo/src/joystick_demo/__init__.py none (the engine's --input-mode chooses what it shows) Bitrot Adventures scripts/bitrotadventures.py -s, --some-game-specific-option Animation Demo scripts/animation_scene_full_demo.py -v, --version What --help Looks Like # uv run bitmappy --help prints a usage line, the options: group ( -h, --help ), then each group in the order the layers add them: Graphics, Diagnostics, Controller, Font and Game Options, then Bitmappy v1.0 Options . argparse leaves out groups with no arguments (App, Sound Mixer and the other reserved groups). Every option it prints, with its help text, is listed in Complete Flag Reference . How to Add Arguments to a New Event Manager # If you are adding arguments to a currently-empty event manager group, follow the existing pattern: # In src/glitchygames/events/mouse.py @classmethod def args ( cls , parser : argparse . ArgumentParser ) -> argparse . ArgumentParser : group = parser . add_argument_group ( 'Mouse Options' ) group . add_argument ( '--mouse-sensitivity' , type = float , default = 1.0 , help = 'Mouse sensitivity multiplier (default: 1.0)' , ) return parser The engine already calls your manager's args() method — you just need to add add_argument() calls to the existing group. How to Create a New Game with Arguments # from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine from glitchygames.scenes import Scene class MyGame ( Scene ): NAME = 'My Game' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): """Add game-specific arguments. Args: parser: An argument group (not the root parser). """ parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) parser . add_argument ( '--difficulty' , choices = [ 'easy' , 'medium' , 'hard' ], default = 'medium' , help = 'game difficulty level' , ) def __init__ ( self , options ): super () . __init__ ( options = options ) # Access your arguments via self.options self . difficulty = self . options [ 'difficulty' ] def main (): GameEngine ( game = MyGame ) . start () Your arguments will automatically appear under "My Game v1.0 Options" in the --help output, separate from all engine-level flags.

docs.text: A game logs at WARNING unless --log-level says otherwise (the owner, 2026-10-28: games default to WARNING, as the replay tools do), so a plain run prints only warnings and worse: the exit code it ended with, whether its seed was rolled or given, and the end-of-run performance reports are INFO, shown with --log-level info . Nothing else sets a level (the logger guards: no level set at import). Each failure a player sees (a crash, exit 70; a failed teardown; a playback that failed) logs one more line after its traceback, exit_codes.BUG_REPORT_HINT : "To report this, run the game again with --log-level info and include the output." The glitchygames command has no --log-level , so its own tool crashes do not say it. Every engine start ( start() or start_async() ) logs the run's whole options dictionary once, at CRITICAL, so it shows at every level ("for now": plans/future-work.md): game.engine - CRITICAL - Options for Paddle Slap (secrets redacted): allow_dirty = False ... log_level = 'warning' ... replay_trace = 'src/games/paddleslap/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz' Names are sorted, one name = value per line, aligned, with values as Python writes them; a nested mapping is indented below its name. Path options (the tools' and the engine's, the set a recording's header stores) are shown relative to the project root when inside it and absolute otherwise. An option whose name holds key, token, secret, password or credential, in any case, shows <redacted> . The environment is never read. A replay's options are the recorded run's. random_seed is the seed the run uses, rolled or given (the owner, 2026-10-28: "The seed should definitely be in the options"), never None, so --random-seed with it plays the run again.

docs.text: from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine from glitchygames.scenes import Scene class MyGame ( Scene ): NAME = 'My Game' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): """Add game-specific arguments. Args: parser: An argument group (not the root parser). """ parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) parser . add_argument ( '--difficulty' , choices = [ 'easy' , 'medium' , 'hard' ], default = 'medium' , help = 'game difficulty level' , ) def __init__ ( self , options ): super () . __init__ ( options = options ) # Access your arguments via self.options self . difficulty = self . options [ 'difficulty' ] def main (): GameEngine ( game = MyGame ) . start () Your arguments will automatically appear under "My Game v1.0 Options" in the --help output, separate from all engine-level flags.

docs.text:
Bitmappy Architecture # Bitmappy is GlitchyGames' pixel art editor. These diagrams show how it is wired up through the engine, from bootstrap to rendering. Its package # Bitmappy is an app, not part of the engine: the first member of the apps layer of the uv workspace , at src/apps/bitmappy/ . The distribution, the import package and the console script are all bitmappy ( uv run bitmappy ), and its scene's logical name, the one a recording holds, is apps.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene . A recording made when the scene lived in the engine ( glitchygames.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene ) is refused by a plain replay, which names the remedy; --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless converts it ( gameplay replay ). Its code is src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ . The engine never imports it, and Bitmappy uses the engine's public API (sprite file-format detection, for one, is the engine's src/glitchygames/sprites/file_format.py ). Its sprite library is 71 sprites in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/sprites/ , shipped as package data and found through bitmappy.SPRITE_CONFIG_DIR . They are also the AI's training data ( load_ai_training_data() below), so they stay in the package. Its other resources (the window icon and bitmappy.cfg ) are beside them, in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/ . Its tests are in src/apps/bitmappy/tests/ , rootless, every file named test_bitmappy_*.py . The Load and Save dialogs (the engine's glitchygames.ui dialog scenes) treat every file the same: the name is used as given, with surrounding whitespace trimmed, and a sprite in the library is opened by its path. The example: prefix they once understood is gone, and Save applies a per-platform rule to : in a file name ( _file_name_problem , the platform passed in and sys.platform by default); the refusal is shown in the editor's debug text and nothing is written: Platform : in a Save name Windows ( win32 , cygwin ) Allowed only in a letter-drive designator ( C:\a.toml , C:/a.toml , C:a.toml , \?\C:\a.toml , \.\C:\a.toml ); anywhere else, including inside a UNC server or share name, it is refused: NTFS would read it as an alternate data stream, so examples:foo.toml would leave an empty file called examples macOS ( darwin ) Refused everywhere: Finder shows : as / (a Classic Mac OS leftover) Linux and others Allowed Browser ( emscripten ) Allowed (Save is a download; the browser sanitizes the name) Load is unchanged (a missing name is reported as "File not found"). Bootstrap & Main Loop # How Bitmappy starts up: entry point through main() , GameEngine initialization, scene setup, and the main loop (one frame per pass, ended by _finish_frame ). The Bitmappy box is the editor's own code ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ ); the Engine box is what every game gets. sequenceDiagram participant User box rgb(255,243,224) Bitmappy participant main as main() participant BES as BitmapEditorScene end box rgb(232,238,255) Engine participant GE as GameEngine participant SM as SceneManager (singleton) end User->>main: uv run bitmappy main->>GE: GameEngine(game=BitmapEditorScene, icon=...) GE->>GE: parse CLI args (GameEngine.args() + BitmapEditorScene.args()) GE->>GE: pygame.init(), create display main->>main: load_ai_training_data() main->>GE: engine.start() GE->>BES: BitmapEditorScene(options=OPTIONS) BES->>BES: EditorSetup.init_undo_redo_system() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_menu_bar() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_canvas(options) BES->>BES: SliderManager.setup_sliders_and_color_well() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_debug_text_box() BES->>BES: FilmStripCoordinator.setup_film_strips() GE->>GE: _initialize_event_managers() GE->>SM: scene_manager.switch_to_scene(game) SM->>BES: setup() (AIManager.setup() starts the AI worker) GE->>SM: scene_manager.start() loop Main Game Loop (while active_scene is not None) Note over SM: dt = the previous frame's start-to-start time SM->>SM: camera.begin_frame() SM->>BES: _update_scene() (Scene.dt_tick: logic and collision) SM->>GE: _process_events() GE->>GE: _pump_events() (active_sources().pump_events(): live, pygame.event.get()) GE->>SM: EVENT_HANDLERS[event.type](event) SM->>BES: on_*_event(event) SM->>SM: _run_supervisor_slot() (supervisors, e.g. a recording's) SM->>SM: _update_frame_services() (shake, rumble) SM->>SM: _aim_active_camera() (camera_target / follow) SM->>SM: _position_active_world_sprites() (world sprites' rect, culling) SM->>SM: _render_scene() (BitmapEditorScene.update: animation, controllers, AI, then draw) SM->>SM: _advance_still_camera_shake() (WORLD shake nothing advanced) SM->>SM: _present_frame() (overlay, display update) SM->>SM: _finish_frame() (pace, then set dt once from perf_counter) end Class Hierarchy # Event dispatch chain (how events reach your scene) # Every scene has every on_*_event() handler, but it gets them a different way from the engine. A Scene inherits them: AllEventStubs gives it a default for each one, which reports the event as unhandled, and your scene overrides the ones it uses. GameEngine and SceneManager inherit no handlers at all. They pass on_*_event() calls along at runtime through __getattr__ . Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class. Dotted arrows are the runtime calls, numbered in the order an event takes them. The Engine box is the engine's classes; the Bitmappy box is the editor's scene. classDiagram direction TB namespace Engine { class EventInterface { <<interface, abc.ABC>> #95;#95;subclasshook#95;#95; counts any class with every handler } class EventInterfaces["MouseEvents, KeyboardEvents, ... (13)"] { <<interface, abc.ABC>> every on#95;#42;#95;event abstract } class EventStubs["MouseEventStubs, KeyboardEventStubs, ... (13)"] { <<mixin>> every on#95;#42;#95;event calls unhandled#95;event } class AllEventStubs { <<mixin>> all 13 stub mixins } class GameOptionsProvider { <<Protocol>> options dict } class Scene { a default for every on#95;#42;#95;event } class ManagerProxy["MouseEventManager.MouseEventProxy (one per manager)"] { implements MouseEvents each on#95;#42;#95;event calls game.on#95;#42;#95;event } class ResourceManager { proxies list #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; forwards to its proxies } class EventManager class GameEngine { process#95;#42;#95;event calls the event manager #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; turns on#95;#42;#95;event into missing#95;event } class SceneManager { #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; sends on#95;#42;#95;event to the active scene } } namespace Bitmappy { class BitmapEditorScene { overrides the handlers it uses } } EventInterface <|-- EventInterfaces EventInterface <|-- EventStubs EventStubs <|-- AllEventStubs AllEventStubs <|-- Scene Scene <|-- BitmapEditorScene EventInterfaces <|-- ManagerProxy ResourceManager <|-- EventManager EventManager <|-- GameEngine EventManager <|-- SceneManager GameEngine ..> ManagerProxy : 1. process#95;mouse#95;event ManagerProxy ..> SceneManager : 2. game.on#95;#42;#95;event SceneManager ..> Scene : 3. #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; forwards it SceneManager ..> GameEngine : 3b. no active scene, missing#95;event EventStubs ..> GameOptionsProvider : unhandled#95;event(game) The interfaces are abstract base classes, not typing.Protocol s, but EventInterface 's __subclasshook__ makes them structural: any class with every handler of an interface counts as one. GameOptionsProvider is a real Protocol : unhandled_event() needs only the scene's options . Both scene classes also inherit SceneInterface (left out to keep the diagram readable). docs.text: Bitmappy is GlitchyGames' pixel art editor. These diagrams show how it is wired up through the engine, from bootstrap to rendering.
docs.title: Bitmappy Architecture

docs.text: Bitmappy is an app, not part of the engine: the first member of the apps layer of the uv workspace , at src/apps/bitmappy/ . The distribution, the import package and the console script are all bitmappy ( uv run bitmappy ), and its scene's logical name, the one a recording holds, is apps.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene . A recording made when the scene lived in the engine ( glitchygames.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene ) is refused by a plain replay, which names the remedy; --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless converts it ( gameplay replay ). Its code is src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ . The engine never imports it, and Bitmappy uses the engine's public API (sprite file-format detection, for one, is the engine's src/glitchygames/sprites/file_format.py ). Its sprite library is 71 sprites in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/sprites/ , shipped as package data and found through bitmappy.SPRITE_CONFIG_DIR . They are also the AI's training data ( load_ai_training_data() below), so they stay in the package. Its other resources (the window icon and bitmappy.cfg ) are beside them, in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/ . Its tests are in src/apps/bitmappy/tests/ , rootless, every file named test_bitmappy_*.py . The Load and Save dialogs (the engine's glitchygames.ui dialog scenes) treat every file the same: the name is used as given, with surrounding whitespace trimmed, and a sprite in the library is opened by its path. The example: prefix they once understood is gone, and Save applies a per-platform rule to : in a file name ( _file_name_problem , the platform passed in and sys.platform by default); the refusal is shown in the editor's debug text and nothing is written: Platform : in a Save name Windows ( win32 , cygwin ) Allowed only in a letter-drive designator ( C:\a.toml , C:/a.toml , C:a.toml , \\?\C:\a.toml , \\.\C:\a.toml ); anywhere else, including inside a UNC server or share name, it is refused: NTFS would read it as an alternate data stream, so examples:foo.toml would leave an empty file called examples macOS ( darwin ) Refused everywhere: Finder shows : as / (a Classic Mac OS leftover) Linux and others Allowed Browser ( emscripten ) Allowed (Save is a download; the browser sanitizes the name) Load is unchanged (a missing name is reported as "File not found").

docs.text: How Bitmappy starts up: entry point through main() , GameEngine initialization, scene setup, and the main loop (one frame per pass, ended by _finish_frame ). The Bitmappy box is the editor's own code ( src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ ); the Engine box is what every game gets. sequenceDiagram participant User box rgb(255,243,224) Bitmappy participant main as main() participant BES as BitmapEditorScene end box rgb(232,238,255) Engine participant GE as GameEngine participant SM as SceneManager (singleton) end User->>main: uv run bitmappy main->>GE: GameEngine(game=BitmapEditorScene, icon=...) GE->>GE: parse CLI args (GameEngine.args() + BitmapEditorScene.args()) GE->>GE: pygame.init(), create display main->>main: load_ai_training_data() main->>GE: engine.start() GE->>BES: BitmapEditorScene(options=OPTIONS) BES->>BES: EditorSetup.init_undo_redo_system() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_menu_bar() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_canvas(options) BES->>BES: SliderManager.setup_sliders_and_color_well() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_debug_text_box() BES->>BES: FilmStripCoordinator.setup_film_strips() GE->>GE: _initialize_event_managers() GE->>SM: scene_manager.switch_to_scene(game) SM->>BES: setup() (AIManager.setup() starts the AI worker) GE->>SM: scene_manager.start() loop Main Game Loop (while active_scene is not None) Note over SM: dt = the previous frame's start-to-start time SM->>SM: camera.begin_frame() SM->>BES: _update_scene() (Scene.dt_tick: logic and collision) SM->>GE: _process_events() GE->>GE: _pump_events() (active_sources().pump_events(): live, pygame.event.get()) GE->>SM: EVENT_HANDLERS[event.type](event) SM->>BES: on_*_event(event) SM->>SM: _run_supervisor_slot() (supervisors, e.g. a recording's) SM->>SM: _update_frame_services() (shake, rumble) SM->>SM: _aim_active_camera() (camera_target / follow) SM->>SM: _position_active_world_sprites() (world sprites' rect, culling) SM->>SM: _render_scene() (BitmapEditorScene.update: animation, controllers, AI, then draw) SM->>SM: _advance_still_camera_shake() (WORLD shake nothing advanced) SM->>SM: _present_frame() (overlay, display update) SM->>SM: _finish_frame() (pace, then set dt once from perf_counter) end

docs.text:
Every scene has every on_*_event() handler, but it gets them a different way from the engine. A Scene inherits them: AllEventStubs gives it a default for each one, which reports the event as unhandled, and your scene overrides the ones it uses. GameEngine and SceneManager inherit no handlers at all. They pass on_*_event() calls along at runtime through __getattr__ . Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class. Dotted arrows are the runtime calls, numbered in the order an event takes them. The Engine box is the engine's classes; the Bitmappy box is the editor's scene. classDiagram direction TB namespace Engine { class EventInterface { <<interface, abc.ABC>> #95;#95;subclasshook#95;#95; counts any class with every handler } class EventInterfaces["MouseEvents, KeyboardEvents, ... (13)"] { <<interface, abc.ABC>> every on#95;#42;#95;event abstract } class EventStubs["MouseEventStubs, KeyboardEventStubs, ... (13)"] { <<mixin>> every on#95;#42;#95;event calls unhandled#95;event } class AllEventStubs { <<mixin>> all 13 stub mixins } class GameOptionsProvider { <<Protocol>> options dict } class Scene { a default for every on#95;#42;#95;event } class ManagerProxy["MouseEventManager.MouseEventProxy (one per manager)"] { implements MouseEvents each on#95;#42;#95;event calls game.on#95;#42;#95;event } class ResourceManager { proxies list #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; forwards to its proxies } class EventManager class GameEngine { process#95;#42;#95;event calls the event manager #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; turns on#95;#42;#95;event into missing#95;event } class SceneManager { #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; sends on#95;#42;#95;event to the active scene } } namespace Bitmappy { class BitmapEditorScene { overrides the handlers it uses } } EventInterface <|-- EventInterfaces EventInterface <|-- EventStubs EventStubs <|-- AllEventStubs AllEventStubs <|-- Scene Scene <|-- BitmapEditorScene EventInterfaces <|-- ManagerProxy ResourceManager <|-- EventManager EventManager <|-- GameEngine EventManager <|-- SceneManager GameEngine ..> ManagerProxy : 1. process#95;mouse#95;event ManagerProxy ..> SceneManager : 2. game.on#95;#42;#95;event SceneManager ..> Scene : 3. #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; forwards it SceneManager ..> GameEngine : 3b. no active scene, missing#95;event EventStubs ..> GameOptionsProvider : unhandled#95;event(game) The interfaces are abstract base classes, not typing.Protocol s, but EventInterface 's __subclasshook__ makes them structural: any class with every handler of an interface counts as one. GameOptionsProvider is a real Protocol : unhandled_event() needs only the scene's options . Both scene classes also inherit SceneInterface (left out to keep the diagram readable). Event flow — how an SDL event reaches your handler in Bitmappy (the stub a missing handler falls to is the engine's): flowchart TD SDL["SDL Event"] --> GE subgraph ENGINE_BITMAPPY_EVENT_FLOW["Engine"] GE["GameEngine
O#40;1#41; EVENT_HANDLERS lookup"] GE --> MGR["Event Manager
e.g. MouseEventManager"] MGR -->|"updates state,
synthesizes events"| SM["SceneManager
forwards to active_scene"] STUB["No handler?
The stub calls unhandled_event#40;#41;"] end subgraph APP_BITMAPPY_EVENT_FLOW["Bitmappy"] BES["BitmapEditorScene
#40;the active scene#41;"] BES --> HANDLER["Your handler runs
on_left_mouse_drag_event#40;#41;"] end SM --> BES BES --> STUB The GameEngine receives every SDL event and does an O(1) dict lookup to find the right event manager. The event manager updates its internal state (button tracking, axis values, drag detection) and may synthesize higher-level events (drag, drop, chord). It then forwards to the SceneManager , which passes everything to the active_scene . In Bitmappy, that's BitmapEditorScene , which overrides handlers like on_key_down_event() , on_left_mouse_button_down_event() , on_left_mouse_drag_event() , and on_controller_button_down_event() . Events it doesn't override hit the stubs, which call unhandled_event() : it does nothing by default, logs each event type once when debug_events is on (the --debug-events flag, off by default), and raises UnhandledEventError under --no-unhandled-events (as the tests run).

docs.text: Engine Context # An engine context is the state one running game owns, so several games can run in one process (the Arcade's demo tiles; design: plans/2026-10-25-engine-context.md ). Ordinary games never create one: they run in the default context, exactly as before. Only the six slots below are per context today; the rest of the process-wide state ( GameEngine and its OPTIONS , SceneManager.OPTIONS , FontManager , ResourceManager , the event managers and the other rows of the audit in plans/2026-10-25-engine-context.md ) is still shared and belongs to later sub-plans. The engine does not switch contexts yet: nothing in src/ calls .active() , only tests do. Rules # Per-context state is a ContextSlot ( src/glitchygames/engine_context.py ), declared once at module level with a unique dotted name and a factory. ContextSlot is internal to the engine: only engine modules declare slots, and games keep their state on their scenes. The tests' COUNTER_SLOT exists only to test the class. Code reads a slot when it needs it, current_context().value(slot=...) , never as its module is imported: the test suite scans the engine and every workspace member for such reads. A context makes each value with the slot's factory the first time it is read there. current_context() is the context switched to last in this thread or asyncio task, else the default context. with context.active(): makes a context current and puts the previous one back when the block ends, also by an exception; switches nest. An asyncio task made inside a switch keeps it, a switch held across an await is never seen by another task, and a thread sees it only when started with context=contextvars.copy_context() (or on an interpreter whose sys.flags.thread_inherit_context is set, such as free-threaded 3.14 builds). A context owns only what its slots hold. The display, the mixer, SDL's event queue and the joystick subsystem are one per process. What belongs to a context today # Slot Module Public functions glitchygames.pixel_snap.default_mode src/glitchygames/pixel_snap.py set_active_default_snap_mode , active_default_snap_mode , resolve_snap_mode glitchygames.backgrounds.default_pattern src/glitchygames/backgrounds.py set_active_default_background_pattern , active_default_background_pattern , paint_default_background glitchygames.input.state.current_input src/glitchygames/input/state.py current_input , set_current_input , reset_current_input glitchygames.randomness.streams src/glitchygames/randomness.py random_stream , numpy_stream , reset_streams , seed_engine_random , engine_random_seed , capture_stream_states , restore_stream_states glitchygames.sources.registry src/glitchygames/sources.py active_sources , install_sources , the scoped sources, the frame clock, held events, observers glitchygames.scenes.scene.scene_managers src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py SceneManager() , SceneManager._reset() tests/test_engine_context.py proves, for every slot, that two contexts in one process never see each other's values; a slot added without such a check fails the suite.

ContextSlot is internal to the engine: only engine modules declare slots, and games keep their state on their scenes. The tests' COUNTER_SLOT exists only to test the class. Code reads a slot when it needs it, current_context().value(slot=...) , never as its module is imported: the test suite scans the engine and every workspace member for such reads. A context makes each value with the slot's factory the first time it is read there. current_context() is the context switched to last in this thread or asyncio task, else the default context. with context.active(): makes a context current and puts the previous one back when the block ends, also by an exception; switches nest. An asyncio task made inside a switch keeps it, a switch held across an await is never seen by another task, and a thread sees it only when started with context=contextvars.copy_context() (or on an interpreter whose sys.flags.thread_inherit_context is set, such as free-threaded 3.14 builds). A context owns only what its slots hold. The display, the mixer, SDL's event queue and the joystick subsystem are one per process.
