Code ExitCode member Meaning 0 SUCCESS Success; the replay matched; the audit is deterministic; the rebaseline was written 1 REPLAY_DIVERGED A replay's frames differ from the recording 2 ARGUMENT_PARSER_ERROR A usage error from argparse; the engine never exits with it itself 3 AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC --audit 's two runs differ from each other or from the recording 4 GENERATION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's generation request 5 EXTRACTION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's frame extraction 6 AUDIO_DROPOUT_RISK scripts/audio_glitch_probe.py found a risk of audio dropouts 7 REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST --rebaseline wrote NEW, but the run never received some of OLD's input (it ended early, or did not pump a recorded batch) 8 PROCESSING_SLOWER A replay matched, but its processing time exceeded the recording's by more than --max-processing-slowdown 64 OPTIONS_REFUSED The engine refuses the options given (a combination it will not run) 65 UNUSABLE_INPUT The recording or input data is unusable (another game's recording, an unsupported format version, a corrupt or unreadable file, a bad server response) 66 MISSING_INPUT The input file does not exist 69 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE A required service (the API server) cannot be reached 70 INTERNAL_ERROR An uncaught exception during a run or its teardown (logged with its traceback, after the teardown), or an audit that could not run 73 CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT An output file or directory cannot be created or written (a rebaseline's new recording could not be moved into place) 129 HANGUP Stopped by SIGHUP (Unix only) 130 INTERRUPTED Stopped by SIGINT (Ctrl-C) 143 TERMINATED Stopped by SIGTERM 149 BREAK Stopped by SIGBREAK (Windows only: Ctrl-Break) 0, 64-70 and 73 have the values of BSD sysexits.h (Python's os.EX_OK , os.EX_USAGE and so on, which exist only on Unix, so the values are defined in the engine). The signal codes are 128 + the signal number. A run stopped by one of those signals exits only after the normal teardown, so a recording is complete: the engine handles SIGTERM, SIGHUP and SIGBREAK for the whole run (unless the game installed its own handler) and turns off SDL's own signal handling ( SDL_NO_SIGNAL_HANDLERS ), which would otherwise turn SIGINT and SIGTERM into a QUIT event. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, Python ignores SIGPIPE, and SIGQUIT keeps its core-dump convention. An engine started off the main thread cannot install its handlers, so SIGTERM then ends it the system's default way, without the teardown. An exception raised before the run starts (while the engine is being constructed) exits with Python's default status 1.
docs.title: Exit codes

docs.text: A recording holds each frame's processing time ( processing_seconds ): the frame's work (logic, events, frame services, positioning and rendering), without presenting it, without the recorder's own writing and without the pacing sleep. The header's latest measurement run ( measurement_runs[0] , see "Content hashes and measurement history" below) names the machine it was measured on (system, version and architecture, never the host name). These are diagnostics: a replay never compares them with the recording to decide whether it matched, and never serves them to the game. The comparison uses the newest entry, processing_seconds[0] . --replay-trace PATH --headless --compare-processing measures this machine's processing time for every replayed frame the same way and prints one line after the replay's report: Replay matched 9800 frames (end of recording) Processing: the replay took 14.2% longer than the recording (9800 frames: 30.410 s against 26.630 s; median frame 3.100 ms against 2.710 ms); slowest against the recording: frame 812 +6.100 ms, frame 813 +5.920 ms, frame 4400 +3.010 ms --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT (which implies --compare-processing ) makes it a check: a replay that matched but took more than PERCENT longer in total exits PROCESSING_SLOWER (8). A divergence still exits REPLAY_DIVERGED (1), and a recording without processing times (made before they were recorded) cannot be checked: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65), with Processing: nothing to compare after the report. Why processing time and not wall-clock time: a live run is paced (most of each frame is the sleep before the next) and a headless replay is not paced at all, so their total times measure different things. Processing time measures the same work in both. It only compares on the same machine, so make the baseline on the machine that will check it (a CI runner); the report says so when the recording names another machine. Pacing still slows the work itself: between paced frames the processor idles and clocks down, so a live recording's frames take longer than the same frames in an unpaced replay (one Clockwork Keep session measured about 65% faster replayed than recorded live). So make the baseline with a rebaseline, which is measured unpaced as every later replay is, and check against it: # Once, on the CI machine: the baseline (the same inputs, measured unpaced) uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --rebaseline baseline.jsonl.gz --headless # On every change: fail if the work got more than 10% slower uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace baseline.jsonl.gz --headless --max-processing-slowdown 10 Replays of the same session against such a baseline land within about 1% of it. The latest measurement run says whether it paced its frames ( processing_paced ; a live run with a target FPS, as recording began) and names its frame-pacing timer, paced or not ( pacing_timer : the timer backend, its final spin and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did; src/glitchygames/timing.py ), and the report adds a note when the baseline was paced. --compare-processing needs --headless (a watched replay presents, steps and rebuilds frames as its viewer asks) and is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) with --audit and with --rebaseline (a rebaseline's NEW records the current code's own processing times anyway). The contract is src/glitchygames/replay/processing.py 's docstring.
docs.title: Comparing processing time (--compare-processing)

docs.text: Every frame a recorder writes carries two histories, newest first, and the header a third (design: plans/2026-10-20-recording-content-hash-and-history.md ; contract: src/glitchygames/recording_history.py ): Where Field Each entry Depth constant (10) frame content_hash the frame's content hash CONTENT_HASH_HISTORY_DEPTH frame processing_seconds its processing time ( null when not measured) PROCESSING_SECONDS_HISTORY_DEPTH header measurement_runs the run's provenance: machine, processing_paced , pacing_timer (its frame-pacing timer, paced or not: backend, final spin, and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did), engine, pygame and Python versions, measured_at , rebaselined_from , hash_scheme , and frame_count (how many frames it wrote; filled in when the next rebaseline stacks onto it, null for the newest run, whose count is the file's) MEASUREMENT_RUNS_HISTORY_DEPTH A fresh recording writes one entry in each. A rebaseline puts its own in front of the replayed recording's and drops the oldest past the depth, so index i means run i in every list. If the runs' depth is tuned below the hash depth, the deeper hashes have no run, so no hash_scheme : treat their scheme as unknown. A reader takes the fields of a run it knows and ignores fields a newer engine added. The content hash is the first 64 bits of SHA-256 of the frame's content fields as a JSON reader decodes them (string keys, lists), encoded as compact, key-sorted JSON (hash scheme 1), so the stored hash is the one a reader recomputes from the frame it reads. Content is everything the game did or took in: dt , the event batches, input, control events, devices, saves, scene starts, the scene and its sprites. Measurements (the two history fields) are left out. Every frame field is one or the other, and the hash refuses a field that is neither, so a new field cannot slip in or out unnoticed. A rebaseline copies the inputs, dt included, so an unchanged game gives the same hash one entry deeper, and a changed one shows exactly which frames changed. Two fresh recordings of the same script differ anyway (each measures its own dt , and the game moves by it). A recording's own hash, for any run, is derived from its frames' hashes: recording_content_hash(frames=..., run_index=i) ; it is not stored. Neither history is compared by a replay or served to the game. They are the record the baselines in the repository keep: behaviour (hashes) and speed (processing times) over time.
docs.title: Content hashes and measurement history

docs.text: Each game's workspace member holds a recorded session of it in <member>/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz (PaddleSlap, Clockwork Keep, Mr. Muncher and Drawing Fire; both Brave Adventurer editions as golden-classic.jsonl.gz and golden-papyrus.jsonl.gz ). scripts/record_scripted_session.py recorded them through the real engine loop (on the engine's scripted-session recorder, the record-session tool below, with our games' input scripts and controls tails from scripts/golden_inputs.py ), with a supervisor posting each game's golden input script, then the game's controls tail: input that presses the controls the script does not, pauses and resumes, and ends with the game's own quit control, so every golden replay ends on a QUIT the game posted and diverges when a control stops working. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py enforces it: every control the game binds (its ActionMaps, plus the keys the engine's pause screen hard-codes) must be pressed in its golden replay, or be listed in UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS with the reason (gamepad controls: no scripted session has a gamepad). Each recording is a test item of its own: the pytest plugin src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py (registered by the engine's pytest11 entry point, glitchygames.testing.replays , in every pytest run with glitchygames installed) collects every .../fixtures/replays/<console-script>/<name>.jsonl.gz as <console-script>/<name> , replays it headless in a child process through the console script's entry point ( --replay-trace PATH --headless ) and fails, with the exit code and the child's output (the divergence report), unless it exits ExitCode.SUCCESS . A directory that is not a console script is a collection error. Another project's games get the plugin the same way, with nothing to configure; loading it by name as well ( pytest_plugins = ['glitchygames.testing.replays'] or -p glitchygames.testing.replays ) still loads it once, and -p no:glitchygames.testing.replays turns it off. The plugin imports no pygame (and prints no banner) until it finds a recording, so a project that is no game gets no item and no output from it. Re-record a fixture only deliberately, after finding out why it stopped replaying; the commands are in the script's docstring. After an intentional change, rebaseline it instead (below), so it keeps its recorded inputs.
docs.title: Golden replays

docs.text: --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless replays OLD's inputs on the current code and writes what that code did to NEW: the same inputs and a new picture. The contract is src/glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py 's docstring. A recording whose game or scene classes moved to another logical module is converted here and only here: the run matches them by qualified name alone, and NEW holds the current logical names (a plain replay refuses it, above). The replay does not stop at a divergence: it runs to OLD's last frame (or until the game ends), counting every frame that differs and naming every sprite that differs in them. NEW holds OLD's inputs as the replay served them: the event batches with their origins (code-posted events stay internal , so replaying NEW delivers nothing twice), dt , input_changes , re-applied control events, and each frame's saves_opened , devices_opened and device_enumeration copied from OLD. Its sprites and markers are the current code's. Its header is OLD's (seed, start time, options, saves, devices) with rebaselined_from naming OLD and this run's engine, pygame and Python versions. A cut-off (truncated) OLD gives NEW source_truncated : NEW ends as truncated too, so its replay exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) at the cut-off, --audit refuses it, and it cannot be a golden fixture (the plugin expects SUCCESS ). Rebaseline a complete recording for those. A version-2 OLD (no input snapshots) gives an honest format-3 NEW: its polled input is the idle input the replay served, recorded as such, and its markers are compared when NEW is replayed (OLD's were not). Input OLD has that the run never received is not moved anywhere else (that would invent an input sequence OLD does not have); it is reported. That is the external events of batches a frame did not pump (the current code pumped fewer times than recorded), and OLD's frames after the game ended early. NEW is written to NEW.partial and moved into place only when the run ends normally; a run that crashes, is interrupted or fails its own exit ( sys.exit(1) ) writes nothing; the game's own successful exit ( sys.exit(0) ) ends it early as quit_game() does (NEW holds the frames that ran, exit REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST ). If the move fails (say NEW is a directory), the finished NEW.partial is kept, its path logged and printed, and the run exits CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73). NEW is never OLD, and NEW.partial is never OLD either. A NEW.partial that cannot be written at all is refused before the replay starts, with one line and CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73), as is an unwritable --record-trace or --replay-digest file. NEW is an original, never a bookmarked copy (OLD's bookmarked_copy_of is dropped), so S on a replay of NEW never rewrites it. It prints one line to stdout and exits SUCCESS (0), however many frames differ: Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: 412 frames differ (first at 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16]); sprites affected: Ball#2, Ball#3 or Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: no frames differ . Lost input (above) is added to the line and logged as a warning, e.g. ; 3 recorded input events not delivered (first at frame 812); ended at frame 500 of 9800 . NEW is still written (it replays clean), but the run exits REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST (7) instead, so a script that replaces fixtures notices that NEW is not a faithful re-run of OLD's session. It is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) without --replay-trace or without --headless (a watched replay holds frames and takes the viewer's keys, so it is refused rather than made headless quietly), when NEW or NEW.partial is OLD's file, and with --record-trace , --audit , --replay-digest (the audit's tools; a rebaseline is not audited) or --replay-fps real (FPS events from this machine's frame times would become the baseline). An unusable OLD is refused like any replay ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , MISSING_INPUT ). NEW replays on the current code with no divergence when the rebaseline replayed all of OLD: a truncated OLD gives a truncated NEW, whose replay matches up to its cut-off and exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) like any truncated recording. Replacing a golden fixture with it stays a deliberate, reviewed step: read the summary, check the change is the intended one, then move NEW over the fixture yourself.
docs.title: Rebaselining (--rebaseline NEW)

docs.text: Every recording, replay and measurement tool belongs to the engine ( src/glitchygames/replay/tools/ ), so a game the engine has never seen can record, replay, verify, rebaseline, measure, report on and graph its recordings with only the glitchygames wheel installed. A game passes itself to the engine ( GameEngine(game=Game) ) and declares nothing else: its package, package directory, console script and git revision all come from that object ( identity.py ). Each tool is reachable two ways, with the same name and the same options: As a flag on the game. GameEngine.args adds every tool to every game's command line ( uv run paddleslap --report session.jsonl.gz ). A tool that does not run the game, or runs it in a harness of its own, runs in place of the game, before the engine starts pygame: no window opens and no scene is built. As the glitchygames command (also python -m glitchygames ), one subcommand per tool ( uv run glitchygames report session.jsonl.gz ). A subcommand whose tool runs the game starts the game as a child process with the tool's flag. Arguments after a bare -- go to that game unchanged ( glitchygames record-trace paddleslap run.jsonl.gz -- --resolution 640x480 ). --project-root DIR is, for the tools that read the project's settings ( verify , measure , unmeasured , clear-published , performance-pages ), the project they work on (default: the nearest directory at or above the current one whose pyproject.toml has [tool.glitchygames] , else the nearest with a pyproject.toml , else the current directory); for record-trace , replay-trace , record-golden-trace and record-session , the directory the game runs in (default: the current directory); report reads only its recording. Both front ends are generated from one table, TOOLS in src/glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py , which is the reference for every flag, option, default and help text ( glitchygames --help lists each tool with its options; glitchygames TOOL --help describes them). tests/replay/tools/test_registry.py walks the table and fails if a tool or option differs between the front ends, and tests/replay/tools/test_an_unseen_game.py runs every tool, both ways, on a stand-in game in its own git repository. Tool Runs the game? On the game As the command record-trace yes --record-trace PATH [--random-seed N] [--headless] glitchygames record-trace GAME PATH with the same options replay-trace yes --replay-trace PATH with --headless , --replay-fps , --replay-pause-at-frame N , --audit , --rebaseline NEW , --compare-processing , --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT , --replay-digest PATH , --random-seed N , --compare-trace OLD , --compare-alpha PERCENT glitchygames replay-trace PATH [the same options] [--game GAME] (the game comes from the recording's header) record-golden-trace in its harness --record-golden-trace PATH --input-script MODULE:NAME --frame-count N [--random-seed N] [--headless] glitchygames record-golden-trace GAME PATH with the same options record-session in its recorder --record-session PATH --input-script MODULE:NAME --frame-count N [--controls-tail MODULE:NAME] [--polled-input] [--input-only-placements] [--random-seed N] [--headless] glitchygames record-session GAME PATH with the same options verify in children --verify [PATH ...] [--only TEXT] (default: the game's own recordings) glitchygames verify [PATH ...] [--only TEXT] [--game GAME ...] (default: [tool.glitchygames] games ) measure in children --measure [PATH ...] [--force] [--allow-dirty \| --skip-dirty] [--only TEXT] [--code-tree TREE] [--rows-directory DIRECTORY] [--pending PATH] glitchygames measure [PATH ...] with the same options [--game GAME ...] unmeasured no --unmeasured [--code-tree TREE] [--rows-directory DIRECTORY] [--pending PATH] glitchygames unmeasured with the same options [--game GAME ...] clear-published no --clear-published [--pending PATH] glitchygames clear-published [--pending PATH] report no --report PATH [--threshold PERCENT] [--minimum-ms MS] [--spans N] glitchygames report PATH with the same options performance-pages no --performance-pages DIRECTORY [--published] glitchygames performance-pages DIRECTORY [--published] An option several tools list is one flag on the game: --random-seed (every tool that runs the game) and --headless (the four that record or replay). --random-seed is never needed: a recording rolls a seed (kept in it) and a replay uses the recording's. verify and measure refuse one (exit 64): they always compare, and measure each recording under its own seed. Rebaseline and audit are options of replay-trace ( --rebaseline NEW , --audit ), since they take the same recording and find the game the same way; so is the onion skin ( --compare-trace OLD , above). --replay-frame-stream PORT:TOKEN is a hidden option the onion skin gives OLD's child; it is in neither front end's help. One tool at a time: a game given two tool flags is refused (exit 64), and so is a tool missing a required option ( --input-script , --frame-count ). Reserved names. Every tool's flag and option is added to every game's parser, so a game must not define an argument of the same name ( --threshold , --spans , --only , --force , ...). A game that does is refused on every run, before anything starts (exit 64), with a message naming the flag and saying the engine reserves it. Our games are checked by a test; the full list is glitchygames --help .
docs.title: Tools for any game

docs.text: The command's GAME (and --game ) takes three forms, read in this order; the command says which one it used ( glitchygames replay-trace: running paddleslap (an installed console script) ): GAME looks like Meaning The child it runs contains / or ends in .py a script path python <path> --<tool> ... contains : an entry point MODULE:CALLABLE python -c calling it, with the flags in sys.argv a plain name an installed console script, else an importable module the console script's entry point, else python -m <module> A plain name matching nothing is refused with all three forms named. Every form ends in the game's own GameEngine(game=Game) , which adds the flags, so the game never knows how it was started. replay-trace takes the game from the recording's header and asks for --game when that game's module no longer imports (a script that moved).
docs.title: GAME

docs.text: --verify and --measure with no paths take the game's own recordings: the goldens that match [tool.glitchygames] golden-globs and that the game's console script replays, plus its bundled demos ( <package>/demos/*.jsonl.gz ; recordings.py ). A golden in fixtures/replays/<console-script>/ is that script's; one directly in a project's tests/fixtures/replays/ is the project's own distribution's ( [project] name in its pyproject.toml , whatever its checkout's directory is called; a directory with no pyproject.toml is read as named after its distribution). The command with no paths runs GAME --verify (or --measure ) for each --game , else for each of [tool.glitchygames] games ; with paths, each recording is replayed by the game its header names (or by the one --game ). With the games from the settings, a golden or demo that none of them replays fails both tools, on a line naming it and why (exit 70): none is skipped without a word. verify replays each recording headless in a child process, prints PASS <name>: <result> or FAIL <name>: <exit code>: <why> per recording and verify: N of M recordings passed , and exits 0 only when every one matched (or none was found, which it says), 1 when the only failures diverged, else the first other failure's code. measure rebaselines each recording headless in a child into the run ledger (see Replay Performance ), skipping what this machine already measured for the game's commit. A row's commit is the game's own (its package directory's checkout), not the engine's. A game with uncommitted changes, or no known commit, is refused (exit 64) unless --allow-dirty (a trial row, never published) or --skip-dirty (nothing measured, exit 0). unmeasured lists what measure would measure, without running a game.
docs.title: A game's own recordings

docs.text: record-golden-trace and record-session drive the game with an input script: --input-script MODULE:NAME names a callable taking no arguments that returns an InputScript ( glitchygames.replay.tools.golden_traces : press / release per frame, and placements), its module looked for in the current directory first. --controls-tail MODULE:NAME (record-session) names the keys played after the script's frames, ending with the game's own quit. A golden trace runs the game's scene in a headless harness at 1/60 second per frame and samples every sprite each frame; a session runs the game for real, at its own pace, with --record-trace . Our five games' scripts and controls tails are test data in scripts/golden_inputs.py ( --input-script scripts.golden_inputs:paddleslap_script , run from the repository root); scripts/record_golden_traces.py and scripts/record_scripted_session.py keep only our games' tables and call the engine.
docs.title: Input scripts

docs.text: A project's settings for the tools live in [tool.glitchygames] in its pyproject.toml ( src/glitchygames/replay/tools/settings.py ). Every key has a default that fits a standard layout, so a project without the table (a player's own local runs) works as it is. Keys are kebab-case, an unknown key is refused by name, and every path is relative to the project root. A path that does not exist yet (no ledger directory before the first measurement) is created by the tool that writes it, or reported; it is never a traceback. Key Default Ours (the root pyproject.toml ) games the project's [project.scripts] the nine members' console scripts golden-globs ["tests/fixtures/replays/**/*.jsonl.gz"] ["src/*/*/tests/fixtures/replays/golden*.jsonl.gz"] ledger-directory "replay-ledger" "quality/replay-ledger" pending-ledger ".glitchygames/pending-ledger.jsonl" "test-results/replay-metrics/pending.jsonl" published-ledger none (nothing published) "origin/gh-pages:quality/metrics/replay-ledger.jsonl" ( REF:PATH ) landed-ref "origin/main" "origin/main" measured-paths ["src", "tests/fixtures/replays", "pyproject.toml"] the same, and uv.lock unmeasured-paths [] the members' tests/ , but for their tests/fixtures/replays/ recording-renames {} each moved recording, old path to new (one hop: refused if a new path is itself an old one; each new path must exist, tests/test_our_stored_paths.py ) game-timeout-seconds 3600 (an hour) the default game-timeout-seconds bounds each game that glitchygames verify and glitchygames measure start ( GAME --verify , GAME --measure , one per game): a game still running after it is stopped (asked first, so it can stop its own replays, then killed), reaped, and failed with a line naming the game and the timeout (exit 70). Each recording's replay inside it has its own timeout too. It guards against a console script that is no game (an editor or a server among [project.scripts] , which games defaults to) hanging the run; it has no flag, since only the command starts a game per child ( --game names the games instead, or set games ). The project's local directory, .glitchygames/ , holds what the tools write and nobody commits; it gets a .gitignore of * when it is made. Stored paths are relative to the project root. The project root is the anchor of every path above and of every path the tools write into a file: a recording header's path options ( --record-trace , --rebaseline , ...), a rebaselined recording's rebaselined_from (in its header and its newest run, which a ledger row copies) and a ledger row's recording. It is the nearest project above the current directory ( find_project_root ), or --project-root where a subcommand takes it; the tools start each game in it. A path inside the project is stored relative to it, POSIX-style. A path inside another checkout of the same project (a clone or a worktree: the nearest directory above the path whose pyproject.toml has the same [project] name ) is stored relative to that checkout's root. Any other path (another project, no project) is stored as its file name only ( stored_path ), so no user name, home or scratch directory is ever written. tests/test_our_stored_paths.py checks every committed recording header and ledger row.
docs.title: Project settings ([tool.glitchygames])

docs.text: The pytest plugin glitchygames.testing.replays registers itself through the engine's pytest11 entry point (named after its module), so every pytest run of a project with glitchygames installed collects that project's recordings (Golden replays, above) with no conftest line. A project that is no game gets no item and no output from it, unless it has a fixtures/replays/<directory>/*.jsonl.gz : a directory there that is not a console script is a collection error. pytest -p no:glitchygames.testing.replays turns the plugin off. Under a wheel install, pytest rewrites the asserts of the whole glitchygames package (it rewrites every module of a distribution that has a pytest11 entry point): harmless, but it writes *-pytest-*.pyc files into site-packages . The engine wheel also ships glitchygames.testing.frame_comparison (comparing the frames test runs presented on different SDL drivers, with glitchygames.testing.frame_fingerprints , which records them); scripts/compare_driver_frames.py and scripts/driver_frame_matrix.py are its command lines.
docs.title: The golden-replay pytest plugin

docs.text: A running game can play a recording to a rebuilt scene and then go on: attract-mode demos, instant replays and ghosts. Demos and instant replays run in a playback scope , not a new engine run ( src/glitchygames/replay/playback.py 's docstring is the contract): the scene is rebuilt from its start (see Scene starts above) on scoped doors that serve the recording, the live scene is stashed untouched, saves are a sandbox, the random streams, clocks and FPS timer are put back afterwards, and the live game's own posts and the player's releases, device and window events are held and handed back when the scope ends. A --record-trace session that plays a scope records it, and replays it exactly. An error inside the scope ends the scope (logged) and the live game goes on. scene_manager.last_playback_outcome says how the last scope ended (its kind, reason and frames played). What belongs to the scope ends with it: supervisors and control event handlers its scene adds (in setup() , cleanup() or an event handler; a live supervisor's additions stay), and the playback scene's own events still queued when it ends (posted in update() or an event handler after its last pump: the live game never receives them, so a goal posted there cannot start a second instant replay). What the live game's own supervisors and handlers post while it plays stays the live game's: a supervisor that calls end_playback() and then posts an event has it delivered to the live game after the scope. Their post_input_event posts of SDL types are the exception: those stand in for the player, so they reach the scope's exit check as the player's presses do (a scripted key ends a demo) and their releases are held with the player's. Their post_input_event posts of other types (a game event) are held and delivered to the live game after the scope, and a replay of the session without the supervisor delivers them at the same frame. A playback never rumbles the player's controllers, and the live scene's synth voices (and those of the game behind a pause screen the instant replay began from) pause behind it and play on after. Inside a scope, a replay of the session still applies the session's breakpoints (a bookmark on a frame a demo played pauses there); the played recording's own breakpoints are never applied again. A --record-trace recording of a session that played a scope replays exactly, but cannot itself be played in-game from a frame inside or after that scope (only an instant-replay journal records what a scene's playback requests got and how it resumed).
docs.title: In-game playback

docs.text: scene_manager . play_recording ( path = DEMO_PATH , then = self ) # any key or button returns to `then` A demo plays at the game's speed from the start of the next frame and ends at the recording's end, at the player's first press (consumed: it never reaches then ), at the recording's own quit, or at a divergence (logged at WARNING as demo diverged: ... , then back to then ). A recording that cannot be played (missing, unreadable, another game's, no scene start) is logged at WARNING and nothing starts. Record a demo with scripts/record_scripted_session.py --script-only --output PATH (it runs --record-trace , so its first frame holds the scene start; --script-only leaves out the controls tail, whose quit would end the demo). Bundled demos are recordings shipped in a game's package as package data, <package>/demos/<name>.jsonl.gz : PaddleSlap's paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz , which its game-over screen plays after 10 seconds without a press. The engine finds them, for any tool or installed game, with glitchygames.bundled_demos.bundled_demos() : each BundledDemo (a frozen record) holds the game's console script (None when no installed console script is in the package), the demo's installed path and its install name ( paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz , the same under any install). It searches the installed packages its caller names (required, with no default: a game's own package for --verify , MEMBER_LAYERS ' for our tests; importlib.util.find_spec , importing no game), leaves out bookmarked copies and sorts them by path. tests/replay/test_bundled_demos.py replays every one headless (through glitchygames.testing.replays.bundled_demo_paths , which refuses a demo nothing replays), so a change that makes a demo diverge fails in CI before it ships; glitchygames measure measures the same demos (each game's --measure takes its own package's, as --verify does).
docs.title: Demos

docs.text: class Match ( Scene ): INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS = 5.0 # opt in: show the last 5 seconds MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS = 60.0 # the default budget def on_goal ( self ): self . scene_manager . instant_replay () # False (logged) when it cannot play A scene class that sets INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS keeps, in memory, the recording of every frame since its first logic frame ( src/glitchygames/instant_replay.py ), sprites included: about 0.5 MB per minute for one sprite moving every frame, about 1.5 MB per minute for PaddleSlap. The journal ends when another scene is presented, and once it holds more frame time than MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS (paused frames count: all are re-simulated), after which instant_replay() returns False ; longer scenes would need state snapshots. instant_replay() rebuilds the scene from its start, runs the frames before the last INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS of frame time unseen, unpaced and silent, shows the rest at the game's pace with their sounds, then the live scene goes on exactly where it was. The player's presses do not end it. To let the player skip it, read the player's input in a supervisor and end the playback there ( end_playback() is honoured only from a supervisor or between frames): class SkipReplayOnPress : def on_frame ( self , * , frame_number , scene ): player_input = scene_manager . playback_player_input # None outside a playback if player_input is not None and player_input . key_pressed ( pygame . K_SPACE ): scene_manager . end_playback () Instant replays can follow one another (a replay after every goal): a playback suspends the journal, which resumes afterwards, and a request the scene's own code makes while its journal plays back gets the answer it got live.
docs.title: Instant replay

docs.text: A ghost is a recorded sprite's path and looks drawn beside live play, a time-trial ghost ( src/glitchygames/replay/ghosts.py 's docstring is the contract). Ghosts are appearance, not play: they have no hitbox and change nothing the game does. from glitchygames.replay.ghosts import ( GhostRecorder , GhostSprite , GhostTrack , images_from_animated_sprite , ) # Recording: from the scene's start until the lap ends recorder = GhostRecorder ( sprite = self . player , scene = self ) ... track = recorder . finish () saves . save ( 'best_lap' , track . to_json ()) # Playing it in the next run of the scene (in setup()) track = GhostTrack . from_json ( saves . load ( 'best_lap' )) ghost = GhostSprite ( track = track , image_for = images_from_animated_sprite ( self . player )) ghost . scene = self # the ghost follows this scene's game_time self . all_sprites . add ( ghost ) # never to a collision group GhostRecorder is a supervisor: once per frame, after the frame's logic, it samples the scene's game_time , the sprite's world_x / world_y , its appearance (animation, frame, horizontal flip and draw offset of an AnimatedSprite ; pass appearance= for anything else) and whether the game shows it ( not hidden ). It samples only live frames of the scene it was given, and only when that scene's game time advanced: not behind the pause screen, not in a demo or instant replay. It reads game state only, so recording a ghost changes nothing. Supervisors added while a demo or instant replay plays belong to that playback and are removed when it ends, so a recorder the rebuilt scene's setup() makes never outlives it. Samples are keyed by Scene.game_time , which stops while the scene is paused. The ghost shows the last sample not after the current game_time , so it lines up with the live run from the scene's start at any frame rate, and waits while the game is paused. GhostSprite is a world-space sprite: the engine positions and culls it. Its position is read from the track whenever the engine reads it, so it is drawn in this frame's place, not last frame's. Its image is image_for(sample) drawn translucent ( alpha , default 96). Hide it with ghost.hidden = True (the game's own flag, as for every world sprite). With nothing to show (before the track's first sample, or a sample the game had hidden) its image is empty, so the engine culls it. A ghost in all_sprites is in a recording's sprite trace like any sprite. Store tracks in saves: a replay serves the saves the recording saw, so a session with a ghost replays exactly.
docs.title: Ghosts

docs.text:
Gameplay Playback # Playback is how GlitchyGames records a play session and runs it again, through the real engine, frame for frame. It is what makes a bug report reproducible, a golden replay a regression test, a demo or an instant replay possible, and a performance measurement repeatable: the same recording, replayed on the same engine, draws the same sprites in every frame ( src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py , whose docstring is the replay's contract). These pages explain how it works. For every flag, option and exit code, the command reference is Gameplay Recording and Replay ; these pages link into it rather than repeat it. The idea in one picture # Everything the engine takes in from the outside world (events, frame time, polled input, devices, saves, the clocks and the random seed) passes through one set of doors ( src/glitchygames/sources.py , EngineSources ). Live play installs the live doors; a recording wraps them and writes down what passes through; a replay installs doors that serve the recording instead. Everything downstream of the doors, the game included, runs unchanged. flowchart LR world["Outside world

"--record-trace wraps" .-> recording recording --> engine recording --> file file --> replay replay --> engine The modes at a glance # Mode How it starts Doors Paced? Compares? Writes? Live play LiveSources yes, to the target FPS no nothing Record --record-trace PATH RecordingSources around LiveSources yes no the recording Headless replay --replay-trace PATH --headless ReplaySources no ( paced_frame_seconds is 0.0) every frame, stops at the first difference nothing Watched replay --replay-trace PATH ReplaySources , driven by the viewer by the viewer's 60 Hz outer tick every frame, pauses at a difference a bookmarked copy, if asked Live play against OLD --compare-trace OLD the live host's doors, plus a headless child replaying OLD yes no (the onion skin only draws) nothing (or --record-trace ) Rebaseline --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless ReplaySources , with a recorder over them no counts every differing frame, never stops NEW Measure glitchygames measure a rebaseline per recording, in a child no as a rebaseline ledger rows Verify glitchygames verify a headless replay per recording, in a child no as a headless replay nothing Audit --replay-trace PATH --audit two headless replays, in fresh processes no the two runs' frame digests nothing Sources: the pacing column is paced_frame_seconds in src/glitchygames/sources.py and rule 13 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py ; the watched replay's tick is CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND in src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py ; live play against OLD is rule 9 of src/glitchygames/replay/tools/compare.py ; the rebaseline is src/glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py ; measure and verify are src/glitchygames/replay/tools/measure.py and verify.py ; the audit is src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py . Which page answers what # How a frame runs : the steps of one frame in SceneManager 's order, where each door is read, and where a replay's sources take over from the live ones. Speeds and timing : live pacing, headless and watched replays, the catch-up rule, --replay-fps real , live play against OLD and step back. A frame's logic is the same at every speed; only the waiting differs. The recording file : the .jsonl.gz layout, every field and why it is kept, what is deliberately not kept, and what is stored versus derived. How we test playback : golden replays, golden traces, the replay-tool tests on stand-in games, verify, measure and rebaseline, the determinism audit, the doors guard and the memory guard. Related: Replay Performance (the graphs built from measured runs) and Event System .

The Recording File # A recording ( --record-trace PATH , or a rebaseline's NEW) is a sprite trace in the format of src/glitchygames/tracing.py , plus what an exact replay needs ( src/glitchygames/recording.py , whose docstring lists every field). The field-by-field command reference is Recording and Content hashes and measurement history . This page explains the layout, and why each part is kept. Layout # gzip-compressed JSON Lines ( tracing.py ): line 1 is the header, then exactly one line per main-loop frame, numbered 0, 1, 2, ... Transition frames, paused frames, frames where nothing changed, and a final frame with no active scene are all included ( recording.py ). The gzip header has mtime 0 and no file name, so identical traces give identical bytes ( tracing.py ). flowchart TD file[("PATH.jsonl.gz")] header["Line 1: header
format_version, source, game (logical name), game_class, game_module,
scene_class, options, screen_size, random_seed, recorded_at,
engine/pygame/Python versions, saves, devices, device_enumeration,
measurement_runs, rebaselined_from"] key["Frame line: keyframe
(frame 0, a new scene object, or forced)
frame, scene, sprites (full list)"] delta["Frame line: delta
changed / added / removed / order
against the previous frame"] always["On every frame line:
dt, event_batches,
content_hash [history], processing_seconds [history]"] sometimes["Only where not empty:
input_changes, control_events, devices_opened,
saves_opened, device_enumeration, scene_start,
redelivered_events"] file --> header file --> key file --> delta key --- always delta --- always key --- sometimes delta --- sometimes A frame's sprite record is {"id": "#", "rect": [x, y, width, height], "visible": bool} for every sprite in the scene's all_sprites , in draw order ( sample_scene_frame , tracing.py ). Delta frames carry only what changed, and an integer rect change is written as rect_delta ( tracing.py ). What each part is for # Field Why it is kept Read by random_seed every random stream derives from it, so the replay draws the same numbers ( src/glitchygames/randomness.py ) replay startup (driver rule 1) options , screen_size the replay applies the recorded options (all but the replay's own) and opens the recorded display size (driver rule 1) replay startup game , scene_start.scene (logical names) the game and scenes are found by logical name, not by where their code lives ( src/glitchygames/logical_names.py ) check_recorded_game , find_scene_class recorded_at the wall clock of the recording, and of its replay, is this stamp plus the frame clock (driver rule 9) clock.wall_clock_time() saves , saves_opened save stores as they were first opened, so a replay never touches real saves (driver rule 7) MemorySaveManager devices , devices_opened , device_enumeration the pads the run saw, and every enumeration answer (driver rule 6) ReplayDeviceRegistry dt the frame time logic received; a replay serves it, so timers and physics replay exactly (driver rule 4) frame_seconds door event_batches every read of SDL's queue in the frame, empty ones too, in order, with each event's origin (driver rule 2) pump_events door input_changes the polled input (keys held, mouse, pads) as changes since the previous frame (driver rule 5) input_snapshot door control_events the supervisor's actions in the frame ( src/glitchygames/supervision.py ), compared at the end of the frame (driver rule 8) end_frame scene_start how a scene began (its arguments, random states and frame clock), so in-game playback can rebuild it ( src/glitchygames/scene_start.py ) playback scopes scene , sprites what the frame drew, sampled: the comparison's fingerprint of the frame (driver rule 8) end_frame measurement_runs each run's provenance (machine, paced or not, versions, commit, machine state) and its summary ( src/glitchygames/recording_history.py ) glitchygames report , measure content_hash , processing_seconds per frame, newest run first: what the frame did and how long its work took, per run report , the ledger What is deliberately not kept # Pixels and audio. A frame is compared by its scene class and each sprite's rect , visible and draw order. Pixels, audio, and game state that is not sampled are not compared, so they are not recorded ( src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py ; sample_scene_frame ). Audio plays during a replay but is not compared ( the reference ). Wall-clock time per frame. Only recorded_at is stored. Every later wall-clock reading is recorded_at plus the frame clock, and the frame clock is the sum of the recorded dt s ( src/glitchygames/clock.py ). Measured durations as inputs. measured_seconds() is real time for logs and metrics. It is never replayed, so it may never decide anything that is drawn, played or recorded ( clock.py ). Processing times are recorded as diagnostics, never compared and never served to the game ( src/glitchygames/replay/processing.py ). The host name. The machine is platform.platform() , with no host name, because recordings are shared and bundled demos ship in the wheel ( machine_description , processing.py ). Pumps after the last frame. Pumps while the engine shuts down belong to no frame ( recording.py ). Anything the replay can recompute , such as which events were delivered, discarded or unhandled. That follows from the batch and the game state, so the replay re-derives it ( recording.py ). Stored, and derived # The rule: store what cannot be recomputed; derive the rest, and store a derived value only where history would otherwise be lost. Stored, because it cannot be recomputed # The inputs : event batches with their origins, the input snapshots ( input_changes ), device answers, save snapshots and supervisor control events. Frame times ( dt ) and the seed and options . These are the run's conditions. Logical names ( game , scene_start.scene ). They name the code, not where it lived. The sampled sprites per frame: the comparison's fingerprint of what each frame drew. Per run, processing times ( processing_seconds[i] ) and provenance ( measurement_runs[i] ). They describe that run on that machine, and are gone once it ends. Derived: where each derived value lives, and why # flowchart LR frames["Frame content
(stored)"] --> hash["content_hash per frame
stored per run, newest first"] hash --> rechash["recording content hash
(recording_content_hash: derived on demand, not stored)"] times["processing_seconds and dt
(stored)"] --> summary["RunSummary
p50/p95/p99/max, total, worst frame,
frames over budget, live frame times,
mean and 5% low/high slice means"] summary --> header["header: measurement_runs[i].summary
(filled in when the next run stacks)"] summary --> row["ledger row (quality/replay-ledger/)
one per recording per run"] row --> pages["performance pages
(built from rows on every docs build)"] summary -. "display only" .-> fps["FPS = 1 / seconds
(fps_from_seconds, never stored)"] Content hash ( frame_content_hash , recording_history.py ): 64 bits of SHA-256 of a frame's content fields. It is stored per frame and per run, because a later rebaseline compares runs frame by frame (behavior changes, same-work speed comparisons: src/glitchygames/recording_metrics.py ). The recording's own hash for a run is derived from those on demand and never stored ( recording_content_hash ). Run summaries ( RunSummary , recording_history.py ): processing p50/p95/p99/max, total, the worst frame and its scene, frames over budget, a live run's frame times (p50/p99/max, late frames), and the mean and the "5% low/high" slice means ( slice_frame_count is the one definition of a slice). A summary could be recomputed from the frames, but each recording keeps only MEASUREMENT_RUNS_HISTORY_DEPTH = 10 runs, so the summary is stored twice to outlive them: in the header, written when the next run stacks ( stacked_measurement_runs ; the newest run's summary is computed on read, recording_run_summaries ); in a ledger row, one per recording per run ( LedgerRow , recording_metrics.py ), each with a per-frame profile ( FrameProfile ). FPS is never stored. Summaries keep seconds, which average correctly, and FPS is one division away, done for display only ( fps_from_seconds , recording_metrics.py ). The ledger and the performance pages are built from rows: every docs build merges the row files, the published ledger and pending rows, and graphs them ( src/glitchygames/replay/tools/performance_pages.py ; Replay Performance ). Adding a derived field # The mean and the 5% slices (2026-10-28) are the worked example: Readers accept its absence. The new field defaults to None ( FrameTimeSummary and RunSummary in recording_history.py ), so every older header and ledger row still reads, and tools show nothing for it rather than failing. The measure and report lines, and the performance pages' FPS charts, leave such rows out. No format version. Header and frame fields added later need none: readers pass through fields they do not use ( tracing.py ), and measurement_runs is read leniently and written strictly ( measurement_run_from ). Older recordings get it at their next rebaseline or stacked run. When a run stacks, each earlier run without a summary gets one from the frames. A stored summary that lacks a newer field is completed from the frames too, keeping every value it already holds ( summary_lacks_fields , completed_summary ). Ledger rows already written are never rewritten, so they keep their absence. One definition, tested by hand. A derived figure is defined in one function and tested with hand-computed vectors ( tests/test_recording_history.py ).

docs.title: What each part is for

docs.text: Pixels and audio. A frame is compared by its scene class and each sprite's rect , visible and draw order. Pixels, audio, and game state that is not sampled are not compared, so they are not recorded ( src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py ; sample_scene_frame ). Audio plays during a replay but is not compared ( the reference ). Wall-clock time per frame. Only recorded_at is stored. Every later wall-clock reading is recorded_at plus the frame clock, and the frame clock is the sum of the recorded dt s ( src/glitchygames/clock.py ). Measured durations as inputs. measured_seconds() is real time for logs and metrics. It is never replayed, so it may never decide anything that is drawn, played or recorded ( clock.py ). Processing times are recorded as diagnostics, never compared and never served to the game ( src/glitchygames/replay/processing.py ). The host name. The machine is platform.platform() , with no host name, because recordings are shared and bundled demos ship in the wheel ( machine_description , processing.py ). Pumps after the last frame. Pumps while the engine shuts down belong to no frame ( recording.py ). Anything the replay can recompute , such as which events were delivered, discarded or unhandled. That follows from the batch and the game state, so the replay re-derives it ( recording.py ).
docs.title: What is deliberately not kept

docs.text: The rule: store what cannot be recomputed; derive the rest, and store a derived value only where history would otherwise be lost.
docs.title: Stored, and derived

docs.text: The inputs : event batches with their origins, the input snapshots ( input_changes ), device answers, save snapshots and supervisor control events. Frame times ( dt ) and the seed and options . These are the run's conditions. Logical names ( game , scene_start.scene ). They name the code, not where it lived. The sampled sprites per frame: the comparison's fingerprint of what each frame drew. Per run, processing times ( processing_seconds[i] ) and provenance ( measurement_runs[i] ). They describe that run on that machine, and are gone once it ends.
docs.title: Stored, because it cannot be recomputed

(fps_from_seconds, never stored)"] Content hash ( frame_content_hash , recording_history.py ): 64 bits of SHA-256 of a frame's content fields. It is stored per frame and per run, because a later rebaseline compares runs frame by frame (behavior changes, same-work speed comparisons: src/glitchygames/recording_metrics.py ). The recording's own hash for a run is derived from those on demand and never stored ( recording_content_hash ). docs.text: The mean and the 5% slices (2026-10-28) are the worked example: Readers accept its absence. The new field defaults to None ( FrameTimeSummary and RunSummary in recording_history.py ), so every older header and ledger row still reads, and tools show nothing for it rather than failing. The measure and report lines, and the performance pages' FPS charts, leave such rows out. No format version. Header and frame fields added later need none: readers pass through fields they do not use ( tracing.py ), and measurement_runs is read leniently and written strictly ( measurement_run_from ). Older recordings get it at their next rebaseline or stacked run. When a run stacks, each earlier run without a summary gets one from the frames. A stored summary that lacks a newer field is completed from the frames too, keeping every value it already holds ( summary_lacks_fields , completed_summary ). Ledger rows already written are never rewritten, so they keep their absence. One definition, tested by hand. A derived figure is defined in one function and tested with hand-computed vectors ( tests/test_recording_history.py ).

docs.text: Speeds and Timing # A frame's logic is identical at every speed; only the waiting differs. Every mode runs the same _run_frame_steps ( How a frame runs ). What changes is whether _finish_frame waits after the work, whether the doors hold the loop between frames, and which dt the logic receives: the measured one live, the recorded one in a replay ( frame_seconds , rule 4 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py ). A replay at 8x runs exactly the frames a replay at 1x runs. It just runs more of them per real second. In the timing charts below, the constants come from the code and are named. Bars labelled work stand for however long a frame's work takes. Their lengths are illustrative, not measurements. The charts' positions are whole milliseconds (Mermaid's time axis), so 16.667 ms is drawn at 17. A paced live frame # Live play paces each frame to the target FPS (the default is 60.01 FPS, DEFAULT_TARGET_FPS in src/glitchygames/timing.py ). With the fast backend, FastTimer.start_frame turns the target into a period in nanoseconds: 16,666,667 ns at 60 FPS, or about 16,664 µs at 60.01. After the frame's work, SceneManager._handle_frame_pacing asks the timer for the next deadline ( compute_deadline ) and sleeps until it ( sleep_until_next ): Sleep. The timer sleeps so that it is predicted to wake DEFAULT_SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS (1 ms) before the deadline. Under --timer-backend auto , the engine's default, the sleep is shortened by this machine's measured SleepModel (how late its sleeps wake: a constant plus a fraction of the length). Spin. It spins the rest. Then _finish_frame takes one perf_counter() reading, which ends this frame and starts the next. gantt title One paced live frame at 60 FPS (period 16.667 ms, FastTimer.start_frame) dateFormat x axisFormat %L ms section Frame N work (_run_frame_steps, illustrative) :w, 0, 6 sleep (sized by the SleepModel) :s, 6, 16 spin (DEFAULT_SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS = 1 ms) :p, 16, 17 section Frame N+1 work (illustrative) :w2, 17, 22 The frame's processing time is the work alone, without presenting and without the pacing ( _run_frame_steps ; src/glitchygames/replay/processing.py ). Its frame time ( dt ) is the whole period, start to start. Paced frames process more slowly than unpaced ones, because the processor idles between them; processing.py explains this, and it is why paced and unpaced timings are never compared. A headless replay # A replay never paces: ReplaySources.paced_frame_seconds returns 0.0, so _handle_frame_pacing returns at once (no deadline, no clock tick), and a headless replay never holds. Frames run back to back. Each frame's logic still receives the recorded dt , so the game "sees" the recorded timing however fast the machine runs it (rules 4 and 13 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py ). gantt title Headless replay: no waits (paced_frame_seconds = 0.0) dateFormat x axisFormat %L ms section Frames frame 0 work (logic gets recorded dt 0) :a, 0, 3 frame 1 work (recorded dt 1) :b, 3, 5 frame 2 work (recorded dt 2) :c, 5, 9 frame 3 work (recorded dt 3) :d, 9, 11 This is the mode every measurement uses: a rebaseline (and so measure ) is headless, and its per-frame processing times are pure work. A watched replay # A watched replay has two loops ( src/glitchygames/replay/viewer.py , whose docstring is the contract): Outer. The viewer ticks at a fixed real-time rate: CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND = 60 ( src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py ), on measured_seconds() , never replayed. Each tick reads the viewer's keys, refreshes the status line and presents one frame. Inner. The recorded game steps at its recorded frame times. Its frames run whole, but are not presented ( presents_frames is False). Before each inner frame the scene manager asks hold_frame : No tick open. Sleep until the next tick (with FastTimer while frames run), then add the real time since the last tick, times the speed, to an accumulator. Tick open. Run another inner frame while the accumulator holds that frame's recorded duration, and consume it. There are two limits per tick: at most MAX_INNER_FRAMES_PER_TICK = 32 frames, and only within INNER_FRAME_BUDGET_SECONDS = 0.011 s of real time, so keys and presenting stay at 60 Hz. The accumulator never owes more than one tick's worth: the excess is dropped, and the status bar shows the real speed while the viewer is behind ( BEHIND_SPEED_FRACTION = 0.95). Otherwise the tick closes and the frame is presented. So at 1x a 60 FPS recording runs one inner frame per tick, at 8x eight, and at ¼x one every fourth tick (the viewer's docstring). The speed keys double or halve the speed ( SPEED_STEP_FACTOR = 2.0), within MIN_SPEED = 0.25 and MAX_SPEED = 8.0 ( ReplayControls , src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py ). The 32-frame cap is what lets the viewer catch up after a stall, in one bounded burst. gantt title Watched replay at 8x: one outer tick (1/60 s) runs several inner frames dateFormat x axisFormat %L ms section Outer tick 1 keys + accumulator (hold_frame) :k1, 0, 1 inner frames, within the 11 ms budget :i1, 1, 7 present the latest frame :p1, 7, 8 sleep until the next tick :s1, 8, 17 section Outer tick 2 keys + accumulator :k2, 17, 18 inner frames (up to 32 per tick) :i2, 18, 24 present :p2, 24, 25 The accumulator only decides when inner frames run, never what they do, so a watched replay is as exact as a headless one ( viewer.py ). --replay-fps real # --replay-fps changes only which frame time the FPS statistics read, never the logic and never the pacing. Under recorded (the default), the FPS events and performance statistics use the recorded dt , so the FPS events are compared exactly. Under real , they use this machine's measured frame time, and FPS events are not compared. Logic still receives the recorded dt (rule 4 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py ; SceneManager._performance_frame_seconds ). The timing chart is therefore the same as the headless or watched replay above. A rebaseline and an audit refuse real ( src/glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py rule 1; src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py ). Flags: --replay-fps . Live play against OLD (the onion skin) # <game> --compare-trace OLD plays live, paced as usual, and draws OLD's items over each presented frame. OLD is replayed headless by a child process that streams its frames back over a loopback socket ( src/glitchygames/replay/tools/compare.py , rules 2-5 and 9): sequenceDiagram participant Game as Live game (parent, paced) participant Sock as Socket on 127.0.0.1 (FRAME_STREAM_HOST) participant Child as OLD's child: --replay-trace OLD --headless Game->>Sock: listen on a port Game->>Child: start with --replay-frame-stream PORT:TOKEN (on the first presented frame) Child->>Sock: connect, send the token first (32 hex characters) Note over Game,Sock: a connection without the token is closed and logged loop each frame OLD replays Child->>Sock: FRAME_HEADER (frame, width, height: 3 x uint32 LE), then RGB pixels end loop each frame the game presents Game->>Sock: read (and drop) until the frame paired by the game-frame clock Game->>Game: blend OLD's items over the frame at --compare-alpha end Note over Game,Child: the parent reads only when it draws: the child blocks on a full socket, so both move together Game->>Child: teardown stops it and waits (OnionSkin.stop) The token is FRAME_STREAM_TOKEN_BYTES = 16 random bytes from secrets , sent as FRAME_STREAM_TOKEN_LENGTH = 32 hex characters. The child has CHILD_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60 s to connect; a child that stalls for CHILD_READ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60 s ends OLD's ghost there, while the game goes on. Frames are paired by the game-frame clock ( src/glitchygames/game_frames.py ), so a pause on either side freezes the ghost rather than drifting (rule 11). The child is headless, so it runs unpaced, as any headless replay does. The parent's reads keep it in lockstep. Flags: Live play against OLD . Step back: rebuild # A replay cannot run backwards, so step back ( , ), Home and D restart the replay in a fresh process, paused at frame N ( src/glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py , whose docstring is the contract): sequenceDiagram participant First as First replay process (becomes the supervisor) participant Child as Restarted replay (--replay-pause-at-frame N) First->>First: viewer presses step back: end the run (restart_frame = N), tear down First->>Child: run the restart command (run_command), with --replay-restart-handoff PATH Note over Child: rebuild: frames 0..N-1 run whole, unpresented, unpaced, silenced loop every REBUILD_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_SECONDS (0.1 s) of real time Child->>Child: present "Rebuilding: frame k / N" end Child->>Child: pause at frame N, showing frame N-1's picture opt the viewer steps back again Child->>First: write a RestartHandoff to PATH and end First->>Child: run the next restart (never more than two processes) end The rebuild is a headless-speed run of the same frames, with the same logic: only presenting, pacing and sound are left out ( Rebuild.silence_frame ; src/glitchygames/replay/silence.py ). With an onion skin, the restarted process's child skips straight to the paired game frame ( compare.py rule 8). Keys: Step back, Home and D . Summary # Mode Waits after a frame Holds between frames Logic's dt FPS statistics read Live to the deadline (sleep, then spin) never measured measured Headless replay never never recorded recorded ( --replay-fps real : measured) Watched replay never until the viewer's tick pays for the frame recorded as headless Rebuild never only to show progress recorded as headless Live vs OLD to the deadline never measured measured OLD's child never never (blocks on a full socket) recorded recorded

How We Test Playback # Each tier checks something the others cannot see. The cheapest checks run on every test run; the real games' replays run as test items too, in child processes, so the engine is exercised the way a player's run exercises it. flowchart TD subgraph suite ["Every test run (pytest / nox -s test)"] goldens["Golden replays

on stand-in games"] doors["Doors guard

(pre-commit replay-metrics)"] rebaseline["--rebaseline
(after an intended change)"] audit["--audit
(determinism)"] end goldens -. "same replay as" .-> verify measure -. "is a rebaseline per recording" .-> rebaseline Golden replays # Intent: every game still plays its scripted session exactly as recorded, and every control it binds still works. Each src///tests/fixtures/replays/golden*.jsonl.gz (the golden-globs setting in pyproject.toml ) is collected as one test item by the replay plugin ( src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py , registered through the engine's pytest11 entry point). The item replays the recording headless in a child process, through the game's console script entry point ( --replay-trace PATH --headless --log-level warning ). It passes only if the child exits SUCCESS ; otherwise it fails with the divergence report. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py checks the fixtures themselves. Its controls rule is that every golden pauses and resumes, exercises every keyboard control the game binds, and ends with the game's own quit control ( test_every_golden_replay_exercises_every_control ), so a control that stops working makes its golden diverge. The goldens are recorded through the real engine by scripts/record_scripted_session.py , with scripts/golden_inputs.py . flowchart LR item["pytest collects

The same frames and sprites are recorded either way. A test that reads the recorded frame times (a watched replay presents frames by them) or the run's pacing ( processing_paced , its live frame times) asks for paced=True , which paces at STAND_IN_GAME_TARGET_FPS = '60' as a player's run is; each such call says why. Replays of either are unpaced, as every replay is ( tests/stand_in_games.py ). Shared recordings. A replay still running after REPLAY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 300 s is stopped ( src/glitchygames/replay/tools/verify.py , children.py ). The test parses every engine source file and follows imports and aliases of the watched modules ( time , datetime , pygame and its event, key, mouse, time and joystick modules, ...; WATCHED_DOOR_MODULES ). The memory guard # Intent: a test that runs CI's 2 GB Linux container out of memory stops the run and names the test, instead of the kernel killing the job silently ( tests/memory_guard.py ; tests/test_memory_guard.py ). It is on only when GLITCHYGAMES_TEST_RSS_LIMIT_MB is set; CircleCI's Linux job sets 1600. It reads the container's memory (cgroup v2) where there is one, else this process's resident memory, and does nothing on macOS or Windows. It matters for playback because the golden replays and the tools' tests start child processes, and the container's figure counts them.

docs.text: Shut down every running AI worker the way a normal quit does (AIManager.cleanup). Bitmappy's main() calls it when the engine stops, so a SIGINT/SIGTERM (which ends the engine with SystemExit and skips the scenes' cleanup) still sends each worker its shutdown message, joins it with a timeout and terminates it only if it does not exit. Workers already shut down by a normal quit are no longer registered, so this then does nothing. Source code in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ai_manager.py 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 def shut_down_running_ai_workers () -> None : """Shut down every running AI worker the way a normal quit does (AIManager.cleanup). Bitmappy's main() calls it when the engine stops, so a SIGINT/SIGTERM (which ends the engine with SystemExit and skips the scenes' cleanup) still sends each worker its shutdown message, joins it with a timeout and terminates it only if it does not exit. Workers already shut down by a normal quit are no longer registered, so this then does nothing. """ for manager in list ( _RUNNING_AI_MANAGERS ): manager . cleanup () AI worker infrastructure for Bitmappy sprite generation. Contains the AI worker process function and all supporting functions for initializing the AI client, managing timeouts, processing requests, and selecting training examples.

docs.text: Build a targeted retry prompt based on validation error. Parameters: original_prompt ( str ) – Original user request validation_error ( str ) – Error message from validate_ai_response() Returns: str – Enhanced prompt with specific corrections Source code in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ai_worker.py 843 844 845 846 847 848 849 850 851 852 853 854 855 856 857 858 859 860 861 862 863 864 865 866 867 868 869 870 871 872 873 874 875 876 877 878 879 880 881 882 883 884 885 886 887 888 889 890 891 892 893 894 def build_retry_prompt ( original_prompt : str , validation_error : str ) -> str : """Build a targeted retry prompt based on validation error. Args: original_prompt: Original user request validation_error: Error message from validate_ai_response() Returns: Enhanced prompt with specific corrections """ # Base prompt retry_prompt = original_prompt + ' \n\n ' # Add specific corrections based on error type error_lower = validation_error . lower () if 'missing [sprite] section' in error_lower : retry_prompt += 'CRITICAL: You must include a [sprite] section at the beginning.' elif 'missing [colors] section' in error_lower : retry_prompt += ( 'CRITICAL: You must include [colors] sections defining every color used in pixels.' ) elif 'truncated' in error_lower or 'incomplete' in error_lower : retry_prompt += ( 'IMPORTANT: Previous response was cut off. ' 'Reduce detail, use fewer frames, or make it smaller to fit within token limits.' ) elif 'mixed' in error_lower and 'format' in error_lower : retry_prompt += ( "CRITICAL: For animated sprites, do NOT include 'pixels' in [sprite] section. " 'Only include pixels in [[animation.frame]] sections.' ) elif 'comma' in error_lower : retry_prompt += ( 'CRITICAL: Color values must use separate fields (red = X, green = Y, blue = Z), ' 'NOT comma-separated tuples.' ) elif 'markdown' in error_lower : retry_prompt += ( 'CRITICAL: Return ONLY raw TOML, no markdown code blocks (```), no explanations.' ) elif 'empty' in error_lower : retry_prompt += 'CRITICAL: You must generate sprite content, not an empty or error message.' else : # Generic retry message retry_prompt += ( f 'IMPORTANT: Previous attempt had an error: ' f ' { validation_error } . Please fix and try again.' ) return retry_prompt

docs.text: Run the AI worker as the editor's background process (AIManager's Process target). Ctrl-C in a terminal sends SIGINT to the whole process group. The worker ignores it so it is not killed by KeyboardInterrupt and instead exits on the shutdown message the editor sends while it shuts down (AIManager.cleanup). terminate() (SIGTERM) still stops it. Parameters: request_queue ( Queue [ AIRequest | None] ) – Queue to receive requests from (None asks the worker to exit). response_queue ( Queue [ tuple [ str , AIResponse ]] ) – Queue to send responses to. Queue [ AIRequest | None ], response_queue : multiprocessing . Queue [ tuple [ str , AIResponse ]], ) -> None : """Run the AI worker as the editor's background process (AIManager's Process target). Ctrl-C in a terminal sends SIGINT to the whole process group. The worker ignores it so it is not killed by KeyboardInterrupt and instead exits on the shutdown message the editor sends while it shuts down (AIManager.cleanup). terminate() (SIGTERM) still stops it. Args: request_queue: Queue to receive requests from (None asks the worker to exit). response_queue: Queue to send responses to. """ signal . signal ( signal . SIGINT , signal . SIG_IGN ) run_ai_worker ( request_queue , response_queue )

Returns: list: The result. """ training_data = ai_training_state [ 'data' ] if not isinstance ( training_data , list ): return [] if len ( training_data ) <= max_examples : return training_data user_lower = user_request . lower () requested_size = get_sprite_size_hint ( user_request ) user_words = set ( user_lower . split ()) wants_alpha = any ( kw in user_lower for kw in [ 'alpha' , 'transparent' , 'transparency' , 'translucent' ] ) scored_examples : list [ tuple [ float , dict [ str , Any ]]] = [] for example in training_data : score = _score_training_example ( example , user_lower , user_words , wants_alpha = wants_alpha , requested_size = requested_size , ) scored_examples . append (( score , example )) scored_examples . sort ( key = operator . itemgetter ( 0 ), reverse = True ) # There are more examples than max_examples (fewer returned above), so this takes # exactly max_examples of them return [ example for _ , example in scored_examples [: max_examples ]] Alpha channel detection and conversion for the Bitmappy editor.

""" import tomllib with config_file . open ( mode = 'rb' ) as f : config_data = tomllib . load ( f ) config_data = normalize_toml_data ( config_data ) sprite_data = { 'name' : config_data . get ( 'sprite' , {}) . get ( 'name' , 'Unknown' ), 'format' : ai_training_state [ 'format' ], 'sprite_type' : 'animated' if 'animation' in config_data else 'static' , 'has_alpha' : False , } if 'sprite' in config_data : sprite_data [ 'pixels' ] = config_data [ 'sprite' ] . get ( 'pixels' , '' ) sprite_data [ 'colors' ] = config_data . get ( 'colors' , {}) sprite_data [ 'has_alpha' ] = _detect_alpha_channel ( config_data . get ( 'colors' , {})) if 'animation' in config_data : sprite_data [ 'animations' ] = config_data [ 'animation' ] sprite_data [ 'has_alpha' ] = _detect_alpha_channel_in_animation ( config_data [ 'animation' ]) return config_data , sprite_data AnimatedCanvasSprite — main pixel-editing canvas for animated sprites.

docs.text: Move the shown frame's pixels one step, as part of the pan gesture in progress. The first step of a gesture (or the first on another frame) starts a new PanSession from the frame's pixels. If the frame changed since the last step (an edit made during the gesture), the gesture continues from the edited pixels, so the edit is kept. A step that would move the gesture's source pixels more than MAX_PAN_DISTANCE is ignored. The moved pixels are written into the frame. Parameters: delta_x ( int ) – Horizontal step (-1 left, 0, or 1 right). delta_y ( int ) – Vertical step (-1 up, 0, or 1 down). Source code in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/animated_canvas.py 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 247 248 249 250 251 252 253 254 255 256 257 258 259 260 261 262 263 264 265 266 267 268 269 270 271 272 273 274 275 276 277 278 279 280 281 282 def pan_canvas ( self , delta_x : int , delta_y : int ) -> None : """Move the shown frame's pixels one step, as part of the pan gesture in progress. The first step of a gesture (or the first on another frame) starts a new PanSession from the frame's pixels. If the frame changed since the last step (an edit made during the gesture), the gesture continues from the edited pixels, so the edit is kept. A step that would move the gesture's source pixels more than MAX_PAN_DISTANCE is ignored. The moved pixels are written into the frame. Args: delta_x: Horizontal step (-1 left, 0, or 1 right). delta_y: Vertical step (-1 up, 0, or 1 down). """ frame = self . _current_sprite_frame () if frame is None : self . log . debug ( 'No frame shown - nothing to pan' ) return frame_pixels = frame . get_pixel_data () session = self . pan_session if session is None or not session . is_for ( animation = self . current_animation , frame_index = self . current_frame , ): session = PanSession . starting_from ( animation = self . current_animation , frame_index = self . current_frame , pixels = frame_pixels , ) elif tuple ( frame_pixels ) != session . panned_pixels : session = session . rebased_on ( pixels = frame_pixels ) new_offset_x = session . offset_x + delta_x new_offset_y = session . offset_y + delta_y if not can_pan_to ( offset_x = new_offset_x , offset_y = new_offset_y ): self . log . debug ( 'Cannot pan to ( %s , %s ) - out of bounds.' , new_offset_x , new_offset_y ) self . pan_session = session return frame_width , frame_height = frame . get_size () panned_pixels = shift_pixels ( pixels = session . source_pixels , width = frame_width , height = frame_height , offset_x = new_offset_x , offset_y = new_offset_y , ) self . pan_session = session . moved_to ( offset_x = new_offset_x , offset_y = new_offset_y , panned_pixels = panned_pixels , ) self . replace_frame_pixels ( animation = self . current_animation , frame_index = self . current_frame , pixels = panned_pixels , )
