docs.text: replay_arguments() returns the constructor arguments the floor was built with, besides options : { 'floor_index' : self . floor_index , 'player_score' : self . starting_player_score , 'player_lives' : self . starting_player_lives } The engine's default is {} , which rebuilds a scene from options alone. That works for the first floor but not for the others: a floor the elevator built would be rebuilt as the --floor floor with score 0 and 3 lives. A scene start ( src/glitchygames/scene_start.py ) keeps these arguments, and rebuild_scene(start=..., scene_class=..., options=...) passes them back to the constructor, so a playback scope (a demo, an instant replay) that starts on floor 2 rebuilds floor 2 with the score and lives it began with. The values are the ones the floor began with ( starting_player_score , starting_player_lives ), not the current ones: cogs collected and lives lost on the floor are what the playback replays, so they must not be in the starting state ( test_floor_replay_arguments_rebuild_the_floor ). They are plain ints, so they round-trip through JSON exactly, as scene starts require.
docs.title: replay_arguments: rebuilding a floor

docs.text: Clockwork Keep is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/clockwork-keep/ (distribution clockwork-keep , import package clockwork_keep ). How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages . Its recordings name it games.clockwork_keep.game:ClockworkKeepScene , its golden replay is src/games/clockwork-keep/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz , its golden trace stays with the engine's trace tests ( tests/world/golden/clockwork_keep.jsonl.gz ), and its browser bundle ships clockwork_keep.zip .
docs.title: Its package

docs.text: Clockwork Keep's own code is the scene, five sprite classes and the floor data, all in src/games/clockwork-keep/src/clockwork_keep/ . The rest comes from the engine: Scene and the built-in PauseScene and GameOverScene ( glitchygames.scenes ), Sprite ( glitchygames.sprites ) and PhysicsBody ( glitchygames.physics ). In the diagram, the Engine box is what every game gets; the Clockwork Keep box is what this game adds. Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class; dotted arrows are how the game uses an engine class; plain arrows are what a game class holds. The scene owns everything on a floor. The five sprite classes all declare COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD , and the scene keeps each kind in a list of its own ( platform_sprites , ...) besides all_sprites . classDiagram direction TB namespace Engine { class Scene { camera, collisions, tweens replay_arguments() } class PauseScene { the frozen floor, dimmed SPACE or Start/A resumes it, ESC or B/Back quits } class GameOverScene { score and high scores SPACE or Start/A restarts, ESC or B/Back quits } class Sprite class PhysicsBody { GravityBehavior AccelerationBehavior BoundsConstraint } } namespace ClockworkKeep { class ClockworkKeepScene { MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05 floor_index, floor_data floor_elapsed_time platform_sprites, elevator_sprites moving_gear_sprites, collectible_sprites actions: ActionMap sounds: SoundBank camera: Camera2D saves: SaveManager victory_platform dt_tick(dt) render(screen) } class ClockworkKeepVictoryScene { the GameOverScene layout titled VICTORY! } class Tinker { lives, score, floor state#95;machine: AnimationStateMachine dt_tick(dt) update() } class Platform class Elevator class MovingGear { moved_x, moved_y dt_tick(dt) } class CogCollectible { points dt_tick(dt) } class FloorData { <<dataclass>> platforms, elevators collectibles, moving_gears } } Scene <|-- PauseScene Scene <|-- GameOverScene Scene <|-- ClockworkKeepScene GameOverScene <|-- ClockworkKeepVictoryScene Sprite <|-- Tinker Sprite <|-- Platform Sprite <|-- Elevator Sprite <|-- MovingGear Sprite <|-- CogCollectible PauseScene <.. ClockworkKeepScene : next_scene on Esc or focus lost GameOverScene <.. ClockworkKeepScene : after the last life ClockworkKeepVictoryScene <.. ClockworkKeepScene : on the top platform PhysicsBody <.. Tinker : physics ClockworkKeepScene --> FloorData : builds its sprites from ClockworkKeepScene --> Tinker : player Tinker 's world_x , world_y , velocity_x , velocity_y , on_ground and facing_right are properties that delegate to its PhysicsBody , so the scene and the engine read the body through the sprite. The debug overlay's physics panel finds the body as sprite.physics .
docs.title: Classes

docs.text: A floor is a FloorData ( levels.py ): one screen wide (800 px), several screens tall, with walls 100 px wide on each side, leaving a 600 px playfield (x 100 to 700). World coordinates start at the floor's top-left; y grows downward, so climbing means a falling world_y . The Tinker spawns at x 400, 60 px above the floor's bottom. Floor Height Platforms Cogs (bronze / silver / gold) Points Way up 0 Boiler Room 960 (2 screens) 14 4 / 1 / 1 190 Elevator at the top 1 Gear Works 1440 (3 screens) 19 5 / 3 / 1 300 Elevator at the top 2 Clock Face 1920 (4 screens) 21 5 / 7 / 2 600 The moving gear, then the victory platform Cogs are worth 10 (bronze), 50 (silver) and 100 (gold) points. There are no enemies. Victory. The Clock Face (the last floor) has no elevator; its highest platform is the floor's victory_platform ( _find_victory_platform ; None on the floors below). When ground collision stands the Tinker on it ( supporting_platform ), dt_tick calls _win() after the cog pickups (so the victory cog above it counts): the floor stops, the camera stops following, the victory chime plays, the high score is saved and the floor fades to ClockworkKeepVictoryScene , the engine's GameOverScene (final score and high scores, Space or a gamepad's Start or A restarts, Esc or B or Back quits) with a gold VICTORY! title. The floor builds its sprites in __init__ , in this order: the parallax background, platforms, elevators, moving gears, cogs, then the player. Sprites of one layer draw in the order they are added, so the order is part of the picture. Each class sets _layer before Sprite.__init__ ( LAYER_TERRAIN 4, LAYER_COLLECTIBLES 5, LAYER_PLAYER 7, the background LAYER_FAR_BACKGROUND 0) for the LayeredDirty group.
docs.title: Floors

docs.text: Every gameplay sprite ( Tinker , Platform , Elevator , MovingGear , CogCollectible ) declares COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD and keeps float world_x / world_y . The game never writes their rect : each frame the engine sets it from the camera, culls sprites more than 32 px off screen, and marks moved sprites dirty. The game reads positions from world_x / world_y and from collision rects, never from rect (except rect.width , which does not move). A cog bobs by moving its world_y , not by shifting pixels in its image. The HUD is not a sprite: render() draws the score (top left), lives (top right) and floor name (top centre) straight onto the screen after the sprites, with a 1 px shadow. Its font is loaded in setup() , so a floor rendered before setup draws no HUD.
docs.title: World-space sprites

docs.text: Setting Value Effect camera.follow(target=player, axes=FollowAxes.BOTH) in setup() The engine aims the camera at the Tinker every frame set_bounds(min_x=0, max_x=0, ...) in __init__ No horizontal scroll: the tower is one screen wide set_bounds(min_y=0, max_y=height - 480) in __init__ The camera stops at the floor's top and bottom lead_y=200 ( CAMERA_LEAD_Y ) in __init__ The camera's top edge sits 200 px above the Tinker's top: a little less view above it than below it on the 480 px screen camera.follow(target=None) at game over The floor stands still during the fade The game never calls camera.update() and has no camera loop ( test_scene_has_no_camera_loop ). setup() does not snap_to the player, so on a fresh start the camera eases down from the floor's top to the spawn; a floor arriving by elevator is snapped to its target by the transition's arrival capture.
docs.title: Camera

docs.text: Each floor has one parallax layer ( camera.add_background_layer , scroll_factor=PARALLAX_FAR = 0.1): the tower walls with brick and windows, plus the floor's machinery (the Boiler Room's furnace glow and pipes, the Gear Works' gears and chain). The engine calls a layer's draw function again only when its offset changes, so these draw functions depend only on the camera position they are given. The Clock Face's layer is different: a working clock whose hands show CLOCK_START_SECONDS (11:58, two minutes to midnight) plus floor_elapsed_time , the floor's game time. Its picture changes while the camera stands still, so that layer is added with animated=True and redraws every frame ( test_only_the_clock_background_is_animated , test_clock_hands_move_on_a_still_camera ). The scene passes a bound method ( _draw_timed_clock_background ) that reads floor_elapsed_time . floor_elapsed_time adds the capped dt in dt_tick , so it stops while paused and after game over.
docs.title: The parallax background and the animated clock

docs.text: Sprite Image Behaviour Platform 12 px tall metal bar in the floor's theme colours, drawn once One-way support: the Tinker jumps up through it and lands on top of it Elevator 60 x 8 px car with caution stripes and an up arrow Supports like a platform; interact while standing on it rides to the next floor MovingGear size x size/4 bar with teeth along its top, dirty = 2 Moves on centre + range * sin(timer * speed) each dt_tick and records moved_x / moved_y CogCollectible 16 px cog, redrawn each tick with spinning teeth Bobs 3 px; picked up when its collision rect overlaps the Tinker's The Clock Face's one moving gear ( MovingGearData : 64 px wide, ±150 px horizontally, speed 1.2, a 5.2 s round trip) is the only way up its final approach: the centre step is 180 px below the last step, beyond a running jump's ~140 px, so the climber hops onto the gear (90 px up), rides it right, and hops off at the end of its sweep, where it pauses. test_the_route_is_within_a_walking_jump and test_climbing_the_final_approach_on_the_gear pin the route.
docs.title: Platforms, elevators, moving gear and cogs
The player: movement, physics and collision

docs.text: Tinker builds a PhysicsBody with: Piece Values GravityBehavior 1200 px/s², terminal fall speed 800 px/s AccelerationBehavior 1600 px/s² toward the target speed, 1200 px/s² to slow down BoundsConstraint The side walls, refitted to the hitbox every tick Speeds Walk 160 px/s, run 280 px/s Jumps -480 px/s (~96 px high), running -580 px/s (~140 px high) move_left / move_right / stop_horizontal only set the acceleration behaviour's target velocity; the body accelerates toward it. jump() sets velocity_y only when on_ground , so an airborne Tinker never jumps again. An AnimationStateMachine picks the pose from the body's animation context: idle , running ( abs(velocity_x) > 0.1 ), jumping ( velocity_y < -10 ) and falling ( velocity_y > 50 and not on the ground).
docs.title: Physics

docs.text: The Tinker's hitbox is its image's visible pixels (the engine's default: transparent pixels trimmed, measured on every query). The figure's transparent margin moves with its pose and facing, so the pose must be drawn before anything collides with it. Tinker.dt_tick does, in order: Fit the wall bounds to the current hitbox, then physics.tick(dt) . Evaluate the state machine. Draw the pose ( _draw_pose : clear the image, draw_tinker(...) ). Refit the wall bounds to the new hitbox and apply them again, so turning toward a wall never puts the hitbox inside it (BUGS.md #64, TestPoseBeforeCollision ). Tinker.update() , which runs in the render phase, only applies the respawn fade ( image.set_alpha ). Drawing the pose there would make the floor's ground and cog checks use the previous frame's pose. All support and pickups use collision rects ( get_sprite_collision_rect ) and collision_rect_offset , not the drawn image: the feet are the hitbox's bottom, and only a hitbox pixel over a platform supports ( TestPlatformSupportUsesHitbox , TestHitboxLooseEnds ). The scene registers two collision layers, player and cogs ; cog pickup is collisions.check_overlap('player', 'cogs', ...) , and the debug overlay's hitbox panel draws the same layers.
docs.title: The pose rule and hitboxes

docs.text: _resolve_ground_collision clears on_ground , then stands the Tinker on the support it finds, falling or at rest ( velocity_y >= 0 ), whose top its feet reached this tick and its hitbox overlapping it horizontally. The fall is swept ( _feet_reach_surface ): the feet must end the tick at or below the support's top, and have started it (before this tick's movement; a gear's ride is not part of the fall) no more than GROUND_SNAP_TOLERANCE (20 px) below it. So a long tick at the 800 px/s terminal speed, which moves the feet up to 40 px at the 50 ms cap, still lands on the platform it crossed instead of passing through it: Platforms (their world_y is their top). Elevators (checked after the platforms, so an elevator standing on its shelf platform wins). Only if neither held it: moving gears, by the gear's collision rect top ( _land_on_moving_gear ), which also sets riding_gear . A gear carries its rider in _ride_moving_gear , which runs after every sprite's dt_tick (the gear has moved) and before ground collision: the rider moves by the gear's moved_x / moved_y , so the collision that follows finds it on the gear again. A jump clears on_ground , so a player leaving the gear is not carried.
docs.title: Ground collision

docs.text: ClockworkKeepScene.MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05 : after a hitch (Cmd-Tab, a slow frame) the engine hands dt_tick and the camera aim at most 50 ms, so the game advances as at 20 FPS at worst instead of jumping. The cap alone does not keep a fast fall out of a platform (40 px in a 50 ms tick); the swept ground check does. The scene manager's own dt (pacing, FPS statistics, shake) stays the raw frame time, and recordings keep the raw dt.
docs.title: MAX_FRAME_SECONDS

docs.text:
The engine runs the frame; the floor's code runs in two places: dt_tick (logic, physics, collision) and the render phase ( update() , then render() ). The Engine box is the engine's frame loop; the Clockwork Keep box is the game's scene and sprites. sequenceDiagram box rgb(232,238,255) Engine participant SM as SceneManager participant GE as GameEngine end box rgb(255,243,224) Clockwork Keep participant CKS as ClockworkKeepScene participant T as Tinker and the other sprites end SM->>SM: camera.begin_frame() SM->>CKS: dt_tick(min(dt, 0.05)) CKS->>T: sprite.dt_tick(dt) for all_sprites Note over CKS: elevator check, movement input,

jump right away, pause, quit SM->>SM: supervisor slot, then shake and rumble SM->>SM: aim the camera at the player SM->>SM: position world sprites from the camera, cull SM->>CKS: update() (Scene: sprite.update(), the Tinker's fade) SM->>CKS: render(screen): fill, draw sprites, HUD SM->>SM: present, then start a pending transition or switch SM->>SM: finish frame (pace, measure dt) Input crosses the frame boundary in two ways. A jump happens in the event handler ( _try_jump ), so its velocity moves the Tinker in the next dt_tick . Interact is read at the top of the next dt_tick with actions.just_pressed('interact') , which is why _check_elevator runs before _process_movement_input calls actions.begin_frame() (which clears the frame's presses). The first result only initializes it, so the arriving floor's off-screen tick during the elevator ride plays nothing, and respawning resets it ( test_first_tick_never_plays_land , test_respawn_does_not_play_land ).

docs.text:
The ride itself is the engine's ( ElevatorTransition , Engine box); the floors and their callbacks are the game's (Clockwork Keep box). sequenceDiagram participant P as Player box rgb(255,243,224) Clockwork Keep participant New as Floor N+1 participant Old as Floor N (ClockworkKeepScene) end box rgb(232,238,255) Engine participant SM as SceneManager participant ET as ElevatorTransition end P->>Old: W / Y (interact) Old->>Old: _check_elevator (next dt_tick):
on an elevator, not the last floor Old->>New: ClockworkKeepScene(floor_index=N+1,
player_score, player_lives, options) Old->>ET: ElevatorTransition(duration=4.0,
easing='ease_in_sine', player_surface=...) Old->>SM: create_voice(owner=transition), motor.start() Old->>SM: transition_to(New, ET)
with a cue at progress 1.0 loop every frame of the ride ET->>Old: on_update: _update_elevator_motor(transition) Old->>SM: rumble.set_sustained(low, high)
scaled by car speed Note over Old: motor pitch 45 to 110 Hz, volume 0.15 to 0.6 end ET->>Old: cue 1.0: _elevator_arrived() Old->>SM: motor.stop_now(), rumble.clear_sustained() Old->>SM: play 'elevator_clank',
SCREEN shakes: bounce + rattle SM->>New: the ride ends, Floor N+1 is active The ride is src/glitchygames/transitions/elevator.py : a tall composite of the old floor, a shaft and the new floor scrolls up while the car and the Tinker (a copy of its image) stay pinned at the screen's centre. ease_in_sine arrives at full speed, so the stop reads as a slam. The car's speed is the easing's slope ( transition.eased_velocity_at(progress) ), divided by its peak (sampled over 101 points when the ride starts), so motor pitch, motor volume and rumble all follow the car. The callbacks run after the old floor's cleanup() , so they touch only SceneManager services: the live voice, the rumble and SCREEN shakes (a WORLD shake would need the old floor's sprites). A ride with no free live voice, or without audio, rides silently but still rumbles ( test_ride_without_free_voice_still_rumbles ). _update_elevator_motor ignores the completing frame (progress 1.0): the arrival cue runs first and clears the rumble, and updating again would restart it. Input pressed during the ride is not delivered to the new floor: a jump pressed and released mid-ride does not jump on arrival ( tests/world/test_transition_input.py ).
docs.title: Riding the elevator

The game decides a death and what follows (Clockwork Keep box); the fade and the game-over screen are the engine's (Engine box). flowchart TB subgraph GAME_DEATH["Clockwork Keep"] direction TB fall["world_y more than 100 px
below the floor's bottom"] --> lose["lives -= 1"] lose --> left{"lives left?"} left -->|yes| deathSound["play 'death'"] deathSound --> fadeOut["_respawn_player: is_respawning,
velocity 0, fade alpha to 0 (0.2 s)"] fadeOut --> respawn["at the spawn point, on the ground,
riding no gear, fade in (0.3 s)"] left -->|no| over["game_over_triggered = True
camera.follow(target=None)"] over --> sounds["play 'game_over'
_save_high_score()"] sounds --> clear["screen_shake.clear()"] clear --> fade["transition_to(game over,
FadeTransition(duration=1.0))"] end subgraph ENGINE_DEATH["Engine"] direction TB deathFadeTransition["FadeTransition
1 s fade"] deathGameOver["GameOverScene(final_score, high_scores)
final score, high scores"] deathFadeTransition --> deathGameOver end fade -.->|uses| deathFadeTransition While is_respawning , movement input is ignored and the pit check is skipped. After game over dt_tick returns early, so dying again changes nothing ( test_dying_after_game_over_changes_nothing ). Every floor's ground spans the playfield wall to wall and the walls stop the hitbox, so a fall lands on the ground: the pit check is a safety net, not a hazard the levels use. Since the ground check sweeps the fall, even a slow frame at terminal speed lands on the ground rather than dropping through it.
docs.title: Death, respawn and game over

docs.text: sounds.py defines seven SoundRecipe s (synthesized tones: oscillators, envelopes, filters, tremolo), played through one SoundBank(ALL_RECIPES) per floor. setup() calls sounds.prerender() , so no sound renders mid-frame (the clank would otherwise render on the slam frame). Sound When jump _try_jump , when the jump happens land The frame the feet touch down cog_pickup A cog is collected death A life is lost and lives remain game_over The last life is lost elevator_clank The elevator arrives (cue at progress 1.0) victory The Clock Face is won ( _win ): the clock tower's chime, struck bells (each a fundamental, its octave and a 2.76x overtone) climbing C5, E5, G5, then C6 ringing over a deep C3 The elevator's motor is not a recipe but a live voice: a low-passed sawtooth with tremolo, made with scene_manager.live_audio.create_voice(owner=transition) and retuned every frame of the ride ( ELEVATOR_MOTOR_* constants). SoundBank.play is a no-op when audio is unavailable.
docs.title: Sound

docs.text: State Where Lifetime player.score , player.lives Tinker Carried to the next floor through the constructor starting_player_score , starting_player_lives ClockworkKeepScene As the floor began (for replay_arguments ) floor_elapsed_time ClockworkKeepScene The floor's capped game time (the clock) game_over_triggered , riding_gear , supporting_platform ClockworkKeepScene Per floor ( game_over_triggered is also set by victory) High scores open_saves(app_name='clockwork-keep') , save high_scores On disk, across runs The game starts with 3 lives ( STARTING_LIVES ). At game over and at victory _save_high_score appends {'score': ..., 'floor': ...} to the saved scores list, keeps the 10 best (best first) and saves it; GameOverScene shows the list. A missing save loads as an empty list. In a replay the saves are a MemorySaveManager seeded from the recording, so a replayed game over never touches real high scores.
docs.title: State, score, lives and saves

docs.text: Feature How Clockwork Keep uses it World space and camera Every gameplay sprite is a WORLD sprite; the engine follows the player and positions everything Parallax layers One layer per floor; the clock layer is animated=True Physics PhysicsBody with gravity, acceleration and a bounds constraint Collision layers player and cogs , with trimmed (visible-pixel) hitboxes ActionMap Scancode bindings for every key, controller buttons for the gamepad Tweens The respawn fade out and in ( self.tweens.tween(...) ) Transitions ElevatorTransition (with on_update and add_cue ), FadeTransition to game over Shake and rumble Two SCREEN shakes on arrival, ELEVATOR_STOP_BOUNCE (BOUNCE, vertical) and ELEVATOR_STOP_RATTLE (NOISE), each with RumbleSettings(scale_with_strength=False) ; sustained rumble during the ride Sound synthesis Six recipes and one live voice Saves open_saves , SaveManager.load / save Built-in scenes PauseScene and GameOverScene Debug overlay No debug_draw of its own: the hitbox panel shows the player and cogs layers (platforms, unlayered, as full rects), the physics panel the Tinker's body, the camera panel the bounds Random streams The game draws no randomness itself; the NOISE rattle shake draws from the engine's shake stream, which --random-seed fixes Recording and replay --record-trace / --replay-trace work unchanged: the game reads input only through events and its ActionMap , time only from the dt it is given, and saves only through open_saves , so the doors serve all of it Scene starts replay_arguments() lets any floor be rebuilt for a playback scope The game does not set INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS , ships no bundled demo, and sets no PIXEL_SNAP_MODE (the default, NEAREST_HALF_UP ).
docs.title: Engine features it uses

docs.text: Clockwork Keep has both of the engine's golden checks: Golden trace ( tests/world/golden/clockwork_keep.jsonl.gz , checked by tests/world/test_golden_traces.py ): a 900-frame scripted run ( clockwork_keep_script in scripts/golden_inputs.py , fixed dt 1/60) recorded before the world-space change. It jumps for a cog, walks both ways, is placed on the first elevator at frame 330 (reaching it takes more platforming than the script holds), presses W at frame 350, rides frames 352-592, then walks and pauses (frames 740-790) on Gear Works. Each sprite's rect and visibility must match the baseline frame by frame; six ExpectedDifference entries explain every difference (engine culling, separate snapping of sprite and camera, and the pose fix's 2 px on frame 0 and during the ride). Golden replay ( src/games/clockwork-keep/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz , 532 frames): the same script's first 330 frames plus a controls tail (run right with Left Shift, jump with Space, interact away from an elevator, pause and resume with Esc / Space, quit with Q), recorded through the real engine loop by scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game clockwork_keep --frames 330 . The replay plugin replays it in a child process ( clockwork-keep --replay-trace ... --headless ) and fails unless it exits SUCCESS . tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py also checks that the golden replays exercise every control the game binds ( ClockworkKeepScene._create_action_map ); the gamepad bindings are listed as unexercised, because the dummy driver has no gamepad. Both harnesses drop the focus-lost event SDL's dummy driver posts at startup, which would otherwise auto-pause the game. Never re-record either baseline to make a change pass.
docs.title: Golden trace and golden replay

docs.text:
Drawing Fire Architecture # Drawing Fire is a stick-figure battle drawn in pencil on paper, the way a child draws a war, written as one of the engine's example games. Two armies face each other across a hilly field: the Pencil Platoon in pencil yellow on the left and the Graphite Brigade in graphite grey on the right, both straight off a school pencil. The computer plays every soldier. When one army is wiped out the winner is announced on the paper (when both fall at once, nobody wins), and a new battle starts on its own. At any moment one or two local players can join : press START (Enter on the keyboard), choose a side and a soldier, and fight as him. A player whose soldier dies takes over another soldier of his side, and a player who has had enough holds Back (Escape) to leave. Every new GlitchyGames game proves a new mechanic for the engine. Drawing Fire proves swatches : recolouring a sprite by palette swap, so one soldier sprite wears both armies' liveries (see Swatches ). This page explains how the game is built, for a developer who wants to understand it or write a game like it. Everything here comes from src/games/drawing-fire/src/drawing_fire/ , and the module docstrings there are the detailed reference. The design, with the full vision and the MVP's decisions, is plans/2026-10-25-drawing-fire-design.md . What comes after the MVP is entry 54 in plans/future-features.md . The game as it is # These are screenshots of the MVP. A battle the computer plays by itself. Each army's name, colour chip and soldier count are at the top. The ground is pencilled with hatching under it, and the sandbags are grey-washed bags: The winner, announced on the paper before the next battle starts: Joining. While a device has no seat, a sticky note invites it to press START (Enter on the keyboard). A player who presses it gets a card where he chooses a side (Random, Platoon or Brigade), then a soldier: Choosing a soldier: a pencil ring highlights one of the side's computer soldiers, LEFT and RIGHT move it, and START takes him: The debug seats view (F3): a tag over every soldier names his driver, and a panel lists each army's drivers and the latest joins, takeovers and leaves. Its last line, held: , names the keys and mouse buttons the game sees held this frame (from current_input() ), so a key the browser keeps from the game shows up missing while you hold it: Where it is going: concept art # These pictures are concept art from the brainstorm, not the game. They show the full vision: a battlefield wider than the screen, tunnels, planes and air drops, and bigger guns. None of this is in the MVP (see plans/future-features.md , entry 54). Running it # uv run drawing-fire # the console script (its member's pyproject.toml) uv run drawing-fire --debug-overlay # start with the debug seats view (F3 toggles it) uv run drawing-fire --random-seed 7 # another battlefield and other battles uv run drawing-fire --record-trace run.jsonl.gz # record the session uv run drawing-fire --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz # watch it again, exactly uv run python -m scripts.simulate_drawing_fire --seeds 20 # headless battles: lengths and winners nox -s browser -- drawing-fire # the browser build main() ( game.py ) is GameEngine(game=DrawingFireScene).start() . The scene adds no options of its own; all its options are the engine's. The battlefield fits the window (800x480 by default), and --random-seed decides the terrain, the sandbags and every soldier's choices. Controls # The keyboard and mouse count as one device, and each game controller as another. Nothing is bound in an ActionMap : players.py reads every control from the frame's polled input ( current_input() ), the keys by scancode, so a key is its physical position on every layout. Seats. Seats.update plays the joins, side and soldier choices and leaves ( Seats ). Drivers. In a battle, the computer decides an Intent (move, aim, fire) for every living soldier, a player's included, so the soldier's memory and random stream stay current and he is handed back cleanly. Then each playing player's device intent replaces his soldier's. The battle. Battle.step(dt, intents) applies every intent the same way, whoever drives the soldier: it moves soldiers (sandbags stop them), fires pistols that are ready, flies the bullets, and returns what happened. A SoldierKilled moves a player whose soldier it was to another soldier. The winner. When the battle is over ( Battle.over : an army is gone), the phase becomes VICTORY and the banner shows for VICTORY_SECONDS (3 s): the winner's name, or, when both armies fell in the same step ( Battle.winner is None), a draw's two lines, "Nobody wins!" and "Everybody loses!" ( DRAW_LINES ). The bullets still in flight are cleared and nobody is drawn mid-stride, so the picture holds still. Then start_battle() builds the next battle: new terrain, sandbags and soldiers from fresh seeded streams, and every joined player chooses a soldier again. Seats treat a draw as they treat a win. render(screen) draws it all from the model, straight onto the screen: the paper and ground (on the background, pencilled once per battle and blitted whole each frame), the sandbags, the fallen and then the standing soldiers, the bullets, the HUD, the seats' note, cards and highlight, and the banner. The numbers were tuned with the simulation (design section 4.7): Constant Value Meaning SOLDIER_HEALTH 6 Hits a soldier takes before he falls PISTOL_COOLDOWN 1.5 s Between a soldier's shots PISTOL_RANGE 420 px How far a bullet flies before it falls away (the computer fires only within it) BULLET_SPEED 600 px/s WALK_SPEED 60 px/s SANDBAG_HEIGHT , SANDBAG_WIDTH 34 px, 48 px A sandbag blocks walking while it stands SAND_PER_HIT 0.25 A sandbag loses sand per hit, sags, and is flattened at none MUZZLE_DISTANCE 12 px The muzzle is this far out from the chest; a bullet never hits a sandbag its shooter stood inside or within this distance of when he fired (his own cover: Bullet.ignored_sandbags ) With these, 200 seeded battles end 110 to 90 for the Platoon, lasting 47 s on average, and 1,000 end 555 to 445 (53 s on average), none of them drawn. Hills block bullets, so the computer neither stands nor fires until the ground leaves a clear line to its target. The computer driver # drivers.py turns the battle into an Intent for one soldier, as a person reads the screen. A soldier targets the nearest enemy (and keeps him unless another is nearer by TARGET_SWITCH_MARGIN ), advances until the enemy is within his own stand-off distance, takes cover behind a sandbag when the enemy is in range and in sight, shoots a sandbag that blocks his way (from SANDBAG_SHOT_DISTANCE , beyond his muzzle's reach, since his shots never hit a bag he stands by; nearer than that he first steps back), keeps his spacing from his friends, and fires when his pistol is ready, after a reaction delay, with an aim error held for the whole shot. A soldier crowded by a friend of higher priority walks on to get off his spot, but never past the enemy's front: within MELEE_PIXELS of it he steps back instead, so friends do not follow a player who walks through the enemy's line. All the computer's randomness (stand-off, reaction delay, aim error) comes from one random stream per soldier ( drawing_fire.soldier.. ), so a player taking a soldier over never shifts anyone else's randomness, and battles replay exactly. Seats: joining, dying and leaving # seats.py keeps every player's seat ( PlayerSeat : his name, P1 or P2, his device, his stage, his side and soldier). It reads ButtonEdges , never pygame, and its only randomness is its own stream, drawing_fire.seats . stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> ChoosingSide : START on a device with no seat ChoosingSide --> ChoosingSide : LEFT / RIGHT cycle Random, Platoon, Brigade ChoosingSide --> ChoosingSoldier : START (Random draws a side) ChoosingSoldier --> ChoosingSoldier : LEFT / RIGHT move the highlight ChoosingSoldier --> Playing : START takes the highlighted soldier Playing --> Playing : his soldier dies, another of his side is free
(drawn from the seats' stream) Playing --> Waiting : his soldier dies, none is free ChoosingSoldier --> Waiting : the battle is over, or no soldier is free Waiting --> ChoosingSoldier : the next battle starts Playing --> ChoosingSoldier : the next battle starts ChoosingSide --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged ChoosingSoldier --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged Playing --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged Waiting --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged Each device does at most one thing a frame, so the START that opens a seat never also confirms its side. The highlight starts on the free soldier nearest the middle of the field, passing over a soldier another chooser of the same side is on. It stays on its soldier by id while he moves. A player who leaves frees his name. His soldier goes back to the computer at once, or to a waiting player of his side. The seat log keeps the latest eight joins, takeovers and leaves with their game time, for the debug panel ( P1 START → PLATOON , P1 took soldier 7 , P1 died → soldier 1 , P1 left ). Swatches: the mechanic this game proves # The soldier sprite is drawn once, in the Pencil Platoon's livery. Its file lists the parts that can be recoloured, beside its palette: [swatches.livery.helmet] colors = [ "h" , "H" ] # the base colour, then its shades role = "primary" swatches.py reads these sets ( load_swatch_sets ), and a Scheme gives colours to the parts by role ( primary , secondary ) or by name. recolor_surface swaps them in by exact RGB: a part's base colour becomes the scheme's colour, and each shade keeps its brightness relative to the base, so the helmet's shadow comes out a darker yellow for the Platoon and a darker grey for the Brigade. RecoloredFrames builds each scheme's frames once and keeps them. The sprite file never changes. In the game, drawing.load_soldier_frames loads the frames with the engine's AnimatedSprite loader, scales them up by whole pixels (so the exact colours survive), adds mirrored copies for a soldier facing left, and draw_soldier asks for his army's livery ( ARMY_LIVERIES[soldier.side] ). A hand-drawn line wanders by wobble(x, y, salt) , a deterministic hash of where it is, never a random stream, so the same picture is drawn every frame and in every replay. Text is rendered once per content, fonts are made once. The colours are the paper ( PAPER_COLOR ), the pencil ( PENCIL_COLOR ), a light hatching under the ground, and the two armies' colours: pencil yellow (242, 194, 48) and graphite grey (125, 127, 133) . How it uses the engine # Engine feature How Drawing Fire uses it Game time and dt Movement, cooldowns, bullets and the victory countdown use the scene's dt (capped at MAX_FRAME_SECONDS , 0.05 s, after a hitch); the seat log uses game_time Random streams Terrain, sandbags, the seats and one stream per soldier per battle, all from random_stream (seeded from --random-seed , kept in recordings) Polled input Every control is read from current_input() (keys by scancode, the mouse, controller axes and buttons), never from pygame, so a replay serves the same input Sprite loading AnimatedSprite loads the soldier's frames; swatches recolour them Debug overlay DrawingFireScene.debug_draw(surface, camera) draws the seat tags and the seats panel when the overlay is on (F3) Recording and replay --record-trace and --replay-trace work as for every game; see below Browser build nox -s browser -- drawing-fire ( scripts/build_browser_bundle.py GAMES ). It has no touch layout yet (exempt in tests/test_browser_touch_controls.py until its dual-stick controls settle) Recording, replay and the golden replay # Everything that decides what happens runs on the frame's dt , the seeded streams and the polled input, so a --record-trace recording replays exactly with --replay-trace . The golden replay src/games/drawing-fire/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz was recorded through the real engine loop by scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game drawing_fire --frames 1600 . The keyboard plays the whole session ( drawing_fire_script ): Enter opens a seat at frame 30, the right arrow moves the side card to the Platoon and Enter confirms it, D and A move the soldier highlight and keypad Enter takes soldier 7 at frame 131. The player fires with the left mouse button (held, let go, held again), the mouse following the nearest enemy ( DrawingFireMouse ), walks right with D, steps back with the left arrow and A, then walks through the Brigade's line with the right arrow and stands there. He is shot down at frame 657 and takes over soldier 1, then dies and takes over again at frames 754 (soldier 6) and 840 (soldier 2). At frame 1232 soldier 2, the Platoon's last, falls: P1 waits, the Graphite Brigade wins, and three seconds later the next battle starts with P1 choosing a Platoon soldier again. He holds Escape (for LEAVE_HOLD_SECONDS and ten frames more) from frame 1500 and leaves at frame 1561. The controls tail ( drawing_fire_controls ) then quits with Q. With the tail, the fixture holds 1,614 frames. Because the game reads its controls from the polled input, which a posted event never changes in SDL, the recorder lays the input it posted over each live snapshot ( PostedPolledInput ), as a real keyboard and mouse would. It does so only for the games in POLLED_INPUT_GAMES (Drawing Fire alone), so every other game's re-recording keeps the snapshots it had. The replay serves the recorded snapshots. The soldiers, bullets and sandbags are drawn, not sprites, so a replay's sprite comparison sees none of the battle. Instead the scene posts an internal GAMEEVENT ( post_event ) for every soldier killed ( SOLDIER_KILLED_SUBTYPE : his id, side and driver) and every seat log entry ( SEAT_CHANGED_SUBTYPE : the change, the player, his soldier and the panel's text). The recording holds them, and a replay in which the battle plays out differently misses one and diverges ("missing internal event"). DrawingFireScene.setup() registers its own subtypes ( DRAWING_FIRE_EVENT_SUBTYPES ) with the scene manager, with a callback ( _take_marker ) that does nothing: they are markers for recordings. The game's own tests/test_drawing_fire_golden_replay.py checks that the fixture holds the player's death and takeover. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py checks that every control the game reads is exercised: its keys by scancode, the mouse's motion and left button, and Q. The controller's controls are excused ( UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS , NO_GAMEPAD_IN_THE_SESSION ), because the scripted session runs on the dummy driver, which has no gamepad. Drawing Fire is in GAMES_WITHOUT_A_PAUSE , so its replay is checked never to reach the pause screen instead of pausing and resuming. One limit, noted in plans/future-features.md entry 54: the fixture is about 185 KB, over the 100 KB the other games keep. The first frame holds every random stream's state (19 of them, twice), about 125 KB compressed on its own. The pytest plugin src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py replays the fixture in a child process ( drawing-fire --replay-trace ... --headless ), and the test fails unless it exits SUCCESS . Re-record the fixture only deliberately (the commands are in the script's docstring), never just to make a failing replay pass. A re-recording without the player's death and takeover fails the test above. Its package # Drawing Fire is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/drawing-fire/ (distribution drawing-fire , import package drawing_fire ). Its soldier sprite ships inside the package as package data ( drawing_fire/sprites/soldier.toml , read through the module's own path), so the member's wheel and its browser archive ( drawing_fire.zip ) hold it. How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages . docs.text: Drawing Fire is a stick-figure battle drawn in pencil on paper, the way a child draws a war, written as one of the engine's example games. Two armies face each other across a hilly field: the Pencil Platoon in pencil yellow on the left and the Graphite Brigade in graphite grey on the right, both straight off a school pencil. The computer plays every soldier. When one army is wiped out the winner is announced on the paper (when both fall at once, nobody wins), and a new battle starts on its own. At any moment one or two local players can join : press START (Enter on the keyboard), choose a side and a soldier, and fight as him. A player whose soldier dies takes over another soldier of his side, and a player who has had enough holds Back (Escape) to leave. Every new GlitchyGames game proves a new mechanic for the engine. Drawing Fire proves swatches : recolouring a sprite by palette swap, so one soldier sprite wears both armies' liveries (see Swatches ). This page explains how the game is built, for a developer who wants to understand it or write a game like it. Everything here comes from src/games/drawing-fire/src/drawing_fire/ , and the module docstrings there are the detailed reference. The design, with the full vision and the MVP's decisions, is plans/2026-10-25-drawing-fire-design.md . What comes after the MVP is entry 54 in plans/future-features.md .

docs.text: uv run drawing-fire # the console script (its member's pyproject.toml) uv run drawing-fire --debug-overlay # start with the debug seats view (F3 toggles it) uv run drawing-fire --random-seed 7 # another battlefield and other battles uv run drawing-fire --record-trace run.jsonl.gz # record the session uv run drawing-fire --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz # watch it again, exactly uv run python -m scripts.simulate_drawing_fire --seeds 20 # headless battles: lengths and winners nox -s browser -- drawing-fire # the browser build main() ( game.py ) is GameEngine(game=DrawingFireScene).start() . The scene adds no options of its own; all its options are the engine's. The battlefield fits the window (800x480 by default), and --random-seed decides the terrain, the sandbags and every soldier's choices.

seats.py keeps every player's seat ( PlayerSeat : his name, P1 or P2, his device, his stage, his side and soldier). It reads ButtonEdges , never pygame, and its only randomness is its own stream, drawing_fire.seats . stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> ChoosingSide : START on a device with no seat ChoosingSide --> ChoosingSide : LEFT / RIGHT cycle Random, Platoon, Brigade ChoosingSide --> ChoosingSoldier : START (Random draws a side) ChoosingSoldier --> ChoosingSoldier : LEFT / RIGHT move the highlight ChoosingSoldier --> Playing : START takes the highlighted soldier Playing --> Playing : his soldier dies, another of his side is free
(drawn from the seats' stream) Playing --> Waiting : his soldier dies, none is free ChoosingSoldier --> Waiting : the battle is over, or no soldier is free Waiting --> ChoosingSoldier : the next battle starts Playing --> ChoosingSoldier : the next battle starts ChoosingSide --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged ChoosingSoldier --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged Playing --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged Waiting --> [*] : BACK held a second, or unplugged Each device does at most one thing a frame, so the START that opens a seat never also confirms its side. The highlight starts on the free soldier nearest the middle of the field, passing over a soldier another chooser of the same side is on. It stays on its soldier by id while he moves. A player who leaves frees his name. His soldier goes back to the computer at once, or to a waiting player of his side. The seat log keeps the latest eight joins, takeovers and leaves with their game time, for the debug panel ( P1 START → PLATOON , P1 took soldier 7 , P1 died → soldier 1 , P1 left ).
docs.title: Seats: joining, dying and leaving

docs.text: The soldier sprite is drawn once, in the Pencil Platoon's livery. Its file lists the parts that can be recoloured, beside its palette: [swatches.livery.helmet] colors = [ "h" , "H" ] # the base colour, then its shades role = "primary" swatches.py reads these sets ( load_swatch_sets ), and a Scheme gives colours to the parts by role ( primary , secondary ) or by name. recolor_surface swaps them in by exact RGB: a part's base colour becomes the scheme's colour, and each shade keeps its brightness relative to the base, so the helmet's shadow comes out a darker yellow for the Platoon and a darker grey for the Brigade. RecoloredFrames builds each scheme's frames once and keeps them. The sprite file never changes. In the game, drawing.load_soldier_frames loads the frames with the engine's AnimatedSprite loader, scales them up by whole pixels (so the exact colours survive), adds mirrored copies for a soldier facing left, and draw_soldier asks for his army's livery ( ARMY_LIVERIES[soldier.side] ). Nothing in swatches.py names the game: it is written to move into src/glitchygames/sprites/ . What that would take is entry 55 in plans/future-features.md .
docs.title: Swatches: the mechanic this game proves

docs.text: Everything is drawn with pygame primitives onto the surface it is given, from the model. A hand-drawn line wanders by wobble(x, y, salt) , a deterministic hash of where it is, never a random stream, so the same picture is drawn every frame and in every replay. Text is rendered once per content, fonts are made once. The colours are the paper ( PAPER_COLOR ), the pencil ( PENCIL_COLOR ), a light hatching under the ground, and the two armies' colours: pencil yellow (242, 194, 48) and graphite grey (125, 127, 133) .
docs.title: The pencil look

docs.text: Everything that decides what happens runs on the frame's dt , the seeded streams and the polled input, so a --record-trace recording replays exactly with --replay-trace . The golden replay src/games/drawing-fire/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz was recorded through the real engine loop by scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game drawing_fire --frames 1600 . The keyboard plays the whole session ( drawing_fire_script ): Enter opens a seat at frame 30, the right arrow moves the side card to the Platoon and Enter confirms it, D and A move the soldier highlight and keypad Enter takes soldier 7 at frame 131. The player fires with the left mouse button (held, let go, held again), the mouse following the nearest enemy ( DrawingFireMouse ), walks right with D, steps back with the left arrow and A, then walks through the Brigade's line with the right arrow and stands there. He is shot down at frame 657 and takes over soldier 1, then dies and takes over again at frames 754 (soldier 6) and 840 (soldier 2). At frame 1232 soldier 2, the Platoon's last, falls: P1 waits, the Graphite Brigade wins, and three seconds later the next battle starts with P1 choosing a Platoon soldier again. He holds Escape (for LEAVE_HOLD_SECONDS and ten frames more) from frame 1500 and leaves at frame 1561. The controls tail ( drawing_fire_controls ) then quits with Q. With the tail, the fixture holds 1,614 frames. Because the game reads its controls from the polled input, which a posted event never changes in SDL, the recorder lays the input it posted over each live snapshot ( PostedPolledInput ), as a real keyboard and mouse would. It does so only for the games in POLLED_INPUT_GAMES (Drawing Fire alone), so every other game's re-recording keeps the snapshots it had. The replay serves the recorded snapshots. The soldiers, bullets and sandbags are drawn, not sprites, so a replay's sprite comparison sees none of the battle. Instead the scene posts an internal GAMEEVENT ( post_event ) for every soldier killed ( SOLDIER_KILLED_SUBTYPE : his id, side and driver) and every seat log entry ( SEAT_CHANGED_SUBTYPE : the change, the player, his soldier and the panel's text). The recording holds them, and a replay in which the battle plays out differently misses one and diverges ("missing internal event"). DrawingFireScene.setup() registers its own subtypes ( DRAWING_FIRE_EVENT_SUBTYPES ) with the scene manager, with a callback ( _take_marker ) that does nothing: they are markers for recordings. The game's own tests/test_drawing_fire_golden_replay.py checks that the fixture holds the player's death and takeover. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py checks that every control the game reads is exercised: its keys by scancode, the mouse's motion and left button, and Q. The controller's controls are excused ( UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS , NO_GAMEPAD_IN_THE_SESSION ), because the scripted session runs on the dummy driver, which has no gamepad. Drawing Fire is in GAMES_WITHOUT_A_PAUSE , so its replay is checked never to reach the pause screen instead of pausing and resuming. One limit, noted in plans/future-features.md entry 54: the fixture is about 185 KB, over the 100 KB the other games keep. The first frame holds every random stream's state (19 of them, twice), about 125 KB compressed on its own. The pytest plugin src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py replays the fixture in a child process ( drawing-fire --replay-trace ... --headless ), and the test fails unless it exits SUCCESS . Re-record the fixture only deliberately (the commands are in the script's docstring), never just to make a failing replay pass. A re-recording without the player's death and takeover fails the test above.
docs.title: Recording, replay and the golden replay

docs.text: Drawing Fire is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/drawing-fire/ (distribution drawing-fire , import package drawing_fire ). Its soldier sprite ships inside the package as package data ( drawing_fire/sprites/soldier.toml , read through the module's own path), so the member's wheel and its browser archive ( drawing_fire.zip ) hold it. How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages .

Mr. Muncher Architecture # Mr. Muncher is a maze chase set in a cinema, written as one of the engine's example games. You are Mr. Muncher, a red-and-white popcorn bucket. You eat the sprockets (small dots drawn like the holes along a film strip) to finish the reel , while four munchers (spiky fuzzballs) hunt you. A snack (a wrapped candy) gives you a sugar rush: for a few seconds the munchers turn dull blue and run away, and you can eat them. Each life is a take , a cleared maze is a CUT! , and the last life ends with THE END . This page explains how the game is built, for a developer who wants to understand it or write a game like it. Everything here comes from src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/ . The module docstrings there are the detailed reference. Running it # uv run mr-muncher # the console script (pyproject.toml [project.scripts]) uv run mr-muncher --debug-overlay # start with the debug overlay (F3 toggles it, F4 cycles panels) uv run mr-muncher --record-trace run.jsonl.gz # record the session uv run mr-muncher --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz # watch it again, exactly main() ( game.py ) is just GameEngine(game=MrMuncherScene).start() . The scene does not define an args() class method, so the game adds no options of its own (the engine logs Game does not implement arguments at INFO, shown with --log-level info ). All its options are the engine's. These are the ones that matter here: Option Effect on Mr. Muncher --resolution WxH (default 800x480 ) The maze is scaled to fit (see Layout ). At 800x480 the tiles are 20 px and the maze starts at x = 130 --target-fps The scene sets no TARGET_FPS , so the default is 60.01. Movement uses dt , so the frame rate does not change the game's speed --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} Which gamepad events reach the ActionMap (both families in auto ) --debug-overlay Shows each muncher's target tile (see Debug overlay ) --random-seed INT Seeds the frightened munchers' random turns --screen-shake-intensity , --rumble-intensity Scale the shake and rumble when a muncher catches you --live-voice-pool The projector sound needs one free live voice --record-trace , --replay-trace , --headless Recording and replay (see Engine features ) Controls # Every keyboard control is bound by scancode ( ActionMap.bind(scancode=...) ), so it is tied to a key's physical position and works the same on every keyboard layout. Input Action Where it is handled Arrow keys, or W A S D Steer. A direction pressed early is remembered and taken at the next junction ActionMap ( move_up , move_left , move_down , move_right ) Gamepad D-pad buttons Steer ActionMap ( CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_* ) Gamepad left stick, pushed past 0.5 Steer ActionMap ( CONTROLLER_AXIS_LEFTX/LEFTY , STICK_THRESHOLD ) Joystick hat (a pad whose D-pad is a hat) Steer, in the direction pushed on_joy_hat_motion_event (no ActionMap ) ESC, P, or gamepad Start Pause (not after the game is over) ActionMap ( pause ) Window loses focus Pause on_window_focus_lost_event Q Quit (on the press) ActionMap ( quit ), then scene_manager.quit() On the pause screen: SPACE or gamepad Start or A / ESC or gamepad B or Back / Q Resume (on release, after a press there) / quit (on the press) / quit (on release) The engine's PauseScene (both gamepad event layers) On the game-over screen: SPACE (release), gamepad A or Start / ESC or gamepad B or Back New game / quit MrMuncherGameOverScene and GameOverScene Note that ESC pauses the game, but ESC on the pause screen quits. The pause and game-over screens are engine scenes and check key codes ( event.key ), not scancodes. Its package # Mr. Muncher is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/mr-muncher/ (distribution mr-muncher , import package mr_muncher ), the first game moved out of the engine. How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages . Its recordings name it games.mr_muncher.game:MrMuncherScene , its golden replay is src/games/mr-muncher/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz , and its browser bundle ships mr_muncher.zip . Where things live # File What it holds src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/__init__.py Re-exports main (the mr-muncher console script's entry point) src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/maze.py MAZE_LAYOUT (the maze as text), tile characters, Direction , DIRECTION_PREFERENCE , Maze (a frozen pydantic model: tile questions, wrapping, distances) src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/levels.py LevelSettings and settings_for_level (the difficulty ramp), the scatter/chase schedule helpers, the frightened flash src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/actors.py MazeGeometry (tiles to pixels), MazeActor (tile-to-tile movement), Player , Muncher , MuncherProfile , Personality , MuncherState , ChaseSituation , chase_target src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/game.py MrMuncherScene (one reel: phases, scoring, input, saves, sound, drawing), Phase , GameProgress , MrMuncherGameOverScene , main src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/drawing.py Every picture, drawn with pygame primitives and cached with functools.cache : maze, bucket, munchers, eyes, sprockets, snacks, bonus reel, film-strip panels src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/scenery.py The sprites that never move ( Sprocket , Picture , SidePanel ) and the text helpers ( bundled_font , fitted_font , render_text ) src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/sounds.py The sound effects and jingles as synth SoundRecipe s src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/autopilot.py Autopilot , a bot that plays the game. The golden replay's script and the tests use it src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher.py The scene: game flow, scoring, input, saves, screens, whole games src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher_maze_and_actors.py The parts: maze, levels, actors, pictures, scenery, sounds, autopilot src/games/mr-muncher/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz The golden replay (2,072 frames) scripts/golden_inputs.py mr_muncher_script and MuncherSteering (the autopilot pressing arrow keys) scripts/record_scripted_session.py , scripts/golden_inputs.py The command that records the fixture (on the engine's scripted-session recorder, src/glitchygames/replay/tools/scripted_sessions.py ); mr_muncher_controls (the golden replay's controls tail) Scenes and how they switch # A game is a chain of scenes. Each reel is a new MrMuncherScene , built from a GameProgress (a frozen pydantic model holding the reel number, score, lives left and whether the extra life has been given). The scene keeps the progress it started with as starting_progress . In the diagram, the Engine box holds the engine's built-in PauseScene ; the Mr. Muncher box holds the game's own scenes ( MrMuncherGameOverScene extends the engine's GameOverScene , see Scene classes ). stateDiagram-v2 direction TB [*] --> Reel : GameEngine(game=MrMuncherScene) state "Mr. Muncher" as MrMuncherScenes { Reel : MrMuncherScene (reel n) NextReel : MrMuncherScene (reel n + 1)
same score and lives GameOver : MrMuncherGameOverScene
(extends the engine's GameOverScene) NewGame : MrMuncherScene (reel 1) } state "Engine" as EngineScenes { Pause : PauseScene } Reel --> Pause : ESC, P, Start or focus lost
next_scene = PauseScene Pause --> Reel : SPACE, Start or A released
(setup() runs again) Reel --> NextReel : CUT! then flash
next_scene = new scene NextReel --> Reel : the same flow Reel --> GameOver : THE END shown for 2.5 s
transition_to(..., FadeTransition(1 s)) GameOver --> NewGame : SPACE released, or A or Start
switch_to_scene Reel --> [*] : Q (scene_manager.quit()) Pause --> [*] : ESC, B, Back or Q GameOver --> [*] : ESC, B or Back Next reel : _go_to_next_level sets next_scene to a new MrMuncherScene with GameProgress(level + 1, score, lives, extra_life_awarded) . It does this only once (it checks that next_scene is still None ). Game over : _show_game_over_screen fades (1 s FadeTransition ) to MrMuncherGameOverScene . This screen shows the engine's GAME OVER layout (score and high score table) plus a headline, either NEW HIGH SCORE! Reel N or You reached reel N . resume() always starts a new game with switch_to_scene(MrMuncherScene(...)) , because the previous scene depends on how the screen was reached. Pause : the engine's PauseScene shows a frozen screenshot of the game. When play resumes, the scene's setup() runs again. That is why setup() shows the ready message only while the phase is still READY . Scene classes # Mr. Muncher's scenes are two classes in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/game.py : MrMuncherScene and MrMuncherGameOverScene . Scene and the built-in PauseScene and GameOverScene come from the engine ( glitchygames.scenes ). In the diagram, the Engine box is what every game gets; the Mr. Muncher box is what this game adds. Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class; dotted arrows are how the game uses an engine class. classDiagram direction TB namespace Engine { class Scene { next_scene transition_to(scene, transition) replay_arguments() } class PauseScene { the frozen game, dimmed SPACE or Start/A resumes it, ESC, B/Back or Q quits } class GameOverScene { score and high scores final_score, high_scores } } namespace MrMuncher { class MrMuncherScene { NAME = 'Mr. Muncher' VERSION = '2.0' MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05 starting_progress : GameProgress phase : Phase actions : ActionMap saves : SaveManager dt_tick(dt) render(screen) } class MrMuncherGameOverScene { level_reached : int setup() replay_arguments() resume() } } Scene <|-- PauseScene Scene <|-- GameOverScene Scene <|-- MrMuncherScene GameOverScene <|-- MrMuncherGameOverScene PauseScene <.. MrMuncherScene : _pause sets next_scene = PauseScene MrMuncherScene ..> MrMuncherGameOverScene : transition_to after THE END MrMuncherGameOverScene ..> MrMuncherScene : resume starts a new game Unlike PaddleSlap, MrMuncherScene names PauseScene itself: _pause sets next_scene = PauseScene(options=self.options) , except once the game is over. Phases inside a reel # Inside one scene, Phase decides what each frame does. _run_phase runs the current phase; each waiting phase moves on once phase_seconds (game time since the phase began) is up. Because the phase clocks run on game time, a paused game also pauses its countdowns. stateDiagram-v2 direction TB [*] --> READY READY : READY

THE END (2.5 s) READY --> PLAYING : time up (_start_playing) PLAYING --> MUNCHER_EATEN : touched a frightened muncher MUNCHER_EATEN --> PLAYING : time up (_resume_after_eating) PLAYING --> DYING : touched by a dangerous muncher DYING --> READY : lives left (take + 1) DYING --> GAME_OVER : last life (high score saved) PLAYING --> LEVEL_CLEAR : last sprocket eaten LEVEL_CLEAR --> [*] : next reel (next_scene) GAME_OVER --> [*] : fade to game-over screen The ready message ( _ready_message_text ) depends on the moment: Situation ready_seconds Message Cue sound New game (reel 1, score 0) 3.6 ( INTRO_READY_SECONDS ) 3 , 2 , 1 (2.8 s split three ways), then ACTION! countdown_beep for each number, then action A later life 2.0 ( READY_SECONDS ) TAKE n , then ACTION! action A later reel 2.0 REEL n , then ACTION! action The message is drawn again only when its text or colour changes ( message_shown ), and each cue plays once, when its text first appears. The maze # Layout as text # MAZE_LAYOUT is a tuple of strings, one per row of tiles: 27 columns by 24 rows. It is symmetric from left to right, every corridor is one tile wide, there are no dead ends, and every open tile can be reached from every other. The tests check all four properties. ########################### #o...........#...........o# #.####.#####.#.#####.####.# #.####.#####.#.#####.####.# T.........................T #.####.##.#######.##.####.# #......##....#....##......# #.####.#####.#.#####.####.# #.#....## ##....#.# #.#.##.## ###-### ##.##.#.# #...##. #HHHHH# .##...# ###.##.## #HHHHH# ##.##.### #......## #HHHHH# ##......# #.####.## ####### ##.####.# #.#....## ##....#.# #.#.##.#####.#.#####.##.#.# #...##.......#.......##...# #.####.#####.#.#####.####.# #o..##.......P.......##..o# ###.##.##.#######.##.##.### #......##....#....##......# #.##########.#.##########.# T.........................T ########################### Character Meaning Player may stand on it # Wall No . Sprocket (252 of them) Yes o Snack (4 of them) Yes space Empty corridor Yes T Tunnel mouth: munchers slow down here Yes H Inside the munchers' house No - The house door: munchers pass through it, the player never does No P Player start (an empty corridor tile) Yes Maze is a frozen pydantic model. Its validator rejects a layout that is not a rectangle or that does not have exactly one P . It knows nothing about pixels. Positions are in tile units : the centre of the tile in column c , row r is (c, r) , so an actor standing on a tile centre has whole-number coordinates. Tunnels. Maze.tile wraps columns, and treats rows outside the maze as wall. Only rows 4 and 22 are open at both edges, so they are the two wrapping tunnels. wrap_x moves an x that has gone more than half a tile past an edge to the other side. tile_distance measures the short way round, so two positions at opposite ends of a tunnel count as close. The house. The door is at (13, 9). house_entrance is the corridor tile above it (13, 8), where munchers leave and come back. house_centre is two tiles below the door (13, 11). Geometry. MazeGeometry ( actors.py ) holds tile_size , left and top , and converts a position in tiles to pixels ( pixel_centre ). maze_geometry ( game.py ) chooses the tile size. Grid movement and turn buffering # Both the player and the munchers are MazeActor s. They move only along corridors, and they choose a direction only when they stand exactly on a tile centre ( is_at_tile_centre : both coordinates are whole numbers). MazeActor.advance(distance=..., choose_direction=...) walks a distance from one tile centre to the next. Each time it reaches a centre, or starts on one, it calls choose_direction to decide the way on ( None means stop). When a step reaches a centre, the coordinate is rounded so it lands exactly on it. Because the walk goes centre to centre, a long frame cannot skip past a turn. The player's turn buffering ( Player.travel and _choose_direction ): wanted_direction is the way the player last asked for. Reversing happens at once , even between centres. If the wanted direction is the opposite of the current one, the player turns round on the spot. On each tile centre the player takes the wanted direction if it is open. Otherwise it goes straight on if it can, and stops against a wall if it cannot. The wanted direction stays remembered until a junction opens that way. A new life starts heading left with left wanted, as in the arcade game. How input sets wanted_direction ( _read_direction_input , at the start of each dt_tick ): a direction just pressed wins (if two are pressed in one frame, the first of up, left, down, right wins). If no direction was just pressed and the wanted direction's key was just released while another direction is still held, the held one becomes wanted, as with a held joystick. Releasing the last key keeps the wanted direction. Then actions.begin_frame() clears the frame's presses and releases. The munchers # There are four munchers ( muncher_profiles ). The chaser comes first in the list, because the flanker aims relative to it. Name Colour Personality Chase target Scatter corner Starts Chomper purple CHASER The player's tile (24, -3), top right Outside, above the door, roaming left Snapper green AMBUSHER 4 tiles ahead of where the player faces (2, -3), top left House centre Gnasher orange FLANKER The pivot 2 tiles ahead of the player, mirrored away from Chomper: 2 * pivot - chaser (26, 24), bottom right House, left seat Nibbles magenta SHY The player's tile while farther than 8 tiles from it, else its own corner (0, 24), bottom left House, right seat The scatter corners lie outside the maze, so a scattering muncher circles the block of walls nearest its corner. Choosing a turn # At each tile centre, a roaming muncher ( Muncher._choose_direction ): Never turns back by itself. The way it came is removed from the options; it is used only at a dead end, and this maze has none. Considers only open corridor tiles (the same test as the player's, so roaming munchers never walk back into the house). If frightened , picks one of the options at random from the seeded stream random_stream('mr_muncher.munchers') , so a replay makes the same choices. Otherwise it takes the option whose next tile is closest in a straight line ( tile_distance , tunnel-aware) to its target . On a tie the order is up, left, down, right ( DIRECTION_PREFERENCE , the arcade game's order). The target ( _target ): the house entrance for eyes, the scatter corner while scattering, chase_target(...) while chasing. The target is stored on muncher.target for the debug overlay. The munchers learn about the game through a ChaseSituation that the scene builds for each step: the player's tile and facing, Chomper's tile, and whether the munchers are chasing. Muncher state machine # MuncherState is where a muncher is in its life. Being frightened is a separate flag ( frightened ), because a muncher waiting in the house or walking out can be frightened too. stateDiagram-v2 direction TB [*] --> WAITING : reset() (house seat) [*] --> ROAMING : reset() (Chomper starts outside) WAITING : WAITING

target = chase_target() Frightened : Frightened
random turns (seeded stream) Scatter --> Chase : schedule phase ends (turns round) Chase --> Scatter : schedule phase ends (turns round) Scatter --> Frightened : snack eaten (turns round) Chase --> Frightened : snack eaten (turns round) Frightened --> Scatter : fright over (scatter phase) Frightened --> Chase : fright over (chase phase) } ROAMING --> EATEN : player touches it while frightened EATEN --> ENTERING : eyes reach the house entrance ENTERING --> LEAVING : reaches the house centre
(no longer frightened) State Movement Speed Can touch the player WAITING _bob : up and down 0.35 tiles around its seat house_speed No LEAVING _walk_out : across to the door's column, then up to the entrance house_speed Yes ROAMING advance through the corridors, turning as above tunnel_speed on a T tile, else frightened_speed if frightened, else hurry_speed (Chomper only, with few sprockets left), else muncher_speed Yes EATEN advance towards the house entrance eyes_speed No ENTERING _walk_in : down to the house centre eyes_speed No A change of mode turns every roaming muncher round . When the schedule's phase changes, or a snack starts a fright, the scene sets reverse_soon , and the muncher reverses on its next step, even between tile centres. This is the only time a muncher reverses. Scatter, chase and fright timing # The scene keeps three clocks per life, all in game time and all reset when a life starts ( _reset_actors ). _advance_timers advances them on every step: life_seconds decides when each muncher waiting in the house is released ( release_seconds , in house order: Snapper, Gnasher, Nibbles). mode_seconds drives the scatter/chase schedule. It stops while the munchers are frightened , so a fright does not use up a scatter phase. munchers_chase(schedule=..., elapsed_seconds=...) gives the mode: phases alternate scatter, chase, scatter, ..., starting with scatter, and after the last phase the munchers chase for good. mode_phase_index detects the change of phase that turns them round. frightened_seconds_left counts down a fright. When it reaches zero, _end_fright clears every muncher's frightened flag. A snack ( _start_fright ) frightens every muncher that is not eyes, resets the count of munchers eaten during this fright (which sets their points), and turns the roaming munchers round. Frightened munchers flash white and blue for the last 2 s of the fright (or all of it, if the fright is shorter), switching every quarter second ( frightened_is_flashing ). Levels and the difficulty ramp # settings_for_level(level) returns a frozen LevelSettings . Each reel is a little faster and meaner than the one before, up to reel 8 ( LAST_RAMP_LEVEL ); after that, every reel plays like reel 8. Speeds are in tiles per second. Setting Reel 1 Each reel adds From reel 8 on Player speed 7.5 +0.15 8.55 Muncher speed (fraction of the player's speed) 0.82 +0.018 (at most 0.95) 0.946 (8.09 tiles/s) Fright length 8.0 s -0.9 s (never below 2.0 s) 2.0 s Chomper hurries when this few sprockets are left 20 +5 55 Bonus reel points 100, 300, 500, 700, 1000, 2000, 3000, 5000 (reels 1 to 8) 5000 Scatter/chase schedule (s) 9, 15, 9, 15, 7, 20, 5, then chase 5, 20, 5, 20, 3, 30, 1, then chase (from reel 2) House release times (s) 0.5, 4.0, 8.0 0.5, 2.5, 5.0 (from reel 2) Other speeds are fixed fractions of the player's speed: frightened munchers 0.55, munchers on a tunnel tile 0.50, munchers moving in or out of the house 0.45, eyes 2.0. During a sugar rush the player is 1.1 times faster, and a hurrying Chomper is 1.08 times faster than the other munchers. Scoring, the bonus reel and lives # Event Points Also Sprocket 10 One of two crunch sounds, alternating Snack 50 Starts a fright ( sugar_rush sound) Frightened muncher 200, 400, 800, 1600 (doubling for each one eaten in the same fright) Everything stops for 0.75 s while the points show ( camera_flash sound). Mr. Muncher and the eaten muncher are hidden meanwhile Bonus film reel The reel's bonus_points Shown for 2 s ( eat_bonus sound) The bonus reel appears on the tile three rows below the house centre ( message_cell , where the messages show too) after the 70 th and the 170 th sprocket of a reel ( BONUS_SPROCKET_COUNTS ), and stays 9.5 s unless eaten. Extra life : one, the first time the score reaches 10,000 ( extra_life sound). The game starts with 3 lives, counting the one in play. Contact : a muncher touches the player when their centres are closer than 0.6 tiles ( CONTACT_DISTANCE_TILES , tunnel-aware). Only munchers that are roaming or leaving the house count. The first muncher found touching settles the step: it is eaten if frightened, otherwise the player is caught. High scores use the engine's saves: open_saves(app_name='mr-muncher') , save name high_scores , stored as {'scores': [{'score': ..., 'level': ...}, ...]} , best first, the best 10 kept. The game is added to the table when the last life is lost. The panel's HIGH SCORE is the larger of the best saved score and the current score. In a replay the saves are an in-memory sandbox seeded from the recording, so a replay never touches real saves. One frame # The engine runs dt_tick (logic) before it processes the frame's events, and update() (render phase) after positioning. Mr. Muncher does all its work in dt_tick and does not override update() . MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05 : after a hitch, such as dragging the window, logic advances at most 50 ms in one frame. In the diagram, the Engine box is the scene manager calling the scene; everything in the Mr. Muncher box is the game's own dt_tick . flowchart TB subgraph ENGINE_FRAME["Engine"] direction TB A["SceneManager: logic phase
