docs.title: PaddleSlap Architecture

docs.text: PaddleSlap is the smallest example game in GlitchyGames: two paddles, one or more balls, and no title screen. It is a two-player Pong in which the players share one score, the rally count (every paddle hit by any ball adds one), and the game ends when the last ball has left the court. Paddle hits can spawn more balls, so a long rally fills the court. It is the reference for a game built from the engine's ready-made parts: BallSprite and VerticalPaddle from glitchygames.game_objects , the collision manager's layers, ActionMap input, the save store, and the built-in pause and game-over scenes. It is also the engine's oldest regression subject: it has a golden trace, a golden replay and a bundled attract-mode demo. This page shows how it is put together, from its scenes down to one frame.
docs.title: PaddleSlap Architecture

docs.text: uv run paddleslap # one ball, extra balls spawned by paddle hits uv run paddleslap --balls 3 # start with three balls uv run paddleslap --ball-spawn-mode none # never spawn: a classic one-ball rally uv run paddleslap --random-seed 42 # the same serves, spawns and colours every run The game adds these options to the engine's own ( Game.args() ; the engine's options, such as --target-fps , --resolution and --input-mode , are in Argument System ): Option Default Meaning -b , --balls N 1 Balls on the court when the game starts --ball-spawn-mode MODE paddle_only When extra balls appear: paddle_only , wall_only , ball_only , frequent , rare , none (see Ball spawning ) -v , --version off Prints Paddle Slap 1.1 and exits before the game starts (argparse's version action) The game sets no TARGET_FPS and no MAX_FRAME_SECONDS , so it runs at the engine's default 60.01 FPS and its logic gets the raw frame time.
docs.title: Running it

docs.text: Action Player 1 (left) Player 2 (right) Paddle up W position, D-pad up, left stick up Up arrow, D-pad up, left stick up Paddle down S position, D-pad down, left stick down Down arrow, D-pad down, left stick down Gamepad the pad with instance id 0 the pad with instance id 1 Scene Key Effect Game Space position (on release) Pause Game Q or Esc (on release) Quit (the base Scene posts QUIT ) Pause Space , or a gamepad's Start or A (press, then release) Resume Pause Esc or a gamepad's B or Back (on press), Q (on release) Quit Pause window focus regained (after 0.5 s paused) Resume Game over Space , or a gamepad's Start or A (press, then release) New game Game over Esc or a gamepad's B or Back (on press), Q (on release) Quit Game over nothing for 10 s of game time Play the attract-mode demo; any key or button ends it The paddle and pause keys are bound by scancode (a physical key position, the same place on every layout: AZERTY players press Z / S ). The quit keys and the pause and game-over screens' Space and Esc are the engine's built-in scenes' key codes . Gamepads only move paddles: the pause and game-over screens answer the keyboard only (a button press on the game-over screen just restarts its idle wait).
docs.title: Controls

docs.text:
PaddleSlap has two scenes of its own and one built in. Scene Module Role Game src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py The court: paddles, balls, collisions, rally count, high scores PauseScene src/glitchygames/scenes/builtin_scenes/pause_scene.py The engine's pause screen: the game's last frame dimmed with PAUSED over it PaddleSlapGameOverScene src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py GameOverScene (score, top 5 high scores) plus the attract-mode demo, and a resume that always starts a new Game In the diagram, the Engine box holds what the engine provides (its pause screen and the playback scope the demo runs in); the PaddleSlap box holds the game's own scenes. stateDiagram-v2 direction TB state "PaddleSlap" as GAME_SCENES { state "Game" as Game state "PaddleSlapGameOverScene
(extends the engine's GameOverScene)" as GameOver state "switch_to_scene(Game(options))" as NewGame } state "Engine" as ENGINE_SCENES { state "PauseScene" as PauseScene state "Demo (playback scope)" as Demo } [*] --> Game : GameEngine(game=Game).start() Game --> PauseScene : Space released
Scene.pause() sets next_scene PauseScene --> Game : Space, Start or A, or focus regained
resume() switches back to the same Game Game --> GameOver : last ball gone
_show_game_over() sets next_scene GameOver --> Demo : 10 s of game time idle
play_recording(then=self) Demo --> GameOver : any key or button,
or the demo's end GameOver --> NewGame : Space, Start or A
resume() NewGame --> Game Game --> [*] : Q or Esc PauseScene --> [*] : Q or Esc GameOver --> [*] : Q, Esc, B or Back Pause and game over switch at the end of the frame. Both set next_scene instead of switching at once, so the scene manager switches after the frame renders. Pausing during event processing would otherwise freeze the previous frame's picture (the comment on Scene.pause() ). PauseScene shows previous_scene.screenshot ; resume() switches back to the same Game object, so the rally goes on where it was. A new game is always a Game . GameOverScene.resume() restarts the type of the scene manager's previous_scene , which a playback scope can change (BUGS.md #81), so PaddleSlapGameOverScene.resume() names Game explicitly. Rebuilding the game-over screen. PaddleSlapGameOverScene.replay_arguments() returns final_score and a copy of high_scores , so a recording that starts on this screen can rebuild it (scene starts, in Gameplay Recording and Replay ).
docs.title: Scenes

docs.text: PaddleSlap has no title screen (a game starts serving at once), so its idle screen is the game-over screen. PaddleSlapGameOverScene.dt_tick compares its game_time with idle_since_game_time ; after GAME_OVER_IDLE_SECONDS (10.0) it plays the bundled recording PADDLESLAP_DEMO_PATH ( src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz , package data) with SceneManager.play_recording(path=..., then=self) . In the diagram, the PaddleSlap box is the game's own screen and the Engine box is what plays the demo; the player is outside both. sequenceDiagram participant Player box rgb(255,243,224) PaddleSlap participant GO as PaddleSlapGameOverScene end box rgb(232,238,255) Engine participant SM as SceneManager participant PB as Playback scope end loop each frame SM->>GO: dt_tick(dt) GO->>GO: idle for 10 s of game_time? end Note over Player,GO: a key or button down restarts the idle wait GO->>SM: play_recording(then=self) Note over GO: the idle wait restarts SM->>PB: start at the next frame (exit_on_input) PB->>PB: rebuild Game, play 450 frames Player->>PB: any press ends it (consumed) PB->>SM: back to the game-over screen Note over GO: its game_time stood still meanwhile The demo is an ordinary recording played in a playback scope: real input reaches only its exit check, saves are a sandbox, and the live game-over screen is stashed, not cleaned up. The press that ends a demo never reaches the game-over screen, so starting a new game after a demo takes a second press (the class docstring). A demo that cannot play is logged at WARNING ("No demo: ...") and nothing starts. A divergence ends it with a WARNING demo diverged: ... .
docs.title: The attract-mode demo

docs.text: PaddleSlap is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/paddleslap/ (distribution paddleslap , import package paddleslap ). How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages . PaddleSlap is one module, so Game is defined in the package itself ( paddleslap/__init__.py ): its recordings name it games.paddleslap:Game , which a Game defined in a submodule would change. Its golden replay is src/games/paddleslap/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz , its bundled demo ships inside the package ( src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz , package data), its golden trace stays with the engine's trace tests ( tests/world/golden/paddleslap.jsonl.gz ), and its browser bundle ships paddleslap.zip .
docs.title: Its package

docs.text: PaddleSlap's own code is two classes in src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py : Game and PaddleSlapGameOverScene . Everything else it uses comes from the engine: Scene and the built-in PauseScene and GameOverScene ( glitchygames.scenes ), Sprite ( glitchygames.sprites ), and the paddles and balls of the engine's game-object library ( glitchygames.game_objects ). In the diagrams, the Engine box is what every game gets; the PaddleSlap box is what this game adds. Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class; dotted arrows are how the game uses an engine class.
docs.title: Classes

docs.text: classDiagram direction TB namespace Engine { class Scene { next_scene pause requests a PauseScene } class PauseScene { the frozen game, dimmed SPACE or Start/A resumes it, ESC or B/Back quits } class GameOverScene { score and high scores SPACE or Start/A restarts, ESC or B/Back quits } } namespace PaddleSlap { class Game { NAME = 'Paddle Slap' VERSION = '1.1' player1, player2 : VerticalPaddle balls : list of BallSprite rally_count : int p1_actions, p2_actions, pause_actions : ActionMap saves : SaveManager ball_spawn_mode : BallSpawnMode flags dt_tick(dt) args(parser) } class PaddleSlapGameOverScene { idle_since_game_time : float dt_tick(dt) replay_arguments() resume() } } Scene <|-- PauseScene Scene <|-- GameOverScene Scene <|-- Game GameOverScene <|-- PaddleSlapGameOverScene Game ..> PauseScene : SPACE calls the inherited pause Game ..> PaddleSlapGameOverScene : next_scene when the last ball is gone PaddleSlapGameOverScene ..> Game : resume starts a new Game Game never names PauseScene : its pause action calls Scene.pause() , which it inherits, and that requests the engine's PauseScene for the end of the frame. PaddleSlap's game-over screen extends the engine's, adding the attract-mode demo after an idle wait and always restarting a new Game (the engine's resume() restarts whatever scene came before, BUGS.md #81).
docs.title: Scenes

docs.text: classDiagram direction TB namespace Engine { class Sprite class BasePaddle { _move : Vertical or Horizontal _sub_pixel_x, _sub_pixel_y } class VerticalPaddle { up() down() stop() dt_tick(dt): move, then clamp } class HorizontalPaddle class BallSprite { COORDINATE_SPACE = WORLD world_x, world_y : float speed : Speed serve_settings, speed_up_settings on_paddle_collision, on_wall_bounce dt_tick(dt) handle_paddle_collision(paddle) } } namespace PaddleSlap { class GameSprites["Game"] { creates the paddles and balls sets the balls' callbacks resolves collisions in dt_tick } } Sprite <|-- BasePaddle BasePaddle <|-- VerticalPaddle BasePaddle <|-- HorizontalPaddle Sprite <|-- BallSprite VerticalPaddle <.. GameSprites : player1, player2 BallSprite <.. GameSprites : balls PaddleSlap defines no sprite classes: both paddles are the engine's VerticalPaddle ( src/glitchygames/game_objects/paddle.py ) and every ball is its BallSprite ( src/glitchygames/game_objects/ball.py ). The game creates them, wires the balls' callbacks ( on_paddle_collision , on_wall_bounce ) to its rally count and sounds, and resolves collisions in Game.dt_tick . HorizontalPaddle is not used by PaddleSlap; it is shown because it shares BasePaddle .
docs.title: Sprites

docs.text: Sprite Space Size and image Who writes rect VerticalPaddle ×2 Screen (no COORDINATE_SPACE ) 20×100 white rectangle; left at x = 0, right at x = screen width − 20, vertically centred The paddle itself: dt_tick rounds its float _sub_pixel_y into rect.y , then clamps it to the screen (stopping it at an edge) BallSprite World ( CoordinateSpace.WORLD ) 20×20 image with colour key 0 and a filled circle of radius 5 in the middle; colour set through the color property, which redraws the circle The engine: each frame position_world_sprites writes rect from the snapped world_x / world_y The camera never moves. Game sets no follow target and no camera_target() , so the camera stays at the origin: world and screen coordinates are the same and the balls are drawn exactly where their logic left them ( TestWorldBallsInTheFrame in tests/world/test_frame_integration.py ). The balls are world sprites anyway, so the engine is the only writer of their rect : game logic reads world_x / world_y , drawn_center() or the collision rect, never rect (which holds where the ball was last drawn). Pixel snapping. The ball's own pixel_snap_mode (default NEAREST_HALF_UP , the scene's default too) rounds its sub-pixel position for drawing and for collision alike. Background. The court is BLACK , named on purpose: a scene that sets no background shows the engine's test pattern. Dirty rendering. All sprites live in one pygame.sprite.LayeredDirty ( all_sprites ). The ball sets dirty = 2 (always redrawn); paddles set dirty = 1 every tick. Pose. Neither sprite changes its image with its state (a ball's image changes only when its colour is set), so the pose rule has nothing to order here. Collision resolution, the other half of that rule, runs in dt_tick (below).
docs.title: Sprites and how they are drawn

docs.text: The collision manager has two layers, balls and paddles (the debug overlay's hitbox panel draws them). Hitboxes are the default visible-pixel trim ( src/glitchygames/collision/bounds.py ): A ball's hitbox is its visible circle's 10×10 box , offset (5, 5) from the drawn position, not its 20×20 image. BallSprite._visible_rect() returns that box with its offset, and every ball test uses it: walls, paddles and other balls meet the circle the players see. A paddle's hitbox is its whole 20×100 rectangle.
docs.title: Hitboxes

docs.text: The engine's frame order is in the Bitmappy page and CLAUDE.md . What PaddleSlap does inside it (the PaddleSlap box is the game's one scene class; the Engine box is the engine's scene manager, game objects and collision manager): sequenceDiagram box rgb(255,243,224) PaddleSlap participant G as Game end box rgb(232,238,255) Engine participant SM as SceneManager participant P as VerticalPaddle x2 participant B as BallSprite (each) participant CM as CollisionManager end SM->>G: dt_tick(dt) G->>G: _process_paddle_input() G->>P: up() / down() / stop() G->>P: dt_tick(dt): move, write rect.y, clamp to the screen G->>B: dt_tick(dt) B->>B: move, wall bounce, kill() past an edge G->>G: _resolve_collisions() G->>CM: check_overlap('balls', 'paddles') CM->>G: _on_ball_paddle_collision(ball, paddle) G->>B: handle_paddle_collision(paddle) B->>G: on_paddle_collision(ball): rally, spawn G->>CM: check_overlap('balls', 'balls') CM->>G: _on_ball_ball_collision(ball1, ball2) G->>G: playable rule, spawns G->>G: drop dead balls, game over? SM->>G: event handlers feed the ActionMaps SM->>SM: position the balls SM->>G: update() (render phase) SM->>SM: draw, present, pace Logic before events. dt_tick runs before the frame's events are pumped, so it reads the held state the ActionMaps reached at the end of the previous frame; a press shows up in the next frame's dt_tick . Collisions in dt_tick , after every sprite moved. The engine positions the balls after dt_tick and before update() renders, so a bounce, or a ball spawned this frame, is drawn this frame (the comment in Game.dt_tick ). update() resolves nothing ( test_update_resolves_no_collisions ). A dead ball stays in the balls layer until _resolve_collisions removes it , so _on_ball_paddle_collision skips balls that are no longer alive() . The paddle's screen clamp runs in its dt_tick . A paddle moved past the top or bottom edge is clamped (and stopped) in the same dt_tick , so this frame's collisions see it on screen (the pose rule keeps update() for visual work; HorizontalPaddle clamps the same way).
docs.title: One frame

docs.text: BallSprite._handle_boundary_collisions bounces the ball off the top and bottom walls only (PaddleSlap constructs every ball with bounce_top_bottom=True, bounce_left_right=False ). A wall counts as hit when the visible box touches it while the ball moves toward it , so a ball still touching a wall the frame after a bounce does not bounce again. A hit flips the vertical speed, plays the bounce sound, applies a WALL_BOUNCE speed-up if configured (PaddleSlap's is not) and calls on_wall_bounce . _keep_inside_playfield then mirrors any overshoot back inside. A ball whose visible box is entirely past the left or right edge calls kill() : that is a score.
docs.title: Ball versus wall

docs.text: The collision manager pairs overlapping collision rects (an AABB broad phase), and BallSprite.handle_paddle_collision(paddle) does the exact test and the response: Circle against rectangle. The ball is the circle inscribed in its visible box; the nearest point of the paddle rectangle to its centre must be within the radius (touching counts). Otherwise nothing happens. Which face. _entered_paddle_from_left looks at where the visible box was before this frame's move ( speed.x × the last tick's dt back). If it was clear of the paddle on one side, the ball came in from that side, even when a long frame carried its centre past the paddle's centre; if it already overlapped, the side of the paddle's centre the ball's centre is on decides. Response. The ball is placed with its visible edge flush against that face, its horizontal speed points away from the paddle, the paddle's slap sound plays, a PADDLE_BOUNCE speed-up is applied, the speed is clamped to max_speed , and on_paddle_collision(ball) is called. PaddleSlap's callback counts the rally hit and may spawn a ball.
docs.title: Ball versus paddle

docs.text: _handle_ball_collisions ticks the per-pair cooldowns, then asks the collision manager for overlapping balls / balls pairs. _on_ball_ball_collision handles each pair: Step Method What it does 1 cooldown check A pair that collided in the last 10 frames (either order) is skipped 2 _calculate_ball_distance Centre distance of the two collision rects; they collide within the sum of the half widths 3 separating check Skipped if the balls are moving apart and no longer overlap 4 _apply_elastic_collision Equal-mass elastic exchange: swap the velocity components along the collision normal, keep the tangential ones (momentum and kinetic energy conserved) 5 _cap_ball_speeds Each ball's speed capped at 500 px/s 6 _separate_overlapping_balls Move both balls apart along the normal (by at least 3 px in total, at least 1 px on each significant axis), in world_x / world_y 7 record Cooldown of 10 frames for the pair; the pair is kept for the two steps below After the pass, two game rules apply to every pair that collided this frame: _keep_collided_balls_playable : exact physics can leave a ball almost stopped, almost vertical (it bounces between the walls and never reaches a paddle) or flat (it slides along a wall). The ball's angle from horizontal is moved into its ServeSettings band (15° to 60°) and its speed raised to at least the serve speed, keeping each component's sign (a zero component points away from the partner). This is deliberately not physics and not part of _apply_elastic_collision , whose physics the collision tests check. _spawn_new_balls_for_ball_collisions : one spawn attempt per pair, if ball-ball hits are a spawn trigger; the speed check uses the pair's faster ball. It runs outside the collision manager's pass, so spawned balls never join it.
docs.title: Ball versus ball

docs.text: Setting Value Used by PADDLESLAP_SERVE ServeSettings() : 250 px/s, 15° to 60° from horizontal, either side, either vertical direction, 50 px margin Opening balls ( reset() in the constructor picks a random position and serve) PADDLESLAP_SPAWN_SERVE ServeSettings(speed=150.0) Spawned balls in a mode with RANDOM_SPEED ( serve() keeps the position the game chose) fixed spawn speed Speed(250.0, 125.0) Spawned balls in a mode without RANDOM_SPEED (no listed mode) PADDLESLAP_SPEED_UP PADDLE_BOUNCE trigger, LOGARITHMIC curve, BOTH axes, multiplier 1.15, max_speed 500 px/s Every ball The logarithmic curve gives big early boosts that taper off, s0 × (1 + 0.15 × ln(1 + n)) after n paddle hits, and scaling both axes keeps the angle the paddle set. Paddles move at 400 px/s.
docs.title: Serves and speed-ups

docs.text:
BallSpawnMode ( src/glitchygames/game_objects/ball.py ) is a set of bit flags: triggers (which events may spawn), conditions (cooldown, speed check, random position, speed and colour) and frequency (the cooldown length). --ball-spawn-mode picks one combination: Option Triggers Cooldown Other flags paddle_only (default) paddle hit 2.0 s speed check, random position, speed and colour wall_only wall bounce 2.0 s as above ball_only ball-ball hit 2.0 s as above frequent all four (paddle, wall, ball, score) 0.5 s as above rare paddle hit 5.0 s as above none none the rally is still counted Every trigger goes through _spawn_new_ball_on_trigger , so all triggers share one cooldown and one speed check. In the diagram, the Engine box is the engine's BallSprite reporting paddle hits and wall bounces through its callbacks; the PaddleSlap box is the game's spawn rule in Game (which serves each new ball with the engine's BallSprite.serve() ): flowchart TB subgraph ENGINE_SPAWN["Engine"] direction TB ballcallback["BallSprite calls on_paddle_collision
or on_wall_bounce"] end subgraph GAME_SPAWN["PaddleSlap"] direction TB gametrigger["Game._resolve_collisions:
ball-ball hit or score"] trigger["_spawn_new_ball_on_trigger(trigger, ball)"] named{"Is it one of the
mode's triggers?"} skip1["No spawn"] cooldown{"COOLDOWN_ENABLED and
game_time - last spawn
under the cooldown?"} skip2["No spawn"] speed{"SPEED_CHECK_ENABLED and
the triggering ball faster
than 1000 px/s?"} skip3["No spawn"] spawn["_spawn_new_ball()"] place["Position: 10 tries for a spot
at least 100 px from every ball
(the last try if none is clear)"] serve["Speed: the engine's serve() at 150 px/s
Colour: from the colour stream"] join["Added to balls, all_sprites
and the 'balls' layer"] end ballcallback --> trigger gametrigger --> trigger trigger --> named named -- no --> skip1 named -- yes --> cooldown cooldown -- yes --> skip2 cooldown -- no --> speed speed -- yes --> skip3 speed -- no --> spawn spawn --> place place --> serve serve --> join The cooldown counts Scene.game_time , so it stops while the game is paused or behind the game-over screen ( test_spawn_cooldown_counts_game_time_only ). A score spawns before the game-over check, so in frequent mode the last ball scoring brings a replacement (when the cooldown and speed check allow it) instead of ending the game. Each new ball is connected to the same paddle-hit and wall-bounce callbacks, so spawned balls spawn too.
docs.title: Ball spawning

docs.text:
Each player has an ActionMap ( src/glitchygames/input/action_map.py ) with up and down ; a third holds pause . _create_action_maps binds, per player, a scancode, a D-pad button and the left stick's vertical axis at a ±0.3 threshold, filtered to the gamepad with instance id 0 (player 1) or 1 (player 2). The keyboard bindings have no instance filter. In the diagram, the Engine boxes are the engine's event dispatch (top) and its ActionMap , VerticalPaddle and base Scene (bottom); the PaddleSlap box is what Game 's handlers and dt_tick add between them: flowchart TB subgraph ENGINE_INPUT_DISPATCH["Engine"] direction TB events["Event dispatch: on_key_down/up_event,
on_controller_button/axis_*_event,
on_joy_button/axis_*_event"] end subgraph GAME_INPUT["PaddleSlap"] direction TB feed["Game feeds each event to the ActionMaps
(keys: all three, gamepad: the two players')"] pause{"Game.on_key_up_event:
pause just released?"} tick["Next frame, Game.dt_tick:
begin_frame(), then reads the held state"] end subgraph ENGINE_INPUT_PARTS["Engine"] direction TB state["ActionMap held state
(held, just pressed, just released)"] paddle["VerticalPaddle: up(), down() or stop()"] pausecall["Scene.pause()"] base["Scene.on_key_up_event
(Q or Esc quits)"] end events --> feed feed --> pause feed -- handle_event --> state tick -- "is_held('up') / is_held('down')" --> state tick --> paddle pause -- yes --> pausecall pause -- "not a pause key" --> base Movement is frame-driven. Handlers only update the ActionMaps; the paddles are moved by _process_paddle_input at the top of dt_tick , from the held state. Input mode. The ActionMaps take the engine's --input-mode (default auto : a mapped pad's controller events and any other device's joystick events, each press once). PaddleSlap handles both families, so a pad works in every mode. Instance ids, not player slots. SDL numbers devices in the order they appear, so the first pad connected drives the left paddle; a pad that is unplugged and plugged back in gets a new instance id and no longer matches its binding. Key repeat. PaddleSlap leaves SDL's key repeat off: movement reads held state and pause acts on the release, so nothing needs repeated key-downs (they would only fill event batches and recordings). Polling. PaddleSlap never polls pygame: everything it knows about input comes through events, which recordings hold, so a replay serves the same input.

docs.text: rally_count counts paddle hits by any ball; it is the game's only score, shared by both players. _spawn_new_ball_with_speed_check counts the hit whatever the spawn mode. At game over, _save_high_score loads the high_scores slot of the paddleslap save store ( open_saves(app_name='paddleslap') ), appends the rally, keeps the ten best (best first) and saves it. Live, that is high_scores.json in the platform's save directory ( ~/Library/Application Support/paddleslap/ on macOS, ~/.local/share/paddleslap/ on Linux, %APPDATA%\paddleslap\ on Windows). The game-over screen shows the final score and the top five. In a replay or a demo the store is a MemorySaveManager seeded from the recording, so the real high scores are never touched (the recordings start from an empty paddleslap store).
docs.title: Score and saves

docs.text: Feature How PaddleSlap uses it Random streams Serves draw from ball.serve ( SERVE_RANDOM_STREAM ), spawn positions from paddleslap.spawn , ball colours from paddleslap.colors : separate streams, so a colour draw never moves where the next ball spawns. --random-seed fixes them all Scene.game_time The spawn cooldown and the game-over idle wait Collision layers balls and paddles , check_overlap for the broad phase World space The balls (identity camera); the paddles stay screen space Save store High scores ( open_saves ) Built-in scenes PauseScene , GameOverScene Playback scope The attract-mode demo ( play_recording ) Debug overlay F3 and F4 work as in every game; the hitbox panel shows the two layers. The ball keeps speed , not a physics body, so the physics panel has nothing to draw Not used Screen shake, rumble, live synth voices, instant replay, ghosts, camera follow

It pauses with Space at frame 450 and resumes at frame 510. The golden replay then adds the controls tail ( paddleslap_controls ): Q and Esc pressed and released, so the recording ends on the game's own QUIT and a replay in which either key no longer quits diverges. Re-record only deliberately, after finding out why a replay diverged (the commands are in the docstring of scripts/record_scripted_session.py ). Replay performance for both recordings is in Replay Performance .

docs.text: glitchygames API Reference # glitchygames.color glitchygames.color provides color utilities like palettes, helpers to do color conversion, etc... glitchygames.engine The glitchygames.engine module handles game initialization, event routing, minimal event loop that calls into the active scene's update method. To start your game, pass your main Scene class to the engine. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Bitrot Adventures.""" import argparse import logging import pathlib import pygame from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine from glitchygames.scenes import Scene # Instantiate a logger called "game" to enable glitchygames # logging module. This is optional, but recommended. LOG = logging . getLogger ( 'game' ) # Think of a scene as an encapsulated pygame screen. # # Each scene can handle its own events, update its own # state, and draw its own graphics. # # The engine will handle switching between scenes # and passing events to the current scene. # # The engine will also handle drawing the current # scene to the screen. class BitrotAdventures ( Scene ): """Draws a pixel to the screen""" NAME = 'Bitrot Adventures' VERSION = '0.0.0' def __init__ ( self , options ): super () . __init__ ( options = options ) # This is called by glitchygames.GameEngine before # the class is instantiated. # # Note that GameEngine defines a few command line # options that are intended to be common across all # games, so it's worth checking your game with --help # before adding new options to ensure that you haven't # clobbered an existing option. @classmethod def args ( cls , parser : argparse . ArgumentParser ): """Game specific command line arguments.""" parser . add_argument ( '-s' , '--some-game-specific-option' , help = 'foo help' ) return parser def main (): # Note that the Scene (BitrotAdventures) is # passed in uninitialized - the engine # will initialize it for you. GameEngine ( game = BitrotAdventures , icon = '/path/to/icon' ) . start () if __name__ == '__main__' : main () When we run ./bitrotadventures.py with the -h flag, we can see our command line option, along with options the engine and scene manager provide to us: $ ./bitrotadventures.py -h pygame-ce 2 .5.8 ( SDL 2 .32.10, Python 3 .14.8 ) usage: Bitrot Adventures version 0 .0.0 [ -h ] [ -f TARGET_FPS ] [ --fps-log-interval-ms FPS_LOG_INTERVAL_MS ] [ -w | --windowed | --no-windowed ] [ -r RESOLUTION ] [ --use-gfxdraw ] [ --update-type { update,flip }] [ --timer-backend { auto,fast,pygame }] [ --sleep-granularity-ns SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS ] [ --windows-timer-1ms ] [ --log-timer-jitter ] [ --perf-trim-percent PERF_TRIM_PERCENT ] [ --fps-histogram { equal-range,target-relative }] [ --debug-overlay | --no-debug-overlay ] [ --debug-events ] [ --record-trace PATH ] [ --replay-trace PATH ] [ --replay-fps { recorded,real }] [ --audit | --no-audit ] [ --compare-processing ] [ --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT ] [ --replay-pause-at-frame N ] [ --rebaseline NEW ] [ --replay-digest PATH ] [ --random-seed RANDOM_SEED ] [ --screen-shake-intensity SCREEN_SHAKE_INTENSITY ] [ --rumble-intensity RUMBLE_INTENSITY ] [ --live-voice-pool LIVE_VOICE_POOL ] [ --default-background { test-pattern,channel-3 }] [ --video-driver { cocoa,offscreen,dummy }] [ --headless ] [ --input-mode { auto,joystick,controller }] [ --font-name FONT_NAME ] [ --font-size FONT_SIZE ] [ --font-bold ] [ --font-italic ] [ --font-antialias ] [ --font-dpi FONT_DPI ] [ --font-system { pygame,freetype }] [ -l { debug,info,warning,error,critical }] [ --no-unhandled-events ] [ -p ] [ -s SOME_GAME_SPECIFIC_OPTION ] options: -h, --help show this help message and exit Graphics Options: -f, --target-fps TARGET_FPS cap the framerate ( default: the game 's TARGET_FPS, else 60.01; 0 = uncapped) --fps-log-interval-ms FPS_LOG_INTERVAL_MS how often to log the FPS counter in ms (default: 1000) -w, --windowed, --no-windowed run in a window; --no-windowed runs fullscreen (default: windowed) -r, --resolution RESOLUTION the resolution to use (default: 800x480) --use-gfxdraw not used yet: stored, but nothing draws with pygame.gfxdraw because of it --update-type {update,flip} update or flip (default: update) --timer-backend {auto,fast,pygame} timer backend for draw loop pacing (default: auto, the fast backend with this machine' s sleep delay measured, so each sleep wakes in time ; fast assumes sleeps wake on time ; pygame is the legacy backend ) --sleep-granularity-ns SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS how long before each frame deadline the fast backend is to wake from its sleep and spin ( ns ) ; 0 spins only --windows-timer-1ms on Windows, request 1ms system timer resolution --random-seed RANDOM_SEED master seed for every engine random stream ( default: a random 64 -bit seed, logged in recordings ) --screen-shake-intensity SCREEN_SHAKE_INTENSITY screen shake strength from 0 .0 ( off ) to 1 .0 ( default: 1 .0 ) --rumble-intensity RUMBLE_INTENSITY controller rumble strength from 0 .0 ( off ) to 1 .0 ( default: 1 .0 ) --live-voice-pool LIVE_VOICE_POOL mixer channels reserved for real-time synth voices ( default: 4 ) --default-background { test-pattern,channel-3 } the background of a scene that sets none: the TV test pattern or the channel 3 blue screen ( default: test-pattern ) --video-driver { cocoa,offscreen,dummy } not applied yet: stored, but SDL picks its video driver from SDL_VIDEODRIVER ( or --headless ) instead Diagnostics Options: --log-timer-jitter log frame pacing jitter statistics periodically --perf-trim-percent PERF_TRIM_PERCENT percent of frames to trim from top and bottom in global FPS report --fps-histogram { equal-range,target-relative } FPS histogram buckets in the shutdown report: equal-range ( 10 equal buckets spanning the analyzed min to max, default ) or target-relative ( 10 % steps of the target FPS ) --debug-overlay, --no-debug-overlay show the debug overlay at startup ( F3 toggles, F4 cycles panels ) --debug-events log a warning the first time each unhandled event type arrives ( --no-unhandled-events raises on one instead ) --record-trace PATH record the session ( sprites, frame times, input events, random seed ) to a gzip JSON Lines trace for inspection and later replay ( default: off ) --replay-trace PATH replay a --record-trace recording exactly through the engine, comparing every frame with it and reporting the first divergence ( default: off ) --replay-fps { recorded,real } with --replay-trace: post FPS events from the recorded frame times ( recorded, the default: exact, and compared with the recording ) or from this machine 's measured frame times (real: what this machine achieves; FPS events are then not compared, and sprites that draw the FPS value may diverge) --audit, --no-audit with --replay-trace: instead of replaying, replay the recording twice in fresh headless processes with different hash seeds and compare every frame with the recording and between the runs; exits 0 when both match, 3 otherwise, 70 if a run could not finish --compare-processing with --replay-trace --headless: measure each frame' s processing time ( its work, without presenting or pacing ) and report how it compares with the recording 's (only meaningful on the machine that recorded) --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT with --replay-trace --headless (implies --compare-processing): a replay that matched but took more than PERCENT longer than the recording' s processing time exits 8 ; a recording without processing times exits 65 --replay-pause-at-frame N with --replay-trace, watched: skip the start screen, run frames 0 to N - 1 without showing them, then pause with frame N next ( what step back restarts with ; ignored with --headless ) --rebaseline NEW with --replay-trace OLD and --headless: replay OLD on the current code without stopping at divergences, write the run 's recording (OLD' s inputs, the current sprites ) to NEW, print a summary of the frames and sprites that changed and exit 0 --replay-digest PATH with --replay-trace: write a SHA-256 of every replayed frame, then the divergence, to PATH as JSON lines ( used by --audit ) --headless run on SDL 's dummy video and audio drivers: no window, no sound. With --replay-trace the replay also runs unpaced and prints its report to stdout (exit 0 when it matches, 1 when it diverges, 65 for a truncated recording) Controller Options: --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} Which gamepads the game sees (default: auto, every device; a mapped pad sends controller events, any other device joystick events; joystick: every device sends joystick events; controller: mapped pads only) Font Options: --font-name FONT_NAME Font to use (default: the bundled Vera; the bundled variants are Vera, VeraBd, VeraIt and VeraBI; any other name is looked up among the system' s fonts ) --font-size FONT_SIZE size of the default font, used by text that asks for no font of its own ( default: 14 ) --font-bold not used yet: stored, but no text is drawn bold because of it --font-italic not used yet: stored, but no text is drawn italic because of it --font-antialias not used yet: stored, but each text widget chooses its own antialiasing --font-dpi FONT_DPI the resolution, in dots per inch, freetype font sizes are scaled at ( sets pygame.freetype ' s default resolution ) ; the pygame font system ignores it ( default: 72 ) --font-system { pygame,freetype } Font system to use: freetype ( enhanced, default ) or pygame ( built-in ) Game Options: -l, --log-level { debug,info,warning,error,critical } set the logging level ( default: warning ; a bug report asks for info ) --no-unhandled-events fail on unhandled events -p, --profile enable profiling Bitrot Adventures v0.0.0 Options: -s, --some-game-specific-option SOME_GAME_SPECIFIC_OPTION foo help glitchygames.events The glitchygames.events module extends the pygame event subsystem by giving you on_ event callbacks. Note that you can use the normal pygame raw event mode by simply implementing a process_event(event) method in your Scene: the engine then calls it once for each raw pygame event, in order, instead of dispatching on _event callbacks. This can be especially useful for porting games to glitchygames, but there are some advantages to using glitchygames' event subsystem. The glitchygames.events subsystem detects events that your game does not handle: each type is reported once (with --debug-events ), raised as an error under --no-unhandled-events , and counted in a table the engine logs at shutdown. See Event System . Note that if you bypass the glitchygames game engine event processing, you'll lose some functionality like esc and q to quit, along with on_*_event handler support. It is recommended that you use the glitchygames event subsystem. TODO: Add some benchmark data comparing the two methods in various user scenarios to highlight the performance implications. glitchygames.fonts The glitchygames.fonts module is a module that extends pygame's font mechanisms. glitchygames.interfaces The glitchygames.interfaces module implements various interfaces, notably the Sprite and Scene interfaces, which provide an API contract for subclasses. Note: Migrating to these interfaces is a work in progress. More to come. glitchygames.movement The glitchygames.movement module defines some common movement schemes. glitchygames.pixels The glitchygames.pixels module provides common pixel manipulation operations such as 565 conversion. glitchygames.sprites The glitchygames.sprites module provides extended subclasses for sprite handling that will enable glitchygames to provide common tools and file formats that are human readable and templatable in addition to common sprite sheet formats and other goodies. glitchygames.ui The glitchygames.ui module provides common UI elements such as menubars, buttons, sliders, etc... Also in the reference: glitchygames.audio (synthesis, recipes, live voices), glitchygames.collision (layers and hitbox-aware detection), glitchygames.effects (easing, tweens, screen shake), glitchygames.input (action maps, devices, the per-frame input snapshot, rumble), glitchygames.physics , glitchygames.replay (gameplay replay), glitchygames.state (saves) and glitchygames.transitions (scene transitions).

what step back restarts with ; ignored with --headless ) --rebaseline NEW with --replay-trace OLD and --headless: replay OLD on the current code without stopping at divergences, write the run 's recording (OLD' s inputs, the current sprites ) to NEW, print a summary of the frames and sprites that changed and exit 0 --replay-digest PATH with --replay-trace: write a SHA-256 of every replayed frame, then the divergence, to PATH as JSON lines ( used by --audit ) --headless run on SDL 's dummy video and audio drivers: no window, no sound. With --replay-trace the replay also runs unpaced and prints its report to stdout (exit 0 when it matches, 1 when it diverges, 65 for a truncated recording) Controller Options: --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} Which gamepads the game sees (default: auto, every device; a mapped pad sends controller events, any other device joystick events; joystick: every device sends joystick events; controller: mapped pads only) Font Options: --font-name FONT_NAME Font to use (default: the bundled Vera; the bundled variants are Vera, VeraBd, VeraIt and VeraBI; any other name is looked up among the system' s fonts ) --font-size FONT_SIZE size of the default font, used by text that asks for no font of its own ( default: 14 ) --font-bold not used yet: stored, but no text is drawn bold because of it --font-italic not used yet: stored, but no text is drawn italic because of it --font-antialias not used yet: stored, but each text widget chooses its own antialiasing --font-dpi FONT_DPI the resolution, in dots per inch, freetype font sizes are scaled at ( sets pygame.freetype ' s default resolution ) ; the pygame font system ignores it ( default: 72 ) --font-system { pygame,freetype } Font system to use: freetype ( enhanced, default ) or pygame ( built-in ) Game Options: -l, --log-level { debug,info,warning,error,critical } set the logging level ( default: warning ; a bug report asks for info ) --no-unhandled-events fail on unhandled events -p, --profile enable profiling Bitrot Adventures v0.0.0 Options: -s, --some-game-specific-option SOME_GAME_SPECIFIC_OPTION foo help glitchygames.events The glitchygames.events module extends the pygame event subsystem by giving you on_ event callbacks. Note that you can use the normal pygame raw event mode by simply implementing a process_event(event) method in your Scene: the engine then calls it once for each raw pygame event, in order, instead of dispatching on _event callbacks. This can be especially useful for porting games to glitchygames, but there are some advantages to using glitchygames' event subsystem. The glitchygames.events subsystem detects events that your game does not handle: each type is reported once (with --debug-events ), raised as an error under --no-unhandled-events , and counted in a table the engine logs at shutdown. See Event System . Note that if you bypass the glitchygames game engine event processing, you'll lose some functionality like esc and q to quit, along with on_*_event handler support. It is recommended that you use the glitchygames event subsystem. TODO: Add some benchmark data comparing the two methods in various user scenarios to highlight the performance implications. glitchygames.fonts The glitchygames.fonts module is a module that extends pygame's font mechanisms. glitchygames.interfaces The glitchygames.interfaces module implements various interfaces, notably the Sprite and Scene interfaces, which provide an API contract for subclasses. Note: Migrating to these interfaces is a work in progress. More to come. glitchygames.movement The glitchygames.movement module defines some common movement schemes. glitchygames.pixels The glitchygames.pixels module provides common pixel manipulation operations such as 565 conversion. glitchygames.sprites The glitchygames.sprites module provides extended subclasses for sprite handling that will enable glitchygames to provide common tools and file formats that are human readable and templatable in addition to common sprite sheet formats and other goodies. glitchygames.ui The glitchygames.ui module provides common UI elements such as menubars, buttons, sliders, etc... Also in the reference: glitchygames.audio (synthesis, recipes, live voices), glitchygames.collision (layers and hitbox-aware detection), glitchygames.effects (easing, tweens, screen shake), glitchygames.input (action maps, devices, the per-frame input snapshot, rumble), glitchygames.physics , glitchygames.replay (gameplay replay), glitchygames.state (saves) and glitchygames.transitions (scene transitions).

docs.text: GlitchyGames API - FastAPI application for sprite generation. This module provides a REST API for generating and rendering pixel art sprites using AI providers via aisuite. Server Usage Run the server # glitchygames-server Or with uvicorn # uvicorn glitchygames.api.main:app --reload Generate a sprite (both TOML and PNG) # curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/sprites/generate \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"prompt": "16x16 red heart", "output_format": ["toml", "png"]}' Generate sprite with TOML only # curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/sprites/generate \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"prompt": "16x16 red heart", "output_format": ["toml"]}' Client Usage Generate a sprite using the CLI client # glitchygames-client "16x16 red heart" Generate with specific output formats # glitchygames-client "16x16 red heart" -f toml -f png Save to a directory # glitchygames-client "16x16 red heart" -o ./sprites create_app () # Create and configure the FastAPI application. Sanitize sprite name for directory/filename safe_name : str = '' . join ( c if c . isalnum () or c in '-_' else '_' for c in sprite_name ) if not safe_name : safe_name = 'sprite' # Create a directory for this sprite sprite_dir = find_available_directory ( base_output_dir / safe_name ) sprite_dir . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) LOG . info ( 'Created sprite directory: %s ' , sprite_dir ) # Save TOML if requested and available if 'toml' in output_formats and response . get ( 'toml_content' ): toml_path = sprite_dir / f ' { safe_name } .toml' toml_path . write_text ( response [ 'toml_content' ], encoding = 'utf-8' ) saved_files . append ( str ( toml_path )) LOG . info ( 'Saved TOML: %s ' , toml_path ) # Extract and save individual frames with metadata extracted_dir = sprite_dir / 'extracted' extracted_dir . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) if rendered_frames : # Use rendered_frames for proper animation-#-frame-#.png naming frame_entries : list [ tuple [ str , str , str , str ]] = [ ( ( f 'animation- { info . get ( "animation_index" , 0 ) } ' f '-frame- { info . get ( "frame_index" , 0 ) } ' ), str ( info . get ( 'animation_index' , 0 )), str ( info . get ( 'frame_index' , 0 )), str ( info . get ( 'png_base64' , '' )), ) for info in rendered_frames ] else : # Save single PNG if requested, available, and no animation frames elif 'png' in output_formats and response . get ( 'png_base64' ): png_path = sprite_dir / f ' { safe_name } .png' png_bytes = base64 . b64decode ( response [ 'png_base64' ]) png_path . write_bytes ( png_bytes ) saved_files . append ( str ( png_path )) LOG . info ( 'Saved PNG: %s ' , png_path ) return saved_files dependencies # docs.text: CLI client for the GlitchyGames Sprite Generation API. Exit codes ( ExitCode , glitchygames/exit_codes.py; logged as Exiting with ... ): SUCCESS . GENERATION_REJECTED / EXTRACTION_REJECTED : the server answered an error status (other than 503) or a response that says the request failed. SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE : the server cannot be reached, stops answering, or answers 503. OPTIONS_REFUSED : --server-url is not a usable URL. MISSING_INPUT : the APNG to extract does not exist. UNUSABLE_INPUT : an input file that cannot be read, or a response that cannot be decoded or is malformed (a missing field or one of the wrong type counts as the server's fault). CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT : an output file or directory cannot be written. INTERNAL_ERROR : any other exception (a client bug), logged with its traceback. argparse's ARGUMENT_PARSER_ERROR for a usage error.

docs.text: Create an APNG (Animated PNG) from a list of base64-encoded PNG frames. Parameters: frames_base64 ( list [ str ] ) – List of base64-encoded PNG frame data frame_delay_ms ( int , default: 100 ) – Delay between frames in milliseconds Returns: bytes – APNG file content as bytes Source code in src/glitchygames/api/client.py 337 338 339 340 341 342 343 344 345 346 347 348 349 350 351 352 353 354 355 356 357 358 359 360 361 362 363 def create_apng_from_frames ( frames_base64 : list [ str ], frame_delay_ms : int = 100 , ) -> bytes : """Create an APNG (Animated PNG) from a list of base64-encoded PNG frames. Args: frames_base64: List of base64-encoded PNG frame data frame_delay_ms: Delay between frames in milliseconds Returns: APNG file content as bytes """ apng = APNG () for frame_base64 in frames_base64 : frame_bytes = base64 . b64decode ( frame_base64 ) # Create PNG from bytes (apng library lacks type stubs) png : PNG = PNG . from_bytes ( frame_bytes ) # Add frame with delay (delay is in milliseconds, APNG uses delay/delay_den) apng . append ( png , delay = frame_delay_ms , delay_den = 1000 ) # Write to bytes buffer buffer = io . BytesIO () apng . save ( buffer ) return buffer . getvalue ()

Args: base_dir: The base directory path (without number) Returns: An available directory path with -NNN suffix """ name = base_dir . name parent = base_dir . parent counter = 1 while counter < MAX_FILE_NUMBERING_ATTEMPTS : # Safety limit new_dir = parent / f ' { name } - { counter : 03d } ' if not new_dir . exists (): return new_dir counter += 1 # Fallback: use timestamp if we somehow hit 999 directories timestamp = int ( clock . wall_clock_epoch_seconds ()) return parent / f ' { name } - { timestamp } '

Sanitize sprite name for directory/filename safe_name : str = '' . join ( c if c . isalnum () or c in '-_' else '_' for c in sprite_name ) if not safe_name : safe_name = 'sprite' # Create a directory for this sprite sprite_dir = find_available_directory ( base_output_dir / safe_name ) sprite_dir . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) LOG . info ( 'Created sprite directory: %s ' , sprite_dir ) # Default: 10 FPS # Create and save APNG apng_path = sprite_dir / f ' { safe_name } .apng' apng_path . write_bytes ( create_apng_from_frames ( frames , frame_delay_ms = frame_delay_ms )) saved_files . append ( str ( apng_path )) LOG . info ( 'Saved APNG: %s ( %s frames, %s ms/frame)' , apng_path , frame_count , frame_delay_ms ) # Extract and save individual frames with metadata extracted_dir = sprite_dir / 'extracted' extracted_dir . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) if rendered_frames : # Use rendered_frames for proper animation-#-frame-#.png naming frame_entries : list [ tuple [ str , str , str , str ]] = [ ( ( f 'animation- { info . get ( "animation_index" , 0 ) } ' f '-frame- { info . get ( "frame_index" , 0 ) } ' ), str ( info . get ( 'animation_index' , 0 )), str ( info . get ( 'frame_index' , 0 )), str ( info . get ( 'png_base64' , '' )), ) for info in rendered_frames ] else : # Fallback to old naming if rendered_frames not available frame_entries = [ ( f 'animation-0-frame- { i } ' , '0' , str ( i ), frame_base64 ) for i , frame_base64 in enumerate ( frames ) ] saved_files . extend ( _save_extracted_frames ( frame_entries = frame_entries , extracted_dir = extracted_dir , frame_count = frame_count , frame_delay_ms = frame_delay_ms , extract_scale = extract_scale , model_used = model_used , ), ) LOG . info ( 'Saved %s frames to: %s (scale: %s x)' , frame_count , extracted_dir , extract_scale ) # Called by run() and by the app's lifespan ( uvicorn glitchygames.api.main:app starts no run() , and a --reload worker imports the module afresh). It was a logging.basicConfig at import: any process importing the API, the test suite included, logged every logger's INFO records from then on, whatever its own level was (BUGS.md #236). basicConfig does nothing once the root logger has a handler, so a process that configured its logging first keeps its own. It was a ``logging.basicConfig`` at import: any process importing the API, the test suite included, logged every logger's INFO records from then on, whatever its own level was (BUGS.md #236). ``basicConfig`` does nothing once the root logger has a handler, so a process that configured its logging first keeps its own. """ logging . basicConfig ( level = logging . INFO , format = SERVER_LOG_FORMAT )

All heavy processing (speech recognition, AI API calls, TTS) runs in a background thread to avoid blocking the game loop. Parameters: controller_audio ( ControllerAudio ) – The controller's audio devices. ai_provider ( str | None , default: None ) – AI provider name for aisuite (default: from env or 'anthropic'). ai_model ( str | None , default: None ) – AI model identifier (default: from env or 'claude-sonnet-4-5'). system_prompt ( str , default: _SYSTEM_PROMPT ) – System prompt for the AI assistant. on_transcription ( Callable [[ str ], None] | None , default: None ) – Callback when speech is transcribed. All heavy processing (speech recognition, AI API calls, TTS) runs in a background thread to avoid blocking the game loop. Args: controller_audio: The controller's audio devices. ai_provider: AI provider name for aisuite (default: from env or 'anthropic'). ai_model: AI model identifier (default: from env or 'claude-sonnet-4-5'). system_prompt: System prompt for the AI assistant. on_transcription: Callback when speech is transcribed. Receives the text. on_response: Callback when AI responds. Receives the response text. on_error: Callback on any error. Receives the error message. Lock () @property def is_listening ( self ) -> bool : """Whether the assistant is currently recording.""" return self . _listening @property def is_processing ( self ) -> bool : """Whether the assistant is processing a request (STT + AI + TTS).""" return self . _processing def start_listening ( self ) -> bool : """Start recording from the controller mic. Returns: True if recording started successfully. """ if self . _listening or self . _processing : return False if not self . _audio . has_microphone : self . _fire_error ( 'No microphone found on controller' ) return False # Haptic feedback: short buzz to confirm mic is active self . _audio . play_haptic ( 'buzz' , duration = 0.08 ) self . _listening = self . _audio . start_capture () if self . _listening : log . info ( 'Voice assistant: listening...' ) return self . _listening def stop_listening_and_respond ( self ) -> None : """Stop recording and process the audio in the background. The pipeline runs in a background thread: audio → speech-to-text → AI → TTS → play through speaker. Results are delivered via callbacks and the update() method. """ if not self . _listening : return audio_data = self . _audio . stop_capture () self . _listening = False self . _processing = True log . info ( 'Voice assistant: processing %d bytes of audio...' , len ( audio_data )) # Run the heavy pipeline in a background thread thread = threading . Thread ( target = self . _process_pipeline , args = ( audio_data ,), daemon = True , ) thread . start () def update ( self ) -> None : """Check for completed responses (call from dt_tick). Delivers pending responses and errors via callbacks on the main thread. """ with self . _lock : response = self . _pending_response error = self . _pending_error self . _pending_response = None self . _pending_error = None if response is not None and self . _on_response is not None : self . _on_response ( response ) if error is not None and self . _on_error is not None : self . _on_error ( error ) def clear_conversation ( self ) -> None : """Reset the conversation history. Safe while a request is in flight: its answer is then not added (BUGS.md #114). """ with self . _lock : self . _conversation . clear () # --- Background pipeline --- def _process_pipeline ( self , audio_data : bytes ) -> None : """Run the full STT → AI → TTS → playback pipeline. Runs in a background thread. Sets _pending_response or _pending_error for the main thread to pick up. Args: audio_data: Raw PCM audio from the controller mic. """ # The thread's boundary: a failure is reported to the main thread, never lost with it try : self . _run_pipeline ( audio_data ) except Exception : log . exception ( 'Voice assistant pipeline error' ) self . _fire_error ( 'Voice assistant error — check logs' ) finally : self . _processing = False def _run_pipeline ( self , audio_data : bytes ) -> None : """Transcribe, ask the AI, deliver the response text and speak it. Args: audio_data: Raw PCM audio from the controller mic. """ # 1. Speech-to-text text = self . _transcribe ( audio_data ) if not text : self . _fire_error ( 'Could not understand speech' ) return log . info ( 'Voice assistant heard: %r ' , text ) if self . _on_transcription is not None : self . _on_transcription ( text ) # 2. AI response response = self . _ask_ai ( text ) if not response : self . _fire_error ( 'No response from AI' ) return log . info ( 'Voice assistant says: %r ' , response ) # 3. Deliver response text with self . _lock : self . _pending_response = response # 4. TTS → speaker self . _speak_response ( response ) def _transcribe ( self , audio_data : bytes ) -> str | None : """Convert raw audio to text via speech_recognition. Args: audio_data: Raw PCM audio bytes. Returns: The transcribed text, or None. """ if sr is None : log . warning ( 'speech_recognition not available' ) return None audio = self . _audio . get_speech_recognizer_audio ( audio_data ) if audio is None : return None recognizer = sr . Recognizer () try : # Use Google's free speech recognition # Could swap to Whisper, etc. return recognizer . recognize_google ( audio ) # type: ignore[no-any-return] # ty: ignore[unresolved-attribute] except sr . UnknownValueError : log . warning ( 'Speech not understood' ) return None except sr . RequestError : log . exception ( 'Speech recognition service error' ) return None def _ask_ai ( self , user_text : str ) -> str | None : """Send text to the AI and get a response. Args: user_text: The player's transcribed speech. Returns: The AI's response text, or None. """ if ai is None : log . warning ( 'aisuite not available' ) return None # Trim the history to the turns kept before the question joins it. The history holds # whole user/assistant pairs (a failed request removes its question below), so dropping # whole pairs from the front keeps it starting with a user message, which some # providers require (BUGS.md #105). With the answer, at most max turns are kept. kept_entry_count = ( self . _max_conversation_turns - 1 ) * 2 # The history is shared with clear_conversation() on the main thread: every change # to it holds the lock (never across the request itself) with self . _lock : if len ( self . _conversation ) > kept_entry_count : dropped_entry_count = len ( self . _conversation ) - kept_entry_count # Round up to a whole pair dropped_entry_count += dropped_entry_count % 2 # Deleted in place: clear_conversation() clears this same list del self . _conversation [: dropped_entry_count ] # Build messages with conversation context question = { 'role' : 'user' , 'content' : user_text } self . _conversation . append ( question ) messages : list [ dict [ str , str ]] = [ { 'role' : 'system' , 'content' : self . _system_prompt }, * self . _conversation , ] try : client : Any = ai . Client () model_string = f ' { self . _ai_provider } : { self . _ai_model } ' response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = model_string , messages = messages , ) response_text : str = response . choices [ 0 ] . message . content except Exception : log . exception ( 'AI request failed' ) # An unanswered question would make the next request send two user messages in a # row (BUGS.md #105). Compared by identity: an earlier question may have the same text with self . _lock : if self . _conversation and self . _conversation [ - 1 ] is question : self . _conversation . pop () return None else : # A clear_conversation() during the request removed the question: the answer # alone would start the history with an assistant message (BUGS.md #114) with self . _lock : if self . _conversation and self . _conversation [ - 1 ] is question : self . _conversation . append ({ 'role' : 'assistant' , 'content' : response_text }) return response_text def _speak_response ( self , text : str ) -> None : """Convert response to speech and play through controller speaker. Args: text: The response text to speak. """ if self . _tts is None : log . info ( 'No TTS backend — response is text-only' ) return if not self . _audio . has_speaker : log . info ( 'No speaker on controller — response is text-only' ) return # Play a click haptic when the response starts, then speak self . _audio . play_haptic ( 'click' ) audio_file = self . _tts . speak_to_file ( text ) if audio_file is not None : self . _audio . play_file ( audio_file , haptic_mode = 'speech' ) def _fire_error ( self , message : str ) -> None : """Set a pending error for the main thread. Args: message: Error description. """ log . warning ( 'Voice assistant: %s ' , message ) with self . _lock : self . _pending_error = message self . _processing = False # --- Factory --- @classmethod def for_controller ( cls , controller_name : str , ** kwargs : Any , ) -> VoiceAssistant | None : """Create a VoiceAssistant for a named controller. Returns None if the controller has no audio devices or required libraries are missing. Args: controller_name: The controller's name string. **kwargs: Additional arguments passed to the constructor. Returns: A VoiceAssistant instance, or None. """ audio = ControllerAudio . for_controller ( controller_name ) if audio is None : return None try : return cls ( controller_audio = audio , ** kwargs ) except Exception : log . exception ( 'Failed to create voice assistant for %r ' , controller_name ) return None @classmethod def discover ( cls , ** kwargs : Any ) -> VoiceAssistant | None : """Auto-discover a controller with audio and create a VoiceAssistant. Scans miniaudio devices for a controller with both microphone and speaker. No engine access needed. Args: **kwargs: Additional arguments passed to the constructor. Returns: A VoiceAssistant for the first matching controller, or None. """ # Volume 5.0 compensates for quiet macOS TTS output (~10% of max) audio = ControllerAudio . discover ( volume = 5.0 ) if audio is None : log . info ( 'No controller with audio devices found' ) return None try : return cls ( controller_audio = audio , ** kwargs ) except Exception : log . exception ( 'Failed to create voice assistant' ) return None

CaptureDevice ( input_format = mi . SampleFormat . Returns: True if haptic playback started. """ if not self . has_speaker or mi is None : return False thread = threading . Args: speaker_samples: Mono samples for the speaker (channel 1). haptic_left: Samples for left grip motor (channel 2). haptic_right: Samples for right grip motor (channel 3). haptic_mix: Speaker-to-haptic bleed (0.0-1.0). """ if mi is None : return # The thread's boundary: a failure is logged, never lost with the thread try : self . _stream_4channel ( speaker_samples = speaker_samples , haptic_left = haptic_left , haptic_right = haptic_right , haptic_mix = haptic_mix , ) except Exception : log . exception ( 'Failed to play 4-channel audio' ) def _stream_4channel ( self , * , speaker_samples : array . array [ int ] | None , haptic_left : array . array [ int ] | None , haptic_right : array . array [ int ] | None , haptic_mix : float , ) -> None : """Build the interleaved 4-channel stream and play it to the end (blocking). Yields: Interleaved sample data for the requested frames. """ nonlocal offset num_requested = yield b '' while True : num_samples = int ( num_requested ) * DUALSENSE_CHANNELS chunk = stream_data [ offset : offset + num_samples ] offset += num_samples if not chunk : break num_requested = yield chunk device : Any = mi . PlaybackDevice ( output_format = mi . SampleFormat . SIGNED16 , nchannels = DUALSENSE_CHANNELS , sample_rate = DUALSENSE_SAMPLE_RATE , device_id = self . playback_device_id , ) generator = _stream_generator () next ( generator ) # Prime the generator device . start ( generator ) duration = num_frames / DUALSENSE_SAMPLE_RATE clock . raw_sleep ( duration + 0.3 ) device . stop () log . info ( 'Played %.2f s through %r (speaker= %s haptic= %s )' , duration , self . controller_name , speaker_samples is not None , haptic_left is not None , ) # --- Factory --- @classmethod def for_controller ( cls , controller_name : str , ** kwargs : Any ) -> ControllerAudio | None : """Create a ControllerAudio if the controller has audio devices. Returns None if neither microphone nor speaker is found. Args: controller_name: The controller's name string. **kwargs: Additional arguments passed to the constructor. Returns: A ControllerAudio instance, or None. """ if mi is None : return None try : audio = cls ( controller_name , ** kwargs ) except Exception : log . exception ( 'Failed to create controller audio for %r ' , controller_name ) return None if not audio . has_microphone and not audio . has_speaker : log . info ( 'No audio devices found for controller %r ' , controller_name ) return None return audio @classmethod def discover ( cls , ** kwargs : Any ) -> ControllerAudio | None : """Auto-discover a controller with audio devices. Finds devices that appear in both the capture (mic) and playback (speaker) device lists by name matching. Args: **kwargs: Additional arguments passed to the constructor. Returns: A ControllerAudio for the first matching controller, or None. """ if mi is None : return None devices = mi . Devices () capture_names = { dev [ 'name' ] for dev in devices . get_captures ()} playback_names = { dev [ 'name' ] for dev in devices . get_playbacks ()} # Devices with both mic and speaker are likely controllers controller_names = capture_names & playback_names for name in controller_names : audio = cls . for_controller ( name , ** kwargs ) if audio is not None : return audio return None

docs.text: Enable the DualSense internal speaker via USB HID output report. On macOS (and Windows), the speaker is not enabled by default. This sends the same HID output report that the Linux kernel driver sends to route audio to the speaker. Parameters: volume ( int , default: _SPEAKER_VOLUME_DEFAULT ) – Speaker volume (effective range 0x3D-0x64). preamp_gain ( int , default: _SPEAKER_PREAMP_GAIN_6DB ) – Preamp gain for bits 0-2 of audio_flags2. Returns: bool – True if the speaker was enabled successfully. Source code in src/glitchygames/audio/controller_audio.py 96 97 98 99 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 143 144 145 146 147 148 149 150 151 152 153 154 155 156 157 158 159 160 161 162 163 164 165 166 167 168 def enable_dualsense_speaker ( volume : int = _SPEAKER_VOLUME_DEFAULT , preamp_gain : int = _SPEAKER_PREAMP_GAIN_6DB , ) -> bool : """Enable the DualSense internal speaker via USB HID output report. On macOS (and Windows), the speaker is not enabled by default. This sends the same HID output report that the Linux kernel driver sends to route audio to the speaker. Args: volume: Speaker volume (effective range 0x3D-0x64). preamp_gain: Preamp gain for bits 0-2 of audio_flags2. Returns: True if the speaker was enabled successfully. """ if hidapi is None : log . warning ( 'hidapi not available — cannot enable DualSense speaker' ) return False # Try DualSense, then DualSense Edge device : Any = hidapi . device () # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType,reportUnknownVariableType] try : device . open ( SONY_VENDOR_ID , DUALSENSE_PRODUCT_ID ) # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType] except OSError : try : device . open ( SONY_VENDOR_ID , DUALSENSE_EDGE_PRODUCT_ID ) # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType] except OSError : log . warning ( 'No DualSense found via HID' ) return False # Build the 63-byte USB output report report = bytearray ( DS_OUTPUT_REPORT_SIZE ) report [ 0 ] = DS_OUTPUT_REPORT_USB # Byte 1: valid_flag0 — enable audio control + speaker volume report [ 1 ] = _FLAG0_AUDIO_CONTROL | _FLAG0_SPEAKER_VOLUME # Byte 2: valid_flag1 — enable audio_control2 (preamp gain) report [ 2 ] = _FLAG1_AUDIO_CONTROL2 # Byte 6: speaker_volume report [ 6 ] = volume # Byte 8: audio_flags — route right channel to speaker, mute HP report [ 8 ] = _AUDIO_PATH_SPEAKER_ONLY << _AUDIO_PATH_SHIFT # Byte 38: audio_flags2 — speaker preamp gain (+6dB) report [ 38 ] = preamp_gain # hidapi answers -1 for a failed write, or raises (OSError; ValueError for a device that is # not open, e.g. disconnected). Either way the device is closed and only the speaker enable # fails: an exception escaping here would lose the controller's whole audio (BUGS.md #108) try : bytes_written : int = device . write ( bytes ( report )) # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType,reportUnknownVariableType] except OSError , ValueError : log . warning ( 'Failed to send speaker enable HID report' , exc_info = True ) return False finally : device . close () # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType] if bytes_written < 0 : log . warning ( 'Failed to send speaker enable HID report' ) return False log . info ( 'DualSense speaker enabled: volume=0x %02X , gain=0x %02X ' , volume , preamp_gain , ) return True

docs.text: Audio glitch diagnostics: analyze rendered samples and measure GIL contention. Two kinds of glitch are covered: DSP glitches live in the samples themselves (gaps, steps, abrupt edges); the pure functions here find them in a recording, and need only numpy. Handover glitches come from the mixer thread waiting for Python's GIL while the main thread is busy (pygame's channel-finished callback takes the GIL to start the next live-voice chunk). A disk-driver recording cannot show these, because that driver is not real-time: a late callback just writes later. measure_lock_wait measures the wait directly instead. See BUGS.md #27 and scripts/audio_glitch_probe.py.

docs.text: Describe the onset and the final cut of a sound. Returns: EdgeReport – The edge report (all zeros for pure silence). Source code in src/glitchygames/audio/diagnostics.py 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 def describe_edges ( samples : FloatArray ) -> EdgeReport : """Describe the onset and the final cut of a sound. Returns: The edge report (all zeros for pure silence). """ non_zero_indices = np . flatnonzero ( samples ) if non_zero_indices . size == 0 : return EdgeReport ( onset_samples = (), final_sample = 0.0 , typical_step = 0.0 , cut_ratio = 0.0 ) first_index = int ( non_zero_indices [ 0 ]) last_index = int ( non_zero_indices [ - 1 ]) sound = samples [ first_index : last_index + 1 ] typical_step = float ( np . median ( np . abs ( np . diff ( sound )))) if sound . size > 1 else 0.0 final_sample = float ( samples [ last_index ]) cut_ratio = final_sample / typical_step if typical_step > 0.0 else 0.0 onset = tuple ( float ( value ) for value in sound [: ONSET_SAMPLE_COUNT ]) return EdgeReport ( onset_samples = onset , final_sample = final_sample , typical_step = typical_step , cut_ratio = cut_ratio , )

docs.text: Say whether the p99 GIL wait reaches risk_fraction of the mixer buffer's duration. The p99 is used rather than the maximum: on a busy machine the maximum is dominated by OS scheduling noise that no GIL setting can remove, while the p99 separates a fixed switch interval (about 2 ms) from the 5 ms default (about 6.4 ms). Returns: bool – True when p99 wait >= risk_fraction x buffer duration (512 samples at 44100 Hz is bool – 11.6 ms, so 5.8 ms by default). Source code in src/glitchygames/audio/diagnostics.py 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 def dropout_risk ( report : LockWaitReport , * , buffer_samples : int = DEFAULT_BUFFER_SAMPLES , sample_rate : int = DEFAULT_SAMPLE_RATE , risk_fraction : float = DEFAULT_RISK_FRACTION , ) -> bool : """Say whether the p99 GIL wait reaches risk_fraction of the mixer buffer's duration. The p99 is used rather than the maximum: on a busy machine the maximum is dominated by OS scheduling noise that no GIL setting can remove, while the p99 separates a fixed switch interval (about 2 ms) from the 5 ms default (about 6.4 ms). Returns: True when p99 wait >= risk_fraction x buffer duration (512 samples at 44100 Hz is 11.6 ms, so 5.8 ms by default). """ buffer_milliseconds = buffer_samples / sample_rate * SECONDS_TO_MILLISECONDS return report . p99_milliseconds >= risk_fraction * buffer_milliseconds

docs.text: Find indices where the absolute second difference exceeds sensitivity x its 99 th percentile. A smooth waveform has a small, steady second difference; a click or step makes a spike. Returns: list [ int ] – Sample indices of the spikes (empty when the signal is too short or perfectly smooth). Source code in src/glitchygames/audio/diagnostics.py 66 67 68 69 70 71 72 73 74 75 76 77 78 79 80 81 82 83 84 def find_discontinuities ( samples : FloatArray , * , sensitivity : float = DEFAULT_DISCONTINUITY_SENSITIVITY ) -> list [ int ]: """Find indices where the absolute second difference exceeds sensitivity x its 99th percentile. A smooth waveform has a small, steady second difference; a click or step makes a spike. Returns: Sample indices of the spikes (empty when the signal is too short or perfectly smooth). """ if samples . size < 3 : # ruff: ignore[magic-value-comparison] return [] second_difference = np . abs ( np . diff ( samples , n = 2 )) threshold = sensitivity * float ( np . percentile ( second_difference , 99 )) if threshold <= 0.0 : return [] # diff(n=2)[i] is centered on sample i + 1 return [ int ( index ) + 1 for index in np . flatnonzero ( second_difference > threshold )]

docs.text: Find runs of exact zeros strictly inside the sound. Leading and trailing silence (before the first and after the last non-zero sample) is not a gap. A real gap means the mixer ran dry between two chunks. Returns: list [ tuple [ int , int ]] – (start index, length) of each run of at least minimum_samples zeros. Leading and trailing silence (before the first and after the last non-zero sample) is not a gap. A real gap means the mixer ran dry between two chunks. Returns: (start index, length) of each run of at least minimum_samples zeros. """ non_zero_indices = np . flatnonzero ( samples ) if non_zero_indices . size == 0 : return [] # Zero runs strictly inside the sound are exactly the spaces between consecutive non-zero # samples: a space of (next - previous - 1) zeros starting at previous + 1. run_lengths = np . diff ( non_zero_indices ) - 1 run_starts = non_zero_indices [: - 1 ] + 1 long_enough = run_lengths >= minimum_samples return [ ( int ( start ), int ( length )) for start , length in zip ( run_starts [ long_enough ], run_lengths [ long_enough ], strict = True ) ]

docs.text: Measure how late a background thread gets the GIL while the main thread plays a game. A background thread wakes every period_seconds and records how much later than requested it resumed (it needs the GIL to resume, exactly like the mixer's channel-finished callback). The calling thread simulates frames: busy Python work for game_logic_seconds, then a FastTimer-style coarse sleep plus final spin up to the frame deadline. The previous switch interval is restored. Returns: LockWaitReport – Median, 99 th percentile and maximum extra wake-up delay in milliseconds. A background thread wakes every period_seconds and records how much later than requested it resumed (it needs the GIL to resume, exactly like the mixer's channel-finished callback). The calling thread simulates frames: busy Python work for game_logic_seconds, then a FastTimer-style coarse sleep plus final spin up to the frame deadline. The previous switch interval is restored. Returns: Median, 99th percentile and maximum extra wake-up delay in milliseconds. """ previous_switch_interval = sys . getswitchinterval () if switch_interval_seconds is not None : sys . setswitchinterval ( switch_interval_seconds ) waits_milliseconds : list [ float ] = [] stop_event = threading . Event () def background_listener () -> None : while not stop_event . is_set (): before_ns = clock . raw_counter_ns () clock . raw_sleep ( period_seconds ) elapsed_ns = clock . raw_counter_ns () - before_ns late_ns = elapsed_ns - int ( period_seconds * 1e9 ) waits_milliseconds . append ( max ( 0.0 , late_ns * NANOSECONDS_TO_MILLISECONDS )) listener = threading . Thread ( target = background_listener , name = 'lock-wait-listener' , daemon = True ) timer = FastTimer () period_ns = timer . start_frame ( target_fps ) try : listener . start () deadline_ns = clock . raw_counter_ns () + period_ns for _ in range ( frames ): busy_python_work ( seconds = game_logic_seconds ) _pace_until ( deadline_ns = deadline_ns , timer = timer , yield_in_spin = yield_in_spin ) deadline_ns = timer . compute_deadline ( deadline_ns , period_ns ) finally : stop_event . set () listener . join () sys . setswitchinterval ( previous_switch_interval ) if not waits_milliseconds : return LockWaitReport ( median_milliseconds = 0.0 , p99_milliseconds = 0.0 , maximum_milliseconds = 0.0 , sample_count = 0 , ) waits = np . array ( waits_milliseconds ) return LockWaitReport ( median_milliseconds = float ( np . median ( waits )), p99_milliseconds = float ( np . percentile ( waits , 99 )), maximum_milliseconds = float ( waits . max ()), sample_count = int ( waits . size ), )

docs.text: Real-time synth voices streamed through reserved mixer channels. pygame has no audio callback, so each voice renders short chunks from the game loop and keeps one chunk queued behind the one playing (pygame holds one queued Sound per channel). The safety margin is the rest of the playing chunk minus one device buffer: about 88 ms at 44100 Hz with a 512-sample buffer and 100 ms chunks. A longer frame underruns; the voice restarts next update. Channel facts this module relies on (pygame-ce 2.5.8): Channel.stop() and Channel.fadeout() start the queued sound, so fades are rendered into the samples and stop_now() calls stop() twice; set_reserved(n) reserves channels 0..n-1; set_num_channels(smaller) stops sounds on the removed channels, so the pool is reserved once at startup and never resized.
