docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. """ content_hash : int | None = self . _content_hash if content_hash is not None : return content_hash # Guard against infinite recursion when __dict__ contains this event (as __eq__ does); # the inner call's stand-in is never cached self_id = id ( self ) if self_id in HashableEvent . _hashing_ids : return hash ( self . type ) HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . add ( self_id ) try : content_hash = hash ( frozenset (( name , _hashable_value ( value )) for name , value in self . __dict__ . items ()) ) finally : HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . discard ( self_id ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( self , content_hash ) return content_hash

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Return the hash of the event's content (its type and fields), cached. Equal events hash alike however they were built. Unhashable values (a game event's lists and dicts) hash by their content. Computed on the first call and kept in a slot (never a field); a copy (pickled, with_fields ) computes its own. Returns: int ( int ) – The hash value. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 915 916 917 918 919 920 921 922 923 924 925 926 927 928 929 930 931 932 933 934 935 936 937 938 939 940 941 942 943 @override def __hash__ ( self : Self ) -> int : """Return the hash of the event's content (its type and fields), cached. Computed on the first call and kept in a slot (never a field); a copy (pickled, ``with_fields``) computes its own. Returns: int: The hash value. """ content_hash : int | None = self . _content_hash if content_hash is not None : return content_hash # Guard against infinite recursion when __dict__ contains this event (as __eq__ does); # the inner call's stand-in is never cached self_id = id ( self ) if self_id in HashableEvent . _hashing_ids : return hash ( self . type ) HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . add ( self_id ) try : content_hash = hash ( frozenset (( name , _hashable_value ( value )) for name , value in self . __dict__ . items ()) ) finally : HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . discard ( self_id ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( self , content_hash ) return content_hash

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Shared-instance aggregator base class for event proxies. A ResourceManager subclass will generally pass all requests through to its proxy object(s), however, for certain types of resources such as joysticks, the subclass will manage things itself. This architecture reduces code footprint, and allows maxium flexibility when needed, at the expense of a bit of abstraction. Unless you're implementing a new pygame event manager, you probably don't need to worry about this. Shared instances ( SHARES_INSTANCE , True for the event managers): a class has one instance, the first one constructed. Constructing it again returns that instance as it is, without running __init__ again (BUGS.md #198), so MouseEventManager() is the manager the GameEngine made to process mouse events with. Each engine run releases them ( release_shared_instances ) before it makes its managers, so a second engine in one process (a recording, then its replay) builds its own. A class that sets SHARES_INSTANCE = False gets a new instance at every construction: the proxies (a manager owns its own, and the controller manager one per controller) and EventManager ( GameEngine and SceneManager , whose own __new__ keeps its singleton). A ResourceManager subclass will generally pass all requests through to its proxy object(s), however, for certain types of resources such as joysticks, the subclass will manage things itself. This architecture reduces code footprint, and allows maxium flexibility when needed, at the expense of a bit of abstraction. Unless you're implementing a new pygame event manager, you probably don't need to worry about this. Shared instances (``SHARES_INSTANCE``, True for the event managers): a class has one instance, the first one constructed. Constructing it again returns that instance as it is, without running ``__init__`` again (BUGS.md #198), so ``MouseEventManager()`` is the manager the GameEngine made to process mouse events with. Each engine run releases them (``release_shared_instances``) before it makes its managers, so a second engine in one process (a recording, then its replay) builds its own. A class that sets ``SHARES_INSTANCE = False`` gets a new instance at every construction: the proxies (a manager owns its own, and the controller manager one per controller) and ``EventManager`` (``GameEngine`` and ``SceneManager``, whose own ``__new__`` keeps its singleton). """ log : ClassVar [ logging . Logger ] = LOG # False: every construction makes a new instance (see the class docstring) SHARES_INSTANCE : ClassVar [ bool ] = True __instances__ : ClassVar [ dict [ type , Any ]] = {} def __init_subclass__ ( cls , ** keyword_arguments : Any ) -> None : """Wrap the subclass's own ``__init__`` so its shared instance is initialized once. Args: **keyword_arguments: Passed on to ``object.__init_subclass__``. Args: cls: The class. *_args: The positional arguments (``__init__`` takes them). **_kwargs: The keyword arguments (``__init__`` takes them). Returns: The shared instance (made now if there is none yet), or a new instance. """ if not cls . SHARES_INSTANCE : return object . __new__ ( cls ) if cls not in ResourceManager . __instances__ : ResourceManager . __instances__ [ cls ] = object . __new__ ( cls ) LOG . debug ( 'Created Resource Manager: %s ' , cls ) return ResourceManager . __instances__ [ cls ] @_initialize_once def __init__ ( self : Self , game : object ) -> None : # ruff: ignore[unused-method-argument] """Initialize the resource manager. Args: game: The game instance (accepted for subclass compatibility). """ super () . __init__ () self . proxies : list [ Any ] = [] @classmethod def release_shared_instances ( cls ) -> None : """Forget every shared instance, so the next construction of each class makes a new one. ``GameEngine`` calls it before it makes its event managers: a new engine run builds managers of its own (opening devices through its own doors), not the earlier run's. docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Return the hash of the event's content (its type and fields), cached. Equal events hash alike however they were built. Unhashable values (a game event's lists and dicts) hash by their content. Computed on the first call and kept in a slot (never a field); a copy (pickled, with_fields ) computes its own. Returns: int ( int ) – The hash value. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 915 916 917 918 919 920 921 922 923 924 925 926 927 928 929 930 931 932 933 934 935 936 937 938 939 940 941 942 943 @override def __hash__ ( self : Self ) -> int : """Return the hash of the event's content (its type and fields), cached. Equal events hash alike however they were built. Unhashable values (a game event's lists and dicts) hash by their content. Computed on the first call and kept in a slot (never a field); a copy (pickled, ``with_fields``) computes its own. Returns: int: The hash value. """ content_hash : int | None = self . _content_hash if content_hash is not None : return content_hash # Guard against infinite recursion when __dict__ contains this event (as __eq__ does); # the inner call's stand-in is never cached self_id = id ( self ) if self_id in HashableEvent . _hashing_ids : return hash ( self . type ) HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . add ( self_id ) try : content_hash = hash ( frozenset (( name , _hashable_value ( value )) for name , value in self . __dict__ . items ()) ) finally : HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . discard ( self_id ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( self , content_hash ) return content_hash

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )
docs.title: __new__

docs.text: Set the state of the object. The event is rebuilt from the state's attributes exactly as init builds it, so it equals and hashes like the event the state came from (BUGS.md #121: this hashed a dict). Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 1049 1050 1051 1052 1053 1054 1055 1056 1057 1058 1059 1060 1061 1062 1063 1064 1065 def __setstate__ ( self : Self , state : builtins . dict [ str , Any ]) -> None : """Set the state of the object. The event is rebuilt from the state's attributes exactly as __init__ builds it, so it equals and hashes like the event the state came from (BUGS.md #121: this hashed a dict). """ attributes = dict ( state ) event_type = attributes . pop ( 'type' ) # A state pickled before BUGS.md #179 carries the hash it stored as an attribute attributes . pop ( '_HashableEvent__hash' , None ) self . __dict__ . clear () # Rebuilt as __new__ builds an event; the cached hash (none yet: pickle builds the # event just before) is cleared, so the event hashes by the state's content fields = self . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = event_type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( self , None )

docs.text: Wrap a pygame event, as its type's class ( EVENT_CLASSES ): the engine's dispatch. The same event the constructor builds ( HashableEvent(pygame_event.type, **pygame_event.dict) ), without unpacking the fields into keyword arguments twice: every dispatched event comes through here, mouse-motion floods included. Parameters: pygame_event ( Event ) – The raw event. Returns: HashableEvent ( HashableEvent ) – The event. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 619 620 621 622 623 624 625 626 627 628 629 630 631 632 633 634 635 636 637 638 639 640 @staticmethod def from_pygame ( pygame_event : pygame . event . Event ) -> HashableEvent : """Wrap a pygame event, as its type's class (``EVENT_CLASSES``): the engine's dispatch. The same event the constructor builds (``HashableEvent(pygame_event.type, **pygame_event.dict)``), without unpacking the fields into keyword arguments twice: every dispatched event comes through here, mouse-motion floods included. Args: pygame_event: The raw event. Returns: HashableEvent: The event. """ event_type = pygame_event . type event = object . __new__ ( EVENT_CLASSES . get ( event_type , HashableEvent )) fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = event_type fields . update ( pygame_event . dict ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) return event

docs.text: Return the hash of the event's content (its type and fields), cached. Equal events hash alike however they were built. Unhashable values (a game event's lists and dicts) hash by their content. Computed on the first call and kept in a slot (never a field); a copy (pickled, with_fields ) computes its own. Returns: int ( int ) – The hash value. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 915 916 917 918 919 920 921 922 923 924 925 926 927 928 929 930 931 932 933 934 935 936 937 938 939 940 941 942 943 @override def __hash__ ( self : Self ) -> int : """Return the hash of the event's content (its type and fields), cached. Equal events hash alike however they were built. Unhashable values (a game event's lists and dicts) hash by their content. Computed on the first call and kept in a slot (never a field); a copy (pickled, ``with_fields``) computes its own. Returns: int: The hash value. """ content_hash : int | None = self . _content_hash if content_hash is not None : return content_hash # Guard against infinite recursion when __dict__ contains this event (as __eq__ does); # the inner call's stand-in is never cached self_id = id ( self ) if self_id in HashableEvent . _hashing_ids : return hash ( self . type ) HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . add ( self_id ) try : content_hash = hash ( frozenset (( name , _hashable_value ( value )) for name , value in self . __dict__ . items ()) ) finally : HashableEvent . _hashing_ids . discard ( self_id ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( self , content_hash ) return content_hash

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool ( bool ) – True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object. subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 1425 1426 1427 1428 1429 1430 1431 1432 1433 1434 1435 1436 1437 1438 1439 1440 1441 1442 1443 1444 1445 1446 1447 1448 1449 1450 1451 1452 1453 1454 1455 1456 1457 1458 1459 1460 1461 1462 1463 1464 1465 1466 1467 1468 1469 @classmethod @override def __subclasshook__ ( cls , subclass : type [ Any ]) -> bool : """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. docs.text: Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to ( EVENT_CLASSES ). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here ( __init__ is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Parameters: type ( int ) – The type of the event. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes ( Any , default: {} ) – The event's fields. Returns: Self ( Self ) – An instance of the type's class: HashableEvent (or the class called) for Self – a type with no class of its own. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event )

docs.text: Allow every event type at SDL, SYSWMEVENT only when the game asked for it. SYSWMEVENT carries the window system's raw messages (on x11 every X event: focus, exposure, property changes; on Windows each window message), which SDL itself leaves disabled. A plain pygame.event.set_allowed(None) would enable them too, flooding the queue (and every recording and instant-replay journal) with messages almost no game reads. A game opts in with NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES = True on its scene class; they then reach on_sys_wm_event as plain HashableEvent s holding pygame's platform fields. Blocked through pygame.event.set_blocked , so pygame.event.get_blocked reports it truthfully afterwards: before any pygame call blocks it, pygame-ce 2.5.8 reports SYSWMEVENT as allowed while SDL ignores it, and a snapshot-and-restore of the blocked types (the replay's input blocking) would then enable it. Parameters: native_window_messages ( bool ) – Whether SYSWMEVENT is allowed too. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 200 201 202 203 204 205 206 207 208 def allow_every_event_type ( * , native_window_messages : bool ) -> None : """Allow every event type at SDL, SYSWMEVENT only when the game asked for it. SYSWMEVENT carries the window system's raw messages (on x11 every X event: focus, exposure, property changes; on Windows each window message), which SDL itself leaves disabled. A plain ``pygame.event.set_allowed(None)`` would enable them too, flooding the queue (and every recording and instant-replay journal) with messages almost no game reads. A game opts in with ``NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES = True`` on its scene class; they then reach ``on_sys_wm_event`` as plain ``HashableEvent``s holding pygame's platform fields. Blocked through ``pygame.event.set_blocked``, so ``pygame.event.get_blocked`` reports it truthfully afterwards: before any pygame call blocks it, pygame-ce 2.5.8 reports SYSWMEVENT as allowed while SDL ignores it, and a snapshot-and-restore of the blocked types (the replay's input blocking) would then enable it. Args: native_window_messages: Whether SYSWMEVENT is allowed too. """ pygame . event . set_allowed ( None ) if native_window_messages : pygame . event . set_allowed ( pygame . SYSWMEVENT ) else : pygame . event . set_blocked ( pygame . SYSWMEVENT )

docs.text: Return a list of supported events. This method is crucial for allowing the game engine to support both older versions of pygame and newer versions. It allows us to enumerate supported pygame events and initialize them dynamically. This ensures that the game engine will work with many versions of pygame. We enumerate all pygame event IDs and then use the pygame.event.event_name() method to get the event name. We then use a regular expression to match the event name against the like parameter. The names are scanned once per process ( pygame_event_names ). Parameters: like ( str , default: '.*' ) – A regular expression to match against the event names. Returns: list [ int ] – A list of pygame events whose names match the regular expression. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 81 82 83 84 85 86 87 88 89 90 91 92 93 94 95 96 97 98 99 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 def supported_events ( like : str = '.*' ) -> list [ int ]: """Return a list of supported events. This method is crucial for allowing the game engine to support both older versions of pygame and newer versions. It allows us to enumerate supported pygame events and initialize them dynamically. This ensures that the game engine will work with many versions of pygame. We enumerate all pygame event IDs and then use the pygame.event.event_name() method to get the event name. We then use a regular expression to match the event name against the like parameter. The names are scanned once per process (``pygame_event_names``). Args: like: A regular expression to match against the event names. Returns: A list of pygame events whose names match the regular expression. """ event_names = pygame_event_names () # Pygame 2.5.1 and maybe others have a bug where the event name lookup # is wrong. # # The error is: # # AttributeError: module 'pygame' has no attribute 'CONTROLLERDEVICEMAPPED'. # Did you mean: 'CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED'? # # This is a workaround for that. # # The controller documentation also indicates that it should be CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED patched_event_names = { 'APPDIDENTERBACKGROUND' : 'APP_DIDENTERBACKGROUND' , 'APPDIDENTERFOREGROUND' : 'APP_DIDENTERFOREGROUND' , 'APPLOWMEMORY' : 'APP_LOWMEMORY' , 'APPWILLENTERBACKGROUND' : 'APP_WILLENTERBACKGROUND' , 'APPWILLENTERFOREGROUND' : 'APP_WILLENTERFOREGROUND' , 'APPTERMINATING' : 'APP_TERMINATING' , 'CONTROLLERDEVICEMAPPED' : 'CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED' , 'RENDERDEVICERESET' : 'RENDER_DEVICE_RESET' , 'RENDERTARGETSRESET' : 'RENDER_TARGETS_RESET' , 'UNKNOWN' : 'K_UNKNOWN' , } event_list : list [ int ] = [] for event_name in list ( event_names ): # If there's a patched event name, use it, otherwise use event_name # # This works around a pygame bug for CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED patched_event_name = patched_event_names . get ( event_name . upper (), event_name ) LOG . info ( 'Adding Event: %s ' , patched_event_name ) if re . match ( like , patched_event_name . upper ()): event_list . append ( getattr ( pygame , patched_event_name . upper ())) return event_list

docs.text: Handle unhandled events. This method is called when an event is not handled by any of the event handlers. Each event type is only logged once to avoid per-frame log spam. Parameters: game ( GameOptionsProvider ) – The game instance. event ( HashableEvent ) – The event that wasn't handled. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – The positional arguments. **_kwargs ( Any , default: {} ) – The keyword arguments. Raises: UnhandledEventError – If no_unhandled_events is enabled and the event is not handled. This method is called when an event is not handled by any of the event handlers. Each event type is only logged once to avoid per-frame log spam. This is helpful for us to debug events that we haven't implemented yet. Args: game: The game instance. event: The event that wasn't handled. *_args: The positional arguments. **_kwargs: The keyword arguments. Raises: UnhandledEventError: If no_unhandled_events is enabled and the event is not handled. """ raw_options = getattr ( game , 'options' , None ) if not isinstance ( raw_options , dict ): # No options available (standalone stub without game context) — silently skip return options : dict [ str , Any ] = cast ( 'dict[str, Any]' , raw_options ) no_unhandled_events : bool | None = options . get ( 'no_unhandled_events' ) # Always raise if configured to treat unhandled events as errors if no_unhandled_events : raise UnhandledEventError ( UNHANDLED_EVENT_MSG . format ( event_name = pygame . event . event_name ( event . type ), event = event , ), ) if no_unhandled_events is None : LOG . error ( 'Error: no_unhandled_events is missing from the game options. ' "This shouldn't be possible." , ) return # Log each unhandled event type only once debug_events : bool | None = options . get ( 'debug_events' ) if debug_events and event . type not in _unhandled_event_types : _unhandled_event_types . add ( event . type ) LOG . warning ( 'Unhandled Event: %s %s ' , pygame . event . event_name ( event . type ), event , ) elif debug_events is None : LOG . error ( "Error: debug_events is missing from the game options. This shouldn't be possible." , )

ABC ): """Abstract base class for event interfaces.""" log : ClassVar [ logging . Logger ] = LOG # Declared here so EventStubs satisfy GameOptionsProvider when passed to # unhandled_event(). At runtime, the concrete class (Scene/GameEngine) # provides the real options dict via the ResourceManager singleton chain. options : dict [ str , Any ] @classmethod @override def __subclasshook__ ( cls , subclass : type [ Any ]) -> bool : """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented

docs.text: Bases: UserDict [ str , Any ] Hashable, immutable event class. Hashable events are cacheable, so we can mitigate some of the performance overhead of glitchygames' event subsystem by caching events, which will result in an immediate return if an identical event is encountered, saving some function overhead and processing. Games are welcome to use the built-in pygame event subsystem, but on_*_event callbacks will not be available in that case. The class is chosen by the event's type: HashableEvent(pygame.MOUSEMOTION, ...) builds a MouseMotionEvent ( EVENT_CLASSES ), so every event of a type is an instance of that type's class however it was built; custom and unknown types stay HashableEvent . The per-type classes only declare their fields (for the type checker): they store, hash, compare, pickle and serialize exactly as this class does. Equality is by type and fields, never by Python class. An event never changes after construction (it is hashed, and its hash is cached): item and attribute assignment, deletion, update , clear , pop , popitem , setdefault and |= raise TypeError; with_fields(**changes) returns a changed copy. Field values should be immutable too: a list or dict inside a game event is hashed by its contents once, so changing it afterwards leaves the cached hash stale. UserDict [ str , Any ]): # ruff: ignore[too-many-public-methods] """Hashable, immutable event class. Hashable events are cacheable, so we can mitigate some of the performance overhead of glitchygames' event subsystem by caching events, which will result in an immediate return if an identical event is encountered, saving some function overhead and processing. Games are welcome to use the built-in pygame event subsystem, but on_*_event callbacks will not be available in that case. The class is chosen by the event's type: ``HashableEvent(pygame.MOUSEMOTION, ...)`` builds a ``MouseMotionEvent`` (``EVENT_CLASSES``), so every event of a type is an instance of that type's class however it was built; custom and unknown types stay ``HashableEvent``. The per-type classes only declare their fields (for the type checker): they store, hash, compare, pickle and serialize exactly as this class does. Equality is by type and fields, never by Python class. An event never changes after construction (it is hashed, and its hash is cached): item and attribute assignment, deletion, ``update``, ``clear``, ``pop``, ``popitem``, ``setdefault`` and ``|=`` raise TypeError; ``with_fields(**changes)`` returns a changed copy. Field values should be immutable too: a list or dict inside a game event is hashed by its contents once, so changing it afterwards leaves the cached hash stale. """ # The cached hash lives in a slot, outside __dict__, so it is never one of the event's # fields (iteration, len, dict(), keys(), __eq__, pickling, to_json; BUGS.md #179 was a # hash stored in __dict__). None until the first __hash__ __slots__ = ( '_content_hash' ,) # Every event has its type (stored in __dict__ with the fields) type : int _content_hash : int | None def __new__ ( cls , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> Self : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Create a hashable event, as the class its type maps to (``EVENT_CLASSES``). Pygames events are not hashable by default. All of the construction happens here (``__init__`` is object's): one Python call per event, which matters for mouse-motion floods. A per-type class called with a type it cannot hold (another family's, or a type without a class of its own) raises ValueError. Args: type: The type of the event. *_args: Additional positional arguments (unused). **attributes: The event's fields. Returns: Self: An instance of the type's class: ``HashableEvent`` (or the class called) for a type with no class of its own. """ type_class = EVENT_CLASSES . get ( type ) if type_class is None : event_class = cls if cls not in _TYPED_EVENT_CLASSES else _refused_class ( cls , type ) elif cls is HashableEvent or cls is type_class : event_class = type_class else : event_class = _event_class_for ( cls = cls , event_type = type , type_class = type_class ) event = object . __new__ ( event_class ) # The event's attributes are exactly its type and fields: nothing else is stored in # __dict__ (a stored hash there showed up as a field, BUGS.md #179). Written through # __dict__ because attribute assignment raises (the event is immutable); the cached # hash is None until the first __hash__ fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = type fields . update ( attributes ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) # event_class is cls or one of its subclasses, so the event is a Self return cast ( 'Self' , event ) if TYPE_CHECKING : # The constructor's signature for the type checker (UserDict's __init__ takes a # mapping); at run time __init__ is object's def __init__ ( self , type : int , * _args : Any , ** attributes : Any ) -> None : # ruff: ignore[builtin-argument-shadowing] """Declare the constructor's arguments (``__new__`` builds the event).""" else : # Everything is done in __new__; object's __init__ accepts the constructor's arguments # (a class that overrides __new__ but not __init__) and does nothing, without a second # Python call per event __init__ = object . __init__ @staticmethod def from_pygame ( pygame_event : pygame . event . Event ) -> HashableEvent : """Wrap a pygame event, as its type's class (``EVENT_CLASSES``): the engine's dispatch. The same event the constructor builds (``HashableEvent(pygame_event.type, **pygame_event.dict)``), without unpacking the fields into keyword arguments twice: every dispatched event comes through here, mouse-motion floods included. Args: pygame_event: The raw event. Returns: HashableEvent: The event. """ event_type = pygame_event . type event = object . __new__ ( EVENT_CLASSES . get ( event_type , HashableEvent )) fields = event . __dict__ fields [ 'type' ] = event_type fields . update ( pygame_event . dict ) _CONTENT_HASH_SLOT . __set__ ( event , None ) return event @property def dict ( self : Self ) -> Mapping [ str , Any ]: """A read-only view of the event's type and fields (pygame's ``Event.dict``).""" return MappingProxyType ( self . __dict__ ) def with_fields ( self : Self , ** changes : object ) -> Self : """Return a copy of the event with some fields changed or added (the same class). Args: **changes: The fields to change or add; ``type`` may be given only unchanged. Returns: Self: The changed copy; this event is left as it was. Raises: TypeError: If ``changes`` gives the event another type. """ fields : dict [ str , object ] = { ** self . __dict__ , ** changes } new_type = fields . pop ( 'type' ) if new_type != self . type : raise TypeError ( EVENT_TYPE_CHANGE_MSG . format ( old = self . type , new = new_type )) return self . __class__ ( self . type , ** fields ) def to_json ( self : Self ) -> builtins . dict [ str , JsonValue ]: """Describe the event as JSON: ``{"type": <number>, "attributes": {...}}``. The attributes are encoded as a recording encodes an event's (``glitchygames.recording.json_safe_value``: tuples as lists, lists, dicts, bytes and non-finite floats tagged), except that a window reference is written as None, as a replay serves one. ``from_json`` reverses it. Returns: dict[str, JsonValue]: The JSON-safe description (``json.dumps`` accepts it). """ # Deferred: glitchygames.recording imports the sources and input modules, which import # the events package from glitchygames.recording import ( EVENT_ATTRIBUTES_FIELD , EVENT_TYPE_FIELD , json_safe_value , ) attributes : dict [ str , JsonValue ] = { name : json_safe_value ( None if isinstance ( value , pygame . Window ) else value ) for name , value in self . __dict__ . items () if name != 'type' } return { EVENT_TYPE_FIELD : self . type , EVENT_ATTRIBUTES_FIELD : attributes } @classmethod def from_json ( cls , record : Mapping [ str , JsonValue ]) -> Self : """Build an event from ``to_json``'s description (or a recording's event record). A recorded window reference (a recording's records hold them) becomes None, as a replay serves it. The class is the type's (``EVENT_CLASSES``), as for the constructor. A malformed record raises the recording's ``TraceFormatError`` (``glitchygames.recording.event_from_record``). Args: record: ``{"type": <number>, "attributes": {...}}``, as read back from JSON. Returns: Self: The event. """ # Deferred: glitchygames.recording imports the sources and input modules, which import # the events package from glitchygames.recording import ( WINDOW_REFERENCE , RecordedReference , event_from_record , ) pygame_event = event_from_record ( dict ( record )) attributes = { name : ( None if isinstance ( value , RecordedReference ) and value . kind == WINDOW_REFERENCE else value ) for name , value in pygame_event . dict . items () } return cls ( pygame_event . type , ** attributes ) def _refuse_change ( self : Self , operation : str ) -> NoReturn : """Raise the TypeError every mutator raises. Args: operation: What the caller tried, for the message. Raises: TypeError: Always: events are immutable. """ raise TypeError ( IMMUTABLE_EVENT_MSG . format ( cls = type ( self ) . __name__ , operation = operation )) @override def __setattr__ ( self : Self , name : str , value : object ) -> None : """Refuse: events are immutable (use ``with_fields``).""" self . _refuse_change ( f 'set { name !r} ' ) @override def __delattr__ ( self : Self , name : str ) -> None : """Refuse: events are immutable.""" self . _refuse_change ( f 'delete { name !r} ' ) @override def __setitem__ ( self : Self , key : str , item : object ) -> None : """Refuse: events are immutable (use ``with_fields``).""" self . _refuse_change ( f 'set { key !r} ' ) @override def __getitem__ ( self : Self , key : str ) -> object : """Get an item from the object. Returns: object: The item at the given index. """ return self . __dict__ [ key ] @override def __len__ ( self : Self ) -> int : """Return the length of the object. Returns: int: The number of items. """ return len ( self . __dict__ ) @override def __delitem__ ( self : Self , key : str ) -> None : """Refuse: events are immutable.""" self . _refuse_change ( f 'delete { key !r} ' ) @override def clear ( self : Self ) -> None : """Refuse: events are immutable.""" self . _refuse_change ( 'clear' ) @override def pop ( self : Self , key : str , default : object = None ) -> NoReturn : """Refuse: events are immutable.""" self . _refuse_change ( f 'pop { key !r} ' ) @override def popitem ( self : Self ) -> NoReturn : """Refuse: events are immutable.""" self . _refuse_change ( 'popitem' ) @override def setdefault ( self : Self , key : str , default : object = None ) -> NoReturn : """Refuse: events are immutable (use ``with_fields``).""" self . _refuse_change ( f 'setdefault { key !r} ' ) @override def update ( self : Self , * args : object , ** kwargs : object ) -> None : """Refuse: events are immutable (use ``with_fields``).""" self . _refuse_change ( 'update' ) @override def __ior__ ( self : Self , other : object ) -> NoReturn : """Refuse: events are immutable (``event | changes`` builds a changed copy).""" self . _refuse_change ( '|=' ) @override def __or__ ( self : Self , other : object ) -> Self : """Return a copy with ``other``'s fields changed or added (``with_fields``). UserDict's own ``|`` read ``self.data``, which this class never sets, so it raised AttributeError. Returns: Self: The changed copy, or NotImplemented when ``other`` is not a mapping. """ if not isinstance ( other , Mapping ): return NotImplemented changes = cast ( 'Mapping[str, object]' , other ) return self . with_fields ( ** changes ) @override def __ror__ ( self : Self , other : object ) -> Self : """Return a copy with ``other``'s fields added where the event has none. docs.text: Shared-instance aggregator base class for event proxies. A ResourceManager subclass will generally pass all requests through to its proxy object(s), however, for certain types of resources such as joysticks, the subclass will manage things itself. This architecture reduces code footprint, and allows maxium flexibility when needed, at the expense of a bit of abstraction. Unless you're implementing a new pygame event manager, you probably don't need to worry about this. Shared instances ( SHARES_INSTANCE , True for the event managers): a class has one instance, the first one constructed. Constructing it again returns that instance as it is, without running __init__ again (BUGS.md #198), so MouseEventManager() is the manager the GameEngine made to process mouse events with. Each engine run releases them ( release_shared_instances ) before it makes its managers, so a second engine in one process (a recording, then its replay) builds its own. A class that sets SHARES_INSTANCE = False gets a new instance at every construction: the proxies (a manager owns its own, and the controller manager one per controller) and EventManager ( GameEngine and SceneManager , whose own __new__ keeps its singleton). Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 334 335 336 337 338 339 340 341 342 343 344 345 346 347 348 349 350 351 352 353 354 355 356 357 358 359 360 361 362 363 364 365 366 367 368 369 370 371 372 373 374 375 376 377 378 379 380 381 382 383 384 385 386 387 388 389 390 391 392 393 394 395 396 397 398 399 400 401 402 403 404 405 406 407 408 409 410 411 412 413 414 415 416 417 418 419 420 421 422 423 424 425 426 427 428 429 430 431 432 433 434 435 436 437 438 439 440 441 442 443 444 445 446 447 448 449 450 class ResourceManager : """Shared-instance aggregator base class for event proxies. A ResourceManager subclass will generally pass all requests through to its proxy object(s), however, for certain types of resources such as joysticks, the subclass will manage things itself. This architecture reduces code footprint, and allows maxium flexibility when needed, at the expense of a bit of abstraction. Unless you're implementing a new pygame event manager, you probably don't need to worry about this. Shared instances (``SHARES_INSTANCE``, True for the event managers): a class has one instance, the first one constructed. Constructing it again returns that instance as it is, without running ``__init__`` again (BUGS.md #198), so ``MouseEventManager()`` is the manager the GameEngine made to process mouse events with. Each engine run releases them (``release_shared_instances``) before it makes its managers, so a second engine in one process (a recording, then its replay) builds its own. A class that sets ``SHARES_INSTANCE = False`` gets a new instance at every construction: the proxies (a manager owns its own, and the controller manager one per controller) and ``EventManager`` (``GameEngine`` and ``SceneManager``, whose own ``__new__`` keeps its singleton). """ log : ClassVar [ logging . Logger ] = LOG # False: every construction makes a new instance (see the class docstring) SHARES_INSTANCE : ClassVar [ bool ] = True __instances__ : ClassVar [ dict [ type , Any ]] = {} def __init_subclass__ ( cls , ** keyword_arguments : Any ) -> None : """Wrap the subclass's own ``__init__`` so its shared instance is initialized once. Args: **keyword_arguments: Passed on to ``object.__init_subclass__``. """ super () . __init_subclass__ ( ** keyword_arguments ) own_initializer = cls . __dict__ . get ( '__init__' ) if own_initializer is not None : # Through type.__setattr__: the subclass's __init__ is replaced by its wrapper, whose # signature a type checker cannot match to the base __init__ it overrides type . __setattr__ ( cls , '__init__' , _initialize_once ( own_initializer )) def __new__ ( cls : type [ Self ], * _args : Any , ** _kwargs : Any ) -> Self : """Return the class's shared instance, or a new instance for an unshared class. Args: cls: The class. *_args: The positional arguments (``__init__`` takes them). **_kwargs: The keyword arguments (``__init__`` takes them). Returns: The shared instance (made now if there is none yet), or a new instance. """ if not cls . SHARES_INSTANCE : return object . __new__ ( cls ) if cls not in ResourceManager . __instances__ : ResourceManager . __instances__ [ cls ] = object . __new__ ( cls ) LOG . debug ( 'Created Resource Manager: %s ' , cls ) return ResourceManager . __instances__ [ cls ] @_initialize_once def __init__ ( self : Self , game : object ) -> None : # ruff: ignore[unused-method-argument] """Initialize the resource manager. Args: game: The game instance (accepted for subclass compatibility). """ super () . __init__ () self . proxies : list [ Any ] = [] @classmethod def release_shared_instances ( cls ) -> None : """Forget every shared instance, so the next construction of each class makes a new one. ``GameEngine`` calls it before it makes its event managers: a new engine run builds managers of its own (opening devices through its own doors), not the earlier run's. """ ResourceManager . __instances__ . clear () def __getattr__ ( self : Self , attr : str ) -> Callable [ ... , Any ]: """Get an attribute from the first proxy that has it. This method is called when an attribute is not found. Args: attr: The attribute to get. Returns: The attribute. Raises: AttributeError: If no proxy has the attribute (or there are no proxies yet). """ # The proxies themselves are an instance attribute: before __init__ sets them there are # none to try (looking them up here would recurse) if attr == 'proxies' : raise AttributeError ( MISSING_ATTRIBUTE_MSG . format ( cls = type ( self ), attr = attr )) # Try each proxy in turn (BUGS.md #198: the lookup returned or raised on the first) for proxy in self . proxies : try : return getattr ( proxy , attr ) except AttributeError : continue if self . proxies : self . log . error ( 'No proxies for %s . %s ' , type ( self ), attr ) raise AttributeError ( NO_PROXIES_MSG . format ( cls = type ( self ), attr = attr ))

docs.text: Allow every event type at SDL, SYSWMEVENT only when the game asked for it. SYSWMEVENT carries the window system's raw messages (on x11 every X event: focus, exposure, property changes; on Windows each window message), which SDL itself leaves disabled. A plain pygame.event.set_allowed(None) would enable them too, flooding the queue (and every recording and instant-replay journal) with messages almost no game reads. A game opts in with NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES = True on its scene class; they then reach on_sys_wm_event as plain HashableEvent s holding pygame's platform fields. Blocked through pygame.event.set_blocked , so pygame.event.get_blocked reports it truthfully afterwards: before any pygame call blocks it, pygame-ce 2.5.8 reports SYSWMEVENT as allowed while SDL ignores it, and a snapshot-and-restore of the blocked types (the replay's input blocking) would then enable it. Parameters: native_window_messages ( bool ) – Whether SYSWMEVENT is allowed too. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 200 201 202 203 204 205 206 207 208 def allow_every_event_type ( * , native_window_messages : bool ) -> None : """Allow every event type at SDL, SYSWMEVENT only when the game asked for it. SYSWMEVENT carries the window system's raw messages (on x11 every X event: focus, exposure, property changes; on Windows each window message), which SDL itself leaves disabled. A plain ``pygame.event.set_allowed(None)`` would enable them too, flooding the queue (and every recording and instant-replay journal) with messages almost no game reads. A game opts in with ``NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES = True`` on its scene class; they then reach ``on_sys_wm_event`` as plain ``HashableEvent``s holding pygame's platform fields. Blocked through ``pygame.event.set_blocked``, so ``pygame.event.get_blocked`` reports it truthfully afterwards: before any pygame call blocks it, pygame-ce 2.5.8 reports SYSWMEVENT as allowed while SDL ignores it, and a snapshot-and-restore of the blocked types (the replay's input blocking) would then enable it. Args: native_window_messages: Whether SYSWMEVENT is allowed too. """ pygame . event . set_allowed ( None ) if native_window_messages : pygame . event . set_allowed ( pygame . SYSWMEVENT ) else : pygame . event . set_blocked ( pygame . SYSWMEVENT )

docs.text: Return the names pygame gives its event ids, scanned once per process. The scan asks pygame.event.event_name for every id below pygame.NUMEVENTS (65,536 calls, about 4 ms), and supported_events runs a dozen times as this module is imported: every process the engine starts paid for it a dozen times. The names are the installed pygame's own (a table compiled into it, the same before and after pygame.init() and pygame.event.custom_type() ), so one scan answers every call. Returns: frozenset [ str ] – The names, duplicates dropped (as supported_events always read them). Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 56 57 58 59 60 61 62 63 64 65 66 67 68 69 70 71 72 73 74 75 76 77 78 @functools . cache def pygame_event_names () -> frozenset [ str ]: """Return the names pygame gives its event ids, scanned once per process. The scan asks ``pygame.event.event_name`` for every id below ``pygame.NUMEVENTS`` (65,536 calls, about 4 ms), and ``supported_events`` runs a dozen times as this module is imported: every process the engine starts paid for it a dozen times. The names are the installed pygame's own (a table compiled into it, the same before and after ``pygame.init()`` and ``pygame.event.custom_type()``), so one scan answers every call. Returns: The names, duplicates dropped (as ``supported_events`` always read them). """ # Get a list of all of the events # by name, but ignore duplicates, and 'Unknown', the name of every id pygame does not name # (it was ``set('Unknown')``, the set of its letters, so 'Unknown' stayed and the patch below # turned it into K_UNKNOWN, a key code: ALL_EVENTS held 0 twice, as NOEVENT and as K_UNKNOWN, # BUGS.md #238) event_name_generator = ( pygame . event . event_name ( event_num ) for event_num in range ( pygame . NUMEVENTS ) ) return frozenset ( set ( event_name_generator ) - { 'Unknown' })

docs.text: Return a list of supported events. This method is crucial for allowing the game engine to support both older versions of pygame and newer versions. It allows us to enumerate supported pygame events and initialize them dynamically. This ensures that the game engine will work with many versions of pygame. We enumerate all pygame event IDs and then use the pygame.event.event_name() method to get the event name. We then use a regular expression to match the event name against the like parameter. The names are scanned once per process ( pygame_event_names ). Parameters: like ( str , default: '.*' ) – A regular expression to match against the event names. Returns: list [ int ] – A list of pygame events whose names match the regular expression. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 81 82 83 84 85 86 87 88 89 90 91 92 93 94 95 96 97 98 99 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 def supported_events ( like : str = '.*' ) -> list [ int ]: """Return a list of supported events. This method is crucial for allowing the game engine to support both older versions of pygame and newer versions. It allows us to enumerate supported pygame events and initialize them dynamically. This ensures that the game engine will work with many versions of pygame. We enumerate all pygame event IDs and then use the pygame.event.event_name() method to get the event name. We then use a regular expression to match the event name against the like parameter. The names are scanned once per process (``pygame_event_names``). Args: like: A regular expression to match against the event names. Returns: A list of pygame events whose names match the regular expression. """ event_names = pygame_event_names () # Pygame 2.5.1 and maybe others have a bug where the event name lookup # is wrong. # # The error is: # # AttributeError: module 'pygame' has no attribute 'CONTROLLERDEVICEMAPPED'. # Did you mean: 'CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED'? # # This is a workaround for that. # # The controller documentation also indicates that it should be CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED patched_event_names = { 'APPDIDENTERBACKGROUND' : 'APP_DIDENTERBACKGROUND' , 'APPDIDENTERFOREGROUND' : 'APP_DIDENTERFOREGROUND' , 'APPLOWMEMORY' : 'APP_LOWMEMORY' , 'APPWILLENTERBACKGROUND' : 'APP_WILLENTERBACKGROUND' , 'APPWILLENTERFOREGROUND' : 'APP_WILLENTERFOREGROUND' , 'APPTERMINATING' : 'APP_TERMINATING' , 'CONTROLLERDEVICEMAPPED' : 'CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED' , 'RENDERDEVICERESET' : 'RENDER_DEVICE_RESET' , 'RENDERTARGETSRESET' : 'RENDER_TARGETS_RESET' , 'UNKNOWN' : 'K_UNKNOWN' , } event_list : list [ int ] = [] for event_name in list ( event_names ): # If there's a patched event name, use it, otherwise use event_name # # This works around a pygame bug for CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED patched_event_name = patched_event_names . get ( event_name . upper (), event_name ) LOG . info ( 'Adding Event: %s ' , patched_event_name ) if re . match ( like , patched_event_name . upper ()): event_list . append ( getattr ( pygame , patched_event_name . upper ())) return event_list

docs.text: Handle unhandled events. This method is called when an event is not handled by any of the event handlers. Each event type is only logged once to avoid per-frame log spam. This is helpful for us to debug events that we haven't implemented yet. Parameters: game ( GameOptionsProvider ) – The game instance. event ( HashableEvent ) – The event that wasn't handled. *_args ( Any , default: () ) – The positional arguments. **_kwargs ( Any , default: {} ) – The keyword arguments. Raises: UnhandledEventError – If no_unhandled_events is enabled and the event is not handled. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 224 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 247 248 249 250 251 252 253 254 255 256 257 258 259 260 261 262 263 264 265 266 267 268 269 270 271 272 273 274 275 276 277 278 279 280 281 282 283 284 def unhandled_event ( game : GameOptionsProvider , event : HashableEvent , * _args : Any , ** _kwargs : Any , ) -> None : """Handle unhandled events. This method is called when an event is not handled by any of the event handlers. Each event type is only logged once to avoid per-frame log spam. This is helpful for us to debug events that we haven't implemented yet. Args: game: The game instance. event: The event that wasn't handled. *_args: The positional arguments. **_kwargs: The keyword arguments. """ raw_options = getattr ( game , 'options' , None ) if not isinstance ( raw_options , dict ): # No options available (standalone stub without game context) — silently skip return options : dict [ str , Any ] = cast ( 'dict[str, Any]' , raw_options ) no_unhandled_events : bool | None = options . get ( 'no_unhandled_events' ) # Always raise if configured to treat unhandled events as errors if no_unhandled_events : raise UnhandledEventError ( UNHANDLED_EVENT_MSG . format ( event_name = pygame . event . event_name ( event . type ), event = event , ), ) if no_unhandled_events is None : LOG . error ( 'Error: no_unhandled_events is missing from the game options.
