Instant replay ( SceneManager.instant_replay , start_instant_replay ): the active scene's instant-replay journal (glitchygames/instant_replay.py) plays in a scope of kind 'instant' from its start_frame , returning to the scene shown (the journal's scene, or the pause screen presenting it), with no exit on input: the player's presses reach nothing, and the game decides when it ends (the journal's end, or SceneManager.end_playback from a supervisor, which reads the player's polled input from SceneManager.playback_player_input ). The frames before the last Scene.INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS of frame time are fast-forwarded ( fast_forward_frame_count ); the rest are shown at the game's pace. Frame time, not game time: the shown part takes that long to watch, a paused stretch in it included. Refused (False, nothing starts) when the scene keeps no journal (it does not offer instant replay, its first logic frame has not run, or a scope plays) or the journal holds more frame time than Scene.MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS . The request is answered as any playback request is (rule 1: a playback of the journal gets the recorded answer and requests nothing), so a scene that asks after every goal plays back across its earlier replays. The journal's recording is taken as the request is made: the frame that asks is not in it (it ends live, before the scope begins). Rumble and live voices: a playback never rumbles the player's real controllers, neither while fast-forwarding nor in the frames it shows (a demo's crash buzzing the player's hands would be the playback's, not the game's). While a scope plays, SceneManager.rumble is a rumble controller of its own (the playback scene's pulses, sustained levels and shakes go there and reach no device); the live game's controller waits untouched and is back when the scope ends, so a playback's pulse never carries into live play. The live scene's synth voices (and those of the scene the scope returns to, and of the previous scene as it began: the game behind a pause screen an instant replay began from) pause behind the scope and play on after it ( LiveAudio.update 's paused_owners ), even when the playback's own scene switches change previous_scene ; the playback scene's own voices end with it. Limits: a live supervisor that posts with post_event (the game's own posts, which a replay expects the replayed code to make again) during a scope makes a session that a --replay-trace replay without that supervisor cannot match. Supervisors post with post_input_event , which replays without them, whatever the event's type (rule 5). A scope that fast-forwards inside a restarted replay's rebuild silences on top of the rebuild's silence: the end of its fast-forward may resume music during the rebuild (which pauses it again after the next frame). A scene must be rebuildable from its start ( Scene.replay_arguments ). Of a scene that arrived by a transition, the arrival step is repeated, but the events the ride delivered to it (releases, window and device events) are not: a scene they change diverges. The first logic frame's earlier posts are counted from the internal-post tracker, so they are exact while posts are tracked (while recording or replaying, and from the first setup of a scene that keeps an instant-replay journal: glitchygames/instant_replay.py, whose JournalRecording a scope plays from its start_frame ). A --record-trace recording of a session that played a scope cannot itself be played in-game from a frame inside or after that scope: a recorder writes no playback_answers or resume_bridge (only an instant-replay journal does), so its scene's playback requests and its resumption after the scope are not known (it replays exactly with --replay-trace , which runs the scope again). Rumble in joystick mode asks the devices door for the joysticks (glitchygames/input/rumble.py); inside a scope each send still asks the scope's door, with a device cache of its own, and then sends to no device (rule 8), so the played recording's answers are taken as it gave them. The scope's rumble controller starts fresh, though: a rumble the live game sent before the played scene began, still running when it was recorded, is not known to it, so its sends (and the counts they ask) can fall on other frames than the recording's; that matters only when the played recording's joystick count changed part way. A rebaseline replays OLD's inputs on the current code and writes what that code did to a new recording, NEW, with a summary of what changed. It is how a recording used as a regression test (tests/fixtures/replays, glitchygames/testing/replays.py) follows an intentional change; replacing OLD with NEW stays a deliberate, reviewed step: NEW is never OLD (refused), and nothing replaces OLD. The rules: Options: --rebaseline NEW needs --replay-trace OLD and --headless (a watched replay holds frames and takes the viewer's keys, so it is refused rather than made headless behind the user's back), and refuses NEW or NEW's partial file (rule 4) naming OLD's file, --record-trace (the rebaseline writes its own recording), --audit and --replay-digest (the audit's tools: a rebaseline is not audited) and --replay-fps real (FPS events from this machine's frame times would be recorded as the new baseline); each refusal exits ExitCode.OPTIONS_REFUSED ( rebaseline_refusal ). An unusable OLD is refused as by any replay ( ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT , ExitCode.MISSING_INPUT ), but for one thing only a rebaseline accepts: a recording made before logical names (no game in its header, glitchygames/logical_names.py) of a game that has moved since. Its game is matched by its class's qualified name, whatever the recorded module, and so are its scene starts without scene ( modules_not_compared in glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 17 there; a name several loaded classes share is still refused); NEW holds the current logical names (rule 3), so it replays strictly. This is the backward-compatibility path for such recordings: a plain replay refuses them, naming this command. A recording whose classes moved to another logical module is converted the same way (the logical modules are not compared, the qualified names are); a plain replay refuses it, naming this command. Replay: OLD is replayed as usual (glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 17 there), but a divergence does not stop it ( ReplayOptions.stop_on_divergence False): it runs to OLD's last frame, or until the game ends, noting every frame that differs and every sprite that differs in them. OLD's input the run never received is never carried elsewhere (that would invent an input sequence OLD does not have); it is counted instead: the external events of batches a frame did not pump (it pumped fewer times than recorded), and OLD's frames after the game ended. Recording: RecordingSources over the replay ( replayed ; glitchygames/recording.py) write NEW with OLD's inputs, as the replay's doors served them: the event batches (origins from the replay's merge, so code-posted events stay internal and replaying NEW delivers nothing twice), dt , input_changes , re-applied control events, and each frame's saves_opened , devices_opened and device_enumeration copied from OLD's frame; and the current code's sprites and markers. The header is OLD's, except the game's names ( game_class , game_module , game ): they are this run's ( rebaseline_header ). NEW's frames stack this run's content hash and processing time in front of OLD's histories, and its header this run's measurement_runs entry in front of OLD's (glitchygames/recording_history.py), so an unchanged game shows the same hash one entry deeper, and a changed one shows which frames changed. Writing: NEW is written to NEW.partial ( glitchygames.output_files.partial_path ) and moved into place once the run ended normally, so NEW is never left half written; a run that a crash, a signal or the game's own failing exit ( sys.exit(1) ) ended early writes nothing (the partial file is removed). The game's own successful exit ( sys.exit(0) , sys.exit() ) is the game ending early, as quit_game() is: NEW holds the frames that ran (not the one it left part way through) and the run exits ExitCode.REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST (rule 5). A partial file that cannot be written is refused before the replay starts, on one line, with ExitCode.CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT ( GameEngine._refuse_unwritable_outputs ). If the final move fails, the finished partial file is kept, its path logged and printed, and the run exits ExitCode.CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT . Each tool is reachable two ways, both built from that one table so their names and options never drift apart: as a flag on any game's own command line ( mygame --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz ), added by GameEngine.args ( registry.add_game_flags ); as a subcommand of the glitchygames command ( glitchygames replay-trace run.jsonl.gz , glitchygames/replay/tools/command.py), which starts the game as a child process (glitchygames/replay/tools/children.py) whenever the game has to run. Nothing is imported here, so importing one tool module loads only what it needs. Importing any of them never imports pytest. children # Games run as child processes: finding a game, and starting it with the engine's flags. Every tool that has to run a game ( glitchygames record-trace , glitchygames replay-trace , the replay pytest plugin, the measurement run) starts it as a child process, with the tool's flag on its command line ( --replay-trace PATH ). The game's GameEngine(game=Game) adds those flags to its own command line (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py), so the game never knows how it was started. Two ways to name the game: By a console script ( [project.scripts] ): game_entry_point finds its entry point, and replay_command loads and calls it in the child the way the installed console script would. recording_console_script tells which console script replays a recording under a fixtures/replays/ directory; console_script_for_game_module which of several starts a recorded game's module. By what the user typed (the command's GAME ): resolve_game reads it as a script path, an entry point MODULE:CALLABLE , an installed console script or an importable module ( GameLaunch ), and launch_game starts it with the tool's arguments. A console script is never run as its installed executable ( bin/<script> ). Its entry point is loaded and called in a python -c child ( entry_point_command ) instead, which is what that executable does. It runs on this interpreter (the one whose packages were searched for the entry point), needs no executable on PATH , and works wherever the metadata is installed: a non-editable install in nox's sessions, or a stand-in game's dist-info in the engine's tests, which has no executable at all. The replay pytest plugin has always started games this way. replay_recording_headless and rebaseline_recording_headless run a recording's replay (or rebaseline) headless through a console script; the replay pytest plugin (glitchygames/testing/replays.py), the bundled demos' test and the measurement run use them. Each frame is told apart on its own, with no memory between frames: OLD's background colors are the exact colors covering at least BACKGROUND_COLOR_SHARE (5%) of OLD's frame (a floor, a wall); OLD's items are the pixels where OLD differs from NEW in a color that is none of them. So a dot OLD ate (OLD shows floor) leaves NEW's dot exact, and a dot NEW ate shows OLD's over NEW's floor (the user's report on D13's rule, which learned a background where the runs agreed and so took both runs' dots for background). Known costs: OLD's sprite pixels in a background color are not shown (a sprite drawn in the floor's color); a background of many small colors (a texture or a gradient, each color under 5%) may show some of them as items; and a single color covering 5% or more of OLD's frame is background even when it is OLD's item (a large sprite, about 139x139 at 800x480, many pickups of one color, a full-screen overlay), so it vanishes from the ghost. Telling the colors apart sorts OLD's frame once per new OLD frame: about 2 ms for a game's frame, up to about 19 ms for one whose every pixel has a color of its own (noise; a textured backdrop falls in between). A held last frame (rule 5) is drawn by the same rule, and the labels are drawn as before. Vectorized with numpy on the presented copy. Pausing freezes the ghost (decisions 18 and 19 as amended, Task D14; the user: "Yes, the games should pause."). Frames are paired by the game-frame clock (glitchygames/game_frames.py), not by the frame number a recording counts: a frame whose logic ran on a pause screen shows the game frame before it, so OLD's frame stays drawn (no label) until the game runs again. UNUSABLE_INPUT , reason = ( f 'OLD was recorded on a { old_size [ 0 ] } x { old_size [ 1 ] } display and NEW on a ' f ' { new_size [ 0 ] } x { new_size [ 1 ] } one: an onion skin needs the same size' ), ) golden_traces # The golden-trace harness: a game driven headless with scripted input, every sprite sampled. A golden trace is the rect and visibility of every sprite in the active scene's all_sprites , recorded after each frame of a scripted, fully deterministic run ( record_trace ). The harness knows a game only by its scene class and its input script ( InputScript ), so it runs any game built on the engine: the record-golden-trace tool (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py) runs it on the game it is given, with an input script named MODULE:NAME ( load_input_script ). Our own games' scripts and their golden traces are this repository's (scripts/golden_inputs.py, scripts/record_golden_traces.py, tests/world/test_golden_traces.py). Determinism Every frame runs with dt fixed at 1/60 second. A game started with --random-seed ( random_seed ; our goldens pass RANDOM_SEED ) draws all the randomness of the engine's named streams ( glitchygames/randomness.py ) from it. Without one the run rolls a random seed, as any run does (the user's seed rule, 2026-10-26), and the trace names it ( random_seed , as a recording's header does), so the golden can be made again under it. Nothing is patched. A game clock read from Scene.game_time is driven by the fixed dt (exactly 1/60 second per unpaused frame), so no clock is patched. Save files go to a fresh temporary directory, so high scores on disk cannot leak in. Events the host environment posts (window focus, window shown, audio devices, ...) are discarded before each frame. SDL's dummy video driver posts a focus-lost event at startup, which would auto-pause a game that pauses on focus loss. Ids: each sprite gets <ClassName>#<n> the first time it is seen, where n counts that class's sprites in order of first appearance over the whole run. Ids never renumber when a sprite is removed (a collected coin, a dead ball). Scope and maintenance GoldenTraceSceneManager.run_frame runs SceneManager._run_frame , the same frame body SceneManager.start() runs (both branches, and the --record-trace hook). Frame pacing, timing and the first frame's measured dt are out of scope: the harness fixes dt at 1/60 and never sleeps. The trace format (gzip JSON Lines with keyframes and deltas, StableSpriteIds , the reader and writer) lives in glitchygames/tracing.py ; identical traces give identical bytes. The harness never chooses the video driver: whoever runs it does (SDL's dummy drivers in the tests and scripts/record_golden_traces.py, --headless on a game). Importing this module imports the engine ( GameEngine ), so the tool table imports it only when the tool runs. A scripted session is a game run for real, frame loop and all, with --record-trace , while a supervisor (glitchygames/supervision.py) plays an input script ( InputScript , glitchygames/replay/tools/golden_traces.py): at the supervisor slot of frame N it posts the script's key events and per-frame input for frame N + 1 with glitchygames.recording.post_input_event , so the recording holds them as external input, exactly what a player's keys are. frame_count plays the script's frames 0 to frame_count - 1. The record-session tool (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py) runs it on the game it is given, with the input script named MODULE:NAME ( load_input_script ); our own games' golden replays are recorded by scripts/record_scripted_session.py. The controls tail ( controls_tail ): after the script's frames the supervisor plays it. Its first frame releases every key the script left held; then it presses whatever it holds (a golden replay's tail exercises the controls the script does not), and it must end with the game's own quit control. The game ends the run: the recording's last frame holds the QUIT the game posted (internal), so a replay whose game no longer quits diverges ("missing internal event"). A game still running QUIT_WAIT_FRAMES after the tail's last input fails the recording ( GameDidNotQuitError ). A session is N + T + 2 frames long, T being the tail frame of its last input (the quit): the game posts QUIT while handling that frame's events, and the next frame (the last) pumps it. Without a tail, at frame N - 1 the supervisor ends the run ( SceneManager.quit_requested , no event), so the recording holds frames 0 to N - 1 and no quit. Unlike the golden-trace harness, the session runs the real frame loop ( SceneManager.start ): frames are paced at the game's target FPS, each frame's dt is measured and FPS events are posted, so a --replay-trace replay of the recording (which runs the same loop) matches it frame for frame. Recording takes real time (about 60 frames a second), and two recordings of the same script never have the same bytes (measured frame times differ). Script placements move sprites directly (they are not input), so a session may not run a frame a placement is scheduled before, unless the placements only steer the script's own input ( input_only_placements : PaddleSlap's release its tracked keys and resume tracking). Input scheduled before frame 0 cannot be posted (there is no supervisor slot before it) and is refused. A game that reads its controls from the frame's polled input ( current_input() ) never sees a posted event there: SDL updates its polled state only for a real device's events. With polled_input the session's live snapshots show the supervisor's posted input ( PostedPolledInput , polled_input_follows ), as a real player's would. Only then: without it a session records the snapshots it always did (held keys absent), so a game's re-recordings keep their content hashes. Host environment events (window shown and focus, audio devices) the dummy video driver posts are external and are recorded; a replay serves them as recorded, so they are harmless. The session drops those queued before the first frame (as the golden-trace harness does), because SDL's dummy driver posts a focus-lost event at startup that would auto-pause a game that pauses on it. The session never chooses the video driver: whoever runs it does (SDL's dummy drivers in the tests and scripts/record_scripted_session.py, --headless on a game). Importing this module imports the engine ( GameEngine ), so the tool table imports it only when the tool runs. Every setting has a default that fits a standard layout, so a project with no such table (a player's own local runs, a game the engine has never seen) works as it is. The keys are kebab-case, as pyproject.toml's are (stage D's settings table): games : the console scripts the tools run when given no game (default: the project's [project.scripts] ). golden-globs : where the golden replays are, as globs relative to the project root. ledger-directory : where measured rows are kept as row files (a git pathspec too, so it is relative). pending-ledger : where measured rows wait to be published (default: in the project's local directory, .glitchygames/ , outside the ledger directory so it is never committed with the rows). published-ledger : where the ledger is published, as REF:PATH (what git show reads), or nothing published (the default). landed-ref : the ref whose commits count as landed. measured-paths and unmeasured-paths : what a code tree holds, as git pathspecs (glitchygames/code_tree.py). recording-renames : recordings that moved, old repository path -> new, so a recording's history follows it. Each path is relative, no new path is itself an old one (lookups are one hop: an old path names the final one directly), and no two old paths are the same path written two ways; refused when read otherwise. recording_renames_problems finds a new path that does not exist (a check of the files, which reading settings never does). game-timeout-seconds : how long glitchygames verify and glitchygames measure wait for each game they start ( GAME --verify , GAME --measure ) before stopping it and failing it (default: an hour, DEFAULT_GAME_TIMEOUT_SECONDS ). A game replays each of its recordings in a child of its own with a timeout of its own ( REPLAY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS ); this bounds what never ends at all, such as an editor or a server among [project.scripts] . Stored paths are relative to the project root. Every path the tools write into a file (a recording header's path options, a run's rebaselined_from , a ledger row's recording) is relative to the project root, the one these settings are read from ( find_project_root : the nearest project; --project-root where a tool's subcommand takes it), POSIX-style; a path inside another checkout of the same project (the same [project] name ) relative to that checkout's root; any other path outside the project as its file name only ( stored_path ), so no user name, home or scratch directory is ever written into a file meant to be committed. Settings only name paths, relative to the project root: nothing is created or checked on disk when they are read. A path that doesn't exist yet (no ledger directory before the first measurement) is created or reported by the tool that writes or reads it. A tool writing into the project's local directory ( .glitchygames/ ) creates it with ensure_local_directory , which puts a .gitignore of * there, as pytest does for its cache, so nothing in it is committed. Two loops share the frame loop of SceneManager.start while a replay is watched (glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 14): OUTER, the viewer ( ReplayViewer ): owns the window. It ticks at a fixed real-time rate ( CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND , on glitchygames.clock.measured_seconds , never replayed), whatever the replay's speed and whether it is paused. Each tick it reads the viewer's keys ( ReplayControls , once per press), refreshes the status line, and presents one frame: the inner game's latest, with the status bar, start screen and debug overlay drawn on a copy. INNER, the recorded game: steps at its recorded frame times and never receives viewer input. Its frames always run in full (events, logic, update, render), exactly as recorded; only their presentation is left to the outer tick ( ReplaySources.presents_frames is False while watched). The contract between them, asked through EngineSources.hold_frame before each inner frame: No tick open: sleep until the next tick is due (while inner frames run, sleep_for : the engine's high-resolution sleep-then-spin timer, glitchygames/timing.py FastTimer ; paused, at the start screen or over, sleep_coarsely , which never spins), open it, let the doors run the tick's work (keys), then add the real time since the last tick, times the speed, to the accumulator. A tick within TICK_SNAP_WINDOW_SECONDS of one period counts as exactly one period, the error carried to the next tick, so wake-up jitter does not turn 1x into ticks of 0 and 2 frames. Only while the inner game is running: paused, at the start screen or over, the accumulator empties, and a restart seeds it with half a frame (so frame boundaries never sit on a tick boundary). Tick open: run one more inner frame ( should_run_inner_frame True) while the accumulator holds the frame's recorded duration, which it then consumes; at most MAX_INNER_FRAMES_PER_TICK per tick, and only within the tick's real-time budget ( INNER_FRAME_BUDGET_SECONDS ), so keys, the status line and presenting stay at 60 Hz however costly inner frames are. The accumulator never owes more than one tick's worth of frames: the excess is dropped (a long stall runs one bounded burst), and while frames are dropped or the budget cuts ticks short the viewer is behind ( is_behind ): the status bar then shows the real speed ( effective_speed ). So 1x runs one inner frame a tick for a 60 FPS recording (but for the true rate mismatch), 8x eight, ¼x one every fourth tick, paused none. While paused a step ( . ) runs exactly one inner frame. The start screen lets frame 0 run first, so its picture is behind the message. Otherwise the tick closes: the doors refresh the status line, the loop presents the outer frame and asks again (step 1). The accumulator only decides when inner frames run, never what they do, so a watched replay is as exact as a headless one. Headless replays have no viewer loop: they never hold and run unpaced. Step back restarts the replay process instead, which rebuilds the inner game up to frame N-1 before the viewer's first tick (glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py; no outer tick opens during the rebuild). Later users of the same contract: Part 3's playback scopes (an inner replay under a live outer game) and audio/video capture (inner frames handed to a sink rather than presented). docs.text: Drive the viewer's outer loop: say whether the next inner frame waits (rule 14). Opens the viewer's next outer tick when none is open (sleeping until it is due, then reading the viewer's keys and refreshing the status line), and runs inner frames from the viewer's accumulator (glitchygames/replay/viewer.py). While a restarted replay rebuilds (rule 15) no outer tick opens: frames run unheld, but for one hold every REBUILD_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_SECONDS of real time, which reads the viewer's keys (Esc and the window's close still end the replay) and presents the progress line. Returns: bool – False when headless (a headless replay never holds), while rebuilding (but at its bool – progress) or when the viewer runs one more inner frame in its open tick; True when bool – the tick closes or the rebuild shows its progress (the loop presents the outer frame bool – and asks again). While a restarted replay rebuilds (rule 15) no outer tick opens: frames run unheld, but for one hold every ``REBUILD_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_SECONDS`` of real time, which reads the viewer's keys (Esc and the window's close still end the replay) and presents the progress line. Returns: False when headless (a headless replay never holds), while rebuilding (but at its progress) or when the viewer runs one more inner frame in its open tick; True when the tick closes or the rebuild shows its progress (the loop presents the outer frame and asks again). """ if self . options . headless : return False if self . _rebuild is not None : # Before frame 0's game code: the game's own music pauses are followed from it self . _rebuild . begin () # An onion skin's OLD rebuilds alongside (rule 20), not after this rebuild if self . onion_skin is not None : self . onion_skin . begin () now = clock . measured_seconds () if not self . _rebuild . progress_is_due ( frame_index = self . _frame_index , now = now ): return False self . _run_control_tick ( now = now ) return True # Nothing has run since the last tick closed: its state decides how the viewer waits now = self . viewer . begin_tick ( is_inner_running = self . _is_inner_running ()) if now is not None : self . _run_control_tick ( now = now ) self . viewer . accrue ( now = now , is_inner_running = self . _is_inner_running ()) runs_inner_frame = self . viewer . should_run_inner_frame ( inner_frame_seconds = self . _inner_frame_seconds (), is_inner_over = self . _is_inner_over (), is_first_inner_frame = self . _frame_index == 0 , ) if not runs_inner_frame : # The tick closed: the status line describes the frame about to be presented self . _refresh_status_line () return not runs_inner_frame

docs.text: The determinism audit ( --audit ): replay a recording twice in fresh processes and compare. --replay-trace PATH --audit does not replay in-process. It runs the same command again ( audit_command : this interpreter, sys.orig_argv with --no-audit and --headless added: no window, no sound, no pacing) as two child processes, each with --replay-digest <temp file> and PYTHONHASHSEED set to one of AUDIT_HASH_SEEDS . Fresh processes are the point: they give fresh engine state and different hash seeds, so set and dict ordering bugs show up. Each child replays as usual (with --replay-fps recorded : the audit refuses real ) and writes its digest file ( write_digest_file ): one SHA-256 per replayed frame ( frame_digest of the frame as the replay sampled it), then its divergence summary. What is compared: the sampled frame only (the active scene's class, and each sprite's rect , visible and draw order), as the recording comparison samples it. Pixels, audio and game state that is not sampled are not compared, so nondeterminism that never moves, hides or reorders a sprite goes unnoticed. The audit fails if either run diverged from the recording or the two digest streams differ (the first differing frame is reported: nondeterminism that slipped past the doors, glitchygames/sources.py). A child that cannot be started, runs longer than AUDIT_REPLAY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS , writes no readable digest file or exits with a status other than ExitCode.SUCCESS (or ExitCode.REPLAY_DIVERGED with a divergence in its digest file) did not finish its replay: an AuditRunError . GameEngine exits with ExitCode.SUCCESS when the audit passes, ExitCode.AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC when it fails and ExitCode.INTERNAL_ERROR on an AuditRunError (glitchygames/exit_codes.py). A truncated recording is refused before any child starts, with ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT : an audit needs the whole recording, and each child would stop at the cut-off. Children are started with run_command (glitchygames/process.py, subprocess.run ): an argument list, never a shell, with the environment set before the child's interpreter starts (PYTHONHASHSEED is read only then). An interpreter started with -E or -I would pass that option on to its children, which would then ignore PYTHONHASHSEED; environment_reaches_children tells the engine to refuse. The plan: plans/2026-10-19-gameplay-replay.md, section 3.5.

docs.text: Watched-replay controls: pause, step, speed, quit, the status bar and the start screen. A watched replay ( --replay-trace without --headless ; glitchygames/replay/driver.py) hands every real key press and release to ReplayControls ; none reaches the game. The keys (plans/2026-10-19-gameplay-replay.md, 4.1): Space: start the replay from the start screen, then pause or resume it. . : while paused, run one frame. , : while paused at frame N, step back to frame N - 1 ( restart_request ). The driver restarts the replay, which rebuilds up to that frame unpresented and pauses there (glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py). Held, it repeats like . , but each repeat only moves the target back one more frame: the restart happens once, after the release ( take_restart_request ), as each restart re-runs the replay from frame 0. Resuming drops a pending step back, and a . step while , is held makes the target count back from the frame the step reaches. Home: restart at frame 0 (paused after frame 0, FIRST_PAUSED_FRAME ). D: restart at the divergence frame, once the replay has found one ( divergence_frame ). ] / [ : double or halve the playback speed, within MIN_SPEED and MAX_SPEED . B: bookmark the current frame ( bookmarks : the frame the status line shows, the one to be served next; kept sorted, once each). S asks the driver to save a copy of the recording with the bookmarks as breakpoint control events ( take_save_request ); a replay of the copy pauses at each ( pause_at_breakpoint , glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 16). Esc: quit the replay (the driver ends it with end_reason = 'quit' ; no event is posted, as a code-posted QUIT would be an internal event the recording does not have). F3 / F4: the debug overlay's keys ( OVERLAY_KEYS ), handed to the overlay. While a restarted replay rebuilds ( rebuild_target_frame ) only Esc and the debug overlay's keys act ( REBUILD_KEYS ), and the presented frame is the rebuild's progress line on a cleared display instead of the status bar. The controls run on their own real-time cadence ( ControlCadence , 60 ticks a second), whatever the replay's speed and whether it is paused: the driver reads the keys and refreshes the status line once per tick. Each key acts once per press: the operating system's key repeat (games turn it on: PaddleSlap calls pygame.key.set_repeat(1) ) is ignored until the key is released. Step keys repeat by themselves instead: after STEP_REPEAT_DELAY_SECONDS held, every STEP_REPEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS . The real time comes from glitchygames.clock.measured_seconds (never replayed), which is sound because the controls never change what is simulated. The status bar, a transient message, the driver's banner and the start screen are drawn on the presented frame after the debug overlay ( SceneManager._present_frame ), so they are never in a screenshot or a trace.

docs.text: The viewer controls' own real-time tick, CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND a second. Independent of the replay's speed and pauses: the replayed frames follow the recording, the controls follow real time ( glitchygames.clock.measured_seconds , never replayed; the controls never change what is simulated). A tick that falls more than one period behind (a long frame) is re-anchored to now instead of being caught up tick after tick. Source code in src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py 180 181 182 183 184 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 200 201 202 203 204 205 206 207 208 209 210 211 212 213 214 215 216 217 218 219 220 221 class ControlCadence : """The viewer controls' own real-time tick, ``CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND`` a second. Independent of the replay's speed and pauses: the replayed frames follow the recording, the controls follow real time (``glitchygames.clock.measured_seconds``, never replayed; the controls never change what is simulated). A tick that falls more than one period behind (a long frame) is re-anchored to now instead of being caught up tick after tick. """ def __init__ ( self : Self ) -> None : """Start with a tick due at once.""" self . _next_tick_seconds : float | None = None def tick_is_due ( self : Self , * , now : float ) -> bool : """Report whether a tick is due at ``now``, and if so schedule the next one. Args: now: The measured time. Returns: True when the controls should run a tick now. """ if self . _next_tick_seconds is not None and now < self . _next_tick_seconds : return False scheduled = ( now if self . _next_tick_seconds is None else self . _next_tick_seconds ) + CONTROL_TICK_SECONDS self . _next_tick_seconds = scheduled if scheduled > now else now + CONTROL_TICK_SECONDS return True def next_tick_seconds ( self : Self , * , now : float ) -> float : """Return when the next tick is due. Args: now: The measured time (the answer before any tick has run). Returns: The measured time of the next tick. """ return now if self . _next_tick_seconds is None else self . _next_tick_seconds

docs.text: Exact replay of a --record-trace recording through the real engine ( --replay-trace ). ReplaySources are the doors (glitchygames/sources.py) a replay installs: everything the recorded run took in is served from the recording, so the real engine and game code run the session again, and every frame's sprites are compared with the recorded frame. The rules (plans/2026-10-19-gameplay-replay.md, sections 3.1-3.3): Startup, in one place ( GameEngine.__init__ ): once the options are parsed, start_replay reads the recording, refuses a recording of another game ( ReplayRefusedError ; the engine logs it and exits with ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT , as for an unreadable file or a malformed one ( decoded_replay_sources ), or ExitCode.MISSING_INPUT for a missing one; glitchygames/exit_codes.py), warns once about a different engine version, applies the recorded options (all but REPLAY_LOCAL_OPTIONS ) and seeds the random streams with the recorded seed. Games read the display's size, so the window opens at the header's screen_size (the size the recorded display had, which a window manager may have made other than the recorded --resolution ): apply_recorded_screen_size sets the resolution option to it, and the engine's normal display set-up opens it (headless or watched). A window that still opens at another size is refused ( display_size_refusal : the engine logs Cannot replay PATH: it was recorded on a 800x600 display, but the window opened at 800x480 ... and exits with ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT ); a screen_size that is not two positive integers is a malformed header ( UNUSABLE_INPUT ). A header without one (not written by the engine's recorder, which always writes it, format 2 included) keeps the recorded --resolution , with a warning. A size that changes during the recorded run is not recorded, so a game that reads the live size every frame can still diverge. The engine installs the sources before the first frame; while installed they own the internal-post tracker (glitchygames/recording.py). Pump: the real queue is drained (through the live doors' pump) and each event classified with the internal-post tracker. From the first drain on, real input, device and window events are blocked at SDL ( REAL_INPUT_EVENT_TYPES , glitchygames/replay/input_blocking.py), so they never enter the queue (each drain blocks them again, as an event manager made mid-run allows its types); the blocked state each type had before comes back when the replay ends ( finish_run , normally or after an error) or is uninstalled. QUIT, the window's close event and the custom range are never blocked, nor, in a watched replay, are KEYDOWN and KEYUP ( WATCHED_REAL_KEY_EVENT_TYPES : the viewer's keys, rule 14). Blocking also refuses posts of those types: game code that fakes input by posting, say, KEYDOWN loses the post, which shows as a missing internal event divergence (the engine's own posts are QUIT and custom types). So game code posting KEYDOWN or KEYUP replays differently watched and headless: watched, the keys are not blocked, the post arrives and matches its recorded internal record; headless (and so --audit ), it is refused and diverges. A recording of such a game can match watched and diverge headless. What external events still arrive (queued before the first drain, the close event, app lifecycle and system notifications) never reach the game: a watched replay's real key presses and releases go to its controls (rule 14), the rest are dropped, except the window's QUIT, kept last so closing the window ends the replay. A control tick of a held frame (rule 14) drains the queue the same way; the internal events it finds wait for the next pump. Pump N serves the recording's batch N in its recorded order: each external record is rebuilt (recorded references mapped to live objects: a window to None, as live events of the display module's window carry it; a joystick to its opened stand-in, an event whose joystick has none being dropped with one warning per instance id), and each internal record is the live internal event the replayed code posted again (equal records). A recorded internal event nobody posted, a posted one the recording does not have, or a frame pumped more or fewer times than recorded is a divergence of the frame. Internal events are matched by encoded record ( event_to_record ), so one carrying a window or joystick reference would compare the recorded and live ids; none of the engine's posts carry one today. Frame indexes: the sources count their own end_frame calls; every recorded frame they serve is picked by that count, never by the scene manager's frame number. Frame time: the current frame's recorded dt ; past the end, the measurement. The FPS events and performance statistics ( performance_frame_seconds ) use it too under --replay-fps recorded (the default), so the FPS events are compared exactly; under --replay-fps real they use this machine's measured frame time, and FPS events are not compared (logic still receives the recorded dt ). Input: the frame's snapshot, rebuilt by applying each frame's input_changes in order (a version-2 recording has none: polled input reads as idle, with one warning). Held keys answer by the key codes the recording machine held them as, whatever this machine's keyboard layout (glitchygames/input/state.py). Devices: a ReplayDeviceRegistry from the header, learning each frame's opened devices and enumeration answers when the frame begins (before any open in it is answered). Saves: a MemorySaveManager per namespace, seeded from the header's saves or the frame's saves_opened (an unknown namespace gets an empty store); real saves are never touched. End of frame: a divergence found by the frame's pumps comes first; then the frame's control events that are not applied again (markers the replayed code records by itself) are compared with the recorded ones, in order; then the scene's sprites are sampled as the recorder samples them and compared with the recorded frame (scene class, then each sprite: present, rect , visible ). The first difference stops a headless replay, as does the last recorded frame; a watched replay pauses there instead (rule 14). Under ReplayOptions.stop_on_divergence False ( --rebaseline , rule 17) a difference stops nothing: the result keeps the first one, counts the frames that differ ( ReplayResult.differing_frame_count ) and names every sprite that differs in them ( ReplayResult.affected_sprite_ids ), and the replay runs on to the last recorded frame. The report's history ends at the first divergent frame either way. A frame that pumped fewer times than recorded never serves its remaining batches (they are not carried into a later pump); their external events are counted ( ReplayResult.undelivered_input_count ). Clocks: the wall clock is the recording's recorded_at plus the frame clock; elapsed seconds are the frame clock, live and replayed alike (glitchygames/clock.py). recorded_frame_fields hands a recording made over the replay ( --rebaseline , rule 17) the frame's recorded saves and device fields, and last_batch_origins each event's origin in the batch the last pump returned. GameEngine._shutdown calls finish_run and reports the result ( ReplayResult.report : printed to stdout under --headless , logged otherwise); GameEngine.start then ends the run with ReplayResult.exit_code(policy=options.exit_policy) . The report of a sprite divergence lists the sprite in the last REPORT_HISTORY_FRAMES frames before it, recorded and replayed (kept by end_frame ). Digests ( --replay-digest PATH , for --audit : glitchygames/replay/audit.py): each compared frame's frame_digest (of the frame as sampled for rule 8) is kept, and finish_run writes them with the divergence summary to the digest file. The engine refuses a digest file it cannot write before the run ( ExitCode.CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT ); one that cannot be written at the end is logged on one line ( digest_write_failed ), and the run exits ExitCode.CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT once the replay is reported. Pacing: the scene manager never paces a replay ( paced_frame_seconds is 0.0). A headless replay ( --headless ) is not paced at all, as its frame times come from the recording. A watched replay is paced by its viewer (glitchygames/replay/viewer.py, whose docstring is the contract): an outer tick 60 times a second of real time ( glitchygames.clock.measured_seconds , never replayed: it only decides when frames run, never what they do) runs the inner recorded frames its accumulator pays for (real time times the speed, consumed by each frame's recorded duration, bounded per tick in frames and real time, never owing more than one tick's worth). Watching (not --headless ): ReplayControls (glitchygames/replay/controls.py) take the viewer's real key presses and releases; none reaches the game. hold_frame drives the viewer: with no outer tick open it sleeps until the next one, drains the real queue and acts on the keys read since the last tick (once per press; a key already down when the replay starts acts only after its release); it then answers False for each inner frame the open tick runs and True when the tick closes, refreshing the status line (showing the real speed while the viewer cannot keep up); the scene manager then presents that frame. Inner frames are not presented ( presents_frames is False). The start screen ( ReplayOptions.wait_for_start ) holds the loop after frame 0, so the first frame's picture is behind the message (frame 0's sounds play before Space, and a one-frame recording reaches its end at the start screen). The loop is also held while paused (until a step) and once the recording is used up. At a divergence or the end the replay pauses with the debug overlay on ( ReplayControls.debug_overlay , the scene manager's, handed over by the engine) and a banner ( ReplayControls.banner ) instead of stopping; Esc stops it (a run that already ended keeps its end reason, else 'quit' ). The status bar is drawn by draw_overlay . A headless replay never holds and has no controls' keys: its KEYDOWN and KEYUP stay blocked. Step back ( , ), Home and D restart the replay (glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py, whose docstring is the contract): a control tick that takes the controls' restart request ( ReplayControls.take_restart_request ) stops the replay with ReplayResult.restart_frame set and the end reason 'restart' , and the engine relaunches it once torn down. A replay given ReplayOptions.pause_at_frame N (watched only: a headless replay ignores it, as nobody could unpause it) rebuilds: without its start screen, frames run unpresented and unpaced in silence ( Rebuild.silence_frame after each; hold_frame never holds, except every REBUILD_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_SECONDS of real time to present the progress line and read the viewer's keys), until frame max(N, FIRST_PAUSED_FRAME) is the next to run; there it pauses. A divergence or the end of the recording on the way pauses it there instead (rule 14). ReplayOptions.viewer_state restores the viewer's speed, debug panel and the divergence frame an earlier run found. Bookmarks (watched): B bookmarks the frame the status line shows ( ReplayControls.bookmarks , frame N meaning paused with frame N next). S ( ReplaySources.bookmarks , saved by the control tick) writes a copy of the recording ( write_bookmarked_copy ) to bookmarked_copy_path , with a {'kind': 'breakpoint', 'label': 'bookmark'} control event appended to frame N - 1 (the frame whose picture was shown) for each bookmark N (one already there is not added again; other control events are kept). The same bookmarks as the last save are not written again (unless that copy was deleted since). The copy's header names its source ( bookmarked_copy_of ); only a file with that field is updated in place (written aside and moved in), so an original is never written, even one named like a copy, nor a copy of another recording; a copy an earlier session saved from the same source keeps its bookmarks (they are added to the viewer's). The copy replays as its source does: a cut-off source gives source_truncated (the copy ends as truncated) and a version-2 source input_capture_format_version (polled input reads as idle, markers are not compared). With no bookmarks nothing is written and the viewer is told so. A breakpoint is re-applied on its frame (glitchygames/supervision.py) and is not compared, so the copy replays exactly as the original; a watched replay pauses when it applies one ( ReplayControls.pause_at_breakpoint , a control event handler the engine registers), except while rebuilding, so a saved copy reopens and stops at each bookmark. A recording's bookmark breakpoints are the viewer's bookmarks from the start, so S keeps them. A restart (rule 15) with bookmarks saves the copy first and replays the copy ( GameEngine._restart_replay , which warns naming the bookmarks if the copy cannot be saved), so bookmarks survive step back. Rebaseline ( --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless ; glitchygames/replay/ rebaseline.py, whose docstring is the contract): start_replay gives the replay stop_on_divergence=False and ReplayExitPolicy.SUCCESS_AFTER_WRITING , and the engine records the run over it into NEW ( RecordingSources with replayed set: origins and the saves and device fields come from this replay, never from the live trackers). It also gives it captures_scene_starts=True , so the scenes the replayed code builds capture their starts and NEW holds them ( scene_start , frame 0's included), as a --record-trace recording does; a recording's scene_start fields are never compared (the replayed code captures its own). A rebaseline is also how a recording made before logical names (glitchygames/logical_names.py: no game in its header, no scene in its scene starts) of a game that has moved since is converted: under --rebaseline such a recording's game is matched by its class's qualified name alone, its module may differ, and so are its scene starts' scenes ( modules_not_compared , the one rule check_recorded_game and find_scene_class share; several loaded classes of that name are still refused); NEW holds the current logical names. A plain replay of such a recording is refused ( ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT ) with a message naming --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless . There is no table of former locations. A recording whose classes moved to another logical module is converted the same way (the logical modules are not compared, the qualified names are); a plain replay refuses it, naming the rebaseline. Playback (Part 3's in-game playback scope, glitchygames/replay/playback.py, whose docstring is the contract): playback_replay_sources builds the sources a scope serves a recording's frames from, starting at ReplayOptions.start_frame N (the frame holding the rebuilt scene's scene_start ). They behave as a headless replay's that nobody watches: no viewer, controls, start screen or overlay; they never hold, pause or pace (the scope uses the installed doors' pacing and presenting) and stop at the recording's end or first divergence; no game check, recorded options or seed are applied, and no report is printed and no exit code given (the scope keeps the result). The frames before N are not served: what they took in is learned when the sources are made (opened devices, saves first opened, the polled input they changed; not enumeration answers, which those frames consumed), and the sprite ids continue the recording's ( StableSpriteIds 's recorded_ids : the ids those frames gave, but those frame N holds, which are the replayed scene's own, sampled already between its setup and its first logic frame), so frame N is compared as recorded. Saves start from the scene start's save view, over the header's. The internal events of frame N's first batch that were posted before the scene began ( ReplayOptions.earlier_internal_event_count , from its start's first logic frame; glitchygames/scene_start.py, rule 7) are served from the recording, as external ones are, and not compared; so are the events frame N's redelivered_events holds (a playback scope's held events, delivered before its first pump: they belong to the frame, but no door pumped them), first in its first batch ( ReplayOptions.serves_redelivered_events ). Frame indexes stay the recording's (rule 3, offset by N): divergences name recording frames, and ReplayResult.frames_replayed counts up to the last compared recording frame. A later frame holding a resume_bridge (an instant-replay journal's: its scene resumed there after a playback scope; glitchygames/instant_replay.py, rule 7) begins as the start frame does: the bridge is kept for the frame ( frame_bridge : the playback scope sets the frame clock, the FPS event timer and the polled input from it at the top of the frame), the polled input before it is the bridge's, the first earlier_internal_event_count internal events of its first batch are served from the recording, uncompared, and its redelivered_events come first in its first pump: the external ones served, the internal ones (the scene's own posts from before the scope, which the playback ran) matched with the live posts. A frame's playback_answers are kept for the frame ( recorded_playback_answers ): the playback scope answers the replayed code's playback requests with them (glitchygames/replay/playback.py, answered_playback_request ). Seed ( --random-seed ; the user's decisions, 2026-10-26): a replay runs under its recording's seed ( random_seed ), unless given another ( ReplayOptions.random_seed , which start_replay reads before the recorded options are applied). Given the recorded one, nothing changes. Given another, the replay is reseeded ( ReplaySources.is_reseeded ): the recording's inputs are played out under it (the engine's streams are seeded with it, here and in the engine), a difference never stops it (as in rule 17), and the run's random_seed option names it. A reseeded rebaseline writes NEW under that seed (NEW's header and options name it); a plain reseeded replay writes nothing and exits SUCCESS whatever it found ( ReplayExitPolicy.SUCCESS_WITHOUT_COMPARING ), its report the rebaseline's summary of what differed. --audit is a check, so the engine refuses one under another seed. Onion skin ( --compare-trace OLD ; glitchygames/replay/tools/compare.py, whose docstring is the contract): a watched replay's onion_skin draws OLD's frame of the same number over the presented copy of the frame shown ( draw_overlay , before the status bar; not while rebuilding, though hold_frame begins it as a rebuild starts, so OLD's child rebuilds alongside), and a headless child's frame_sink takes each replayed game frame (glitchygames/game_frames.py) as it is presented: the engine makes such a replay draw its overlay ( draws_overlay ), and its draw_overlay hands the presented frame over instead of drawing (a scene switched to after the frame was presented never shows in it); False back stops the replay at the frame's end ( frame_sink_closed : nobody reads). Neither changes what is replayed or compared.

""" def __init__ ( self : Self , * , controls : ReplayControls , recording_path : Path | None , is_bookmarked_copy : bool , ) -> None : """Keep what a save needs. Args: controls: The watched replay's controls (their ``bookmarks``, and where the outcome is shown); their bookmarks start as the recording's own. recording_path: The file the recording was read from (``ReplayOptions.recording_path``), or None. is_bookmarked_copy: True when the recording is a bookmarked copy: its bookmarks are already saved in it. """ self . _controls = controls self . _recording_path = recording_path # The bookmarks last saved and where (a save of the same ones writes nothing) self . _saved_bookmarks : list [ int ] | None = None self . _saved_path : Path | None = None if is_bookmarked_copy and recording_path is not None : self . _saved_bookmarks = list ( controls . bookmarks ) self . _saved_path = recording_path def save ( self : Self ) -> Path | None : """Save a copy of the recording with the bookmarks as breakpoints. The viewer is told the outcome (``ReplayControls.show_message``), and it is logged. The same bookmarks as the last save (or as a bookmarked copy being replayed holds) are not written again, unless that copy has been deleted since. Returns: The copy's path (already saved, or just written), or None when there is no copy: no bookmarks, no recording file (sources made from frames in memory), or the copy could not be written. """ bookmarks = list ( self . _controls . bookmarks ) if not bookmarks : self . _controls . show_message ( text = NO_BOOKMARKS_MESSAGE ) return None if self . _recording_path is None : self . _controls . show_message ( text = NO_RECORDING_FILE_MESSAGE ) return None if ( self . _saved_path is not None and bookmarks == self . _saved_bookmarks # A copy deleted since it was saved is written again and self . _saved_path . exists () ): self . _controls . show_message ( text = ALREADY_SAVED_MESSAGE . format ( name = self . _saved_path . name ) ) return self . _saved_path destination = bookmarked_copy_path ( recording_path = self . _recording_path ) try : write_bookmarked_copy ( recording_path = self . _recording_path , bookmarks = bookmarks , destination = destination ) # A TraceFormatError (the file changed since it was read) is a ValueError except ( OSError , ValueError ) as error : LOG . exception ( 'Could not save bookmarks %s to %s ' , bookmarks , destination ) self . _controls . show_message ( text = f 'could not save bookmarks: { error } ' ) return None LOG . info ( 'Saved bookmarks %s to %s ' , bookmarks , destination ) self . _controls . show_message ( text = f 'bookmarks saved to { destination . name } ' ) self . _saved_bookmarks = bookmarks self . _saved_path = destination return destination

docs.text: How a replay went so far. Attributes: frames_replayed ( int ) – How many recorded frames were run and compared. divergence ( Divergence | None ) – The first difference, or None. end_reason ( str ) – 'running' , 'end_of_recording' , 'diverged' , 'truncated' (the last complete frame of a cut-off file was replayed), 'quit' (the window was closed, or Esc was pressed in a watched replay, before the end) or 'restart' (the viewer stepped back before the end: rule 15). restart_frame ( int | None ) – The frame the replay restarts at (rule 15), or None. docs.text: Refuse a recording of another game. A recording holding game (the game class's logical name, glitchygames/logical_names.py) must name the started game's logical name; the qualified names must be equal, and so must the logical modules unless modules_not_compared says otherwise ( __main__ on either side: a game file run as a script, python paddleslap.py , is the same game as its console script; or a --rebaseline , the game having moved to another logical module). A plain replay of a recording whose game moved is refused with a message naming the rebaseline. A recording without game (made before logical names) must name the started game's class name, and its module too unless modules_not_compared says otherwise: under --rebaseline the module may differ (the game moved since; the new recording holds its logical name), while a plain replay of such a recording is refused with a message naming the rebaseline that converts it. Convert the recording with { REBASELINE_REMEDY } ' ) raise ReplayRefusedError ( message ) recorded_place = str ( recorded_logical_name ) else : recorded_module = header . get ( GAME_MODULE_HEADER_FIELD ) # The header's class name (game_class.__name__ when recorded): a game class is a # module's top-level class, so its qualified name differs = recorded_game != game_class . __name__ modules_differ = recorded_module != game_class . __module__ and not modules_not_compared ( recorded_module = recorded_module , loaded_module = game_class . __module__ , is_rebaseline = is_rebaseline , ) if not differs and modules_differ : message = ( f 'The recording was made before logical names, by the game { recorded_game } in ' f ' { recorded_module } , and this game ( { started_logical_name } ) is in ' f ' { game_class . __module__ } : if it is this game, the game has since moved, and a ' 'replay cannot tell it from another game of that name. Convert the recording ' f 'with { REBASELINE_REMEDY } ' ) raise ReplayRefusedError ( message ) recorded_place = f ' { recorded_game } ( { recorded_module or "module not recorded" } )' if differs : message = ( f 'The recording is of the game { recorded_place } , not { started_logical_name } ; ' 'refusing to replay it' ) raise ReplayRefusedError ( message )

docs.text: Make replay sources from a decoded recording, refusing a malformed one (rule 1). What the sources decode as they are made (the header's devices, enumeration answers and saves, the frames before the start frame and the start frame itself: their devices, saves, input changes and resume bridge) is checked here, so a malformed recording raises TraceFormatError, which the engine refuses with ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT as it does an unreadable file ( ReplaySources.from_path ), and a playback refuses as it does any recording it cannot play ( playback_replay_sources ). Known limitation: the catch covers the whole ReplaySources.__init__ , so a genuine engine bug there that raises AttributeError, KeyError, TypeError or ValueError is reported as a malformed recording ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , 65), not as INTERNAL_ERROR (70); the message keeps the original exception ( repr ), and it is chained as the cause. docs.text: Return whether a record is matched by qualified name alone. docs.text: Write a copy of a recording with a breakpoint for each bookmark (rule 16). The recording's header and complete frames are copied as read; for each bookmark N, frame N - 1 gets BOOKMARK_CONTROL_EVENT appended to its control events, unless it already has it, and its newest content hash ( content_hash[0] , glitchygames/recording_history.py) is recomputed to describe the breakpoint. The header gains bookmarked_copy_of (the source's file name, kept from a copy), source_truncated when the source was cut off, and input_capture_format_version when the source is older than format version 3, so the copy replays as its source does. A copy an earlier session saved from the same source keeps its bookmarks: they are added to bookmarks (a copy of another recording is never written over). The copy is written aside, then moved into place ( glitchygames.output_files.write_aside_then_replace ), so destination is never left half written, even when it is recording_path . Parameters: recording_path ( Path ) – The recording to copy (never written, unless it is a bookmarked copy and destination ). bookmarks ( list [ int ] ) – The bookmarked frames ( ReplayControls.bookmarks ), each 1 to the recording's frame count. destination ( Path ) – The copy's path ( bookmarked_copy_path ): a new file or a bookmarked copy. Raises: ValueError – If destination exists but is not a bookmarked copy of recording_path , or a bookmark is outside the recording (nothing is written either way). docs.text: Ghosts: one sprite's recorded path and looks, drawn beside live play (a time-trial ghost). A ghost is appearance, not play (plans/2026-10-19-gameplay-replay.md, section 5.5). The rules: Recording: GhostRecorder(sprite=..., scene=...) is a supervisor (glitchygames/supervision.py); it registers itself with SceneManager().add_supervisor as it is made and removes itself in finish() , which returns the GhostTrack . At each frame's supervisor slot (after the frame's logic and events, before the camera aim and positioning) it keeps one GhostSample : the scene's game_time , the sprite's world_x / world_y , its appearance(sprite) ( default_appearance : animation, frame, horizontal flip and draw offset of an AnimatedSprite ; kept as a read-only copy) and whether the game shows it ( not hidden for a world-space sprite: its visible is the engine's culling, which says where the camera was, not whether the sprite was shown; visible for any other sprite). Only live frames of its scene are sampled: frames whose active scene is the scene it was given (another scene has its own game time), in which that scene's game time advanced (not behind the pause screen, not the frame a resume switches back to it), and never inside a playback scope (a demo or an instant replay plays a rebuilt scene; glitchygames/replay/playback.py). A recorder made while a scope plays (by the rebuilt scene's setup() , say) belongs to the scope: the scene manager removes it when the scope ends (glitchygames/supervision.py), and it samples nothing. A recorder stays registered until finish() , even once its scene is gone: a scene left (for the pause screen, or for another the game comes back from) may return, so the engine cannot tell it is over; a recorder never finished samples nothing more, but is kept (with its scene) until the game calls finish() , typically when the run it records ends. The recorder reads game state only: it draws no randomness, posts no event and records no control event, so recording a ghost changes nothing a --record-trace recording holds or a replay compares. Timing: samples are keyed by Scene.game_time , the sum of the scene's (capped) dt since it started, which stops while the scene is paused. A ghost drawn in a later run of the same scene shows, at each moment, the last sample not after that run's game_time ( GhostTrack.sample_at ), so it lines up with the live run from the scene's start whatever the frame rate, and stands still while the game is paused. With the same dt every frame, the ghost is drawn exactly where the recorded sprite was drawn. Storing: GhostTrack.to_json() / from_json() (frozen pydantic models; unknown fields are refused). The game stores tracks, typically in its saves ( glitchygames.state. open_saves ): a replay serves the saves the recording saw (a sandbox), so the replayed ghost is the recorded one. A track read from anywhere else must be the same file when the session is replayed. Drawing: GhostSprite(track=..., image_for=...) is a world-space sprite ( COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD ): the engine positions and culls it like any world sprite and is the only writer of its rect's position. The game sets ghost.scene to the scene it adds the ghost to (whose game_time it follows) and adds it to the scene's all_sprites . Its world_x , world_y and draw_offset are read from the track at the scene's current game_time whenever they are read, and that read brings its image and rect size up to date, so the engine's positioning (which runs before update() ) places and culls this frame's sample, never the last frame's. Its image is image_for(sample) as a translucent copy ( alpha ), made once per distinct appearance (keyed by the appearance's JSON), and the rect takes its size (its top-left stays the engine's). With nothing to show (no scene, before the track's first sample, or a sample that is not visible) its image is empty (0 x 0), which the engine's culling hides ( visible 0). hidden is the game's own flag only, as for every world sprite (set hidden = True to hide it, never visible = False ), so saving and restoring it is safe. It has no hitbox: never add it to a collision group. In traces: a ghost in all_sprites is sampled like every sprite (its rect and visible ), and it is deterministic: its track comes from saves (rule 4) and its position from the replayed game_time , so a session with a ghost replays without divergence. Inside an instant replay the rebuilt scene adds its own ghost as the live scene did (from the sandboxed saves), following its own game_time .

""" self . _sprite = sprite self . _scene = scene self . _appearance = appearance self . _samples : list [ GhostSample ] = [] self . _track : GhostTrack | None = None SceneManager () . add_supervisor ( supervisor = self ) def on_frame ( self : Self , * , frame_number : int , scene : Scene | None ) -> None : """Sample the sprite, if this frame ran the recorded scene's logic live. """ del frame_number # A supervisor earlier in the slot may have finished this recorder this frame if self . _track is not None or scene is not self . _scene : return if SceneManager () . in_playback_scope : return game_seconds = self . _scene . game_time if self . _samples and game_seconds <= self . _samples [ - 1 ] . game_seconds : return sprite = self . _sprite if is_world_positioned ( sprite ): shown = not getattr ( sprite , 'hidden' , False ) else : shown = bool ( getattr ( sprite , 'visible' , True )) self . _samples . append ( GhostSample ( game_seconds = game_seconds , world_x = sprite . world_x , world_y = sprite . world_y , appearance = self . _appearance ( sprite ), visible = shown , ) ) def finish ( self : Self ) -> GhostTrack : """Stop recording: leave the supervisor slot and return the track (the same each call). Returns: The recorded track. """ if self . _track is None : SceneManager () . remove_supervisor ( supervisor = self ) self . _track = GhostTrack ( samples = tuple ( self . _samples )) return self . _track

docs.text: Block real input at SDL while recorded input is served, then put the earlier state back. A replay (glitchygames/replay/driver.py) serves every external event from its recording, so real input, device and window events are blocked at SDL ( pygame.event.set_blocked ): they never enter the queue. EventTypeBlock records each type's blocked state before blocking it and restores exactly that state, so a type a game had already blocked stays blocked. Event managers made mid-run (a scene's widgets) call pygame.event.set_allowed , so the replay blocks the types again on every pump ( reassert ). Part 3's playback scope can reuse it. Blocking a type also refuses posts of it ( pygame.event.post returns False), including the game's own: game code that fakes input by posting, say, KEYDOWN loses those posts during a replay. The engine's own posts are QUIT and custom types, which are never blocked.

docs.text: Blocks event types at SDL and restores each one's blocked state at block() time. restore() returns every type to the state it had when block() ran, overriding any pygame.event.set_allowed or set_blocked calls made for those types in between. Attributes: event_types ( tuple [ int , ...] ) – The types block() blocks. Source code in src/glitchygames/replay/input_blocking.py 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 143 144 145 146 147 148 149 150 151 152 153 154 155 156 157 158 159 160 161 162 163 164 165 class EventTypeBlock : """Blocks event types at SDL and restores each one's blocked state at ``block()`` time. ``restore()`` returns every type to the state it had when ``block()`` ran, overriding any ``pygame.event.set_allowed`` or ``set_blocked`` calls made for those types in between. Attributes: event_types: The types ``block()`` blocks. """ def __init__ ( self : Self , * , event_types : Iterable [ int ]) -> None : """Prepare to block ``event_types`` (nothing is blocked until ``block()``). Args: event_types: The event types to block. """ self . event_types : tuple [ int , ... ] = tuple ( event_types ) # Type -> whether it was blocked before block(); None while not active self . _blocked_before : dict [ int , bool ] | None = None @property def is_active ( self : Self ) -> bool : """True between ``block()`` and ``restore()``.""" return self . _blocked_before is not None def block ( self : Self ) -> None : """Record each type's blocked state, then block every type (a no-op while active).""" if self . is_active : return self . _blocked_before = { event_type : pygame . event . get_blocked ( event_type ) for event_type in self . event_types } pygame . event . set_blocked ( list ( self . event_types )) def reassert ( self : Self ) -> None : """Block every type again, keeping the snapshot ``block()`` took (a no-op unless active). Undoes ``pygame.event.set_allowed`` calls made since (an event manager made mid-run). """ if self . _blocked_before is None : return pygame . event . set_blocked ( list ( self . event_types )) def restore ( self : Self ) -> None : """Return each type to its state at ``block()`` time (a no-op unless active). Types blocked then stay blocked; the others are unblocked, whatever was set in between. """ if self . _blocked_before is None : return pygame . event . set_allowed ([ event_type for event_type , was_blocked in self . _blocked_before . items () if not was_blocked ]) self . _blocked_before = None
