docs.text: In-game playback: a running game plays a recording to a rebuilt scene, then goes on. Demos and instant replays run inside a playback scope, not a new engine run (plans/2026-10-19-gameplay-replay.md, section 5.2). The rules: Starting ( start_playback ; start_playback_from_recording reads a file first): the frame played first ( PlaybackOptions.start_frame ) must hold a scene_start (glitchygames/scene_start.py) with its first logic frame (rule 7 there: a recording writes a start on the scene's first logic frame, so the start's frame is where its logic began), and its scene class must be found among the loaded Scene subclasses ( find_scene_class : by the start's logical name (glitchygames/logical_names.py) when it holds one, else by module and qualified name, else, where the modules are not compared ( modules_not_compared : none recorded, __main__ on either side, or a --rebaseline , which converts recordings made before logical names), by a name no other such scene shares); otherwise nothing starts (logged; False), as for a recording that cannot be replayed (a malformed one included). The replay sources are made ( playback_replay_sources , rule 18 of glitchygames/replay/driver.py) and the scope is requested ( SceneManager. request_playback ): the scene manager enters it at the start of the next frame, so the rebuilt scene's first frame is a whole frame, as recorded, and the frame that asked ends on the live doors. A request made while a transition plays waits for its end. A request made in a frame whose end switches scenes ( next_scene ) is dropped, logged: the scene to return to has gone. Scopes do not nest: inside a scope, a request is answered with the answer the frame being played recorded (an instant-replay journal's playback_answers ) and requests nothing, or, without one, refused ( answered_playback_request ; glitchygames/instant_replay.py, rule 8). Entering ( SceneManager._enter_playback ): the random streams, the frame clock, the FPS event timer and the scene manager's previous_scene are saved ( PlaybackRequest.begin_session ); the live scene is stashed without cleanup() ; PlaybackSources are pushed on top of the installed doors ( push_scoped_sources ; glitchygames/sources.py); a playback control event is recorded (a marker: replaying the session starts the scope again from the recorded input, so it is compared, never applied again); the scene is rebuilt ( rebuild_scene ) and made active as a switch would, a transition's arrival step is repeated for a scene that arrived by one; then the streams, the frame clock and the FPS event timer are set as the scene's first logic frame began, the frame takes the recording's dt, and the current polled input becomes the recording's before that frame (idle before frame 0), so the live input never leaks in. Frames: PlaybackSources serve the recording to the scene (rule 5) and the scene manager runs every frame as always, paced and presented by the installed doors (a demo plays at the game's speed), but for the fast-forwarded frames (rule 6). Ending: after each frame, the scope ends when its doors found a reason ( PlaybackSources.end_reason ): the player's press ( exit_on_input : any key or button, PLAYBACK_EXIT_EVENT_TYPES ), the recording's quit (its window's QUIT or the playback scene's own quit_game() : the scope ends, the game does not quit), the game's request ( SceneManager.end_playback , 'ended_by_game' : from a supervisor, the scope ends once that frame ended; between frames, at once; from the played scene's own code, ignored, as its original call did nothing), or the recording's end or divergence (the replay stops there; a playback never pauses). An error in the scope's part of a frame (its frame, the comparison, or entering) ends it too, logged ( SceneManager._run_frame contains it); an error of the installed doors (a session recorder that cannot write) propagates as it would outside a scope. The run's end ( SceneManager.terminate , after the player's QUIT) ends a scope in progress first and drops a requested one, so the live scene is the one torn down. Ending ( SceneManager._exit_playback ) keeps the replay's result ( SceneManager.last_playback_result ) and a PlaybackOutcome ( SceneManager.last_playback_outcome : the kind, the reason and the frames played), cleans up the playback's scene, removes every supervisor and control event handler the scope's code added while it played (the rebuilt scene's setup(), event handlers or cleanup() may add one, a ghost recorder say: SceneManager.add_supervisor gives it to the scope; those added before the scope began, or by the live game's own supervisors and handlers while it played, stay; SceneManager.in_playback_scope , true while the scoped doors are pushed, is the one answer to "is a scope playing"), pops the scoped doors, restores the streams, the frame clock, the FPS event timer, the scene manager's previous_scene , its rumble controller (rule 8) and the live polled input (the installed doors' latest snapshot), posts again the live game's posts the scope drained and hands back the player's held events (rule 5), drops the playback scene's own posts still queued (made after its frame's last pump: in update() , an event handler, a supervisor or handler the scope owns, its cleanup; sources.discard_scope_posts : they stop being pending posts, and the live doors' next read of SDL's queue loses them before a recording, the instant-replay journal or the game sees the batch; a replay of the session drops them the same way as its playback scene posts them again), posts again, in posting order, the posts the live game's own supervisors and handlers made while it played ( held_live_game_posts and those still queued, made in its last frame: a supervisor that calls end_playback() and then posts for the live game, say; the queued copies are dropped as the scope's are, so each arrives once, after the held events, at the live doors' next pump; pending then, a later instant replay across the scope serves them uncompared as its resume bridge's earlier events), then makes the live scene active again exactly as it was (no setup() again: only its snap mode, event proxies, caption and a full redraw), or switches to then when that is another scene. The frame that ends the scope still finishes afterwards, so the restored live frame clock resumes one frame later (it advances by that frame's dt). The scoped doors ( PlaybackSources ): pump_events : the installed doors pump once per pump of the frame (the real queue live; the session's recorded batch when the session is replayed, so the exit press replays too). Their batch is sorted with the internal-post tracker. The player's QUIT (and one the live game posted) is kept: it quits the game. Internal events, the playback scene's own posts, go to the replay ( ReplaySources.pump_events(real_events=...) ), which matches them with the recorded ones. Internal events posted before the scope began (the live game's last FPS event, say: they are the live game's, and would be divergences of the recording's first frame) are held, as are the external events the live game must not lose (releases, device and window events, PLAYBACK_HELD_EVENT_TYPES ): one list ( held_live_events ), in the order they were pumped, each with its origin, delivered in that order before the first pump after the scope ( sources.redeliver_events ; a recording writes them into that frame's redelivered_events ). Events still waiting to be redelivered when a scope begins (a demo that ended into a scene starting the next one) are taken into the new scope's list first, so they reach the live game, never a playback scene. When the run ends during a scope ( terminate ) they are dropped: no frame follows to deliver them. The posts the live game's own supervisors and control event handlers make while the scope plays ( recording.live_game_posts : post_event marks them while SceneManager runs live code in a scope, rule 4; the played recording never held them) are held apart ( held_live_game_posts ) and posted again as the scope ends (rule 4). The live game's input posts ( recording.post_input_event : a supervisor or tool standing in for the player) of an SDL type (below USEREVENT ), made during the scope or before it, are the player's input (BUGS.md #196): a press reaches the exit check (it ends a demo), releases, device and window events are held with the player's ( held_live_events , external), and the rest reach nothing. A replay of the session runs without the poster and serves those events from the recording as the player's, so the two agree. Its input posts of a type SDL never generates (no player makes one: a game event, a menu event, any custom_type() ) are held as its other posts are, and posted (or redelivered) as input again after the scope. A replay of the session serves those from the recording too (external), and the scope holds a served event of such a type that matches no post the same way, told by its recorded origin ( replayed_batch_origins : the type alone would call it internal), so it reaches the live game after the scope there as well. The rule: a supervisor may post any event ( post_input_event ); input of an SDL type during a scope counts as the player's; everything else reaches the game (after the scope if one is playing), live and replayed alike. The scope's code's own input posts (a supervisor the played scene added again) are dropped: the recording holds them as external and the replay serves them, so each arrives once. External events reach only the exit check, never the scene; presses and motion are dropped. The batch is the replay's (recorded external events, matched internal ones) without any QUIT (a QUIT in it ends the scope: recording_quit ), then the kept QUIT. input_snapshot : the installed doors' snapshot is read (a recording of the session records the player's polled input; it is kept as last_base_snapshot ), the replay's is returned. frame_seconds : the replay's (the recording's dt; past its end, the installed doors' measurement), asked after the installed doors were asked as always. Their answer is kept ( installed_frame_seconds ) for their end_frame . saves , devices , wall_clock_time , random_seed , opened_save_namespaces : the replay's (saves are a sandbox seeded from the scene start's save view: real saves are never touched). control_events_for_frame : the installed doors' (a replay of the session re-applies its breakpoints on the scope's frames too); the played recording's re-applied control events are never applied again (they were applied in the session that recorded them) and never compared (glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 8). end_frame is compare_frame (the replay compares the frame, its playback marker left out: the recording never holds it), then the installed doors' end_frame (a recording of the session writes it; glitchygames/recording.py, Playback scopes) with their own frame time ( installed_frame_seconds ), not the played recording's dt the frame ran with: the scope's first frame's time was read as the live frame before it ended, on the installed doors, and advanced the live frame clock and FPS event timer there, so a replay of the session must be served that time as that frame ends (BUGS.md #196). The scene manager calls the two itself, so only the comparison's errors end the scope. captures_scene_starts is True; stop_requested , pacing, holding, presenting and the overlay are the installed doors' (the scope never stops the run), except while fast-forwarding (rule 6). Fast-forward ( PlaybackOptions.fast_forward_frames ): the scope's first N frames run in full but unseen and unheard. While PlaybackSources.is_fast_forwarding (fewer frames compared than N), presents_frames is False and paced_frame_seconds() is 0.0, the doors a headless replay uses (the scene manager neither presents nor waits; the next presented frame updates the whole display), and after each such frame every sound it started is stopped and music is paused ( FrameSilencer , glitchygames/replay/silence.py, the code path a restarted replay's rebuild uses; it follows the game's own music pauses from the scope's start, and the live game's sounds playing then play on, live voices aside). After the Nth frame the silence ends (music the silencer paused plays on, unless the game paused it) and the frames play as rule 3 says, heard as the game plays them; so does a scope that ends during the fast-forward. Music is the one mixer's: the scope neither saves nor restores it, so music the playback's scene starts or stops is the live game's too. The scope's first frame is paced as the live doors pace it (the loop asks before the frame enters the scope). None of this changes what a frame does, so a recording or replay of the session (watched or headless) is unchanged. Instant replay ( SceneManager.instant_replay , start_instant_replay ): the active scene's instant-replay journal (glitchygames/instant_replay.py) plays in a scope of kind 'instant' from its start_frame , returning to the scene shown (the journal's scene, or the pause screen presenting it), with no exit on input: the player's presses reach nothing, and the game decides when it ends (the journal's end, or SceneManager.end_playback from a supervisor, which reads the player's polled input from SceneManager.playback_player_input ). The frames before the last Scene.INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS of frame time are fast-forwarded ( fast_forward_frame_count ); the rest are shown at the game's pace. Frame time, not game time: the shown part takes that long to watch, a paused stretch in it included. Refused (False, nothing starts) when the scene keeps no journal (it does not offer instant replay, its first logic frame has not run, or a scope plays) or the journal holds more frame time than Scene.MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS . The request is answered as any playback request is (rule 1: a playback of the journal gets the recorded answer and requests nothing), so a scene that asks after every goal plays back across its earlier replays. The journal's recording is taken as the request is made: the frame that asks is not in it (it ends live, before the scope begins). Rumble and live voices: a playback never rumbles the player's real controllers, neither while fast-forwarding nor in the frames it shows (a demo's crash buzzing the player's hands would be the playback's, not the game's). While a scope plays, SceneManager.rumble is a rumble controller of its own (the playback scene's pulses, sustained levels and shakes go there and reach no device); the live game's controller waits untouched and is back when the scope ends, so a playback's pulse never carries into live play. The live scene's synth voices (and those of the scene the scope returns to, and of the previous scene as it began: the game behind a pause screen an instant replay began from) pause behind the scope and play on after it ( LiveAudio.update 's paused_owners ), even when the playback's own scene switches change previous_scene ; the playback scene's own voices end with it. Limits: a live supervisor that posts with post_event (the game's own posts, which a replay expects the replayed code to make again) during a scope makes a session that a --replay-trace replay without that supervisor cannot match. Supervisors post with post_input_event , which replays without them, whatever the event's type (rule 5). A scope that fast-forwards inside a restarted replay's rebuild silences on top of the rebuild's silence: the end of its fast-forward may resume music during the rebuild (which pauses it again after the next frame). A scene must be rebuildable from its start ( Scene.replay_arguments ). Of a scene that arrived by a transition, the arrival step is repeated, but the events the ride delivered to it (releases, window and device events) are not: a scene they change diverges. The first logic frame's earlier posts are counted from the internal-post tracker, so they are exact while posts are tracked (while recording or replaying, and from the first setup of a scene that keeps an instant-replay journal: glitchygames/instant_replay.py, whose JournalRecording a scope plays from its start_frame ). A --record-trace recording of a session that played a scope cannot itself be played in-game from a frame inside or after that scope: a recorder writes no playback_answers or resume_bridge (only an instant-replay journal does), so its scene's playback requests and its resumption after the scope are not known (it replays exactly with --replay-trace , which runs the scope again). Rumble in joystick mode asks the devices door for the joysticks (glitchygames/input/rumble.py); inside a scope each send still asks the scope's door, with a device cache of its own, and then sends to no device (rule 8), so the played recording's answers are taken as it gave them. The scope's rumble controller starts fresh, though: a rumble the live game sent before the played scene began, still running when it was recorded, is not known to it, so its sends (and the counts they ask) can fall on other frames than the recording's; that matters only when the played recording's joystick count changed part way.

docs.text: Answer a playback request as recorded inside a scope, else make it and keep its answer. The scene's code gets the same answers when its instant-replay journal is played back (glitchygames/instant_replay.py, rule 8): live, the answer is kept in the journal's frame ( SceneManager.note_playback_answer ); inside a scope playing the journal, the frame's recorded answer is returned ( SceneManager.recorded_playback_answer ) and the request is not made (scopes do not nest). Inside a scope whose recording holds no answer (a demo), the request is made, and refused as a nested scope. Parameters: manager ( SceneManager ) – The running scene manager. request ( Callable [[], bool ] ) – Makes the request; returns whether a scope will begin. Returns: bool – The answer. Source code in src/glitchygames/replay/playback.py 1188 1189 1190 1191 1192 1193 1194 1195 1196 1197 1198 1199 1200 1201 1202 1203 1204 1205 1206 1207 1208 1209 1210 1211 def answered_playback_request ( * , manager : SceneManager , request : Callable [[], bool ]) -> bool : """Answer a playback request as recorded inside a scope, else make it and keep its answer. The scene's code gets the same answers when its instant-replay journal is played back (glitchygames/instant_replay.py, rule 8): live, the answer is kept in the journal's frame (``SceneManager.note_playback_answer``); inside a scope playing the journal, the frame's recorded answer is returned (``SceneManager.recorded_playback_answer``) and the request is not made (scopes do not nest). Inside a scope whose recording holds no answer (a demo), the request is made, and refused as a nested scope. Args: manager: The running scene manager. request: Makes the request; returns whether a scope will begin. Returns: The answer. """ recorded_answer = manager . recorded_playback_answer () if recorded_answer is not None : return recorded_answer granted = request () manager . note_playback_answer ( granted = granted ) return granted

docs.text: Return how many frames an instant replay fast-forwards before the seconds it shows. A frame is shown when the frame time from its start to the recording's end (its dt and every later frame's, summed exactly, then rounded once to a float) is at most shown_seconds ; every earlier frame from start_frame is fast-forwarded (rule 7). So ten frames of dt d are shown for shown_seconds 10 * d, whatever float rounding a running sum would add. Parameters: frames ( Sequence [ dict [ str , Any ]] ) – The recording's decoded frames. start_frame ( int ) – The frame the playback starts at. shown_seconds ( float ) – The frame time to show ( Scene.INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS ). Returns: int – The number of frames, from start_frame , to fast-forward. Source code in src/glitchygames/replay/playback.py 1269 1270 1271 1272 1273 1274 1275 1276 1277 1278 1279 1280 1281 1282 1283 1284 1285 1286 1287 1288 1289 1290 1291 1292 1293 1294 1295 1296 def fast_forward_frame_count ( * , frames : Sequence [ dict [ str , Any ]], start_frame : int , shown_seconds : float ) -> int : """Return how many frames an instant replay fast-forwards before the seconds it shows. A frame is shown when the frame time from its start to the recording's end (its ``dt`` and every later frame's, summed exactly, then rounded once to a float) is at most ``shown_seconds``; every earlier frame from ``start_frame`` is fast-forwarded (rule 7). So ten frames of ``dt`` d are shown for ``shown_seconds`` 10 * d, whatever float rounding a running sum would add. Args: frames: The recording's decoded frames. start_frame: The frame the playback starts at. shown_seconds: The frame time to show (``Scene.INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS``). Returns: The number of frames, from ``start_frame``, to fast-forward. """ first_shown_frame = len ( frames ) seconds_to_end = Fraction ( 0 ) for frame_index in range ( len ( frames ) - 1 , start_frame - 1 , - 1 ): seconds_to_end += Fraction ( frames [ frame_index ][ DT_FIELD ]) if float ( seconds_to_end ) > shown_seconds : break first_shown_frame = frame_index return first_shown_frame - start_frame

docs.text: Return the loaded Scene subclass a start names (rule 1). Only loaded classes are searched: nothing is imported from recording data. A start that holds a logical name ( SceneStart.scene , glitchygames/logical_names.py) is decided by it: the class named name whose logical name is logical is taken when exactly one is loaded, so a scene whose code moved is still found; under a --rebaseline one at another logical module is taken by its qualified name alone ( modules_not_compared , as below). Without one (recordings made before logical names), the class defined in module with the qualified name name is taken when exactly one is loaded. Otherwise a class is taken by its qualified name alone only where modules_not_compared (glitchygames/replay/driver.py, the rule check_recorded_game applies to a recording's game) says so: no module recorded, a game run as a script ( __main__ ) on either side, or a --rebaseline (a scene that moved since it was recorded); then the one such class is taken and several are refused. Outside a rebaseline, a class of that name from another module is another game's scene: refused. docs.text: Compare a replay's processing time with its recording's, frame by frame. A recording made through the engine ( --record-trace , --rebaseline , the scripted sessions) holds each frame's processing time ( processing_seconds , a newest-first history across rebaselines: glitchygames/recording_history.py; this module compares [0] ): the frame's work (logic, events, frame services, positioning and rendering), without presenting it, without the doors' own end_frame (writing the recording, comparing the replay) and without the pacing sleep. It is a diagnostic field: a replay never compares it and never serves it to the game (it is measured with clock.measured_seconds ). The header's latest measurement run ( measurement_runs[0] ) names the machine that measured them ( machine_description , never the host name). --replay-trace PATH --headless --compare-processing measures this machine's processing time for every replayed frame the same way and reports how the two compare ( ProcessingSummary.describe ), after the replay's own report. --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT (which implies --compare-processing ) turns it into a check: a replay that matched but whose total processing time exceeds the recording's by more than PERCENT exits ExitCode.PROCESSING_SLOWER ; a recording with no processing times cannot be checked ( ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT ). Live runs are paced and headless replays are not, so totals of wall-clock time would not compare; processing times do. They only compare on the same machine (CI against a baseline recorded on its hardware): the report says when the machines differ. Pacing changes processing time too: between paced frames the processor idles and slows down, so a live recording's frames take longer than the same work in an unpaced replay (a 330-frame Clockwork Keep session measured about 65% faster replayed than recorded live, on one machine). The latest measurement run says whether it paced its frames as recording began ( processing_paced : a live run with a target FPS, True; a --rebaseline , a headless replay, False). The fair baseline is a --rebaseline of the session made on the machine that checks it: its times are measured unpaced, as a replay's are (the same session then compares within about 1%). Comparing against a paced recording, the report says so.

docs.text: Rebaseline: --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless . A rebaseline replays OLD's inputs on the current code and writes what that code did to a new recording, NEW, with a summary of what changed. It is how a recording used as a regression test (tests/fixtures/replays, glitchygames/testing/replays.py) follows an intentional change; replacing OLD with NEW stays a deliberate, reviewed step: NEW is never OLD (refused), and nothing replaces OLD. The rules: Options: --rebaseline NEW needs --replay-trace OLD and --headless (a watched replay holds frames and takes the viewer's keys, so it is refused rather than made headless behind the user's back), and refuses NEW or NEW's partial file (rule 4) naming OLD's file, --record-trace (the rebaseline writes its own recording), --audit and --replay-digest (the audit's tools: a rebaseline is not audited) and --replay-fps real (FPS events from this machine's frame times would be recorded as the new baseline); each refusal exits ExitCode.OPTIONS_REFUSED ( rebaseline_refusal ). An unusable OLD is refused as by any replay ( ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT , ExitCode.MISSING_INPUT ), but for one thing only a rebaseline accepts: a recording made before logical names (no game in its header, glitchygames/logical_names.py) of a game that has moved since. Its game is matched by its class's qualified name, whatever the recorded module, and so are its scene starts without scene ( modules_not_compared in glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 17 there; a name several loaded classes share is still refused); NEW holds the current logical names (rule 3), so it replays strictly. This is the backward-compatibility path for such recordings: a plain replay refuses them, naming this command. A recording whose classes moved to another logical module is converted the same way (the logical modules are not compared, the qualified names are); a plain replay refuses it, naming this command. Replay: OLD is replayed as usual (glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 17 there), but a divergence does not stop it ( ReplayOptions.stop_on_divergence False): it runs to OLD's last frame, or until the game ends, noting every frame that differs and every sprite that differs in them. OLD's input the run never received is never carried elsewhere (that would invent an input sequence OLD does not have); it is counted instead: the external events of batches a frame did not pump (it pumped fewer times than recorded), and OLD's frames after the game ended. Recording: RecordingSources over the replay ( replayed ; glitchygames/recording.py) write NEW with OLD's inputs, as the replay's doors served them: the event batches (origins from the replay's merge, so code-posted events stay internal and replaying NEW delivers nothing twice), dt , input_changes , re-applied control events, and each frame's saves_opened , devices_opened and device_enumeration copied from OLD's frame; and the current code's sprites and markers. The header is OLD's, except the game's names ( game_class , game_module , game ): they are this run's ( rebaseline_header ). NEW's frames stack this run's content hash and processing time in front of OLD's histories, and its header this run's measurement_runs entry in front of OLD's (glitchygames/recording_history.py), so an unchanged game shows the same hash one entry deeper, and a changed one shows which frames changed. Writing: NEW is written to NEW.partial ( glitchygames.output_files.partial_path ) and moved into place once the run ended normally, so NEW is never left half written; a run that a crash, a signal or the game's own failing exit ( sys.exit(1) ) ended early writes nothing (the partial file is removed). The game's own successful exit ( sys.exit(0) , sys.exit() ) is the game ending early, as quit_game() is: NEW holds the frames that ran (not the one it left part way through) and the run exits ExitCode.REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST (rule 5). A partial file that cannot be written is refused before the replay starts, on one line, with ExitCode.CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT ( GameEngine._refuse_unwritable_outputs ). If the final move fails, the finished partial file is kept, its path logged and printed, and the run exits ExitCode.CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT . Output: the summary ( RebaselineSummary.describe ) is printed to stdout instead of the replay's report, e.g. Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: 412 frames differ (first at 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16]); sprites affected: Ball#2, Ball#3 or Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: no frames differ , followed by the lost input (rule 2) when there is any, e.g. ; 3 recorded input events not delivered (first at frame 812); ended at frame 500 of 9800 , which is also logged as a warning. The run exits ExitCode.SUCCESS ( ReplayExitPolicy.SUCCESS_AFTER_WRITING ) however many frames differ, but ExitCode.REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST when input was lost ( ReplayResult.has_lost_input ), so a script notices: NEW is still written (it replays clean), but it is not a faithful re-run of OLD's session. NEW replays on the current code with no divergence, as long as the rebaseline replayed all of OLD: a truncated OLD gives a truncated NEW ( source_truncated ), whose replay matches to its cut-off and exits ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT , as any truncated recording does; and a run that ended before OLD's last frame (the lost input of rule 2) records only the frames it ran.

docs.text: Step back in a watched replay: restart the replay process and rebuild up to a frame. A replay cannot run backwards, and the engine cannot be rebuilt in-process (its scenes, sprites and singletons hold the state of every frame run so far). So , (step back), Home and D (glitchygames/replay/controls.py) restart the replay in a fresh process at a pause frame N: The watched replay ends its run with ReplayResult.restart_frame set (the result's end reason is 'restart' , unless it already diverged or ended) and tears down as usual, which closes its window; the end-of-run performance and unhandled-event reports are skipped. GameEngine._restart_replay builds the restart's command ( restart_command ): this process's own command line ( sys.orig_argv , so every option is kept, replay-local ones such as --replay-fps included) with --replay-trace (the recording) and --replay-pause-at-frame N replaced, an explicit --debug-overlay or --no-debug-overlay (whether the overlay was shown) and --replay-viewer-state (the speed, the debug overlay's panel and the divergence found so far, so D works at once: ViewerState ). They are appended, the last occurrence of an option winning (an earlier abbreviation such as --debug-o included), before any bare -- . relaunch_replay runs it, with the engine's signal handlers installed again (a SIGTERM or SIGHUP raises SystemExit, and subprocess.run then kills the child with SIGKILL, without its teardown, and reaps it: acceptable, as a replay never records). The first replay process becomes the supervisor: it runs each restarted replay as a child with glitchygames.process.run_command (the engine's one child-process launcher), adding --replay-restart-handoff PATH . A child that steps back again does not start a grandchild: it writes a RestartHandoff (its restart command and its own result's exit code) to that file, whole (written aside, then moved into place), and ends; the supervisor runs it next. So there are never more than two replay processes, however often the viewer steps back, and no process restarts itself. The supervisor exits with the last child's status, but a divergence in any earlier run is kept: when the last child ends with SUCCESS , the first non-success result handed over (or the first run's own) is the status. An unreadable handoff or a child that cannot start is logged and exits ExitCode.INTERNAL_ERROR . The supervisor keeps the memory its own replay used (the engine's scenes, sprites, the recording's frames and pygame's modules: pygame is quit, the rest is not released) while the children run; only the first process supervises, so this is paid once, not per restart. 4. The restarted replay ( ReplayOptions.pause_at_frame ) skips the start screen (the viewer already started it) and rebuilds: frames 0 to N - 1 run in full but unpresented and unpaced, in silence ( FrameSilencer , glitchygames/replay/silence.py, which an instant replay's fast-forward shares: Rebuild.silence_frame stops every sound a frame started after it, as Sound.play() gives its channel full volume again, and music is paused until the rebuild ends; Rebuild.begin follows the game's own music pauses, so music the game paused itself stays paused), presenting Rebuilding: frame k / N every REBUILD_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_SECONDS of real time and printing it every REBUILD_PROGRESS_PRINT_INTERVAL_SECONDS ( Rebuild.progress_is_due ), so the window does not look frozen. At frame N it pauses, showing frame N - 1's picture. Frame 0 always runs first ( FIRST_PAUSED_FRAME ), so a pause frame of 0 (Home) pauses after it. A game that asks the mixer what is playing may get a different answer during the rebuild than when it was recorded (glitchygames/replay/ silence.py says why the replay is unaffected). os.execv would replace the process in place, but it is not used: starting a process without a shell is a security lint finding everywhere but the one authorised launcher ( glitchygames.process.run_command ).

docs.text: Run frames in silence: a rebuild's frames and an instant replay's fast-forward. Frames that run but are not shown (a restarted replay rebuilding up to its pause frame, glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py; an instant replay fast-forwarding to the seconds it shows, glitchygames/replay/playback.py) must not be heard either. FrameSilencer is the one code path both use: begin follows the game's own pygame.mixer.music.pause() and unpause() calls, so music the game paused itself stays paused at the end. With spares_playing_sounds it also notes the sound each busy channel plays then (the live game's, playing on under a scope). silence_frame , after each silent frame, stops every sound the frame started (a channel's stop() : Sound.play() gives its channel full volume again, so lowering volumes would not do) and pauses the music. Without spares_playing_sounds every channel is stopped ( pygame.mixer.stop() , the rebuild's way: nothing of the live game plays under it). With it, a channel still playing the sound noted at begin plays on; a channel that went idle or plays another sound loses its note and is stopped. A live voice (glitchygames/audio/live.py) queues a new chunk every 100 ms, so its channel soon plays another sound and is stopped, as without sparing. finish stops following the music controls and resumes the music it paused, unless the game's last call paused it. Silencers may stack (a fast-forward inside a rebuild): one pair of wrappers replaces pygame's pause and unpause while any silencer follows them. The wrappers tell every following silencer about the game's call and then call pygame's own functions, captured once when the first silencer began; the last silencer to stop puts pygame's functions back, provided the wrappers are still in place (code that replaced them since keeps its own). A silencer's own pause and resume always call pygame's functions, never the wrappers, so no silencer takes another's for the game's. A game that asks the mixer what is playing ( get_busy , Channel.get_busy ) may get a different answer during silent frames than when they were recorded; audio is played, never compared, so a replay is unaffected unless game logic depends on it (which no recording could replay exactly anyway). Nothing happens without a mixer.

docs.text: Keeps frames silent while they run unseen (see the module docstring). Source code in src/glitchygames/replay/silence.py 150 151 152 153 154 155 156 157 158 159 160 161 162 163 164 165 166 167 168 169 170 171 172 173 174 175 176 177 178 179 180 181 182 183 184 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 200 201 202 203 204 205 206 207 208 209 210 211 212 213 214 215 216 217 218 219 220 221 222 223 224 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 class FrameSilencer : """Keeps frames silent while they run unseen (see the module docstring).""" def __init__ ( self : Self , * , spares_playing_sounds : bool = False ) -> None : """Start with nothing silenced and the game's music controls not followed. Args: spares_playing_sounds: True to let the sounds playing at ``begin`` play on (an instant replay's fast-forward); False to stop every sound (a rebuild). """ self . spares_playing_sounds = spares_playing_sounds # True while music is paused by the silencer (silence_frame), not by the game self . _paused_music = False # Whether the game's last music.pause() / unpause() call while followed paused it self . _game_paused_music = False self . _is_following_music = False # Channel index -> the sound it played at begin (spares_playing_sounds) self . _spared_sounds : dict [ int , pygame . mixer . Sound ] = {} def begin ( self : Self ) -> None : """Follow the game's music controls; note the sounds playing (``spares_playing_sounds``). Until ``finish`` (or ``stop_following_music``), the game's ``pause`` and ``unpause`` calls are noted, so ``finish`` resumes music only when the game did not pause it itself. A game that bound the functions before (``from pygame.mixer.music import pause``) is not followed. Again: nothing. """ if self . _is_following_music : return self . _is_following_music = True _MUSIC_FOLLOWING . add ( silencer = self ) if self . spares_playing_sounds and pygame . mixer . get_init () is not None : for channel_index in range ( pygame . mixer . get_num_channels ()): playing_sound = pygame . mixer . Channel ( channel_index ) . get_sound () if playing_sound is not None : self . _spared_sounds [ channel_index ] = playing_sound def note_game_music_pause ( self : Self , * , paused : bool ) -> None : """Note the game's own music pause (True) or resume (False), while followed. Args: paused: Whether the game's call paused the music. """ self . _game_paused_music = paused def stop_following_music ( self : Self ) -> None : """Stop following the game's music controls (``begin``).""" if not self . _is_following_music : return self . _is_following_music = False _MUSIC_FOLLOWING . remove ( silencer = self ) def silence_frame ( self : Self ) -> None : """Stop every sound the silent frame just run started, and pause any music. Music the silencer paused plays on at ``finish``. Nothing happens without a mixer. """ if pygame . mixer . get_init () is None : return if self . spares_playing_sounds : self . _stop_unspared_channels () else : pygame . mixer . stop () if pygame . mixer . music . get_busy (): # pygame's own pause: the silencer's, not the game's _MUSIC_FOLLOWING . pygame_pause ()() self . _paused_music = True def _stop_unspared_channels ( self : Self ) -> None : """Stop each busy channel not still playing the sound it played at ``begin``.""" for channel_index in range ( pygame . mixer . get_num_channels ()): channel = pygame . mixer . Channel ( channel_index ) spared_sound = self . _spared_sounds . get ( channel_index ) if not channel . get_busy (): self . _spared_sounds . pop ( channel_index , None ) elif spared_sound is None or channel . get_sound () is not spared_sound : self . _spared_sounds . pop ( channel_index , None ) channel . stop () def finish ( self : Self ) -> None : """End the silence: music the silencer paused plays on, unless the game paused it last.""" self . stop_following_music () self . _spared_sounds = {} if ( self . _paused_music and not self . _game_paused_music and pygame . mixer . get_init () is not None ): # pygame's own unpause: other silencers still following must not take it for the # game's _MUSIC_FOLLOWING . pygame_unpause ()() self . _paused_music = False
