docs.text: The engine's recording, replay and measurement tools, described once ( registry.TOOLS ). Each tool is reachable two ways, both built from that one table so their names and options never drift apart: as a flag on any game's own command line ( mygame --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz ), added by GameEngine.args ( registry.add_game_flags ); as a subcommand of the glitchygames command ( glitchygames replay-trace run.jsonl.gz , glitchygames/replay/tools/command.py), which starts the game as a child process (glitchygames/replay/tools/children.py) whenever the game has to run. Nothing is imported here, so importing one tool module loads only what it needs. Importing any of them never imports pytest.
docs.title: tools

docs.text: Games run as child processes: finding a game, and starting it with the engine's flags. Every tool that has to run a game ( glitchygames record-trace , glitchygames replay-trace , the replay pytest plugin, the measurement run) starts it as a child process, with the tool's flag on its command line ( --replay-trace PATH ). The game's GameEngine(game=Game) adds those flags to its own command line (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py), so the game never knows how it was started. Two ways to name the game: By a console script ( [project.scripts] ): game_entry_point finds its entry point, and replay_command loads and calls it in the child the way the installed console script would. recording_console_script tells which console script replays a recording under a fixtures/replays/ directory; console_script_for_game_module which of several starts a recorded game's module. By what the user typed (the command's GAME ): resolve_game reads it as a script path, an entry point MODULE:CALLABLE , an installed console script or an importable module ( GameLaunch ), and launch_game starts it with the tool's arguments. A console script is never run as its installed executable ( bin/<script> ). Its entry point is loaded and called in a python -c child ( entry_point_command ) instead, which is what that executable does. It runs on this interpreter (the one whose packages were searched for the entry point), needs no executable on PATH , and works wherever the metadata is installed: a non-editable install in nox's sessions, or a stand-in game's dist-info in the engine's tests, which has no executable at all. The replay pytest plugin has always started games this way. replay_recording_headless and rebaseline_recording_headless run a recording's replay (or rebaseline) headless through a console script; the replay pytest plugin (glitchygames/testing/replays.py), the bundled demos' test and the measurement run use them. Moved from glitchygames/testing/replays.py (Part 3, Stage D, Task D1), unchanged in behavior: that module imports pytest, and the glitchygames command must not. Importing this module never imports pytest; it imports pygame (through glitchygames.replay ), a required dependency, but opens no display.
docs.title: children

docs.text: The glitchygames command: the engine's tools as subcommands ( registry.TOOLS ). glitchygames <tool> ... runs the tool of that name with the same options its game flag takes ( glitchygames replay-trace run.jsonl.gz --headless is mygame --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz --headless ). A tool that runs the game starts it as a child process; arguments after a bare -- go to that game unchanged. The tool runs inside the crash boundary a game flag's tool runs in ( game_engine.run_inside_tool_crash_boundary ), so both front ends end alike: an uncaught exception exits ExitCode.INTERNAL_ERROR (logged with its traceback), Ctrl-C ExitCode.INTERRUPTED , and a terminating signal (SIGTERM, SIGHUP) its own code, after a child game the tool waits for is stopped and reaped. A child killed by a signal is reported as a shell reports it, 128 + the signal ( exit_codes.shell_exit_status ). A missing required option is refused as on the game ( registry.missing_required_options : ExitCode.OPTIONS_REFUSED ). Started as the glitchygames console script or as python -m glitchygames , both through glitchygames/ main .py, which hides pygame's banner before anything imports pygame (importing this module does, through glitchygames.replay ).
docs.title: command

docs.text: --compare-trace OLD : the onion skin, OLD's frames drawn over a watched replay or live play. The contract (decision 18 of plans/2026-10-26-workspace-packages-3-demos.md, Task D11): What is shown. --replay-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD [--compare-alpha PERCENT] (on the game, or glitchygames replay-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD ... ) replays NEW watched, as any watched replay, drawn solid. On each presented frame, OLD's items of the frame of the same number are drawn over it at PERCENT opacity ( DEFAULT_COMPARE_ALPHA_PERCENT when not given; 0 to 100, the parser refuses any other: argument_types.percent_from_zero_to_one_hundred ; which pixels are items: rule 10), then the viewer's status bar over both ( ReplaySources.draw_overlay ; the debug overlay, drawn before the doors' overlay, is under OLD too). Only the presented copy is drawn on, so nothing in NEW's replay changes: its frames, comparisons, result and exit code are a plain watched replay's. While a restarted replay rebuilds, nothing is drawn over its progress screen. OLD's child. OLD is replayed headless by a child process ( OnionSkin ): OLD's own game, the console script that starts the module its header names ( traces.find_recorded_game ), or, when none does (a game started as a script), this game started again ( children.running_game_command ), with --replay-trace OLD --headless and the hidden --replay-frame-stream PORT:TOKEN . It replays under OLD's own seed, so it compares as a plain headless replay does and stops at its first divergence (it then ends there, and its exit and output are logged). The child is started inside the run ( OnionSkin.begin ): on the first presented frame, or as a restarted replay's rebuild begins (rule 8), never before, so every refusal comes before it, and the run's teardown ( GameEngine._shutdown ) always stops it and waits for it ( OnionSkin.stop ): when the replay ends, fails, is interrupted or restarts. The frame stream. The parent listens on a port of FRAME_STREAM_HOST (loopback only), and the child connects to it ( FrameStream ) before its first frame and sends the run's token first ( FRAME_STREAM_TOKEN_LENGTH hex characters, drawn per child from secrets ): a connection without it (another local process) is closed and logged, and the parent goes on waiting for its child. After each replayed frame, ReplaySources.end_frame hands the display surface (the frame as presented, overlays never on it) to the stream, which writes FRAME_HEADER (the frame's number, width and height: three little-endian unsigned 32-bit integers), then its pixels: width x height x 3 bytes of RGB, rows top to bottom ( pygame.image.tobytes , FRAME_PIXEL_FORMAT ). A socket, not an inherited pipe: the one child launcher ( glitchygames.process.start_command ) passes no descriptors, and a socket works the same on every platform. Lockstep. The parent reads frames only when it draws one: it reads (and drops) OLD's frames until it holds the one numbered as the frame presented, and keeps that one (memory holds one frame, as sent: only a frame drawn is decoded ( decode_frame_pixels ), once; a header whose size is not NEW's presented frame's ends OLD there, before its pixels are read). Paused, it reads nothing, so the child blocks on the full socket within a few frames: the two runs move together, through pause and frame steps too. OLD shorter than NEW. When OLD's stream ends, its last frame stays, labelled OLD_ENDED_LABEL ("OLD ended at frame N"). NEW shorter: NEW's replay ends as usual and the teardown stops the child. A child that streams nothing (it exits or never connects within CHILD_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS ) draws nothing over NEW, labelled OLD_NOT_REPLAYED_LABEL , with its output logged. A child that stalls (alive, but nothing arrives within CHILD_READ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS ) ends OLD there, labelled and logged as any end, and is stopped at once: NEW's replay goes on (its viewer is held only while a read waits). Refused before anything runs ( compare_trace_refusal , old_recording_refusal ): with --headless (an onion skin is watched; a headless replay under another seed, or --rebaseline , is the headless way to see what changed), --audit or --rebaseline ( ExitCode.OPTIONS_REFUSED ); an OLD recorded on a display of another size than NEW's, or that is not a readable recording, a header whose seed or size is missing or malformed included ( ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT : its child could not replay it); a missing OLD ( ExitCode.MISSING_INPUT ). A header without a screen size (not the engine's recorder's) lets the sizes go uncompared, with a warning. A frame stream without --headless , or whose value is not PORT:TOKEN , is refused too ( frame_stream_refusal ): it is a headless child's. Every seed row. NEW may be OLD itself under another seed ( --replay-trace OLD --random-seed N --compare-trace OLD : the seed rule's row 5, which compares and writes nothing), so OLD's run under its own seed is shown over the new seed's. Step back. The viewer's step back (and Home, D) restarts NEW's process with --replay-pause-at-frame N (glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py), keeping every other option, --compare-trace included, and names in its viewer state the game frame (rule 11) the restart shows paused ( ViewerState.compare_first_game_frame , from the game frame each frame showed, ReplayResult.shown_game_frames ). The restarted process gives its own child --replay-pause-at-frame G + 1 for that game frame G ( GameEngine._olds_pause_at_frame ): a headless replay does not pause, but its stream then writes no game frame before G ( first_streamed_frame , read in game frames by the stream), so the child runs on through the frames NEW rebuilds unshown. Without that viewer state (a pause frame given by hand) the child streams from OLD's first frame. The restarted replay starts the child as its rebuild begins ( ReplaySources.hold_frame ), so the two rebuilds run at once instead of one after the other. Live play (decision 19, Task D12). <game> --compare-trace OLD [--compare-alpha PERCENT] without --replay-trace plays the game live, with real input, and draws OLD over each live presented frame as rules 1 to 5 draw it over NEW (the same child, stream, token, size cap and timeouts), through the live host's doors ( HostSources.overlay , glitchygames/host.py). A live frame is paired by the game frame it shows (rule 11), as a replay's is, so --record-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD and a later --replay-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD pair the same frames. The game plays under OLD's recorded seed ( OldRecording.random_seed ), so OLD's ghost starts in the same world, unless --random-seed N is given; logged either way. Refused before anything runs as rule 6 says ( --headless ; --audit and --rebaseline need --replay-trace anyway), OLD's size checked against the live window once it opens, before the first frame. --record-trace NEW may go with it. Live play has no step back. Only OLD's items (decision 18 as amended, Tasks D13 and D16; the user: "Just draw the items from the other game at 50% on top of my game regardless of what else is going on"). NEW stays fully opaque; OLD's background never fades it ( GhostCompositor ). Each frame is told apart on its own, with no memory between frames: OLD's background colors are the exact colors covering at least BACKGROUND_COLOR_SHARE (5%) of OLD's frame (a floor, a wall); OLD's items are the pixels where OLD differs from NEW in a color that is none of them. They are blended over NEW at PERCENT (an alpha blit's arithmetic, blend_over ), whatever NEW has there; every other pixel is NEW's, unchanged. So a dot OLD ate (OLD shows floor) leaves NEW's dot exact, and a dot NEW ate shows OLD's over NEW's floor (the user's report on D13's rule, which learned a background where the runs agreed and so took both runs' dots for background). Known costs: OLD's sprite pixels in a background color are not shown (a sprite drawn in the floor's color); a background of many small colors (a texture or a gradient, each color under 5%) may show some of them as items; and a single color covering 5% or more of OLD's frame is background even when it is OLD's item (a large sprite, about 139x139 at 800x480, many pickups of one color, a full-screen overlay), so it vanishes from the ghost. Telling the colors apart sorts OLD's frame once per new OLD frame: about 2 ms for a game's frame, up to about 19 ms for one whose every pixel has a color of its own (noise; a textured backdrop falls in between). A held last frame (rule 5) is drawn by the same rule, and the labels are drawn as before. Vectorized with numpy on the presented copy. Pausing freezes the ghost (decisions 18 and 19 as amended, Task D14; the user: "Yes, the games should pause."). Frames are paired by the game-frame clock (glitchygames/game_frames.py), not by the frame number a recording counts: a frame whose logic ran on a pause screen shows the game frame before it, so OLD's frame stays drawn (no label) until the game runs again. Every side reads the same clock: live play ( HostSources.draw_overlay ), a watched replay ( ReplaySources.draw_overlay ) and OLD's child, whose stream sends only game frames, numbered by it ( ReplaySources 's frame sink), so OLD's own pauses are skipped too and NEW's game frame N pairs with OLD's game frame N. Recordings are unchanged: they count every frame.
docs.title: compare

docs.text: The golden-trace harness: a game driven headless with scripted input, every sprite sampled. A golden trace is the rect and visibility of every sprite in the active scene's all_sprites , recorded after each frame of a scripted, fully deterministic run ( record_trace ). The harness knows a game only by its scene class and its input script ( InputScript ), so it runs any game built on the engine: the record-golden-trace tool (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py) runs it on the game it is given, with an input script named MODULE:NAME ( load_input_script ). Our own games' scripts and their golden traces are this repository's (scripts/golden_inputs.py, scripts/record_golden_traces.py, tests/world/test_golden_traces.py). Determinism Every frame runs with dt fixed at 1/60 second. A game started with --random-seed ( random_seed ; our goldens pass RANDOM_SEED ) draws all the randomness of the engine's named streams ( glitchygames/randomness.py ) from it. Without one the run rolls a random seed, as any run does (the user's seed rule, 2026-10-26), and the trace names it ( random_seed , as a recording's header does), so the golden can be made again under it. Nothing is patched. A game clock read from Scene.game_time is driven by the fixed dt (exactly 1/60 second per unpaused frame), so no clock is patched. Save files go to a fresh temporary directory, so high scores on disk cannot leak in. Events the host environment posts (window focus, window shown, audio devices, ...) are discarded before each frame. SDL's dummy video driver posts a focus-lost event at startup, which would auto-pause a game that pauses on focus loss. Ids: each sprite gets <ClassName>#<n> the first time it is seen, where n counts that class's sprites in order of first appearance over the whole run. Ids never renumber when a sprite is removed (a collected coin, a dead ball). Scope and maintenance GoldenTraceSceneManager.run_frame runs SceneManager._run_frame , the same frame body SceneManager.start() runs (both branches, and the --record-trace hook). Frame pacing, timing and the first frame's measured dt are out of scope: the harness fixes dt at 1/60 and never sleeps. The trace format (gzip JSON Lines with keyframes and deltas, StableSpriteIds , the reader and writer) lives in glitchygames/tracing.py ; identical traces give identical bytes. The harness never chooses the video driver: whoever runs it does (SDL's dummy drivers in the tests and scripts/record_golden_traces.py, --headless on a game). Importing this module imports the engine ( GameEngine ), so the tool table imports it only when the tool runs. Moved from scripts/record_golden_traces.py (Stage D, Task D4a), re-keyed from our game keys to a scene class and an input script.
docs.title: golden_traces

docs.text: A game's identity, read from the game object alone: its package, directory and console script. The game passes itself to the engine ( GameEngine(game=Game) ) and declares nothing else (stage D's decision 13); the tools find what they need about it from that object: package : the top-level package of the scene class's module ( paddleslap for paddleslap.game ; __main__ for a game run as a script); package directory : where that package is, from importlib.util.find_spec (looked up, never imported), or the loaded module's file when the import system can't find it (a script's __main__ ); console script : the installed console script whose entry point ( module:function ) is in that package and starts the game's module ( children.console_script_for_game_module ); distribution : the installed distribution that holds the package ( importlib.metadata.packages_distributions ), else the console script's distribution (an editable install's metadata lists no packages, only its .pth file); looked up when first read, never as the identity is made: the lookup scans every installed file (0.6 s here, and far more on a loaded machine), and no tool reads it; source revision ( game_source_revision ): the package directory's commit, looked up as the engine's own is; each run records it beside the engine's, and a ledger row names it. Whatever isn't found is None: a game no console script starts, or one no distribution holds, still has an identity.
docs.title: identity

docs.text: The measure , unmeasured and clear-published tools: recordings in the run ledger. Design: plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics-1-frame-performance-history.md (Part 1 of plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics.md); moved here from scripts/replay_metrics.py (Part 3, Stage D, Task D6). The run ledger keeps one row per recording per run ( glitchygames.recording_metrics.LedgerRow ) beyond the ten runs a recording holds. A project may publish it ( [tool.glitchygames] published-ledger : ours, with the docs site on gh-pages); rows measured here wait in the pending ledger ( pending-ledger ) until a publish takes them, or go into the ledger directory as row files ( --rows-directory : our pre-commit hook, scripts/measure_staged_replays.py). measure ( nox -s replay-metrics ; nox -s docs-deploy runs it first): refuses a game whose commit is unknown, and one with uncommitted changes, unless --allow-dirty (the rows say so; such a trial never counts as measuring its commit) or --skip-dirty (measure nothing and succeed: what docs-deploy passes). The revision is the game's ( identity.game_source_revision ; the engine's for a game whose package isn't found), the commit a ledger row names (Task D3), so a game outside the engine's checkout is judged by its own; for each of the game's recordings ( recordings.game_recordings : its goldens in the project and its bundled demos; or the PATHs given) not already measured for this commit on this machine (published, pending or a row file; --force measures again): rebaselines it headless into a temporary file through the game's console script ( children.rebaseline_recording_headless ), so the run measures every frame's processing time and records its provenance. Each replays under its own recorded seed (Stage D's decision 17): --random-seed is refused, as verify refuses it; appends the rebaselined recording's rows ( ledger_rows_from_rebaseline : the measurement, then each run the recording held, unless already in the ledger) to the pending ledger. A run the recording held is written (to the pending file, or with --rows-directory as row files) only if it landed ( rows_to_write : measured on a commit that is on the project's landed-ref without uncommitted changes; none at all without that ref, said once). "Already in the ledger" compares rows with a moved recording's old path resolved to its new one ( LedgerRow.held_key , by the project's recording-renames ). The children must run the game's own package (an editable install, as uv run gives), or they cannot name its commit: a row whose commit is not the game's is a failure. unmeasured lists the recordings measure would measure (without --force ): one ledger name per line on standard output, then a summary on standard error. clear-published (after a publish succeeded) removes the pending rows the published ledger now holds; the rest stay pending. The front ends (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py): On the game : --measure [PATH ...] ( measure_on_the_game ), --unmeasured and --clear-published run from GameEngine.__init__ , before the engine starts pygame: the game is neither built nor shown. With no PATHs, --measure measures the game's own recordings, as --unmeasured lists them. The command : glitchygames measure [PATH ...] [--game GAME ...] ( measure_command ) starts each game ( --game , else the project's [tool.glitchygames] games ) as a child with --measure and combines their exit codes ( combined_exit_code ); with PATHs, each is measured by the game its header names, or by the one --game . When the games come from the settings, a golden none of them replays is a failure, named with why (a workspace member that is not installed: uv sync --all-packages ). glitchygames unmeasured [--game GAME ...] reads the recordings and the ledger itself, without starting a game it can name by its console script; glitchygames clear-published is the game flag's work. Every tool finds the project as verify does ( verify.verify_project_root : the nearest directory with [tool.glitchygames] , else the nearest pyproject.toml) and reads its settings from there; a pending ledger or rows directory in the project's local directory ( .glitchygames/ ) is created through settings.ensure_local_directory . Exit codes: SUCCESS ; OPTIONS_REFUSED for an unknown commit or uncommitted changes (and for a seed, --allow-dirty with --skip-dirty , a game no console script starts given PATHs, or a GAME that names nothing); UNUSABLE_INPUT for settings that can't be read, or a pending ledger that exists but can't be read (no permission, not UTF-8: UnreadableLedgerError , naming it, as performance-pages says it); INTERNAL_ERROR when a recording could not be measured (the others are still measured).
docs.title: measure

docs.text: The performance-pages tool: the run ledger's graph pages, one per recording. Design: plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics-1-frame-performance-history.md; moved here from scripts/generate_performance_graphs.py (Part 3, Stage D, Task D7), which keeps only our docs site's paths and the snippet its page includes, and calls this module: merged_ledger : the project's ledger rows from every source, each row once ( glitchygames.recording_metrics.merge_ledgers ), driven by its [tool.glitchygames] settings (passed in, never read here from any one project): the row files in its ledger-directory (labelled with the commit their code landed in: landed_rows , by the git history of the measured-paths ), the ledger it publishes ( published-ledger , git show REF:PATH of the local ref; nothing is fetched) and its pending-ledger . Rows measured on uncommitted changes ( LedgerRow.from_uncommitted_changes ), and row files whose code never landed, are left out of a build that is published ( include_uncommitted_changes False) and shown, labelled, in a local one; write_performance_pages : the merged ledger as one file ( ledger_file_name : the published ledger's name, so a deploy publishes it where it is read back), then one graph page per recording ( <console-script>-<name>.html ): processing time per frame (p50, p99 and max) by commit, frames over budget by commit, and the live runs' frame times (how steady pacing was), one line per machine and kind of run ( performance_series : times compare only on one machine, and paced frames process slower than replayed ones); FPS by commit ( fps_charts : live runs' achieved FPS solid, replays' headroom FPS dashed, each point the average with its 5% low and 5% high as an error bar, and a line at the target FPS from budget_seconds ); and the machines view ( machines_chart : each machine's latest replay as a bar of average headroom FPS with its 5% low and high, CI machines marked). FPS is read from the rows' seconds with fps_from_seconds ; rows from before the slice means (2026-10-28) have no FPS point. The x axis is the commits in commit-date order, labelled with their short hash; plotly.js comes from jsDelivr ( PLOTLY_JS_URL ), so rendering imports nothing beyond the engine's own dependencies. Then a frame x commit heatmap per machine from the rows' per-frame profiles ( FrameProfile : each bucket's slowest frame); rows without one (older rows, a recording's own runs) have no heatmap line. A file is rewritten only when its text changed ( write_if_changed ), and graph pages of recordings no longer in the ledger are removed. build_performance_pages is one build, local or published: the tool and our docs site's mkdocs hook (scripts/generate_performance_graphs.py: published for gh-deploy ) both build through it, so a deploy's pages are the tool's --published ones. The front ends (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py) write the project's pages into DIRECTORY: a local build (rows from uncommitted changes shown, labelled), or with --published what a deploy publishes. They run no game: On the game : mygame --performance-pages DIRECTORY [--published] ( performance_pages_on_the_game ) runs from GameEngine.__init__ , before the engine starts pygame: the game is neither built nor shown. The command : glitchygames performance-pages DIRECTORY [--published] ( performance_pages_command ). Both find the project as verify does ( verify.verify_project_root ) and read its settings from there; a DIRECTORY in the project's local directory ( .glitchygames/ ) is made through settings.ensure_local_directory ( measure.ensure_directory ). Exit codes: SUCCESS ; UNUSABLE_INPUT for settings that can't be read, a pending ledger that can't be read (no permission, not UTF-8: UnreadableLedgerError , naming it), or row files git can't date (no repository); CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT when DIRECTORY can't be written.
docs.title: performance_pages

docs.text: A game's own recordings: its goldens in the project and the demos bundled in its package. What --verify with no paths replays (glitchygames/replay/tools/verify.py), found from the game alone (its GameIdentity ) and the project's settings, so a game the engine has never seen finds its recordings with nothing declared: goldens : the files the project's golden-globs match ( [tool.glitchygames] ; by default tests/fixtures/replays/**/*.jsonl.gz ) that this game's console script replays ( children.recording_console_script : a workspace member's directory names its distribution, another project's fixtures/replays/<console-script>/ its console script). A golden another game replays, or one whose console script can't be told, is not this game's; demos : <package>/demos/*.jsonl.gz in the game's own installed package ( glitchygames.bundled_demos.bundled_demos , given that one package). Bookmarked copies ( glitchygames.tracing.is_bookmarked_copy ) are neither. A game no console script starts has no recordings found this way: no golden can be told to be its, and none could be replayed by name.
docs.title: recordings

docs.text: The table of the engine's tools ( TOOLS ) and the two front ends built from it. Every recording, replay and measurement tool is described once, as a Tool with its ToolOption s, and both front ends are generated from that description, so a tool's name, options, defaults and help can't differ between them (tests/replay/tools/test_registry.py walks the table to check): On the game ( add_game_flags ): GameEngine.args adds each tool to the game's own command line as --<name> (with the tool's options as flags of their own), so any game the engine runs has them without declaring anything. A tool with a game handler runs in place of the game's own run ( run_game_flag_tool , from GameEngine.__init__ , before the engine starts pygame): one that runs no game, or one that runs the game in a harness of its own ( --record-golden-trace , --record-session ). A tool without one is the game's run, which the engine already handles ( --record-trace , --replay-trace ). As the glitchygames command ( build_command_parser , glitchygames/replay/tools/ command.py): each tool is a subcommand with the same name and options, plus the command's own arguments (the game to run, --project-root ). A subcommand whose tool runs the game starts it as a child process with the tool's flag (glitchygames/replay/tools/children.py). An option may be listed under several tools (the same ToolOption : --headless is record-trace's and replay-trace's); it is one flag on the game and an option of each tool's subcommand. The engine's general flags that no tool lists ( --resolution , ...) stay in GameEngine.args ; the command passes them to the game after a bare -- . Only one tool runs at a time: a game given two tool flags is refused ( run_game_flag_tool ).
docs.title: registry

docs.text: The report tool: a recording's runs, speed changes and behaviour-change map. Design: plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics-2-behaviour-change-map.md (Part 2 of plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics.md); moved here whole from scripts/recording_report.py (Part 3, Stage D, Task D7). A recording holds up to ten runs (each --rebaseline stacks one; glitchygames/recording_history.py); this prints, newest first: Runs: each run's commit (abbreviated, with uncommitted changes when the checkout had them), machine (CPU model), power source, when it measured and what it rebaselined, then its summary (stored in the header, else computed from the frames): processing p50/p95/p99/max, the worst frame and its scene, frames over budget, the headroom FPS of its processing times (average, 5% low and 5% high: recording_metrics.describe_processing_fps ), and a live run's frame times with the FPS it achieved ( describe_frame_time_fps ). A summary from before the slice means (2026-10-28) shows no FPS. Processing: for each adjacent pair of runs, the frames that did the same work (equal content hashes) and how their time changed; spans of frames that got slower or faster by more than --threshold percent and --minimum-ms milliseconds. Frames whose hash changed are different work, never a speed change. Behaviour changes: for each adjacent pair of runs, the spans of frames whose content hash differs, with the first changed frame's scene and both runs' commits: where to look, and the commit range to bisect. The analysis is glitchygames/recording_metrics.py; this is its command line, on both front ends (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py). It runs no game: On the game : mygame --report PATH [--threshold PERCENT] [--minimum-ms MS] [--spans N] ( report_on_the_game ) runs from GameEngine.__init__ , before the engine starts pygame: the game is neither built nor shown. The command : glitchygames report PATH [same options] ( report_command ). Usage uv run glitchygames report src/games/paddleslap/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz uv run glitchygames report PATH --threshold 10 --minimum-ms 0.1 --spans 50 Exit codes: SUCCESS ; MISSING_INPUT when the file does not exist; UNUSABLE_INPUT when it is not a readable recording.
docs.title: report

docs.text: Record a scripted session of a game through the real engine ( GameEngine.start ). A scripted session is a game run for real, frame loop and all, with --record-trace , while a supervisor (glitchygames/supervision.py) plays an input script ( InputScript , glitchygames/replay/tools/golden_traces.py): at the supervisor slot of frame N it posts the script's key events and per-frame input for frame N + 1 with glitchygames.recording.post_input_event , so the recording holds them as external input, exactly what a player's keys are. frame_count plays the script's frames 0 to frame_count - 1. The record-session tool (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py) runs it on the game it is given, with the input script named MODULE:NAME ( load_input_script ); our own games' golden replays are recorded by scripts/record_scripted_session.py. The controls tail ( controls_tail ): after the script's frames the supervisor plays it. Its first frame releases every key the script left held; then it presses whatever it holds (a golden replay's tail exercises the controls the script does not), and it must end with the game's own quit control. The game ends the run: the recording's last frame holds the QUIT the game posted (internal), so a replay whose game no longer quits diverges ("missing internal event"). A game still running QUIT_WAIT_FRAMES after the tail's last input fails the recording ( GameDidNotQuitError ). A session is N + T + 2 frames long, T being the tail frame of its last input (the quit): the game posts QUIT while handling that frame's events, and the next frame (the last) pumps it. Without a tail, at frame N - 1 the supervisor ends the run ( SceneManager.quit_requested , no event), so the recording holds frames 0 to N - 1 and no quit. Unlike the golden-trace harness, the session runs the real frame loop ( SceneManager.start ): frames are paced at the game's target FPS, each frame's dt is measured and FPS events are posted, so a --replay-trace replay of the recording (which runs the same loop) matches it frame for frame. Recording takes real time (about 60 frames a second), and two recordings of the same script never have the same bytes (measured frame times differ). Script placements move sprites directly (they are not input), so a session may not run a frame a placement is scheduled before, unless the placements only steer the script's own input ( input_only_placements : PaddleSlap's release its tracked keys and resume tracking). Input scheduled before frame 0 cannot be posted (there is no supervisor slot before it) and is refused. A game that reads its controls from the frame's polled input ( current_input() ) never sees a posted event there: SDL updates its polled state only for a real device's events. With polled_input the session's live snapshots show the supervisor's posted input ( PostedPolledInput , polled_input_follows ), as a real player's would. Only then: without it a session records the snapshots it always did (held keys absent), so a game's re-recordings keep their content hashes. Host environment events (window shown and focus, audio devices) the dummy video driver posts are external and are recorded; a replay serves them as recorded, so they are harmless. The session drops those queued before the first frame (as the golden-trace harness does), because SDL's dummy driver posts a focus-lost event at startup that would auto-pause a game that pauses on it. The session never chooses the video driver: whoever runs it does (SDL's dummy drivers in the tests and scripts/record_scripted_session.py, --headless on a game). Importing this module imports the engine ( GameEngine ), so the tool table imports it only when the tool runs. Moved from scripts/record_scripted_session.py (Stage D, Task D4b), re-keyed from our game keys to a scene class, an input script and flags ( polled_input , input_only_placements ).
docs.title: scripted_sessions

docs.text: A project's settings for the engine's tools, from [tool.glitchygames] in its pyproject.toml. Every setting has a default that fits a standard layout, so a project with no such table (a player's own local runs, a game the engine has never seen) works as it is. The keys are kebab-case, as pyproject.toml's are (stage D's settings table): games : the console scripts the tools run when given no game (default: the project's [project.scripts] ). golden-globs : where the golden replays are, as globs relative to the project root. ledger-directory : where measured rows are kept as row files (a git pathspec too, so it is relative). pending-ledger : where measured rows wait to be published (default: in the project's local directory, .glitchygames/ , outside the ledger directory so it is never committed with the rows). published-ledger : where the ledger is published, as REF:PATH (what git show reads), or nothing published (the default). landed-ref : the ref whose commits count as landed. measured-paths and unmeasured-paths : what a code tree holds, as git pathspecs (glitchygames/code_tree.py). recording-renames : recordings that moved, old repository path -> new, so a recording's history follows it. Each path is relative, no new path is itself an old one (lookups are one hop: an old path names the final one directly), and no two old paths are the same path written two ways; refused when read otherwise. recording_renames_problems finds a new path that does not exist (a check of the files, which reading settings never does). game-timeout-seconds : how long glitchygames verify and glitchygames measure wait for each game they start ( GAME --verify , GAME --measure ) before stopping it and failing it (default: an hour, DEFAULT_GAME_TIMEOUT_SECONDS ). A game replays each of its recordings in a child of its own with a timeout of its own ( REPLAY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS ); this bounds what never ends at all, such as an editor or a server among [project.scripts] . Stored paths are relative to the project root. Every path the tools write into a file (a recording header's path options, a run's rebaselined_from , a ledger row's recording) is relative to the project root, the one these settings are read from ( find_project_root : the nearest project; --project-root where a tool's subcommand takes it), POSIX-style; a path inside another checkout of the same project (the same [project] name ) relative to that checkout's root; any other path outside the project as its file name only ( stored_path ), so no user name, home or scratch directory is ever written into a file meant to be committed. Settings only name paths, relative to the project root: nothing is created or checked on disk when they are read. A path that doesn't exist yet (no ledger directory before the first measurement) is created or reported by the tool that writes or reads it. A tool writing into the project's local directory ( .glitchygames/ ) creates it with ensure_local_directory , which puts a .gitignore of * there, as pytest does for its cache, so nothing in it is committed. Part 3, Stage D, Task D2: these replaced the module constants of glitchygames/code_tree.py and glitchygames/recording_metrics.py ( LEDGER_DIRECTORY , MEASURED_PATHS , the member-test pathspecs, ORIGIN_MAIN , PUBLISHED_LEDGER_PATH / _REF , PENDING_LEDGER_RELATIVE_PATH and RECORDING_PATH_RENAMES ), whose values are now ours in the root pyproject.toml.
docs.title: settings

docs.text: glitchygames record-trace , replay-trace , record-golden-trace , record-session . Each of these tools runs the game, so its subcommand starts it as a child process with the tool's flag ( Tool.child_arguments : --record-trace PATH , --replay-trace PATH , --record-golden-trace PATH , --record-session PATH and the options given), where the game's own engine records or replays exactly as the flag on the game does. The child's exit status is the command's. record-trace GAME PATH : GAME is read by children.resolve_game (a script path, an entry point, a console script or a module). record-golden-trace GAME PATH --input-script MODULE:NAME --frame-count N : GAME is read as record-trace 's is. On the game, the flag runs the golden-trace harness in place of the game's own run ( record_golden_trace_on_the_game ): the game's scene class, driven by the input script for N frames at a fixed 1/60 second, every sprite sampled each frame (glitchygames/replay/tools/golden_traces.py). record-session GAME PATH --input-script MODULE:NAME --frame-count N : GAME is read as record-trace 's is. On the game, the flag records a scripted session in place of the game's own run ( record_session_on_the_game ): the game's scene class run for real, its own frame loop recorded with --record-trace , while a supervisor plays the input script (and a --controls-tail ) as a player's input (glitchygames/replay/tools/scripted_sessions.py). replay-trace PATH : the game is the one the recording's header names: the installed console script that starts its module ( children.console_script_for_game_module ). When that module no longer imports (a moved script), or no console script starts it, the command asks for --game GAME , read as record-trace 's GAME is. Arguments after a bare -- go to the game unchanged ( --resolution 640x480 ). The command says on standard error which game it runs and how it read it.
docs.title: traces

docs.text: The verify tool: replay recordings headless and say, one line each, whether they matched. Each recording is replayed by the game in a child process ( --replay-trace PATH --headless , children.headless_replay_arguments ), never with a seed of its own, so every replay compares with its recording (Stage D's decision 17). One line per recording goes to standard output: PASS tests/fixtures/replays/rally/serve.jsonl.gz: Replay matched 450 frames (end of recording) FAIL tests/fixtures/replays/rally/lob.jsonl.gz: REPLAY_DIVERGED (1): Replay diverged at ... then verify: N of M recordings passed . A recording inside the project is named by its path relative to the project, any other (a demo installed in site-packages) by its path. With no recordings to verify it says so ( verify: no recordings found ... ) and succeeds. The exit code ( verification_exit_code ): ExitCode.SUCCESS : every recording matched, or there was none; ExitCode.REPLAY_DIVERGED : some diverged, and nothing else went wrong; otherwise the first other failure's own code: MISSING_INPUT (no such recording), UNUSABLE_INPUT (not a recording, another game's, or settings that can't be read), OPTIONS_REFUSED (its game can't be found), INTERNAL_ERROR (a replay that crashed inside the engine, ran too long, or exited with a status that is no ExitCode ), and so on. A replay that crashes before its engine starts (in the game's own code before GameEngine.start() , where no exit code is mapped) exits with Python's 1, which is REPLAY_DIVERGED 's: it counts as a divergence (the user's ruling, 2026-10-27: "Yes, crashes count as divergences"). Its line still ends with the exception. Both front ends find the project the same way ( verify_project_root ): --project-root when the command is given it, else the nearest directory at or above the current one whose pyproject.toml has [tool.glitchygames] , else the nearest with a pyproject.toml ( settings.find_project_root : inside a workspace member, the workspace root), else the current directory. When settings are read there (no PATHs) and it has no pyproject.toml , they say the defaults are used. A seed is refused on both front ends ( seed_refusal ), before any replay runs, with ExitCode.OPTIONS_REFUSED : a replay under another seed compares nothing and succeeds (rule 19 of glitchygames/replay/driver.py), so a tampered recording would pass. --random-seed given to the tool, among the game's own arguments beside --verify , or after the command's -- is refused alike (the user's rule: verify always compares). Both pass the game's other arguments on to every game they start: the command those after a bare -- , the game those on its own command line beside --verify ( registry.tool_free_arguments ). The two front ends (glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py): On the game , --verify [PATH ...] [--only TEXT] ( verify_on_the_game ) runs from GameEngine.__init__ , before the engine starts pygame: the game is neither built nor shown. It replays each recording by starting itself again ( children.running_game_command ), so a game run as a script verifies too. With no PATHs: its own recordings ( recordings.game_recordings ) in the project. The command , glitchygames verify [PATH ...] [--only TEXT] [--game GAME ...] ( verify_command ): with no PATHs, each game ( --game , given once per game, else the project's [tool.glitchygames] games ) is started as a child with --verify and verifies its own; with PATHs, each is replayed by the game its header names (as replay-trace finds it), or by the one --game . --game is the command's own: a game verifying itself needs none.
docs.title: verify

docs.text: The replay viewer: a watched replay is a read-only game inside a game. Two loops share the frame loop of SceneManager.start while a replay is watched (glitchygames/replay/driver.py, rule 14): OUTER, the viewer ( ReplayViewer ): owns the window. It ticks at a fixed real-time rate ( CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND , on glitchygames.clock.measured_seconds , never replayed), whatever the replay's speed and whether it is paused. Each tick it reads the viewer's keys ( ReplayControls , once per press), refreshes the status line, and presents one frame: the inner game's latest, with the status bar, start screen and debug overlay drawn on a copy. INNER, the recorded game: steps at its recorded frame times and never receives viewer input. Its frames always run in full (events, logic, update, render), exactly as recorded; only their presentation is left to the outer tick ( ReplaySources.presents_frames is False while watched). The contract between them, asked through EngineSources.hold_frame before each inner frame: No tick open: sleep until the next tick is due (while inner frames run, sleep_for : the engine's high-resolution sleep-then-spin timer, glitchygames/timing.py FastTimer ; paused, at the start screen or over, sleep_coarsely , which never spins), open it, let the doors run the tick's work (keys), then add the real time since the last tick, times the speed, to the accumulator. A tick within TICK_SNAP_WINDOW_SECONDS of one period counts as exactly one period, the error carried to the next tick, so wake-up jitter does not turn 1x into ticks of 0 and 2 frames. Only while the inner game is running: paused, at the start screen or over, the accumulator empties, and a restart seeds it with half a frame (so frame boundaries never sit on a tick boundary). Tick open: run one more inner frame ( should_run_inner_frame True) while the accumulator holds the frame's recorded duration, which it then consumes; at most MAX_INNER_FRAMES_PER_TICK per tick, and only within the tick's real-time budget ( INNER_FRAME_BUDGET_SECONDS ), so keys, the status line and presenting stay at 60 Hz however costly inner frames are. The accumulator never owes more than one tick's worth of frames: the excess is dropped (a long stall runs one bounded burst), and while frames are dropped or the budget cuts ticks short the viewer is behind ( is_behind ): the status bar then shows the real speed ( effective_speed ). So 1x runs one inner frame a tick for a 60 FPS recording (but for the true rate mismatch), 8x eight, ¼x one every fourth tick, paused none. While paused a step ( . ) runs exactly one inner frame. The start screen lets frame 0 run first, so its picture is behind the message. Otherwise the tick closes: the doors refresh the status line, the loop presents the outer frame and asks again (step 1). The accumulator only decides when inner frames run, never what they do, so a watched replay is as exact as a headless one. Headless replays have no viewer loop: they never hold and run unpaced. Step back restarts the replay process instead, which rebuilds the inner game up to frame N-1 before the viewer's first tick (glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py; no outer tick opens during the rebuild). Later users of the same contract: Part 3's playback scopes (an inner replay under a live outer game) and audio/video capture (inner frames handed to a sink rather than presented).
docs.title: viewer

docs.text: The outer loop of a watched replay (module docstring). Attributes: controls – The viewer's controls (keys, state and status bar). cadence – The outer tick's real-time cadence. accumulated_seconds – Inner game time owed to the inner game (real time times speed, consumed by each inner frame's recorded duration). ticks_externally – True when something outside waits for each tick (a browser's animation frames, run_watched_replay_async ): a tick then opens at once, never sleeping or following cadence , and owes the real time since the last, so the replay keeps its speed at any display rate. Source code in src/glitchygames/replay/viewer.py 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 143 144 145 146 147 148 149 150 151 152 153 154 155 156 157 158 159 160 161 162 163 164 165 166 167 168 169 170 171 172 173 174 175 176 177 178 179 180 181 182 183 184 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 200 201 202 203 204 205 206 207 208 209 210 211 212 213 214 215 216 217 218 219 220 221 222 223 224 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 247 248 249 250 251 252 253 254 255 256 257 258 259 260 261 262 263 264 265 266 267 268 269 270 271 272 273 274 275 276 277 278 279 280 281 282 283 284 285 286 287 288 289 290 291 292 293 294 295 296 297 298 299 300 301 302 303 304 305 306 307 308 309 310 311 312 313 314 315 316 317 318 319 320 321 322 323 324 325 326 327 328 329 330 331 332 333 334 335 336 337 338 339 340 341 342 343 344 345 346 347 348 349 350 351 352 353 354 355 356 357 358 359 360 361 362 363 364 365 366 class ReplayViewer : """The outer loop of a watched replay (module docstring). Attributes: controls: The viewer's controls (keys, state and status bar). cadence: The outer tick's real-time cadence. accumulated_seconds: Inner game time owed to the inner game (real time times speed, consumed by each inner frame's recorded duration). ticks_externally: True when something outside waits for each tick (a browser's animation frames, ``run_watched_replay_async``): a tick then opens at once, never sleeping or following ``cadence``, and owes the real time since the last, so the replay keeps its speed at any display rate. """ def __init__ ( self : Self , * , controls : ReplayControls ) -> None : """Start with no tick open; the first tick is due at once. Args: controls: The viewer's controls. """ self . controls = controls self . cadence = ControlCadence () self . accumulated_seconds = 0.0 self . ticks_externally = False self . _is_tick_open = False self . _inner_frames_this_tick = 0 self . _tick_start_seconds = 0.0 # The tick time the next tick's elapsed time is measured from (snapping carries error) self . _last_tick_seconds : float | None = None # True when the inner game (re)starts running: the accumulator gets half a frame self . _needs_phase_offset = True # Ticks left during which the viewer counts as behind (frames dropped or cut short) self . _behind_ticks_left = 0 # Per running tick over the last second: its real seconds and the inner seconds it ran self . _recent_real_seconds : collections . deque [ float ] = collections . deque ( maxlen = EFFECTIVE_SPEED_WINDOW_TICKS ) self . _recent_inner_seconds : collections . deque [ float ] = collections . deque ( maxlen = EFFECTIVE_SPEED_WINDOW_TICKS ) # The open tick: whether the inner game runs in it, the real time it pays for and the # inner seconds it ran self . _tick_is_running = False self . _tick_elapsed_seconds = 0.0 self . _inner_seconds_this_tick = 0.0 # The viewer's key presses and releases (event type, key) read since the last tick self . _key_events : list [ tuple [ int , int ]] = [] @property def is_behind ( self : Self ) -> bool : """True while the inner game cannot keep up with the speed (in the last second).""" return self . _behind_ticks_left > 0 def effective_speed ( self : Self ) -> float : """Return the speed the inner game really ran at over the last second of ticks. Returns: Inner seconds run over real seconds passed (0.0 before any time passed). """ real_seconds = sum ( self . _recent_real_seconds ) if real_seconds <= 0 : return 0.0 return sum ( self . _recent_inner_seconds ) / real_seconds def real_speed_if_behind ( self : Self ) -> float | None : """Return the real speed when the inner game meaningfully cannot keep up, for the status. Returns: ``effective_speed()`` while behind and below ``BEHIND_SPEED_FRACTION`` of the speed, else None (keeping up, slightly slow, or no running ticks measured yet). """ if not self . is_behind or not self . _recent_real_seconds : return None real_speed = self . effective_speed () if real_speed >= self . controls . speed * BEHIND_SPEED_FRACTION : return None return real_speed def queue_key_event ( self : Self , * , event_type : int , key : int ) -> None : """Keep a real KEYDOWN or KEYUP for the next tick (keys act once per tick at most). Args: event_type: ``pygame.KEYDOWN`` or ``pygame.KEYUP``. key: The key. """ self . _key_events . append (( event_type , key )) def begin_tick ( self : Self , * , is_inner_running : bool ) -> float | None : """Open the next outer tick if none is open, first sleeping until it is due. Args: is_inner_running: Whether the inner game was running when the last tick closed: the wait spins only then (``sleep_for``); paused, at the start screen or over it is a plain sleep (``sleep_coarsely``). Returns: The tick's measured time when a tick was opened (the doors then run its work and call ``accrue``), or None while a tick is open. """ if self . _is_tick_open : return None now = clock . measured_seconds () if self . ticks_externally : return self . _open_tick ( now = now ) remaining_seconds = self . cadence . next_tick_seconds ( now = now ) - now if remaining_seconds > 0 : if is_inner_running : sleep_for ( seconds = remaining_seconds ) else : sleep_coarsely ( seconds = remaining_seconds ) now = clock . measured_seconds () self . cadence . tick_is_due ( now = now ) return self . _open_tick ( now = now ) def _open_tick ( self : Self , * , now : float ) -> float : """Open a tick at ``now``. Returns: ``now``. """ self . _is_tick_open = True self . _inner_frames_this_tick = 0 self . _tick_start_seconds = now return now def apply_key_events ( self : Self , * , now : float ) -> None : """Act on the keys read since the last tick, then repeat held step keys. Args: now: The tick's measured time. """ for event_type , key in self . _key_events : if event_type == pygame . KEYDOWN : self . controls . press_key ( key = key , now = now ) else : self . controls . release_key ( key = key ) self . _key_events = [] self . controls . repeat_held_keys ( now = now ) def accrue ( self : Self , * , now : float , is_inner_running : bool ) -> None : """Owe the inner game the real time since the last tick, times the speed. Args: now: The tick's measured time. is_inner_running: False while paused, at the start screen or over: the accumulator empties instead. """ if self . _last_tick_seconds is None : elapsed_seconds = 0.0 self . _last_tick_seconds = now else : elapsed_seconds = now - self . _last_tick_seconds if abs ( elapsed_seconds - CONTROL_TICK_SECONDS ) <= TICK_SNAP_WINDOW_SECONDS : # On time within the window: exactly one period, the error carried elapsed_seconds = CONTROL_TICK_SECONDS self . _last_tick_seconds += CONTROL_TICK_SECONDS else : self . _last_tick_seconds = now self . _behind_ticks_left = max ( 0 , self . _behind_ticks_left - 1 ) self . _tick_is_running = is_inner_running self . _tick_elapsed_seconds = elapsed_seconds self . _inner_seconds_this_tick = 0.0 if not is_inner_running : self . accumulated_seconds = 0.0 self . _needs_phase_offset = True self . _recent_real_seconds . clear () self . _recent_inner_seconds . clear () self . _behind_ticks_left = 0 return self . accumulated_seconds += elapsed_seconds * self . controls . speed def should_run_inner_frame ( self : Self , * , inner_frame_seconds : float , is_inner_over : bool , is_first_inner_frame : bool ) -> bool : """Decide whether the open tick runs one more inner frame; if not, close the tick. Args: inner_frame_seconds: The recorded duration of the inner frame that would run. is_inner_over: True once the replay stopped or the recording is used up (a step then does nothing). is_first_inner_frame: True before the inner game's frame 0. Returns: True to run one inner frame now. docs.text: Run a watched replay's frames, giving control back to the caller between outer ticks. For a host that must not block (a browser). Each awaited wait_for_tick() is one outer tick of viewer ( ticks_externally : the viewer never sleeps): the tick's inner frames run, then the viewer holds and the outer frame is presented ( SceneManager.run_frame_step steps until last_step_was_held ). Frames run unpaced, as the blocking loop runs them in a watched replay: the viewer's accumulator decides when they run. Parameters: scene_manager ( SceneManager ) – The replayed game's scene manager. viewer ( ReplayViewer ) – The watched replay's viewer. wait_for_tick ( Callable [[], Awaitable [ float ]] ) – Waits for the next outer tick (a browser animation frame). For a host that must not block (a browser). Each awaited ``wait_for_tick()`` is one outer tick of ``viewer`` (``ticks_externally``: the viewer never sleeps): the tick's inner frames run, then the viewer holds and the outer frame is presented (``SceneManager.run_frame_step`` steps until ``last_step_was_held``). Frames run unpaced, as the blocking loop runs them in a watched replay: the viewer's accumulator decides when they run. Args: scene_manager: The replayed game's scene manager. viewer: The watched replay's viewer. wait_for_tick: Waits for the next outer tick (a browser animation frame). """ viewer . ticks_externally = True frame_start_seconds = scene_manager . begin_frames () while scene_manager . should_run_frames (): await wait_for_tick () while scene_manager . should_run_frames (): frame_start_seconds = scene_manager . run_frame_step ( frame_start_seconds = frame_start_seconds , paced = False ) if scene_manager . last_step_was_held : break scene_manager . end_frames ()

docs.text: Logic seconds since this scene started: the sum of the dt its dt_tick received. Capped by MAX_FRAME_SECONDS where set, and it does not advance while the scene is not running (paused, or switched away), so cooldowns and timers measured with it pause with the game and replay exactly. Use it for gameplay timing instead of the wall clock.

docs.text: Every joystick and game controller the game sees, by instance id. Each InputDevice reads the frame's input snapshot on its joystick layer and, for a mapped pad, its controller layer; its events reach on_*_event from one layer only (glitchygames/input/input_devices.py). Empty without an engine.

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool ( bool ) – True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object. subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 1425 1426 1427 1428 1429 1430 1431 1432 1433 1434 1435 1436 1437 1438 1439 1440 1441 1442 1443 1444 1445 1446 1447 1448 1449 1450 1451 1452 1453 1454 1455 1456 1457 1458 1459 1460 1461 1462 1463 1464 1465 1466 1467 1468 1469 @classmethod @override def __subclasshook__ ( cls , subclass : type [ Any ]) -> bool : """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented

docs.text: Pause the current scene. Default implementation requests a PauseScene for the end of this frame. Scenes can override this method to provide custom pause behavior. The switch happens after this frame renders (via next_scene), not immediately: pause() usually runs during event processing, after sprites have moved this frame, so an immediate switch would freeze the previous frame's picture one frame behind the game. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 4192 4193 4194 4195 4196 4197 4198 4199 4200 4201 4202 4203 4204 4205 4206 4207 4208 @override def pause ( self : Self ) -> None : """Pause the current scene. Default implementation requests a PauseScene for the end of this frame. Scenes can override this method to provide custom pause behavior. The switch happens after this frame renders (via next_scene), not immediately: pause() usually runs during event processing, after sprites have moved this frame, so an immediate switch would freeze the previous frame's picture one frame behind the game. """ from .builtin_scenes.pause_scene import PauseScene self . next_scene = PauseScene ( options = self . options ) self . log . info ( 'Scene pause requested' )

Logger = LOG def __init__ ( self : Self , event_source : object ) -> None : """Initialize the event proxy. Args: event_source: The event source. """ super () . __init__ () # No proxies for the root class. self . proxies : list [ Any ] = [] # This is used for leave objects which # don't have their own proxies. # # Subclassed managers that set their own proxy # will not have this. self . event_source = event_source def unhandled_event ( self : Self , * _args : Any , ** kwargs : Any ) -> None : """Handle unhandled events. This method is called when an attribute is not found. Args: attr: The attribute to get. Returns: The attribute. """ return self . unhandled_event

docs.text: Proxy calls to the active scene. Parameters: attr ( str ) – The attribute to proxy. Returns: Callable [..., Any ] – Callable[..., Any]: The callable object. Raises: AttributeError – If the attribute is not an on_*_event method. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 2549 2550 2551 2552 2553 2554 2555 2556 2557 2558 2559 2560 2561 2562 2563 2564 2565 2566 2567 2568 2569 2570 2571 2572 2573 @override def __getattr__ ( self : Self , attr : str ) -> Callable [ ... , Any ]: """Proxy calls to the active scene. Args: attr (str): The attribute to proxy. Returns: Callable[..., Any]: The callable object. Raises: AttributeError: If the attribute is not an on_*_event method. """ # Attempt to proxy the call to the active scene. if attr . startswith ( 'on_' ) and attr . endswith ( '_event' ): try : # Pass it to the active scene for handling return getattr ( self . active_scene , attr ) except AttributeError : # Pass it to the game engine for suppression return getattr ( self . game_engine , attr ) else : message = f "' { type ( self ) } ' object has no attribute ' { attr } '" raise AttributeError ( message )

docs.text: End the playback scope in progress (a demo, an instant replay); the game goes on. Honoured from a supervisor ( add_supervisor ; the scope then ends once that frame ended, so the frame is played and compared whole) and between frames (at once). Its outcome's reason is 'ended_by_game' . Asked anywhere else in a frame, it is ignored (logged at DEBUG): inside a scope the only scene code running is the played scene's, whose call did nothing in its original run (no scope was playing then), as recorded_playback_answer keeps a playback request's answer. A control event handler's call ( add_control_event_handler ) is honoured only when a supervisor's own record_control_event ran it, inside the slot; the handlers of a frame's re-applied control events (a replayed breakpoint) run before the supervisors, outside the slot, so their call is ignored. Nothing when no scope is in progress (a requested one still begins). The player's presses reach no scene during an instant replay; a supervisor reads the player's polled input from playback_player_input to decide when to end it. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 781 782 783 784 785 786 787 788 789 790 791 792 793 794 795 796 797 798 799 800 801 802 803 804 805 806 807 808 809 810 811 812 def end_playback ( self : Self ) -> None : """End the playback scope in progress (a demo, an instant replay); the game goes on. Honoured from a supervisor (``add_supervisor``; the scope then ends once that frame ended, so the frame is played and compared whole) and between frames (at once). Its outcome's reason is ``'ended_by_game'``. Asked anywhere else in a frame, it is ignored (logged at DEBUG): inside a scope the only scene code running is the played scene's, whose call did nothing in its original run (no scope was playing then), as ``recorded_playback_answer`` keeps a playback request's answer. A control event handler's call (``add_control_event_handler``) is honoured only when a supervisor's own ``record_control_event`` ran it, inside the slot; the handlers of a frame's re-applied control events (a replayed breakpoint) run before the supervisors, outside the slot, so their call is ignored. Nothing when no scope is in progress (a requested one still begins). The player's presses reach no scene during an instant replay; a supervisor reads the player's polled input from ``playback_player_input`` to decide when to end it. """ session = self . _playback_session if session is None : return if not self . _frame_in_progress : self . _exit_playback ( reason = 'ended_by_game' ) return if not self . _in_supervisor_slot : LOG . debug ( 'end_playback() asked by the played scene is ignored: it did nothing live' ) return sources = session . sources # First reason found wins, as PlaybackSources._note_end keeps it (the class has no # room for a public method that would do this) if sources . end_reason is None : sources . end_reason = 'ended_by_game'
docs.title: end_playback

docs.text: Show the active scene's last INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS , then go on where it was. The scene is rebuilt from its start in a playback scope from the start of the next frame and plays its instant-replay journal (glitchygames/instant_replay.py): the frames before the last INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS of frame time run unseen, unpaced and silent, the rest are shown at the game's pace, then the live scene, never touched, goes on exactly where it was (glitchygames/replay/playback.py, rules 6 and 7). The player's presses do not end it; the game may, with end_playback . How it ended: last_playback_outcome . Returns: bool – True when the instant replay will begin. False (logged; nothing happens) when the bool – active scene keeps no journal (its class sets no INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS , or bool – its first logic frame has not run), the journal is past the scene's bool – MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS , or a playback is already starting or bool – playing. Inside a playback of the journal, what the recorded scene was answered bool – (nothing is requested: scopes do not nest). Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 756 757 758 759 760 761 762 763 764 765 766 767 768 769 770 771 772 773 774 775 776 777 778 779 def instant_replay ( self : Self ) -> bool : """Show the active scene's last ``INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS``, then go on where it was. The scene is rebuilt from its start in a playback scope from the start of the next frame and plays its instant-replay journal (glitchygames/instant_replay.py): the frames before the last ``INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS`` of frame time run unseen, unpaced and silent, the rest are shown at the game's pace, then the live scene, never touched, goes on exactly where it was (glitchygames/replay/playback.py, rules 6 and 7). The player's presses do not end it; the game may, with ``end_playback``. How it ended: ``last_playback_outcome``. Returns: True when the instant replay will begin. False (logged; nothing happens) when the active scene keeps no journal (its class sets no ``INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS``, or its first logic frame has not run), the journal is past the scene's ``MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS``, or a playback is already starting or playing. Inside a playback of the journal, what the recorded scene was answered (nothing is requested: scopes do not nest). """ # Function-level import, for layering (as in play_recording) from glitchygames.replay.playback import start_instant_replay return start_instant_replay ( manager = self )

docs.text: Handle the debug overlay keys, then forward key-down events as the proxy would. F3 toggles the overlay and F4 cycles its panels, unless a sprite in the active scene has keyboard focus (is_active), so typing into text fields is never intercepted. Every other key goes to the active scene (every Scene has the handler, and records the press first), or to the game engine when there is no active scene. Parameters: event ( KeyEvent ) – The key-down event. Raises: AttributeError – If there is no active scene and the game engine has no handler. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 1322 1323 1324 1325 1326 1327 1328 1329 1330 1331 1332 1333 1334 1335 1336 1337 1338 1339 1340 1341 1342 1343 1344 1345 1346 1347 1348 1349 1350 1351 def on_key_down_event ( self : Self , event : events . KeyEvent ) -> None : """Handle the debug overlay keys, then forward key-down events as the proxy would. F3 toggles the overlay and F4 cycles its panels, unless a sprite in the active scene has keyboard focus (is_active), so typing into text fields is never intercepted. Every other key goes to the active scene (every Scene has the handler, and records the press first), or to the game engine when there is no active scene. Args: event (KeyEvent): The key-down event. Raises: AttributeError: If there is no active scene and the game engine has no handler. """ if event . key in OVERLAY_KEYS and not self . _active_scene_has_focused_sprite (): self . debug_overlay . handle_key ( key = event . key ) return if self . active_scene is not None : # Recorded before dispatch, so a quit-key release knows this scene saw the press self . active_scene . record_key_press ( key = event . key ) self . active_scene . on_key_down_event ( event ) elif self . game_engine is not None and hasattr ( self . game_engine , 'on_key_down_event' ): self . game_engine . on_key_down_event ( event ) else : message = ( f "' { type ( self ) } ' object has no attribute 'on_key_down_event': neither the " 'active scene nor the game engine provides it' ) raise AttributeError ( message )

docs.text: Play a recording as an attract-mode demo, then return to then . The demo plays in a playback scope (glitchygames/replay/playback.py) from the start of the next frame, at the game's speed, and ends at the recording's end, at the first key or button press ( exit_on_input ), at a divergence (logged at WARNING, demo diverged: <description> ) or at the recording's own quit. A recording cut off part way plays to its last complete frame and ends as truncated . A recording that cannot be played (missing, unreadable, of another game, with no scene start to begin at) is logged at WARNING, naming the demo and the reason, and nothing starts; so is a request while another playback is starting or playing. How it ended: last_playback_outcome . Parameters: path ( Path ) – The recording. then ( Scene ) – The scene to make active when the demo ends (usually the scene asking). docs.text: Run one step of the frame loop: one frame, or a held frame presented again. Parameters: frame_start_seconds ( float ) – The perf_counter() reading this frame starts at (the previous step's return value, or begin_frames '). paced ( bool , default: True ) – True ( start ) paces the frame as always: the timer backend's deadline, else the pygame clock, or the doors' pacing. False (an outer driver that waits for its own tick, GameHost.run_async ) never waits or calibrates a timer: the wait for the next tick is the pacing, and is measured into the next frame's start-to-start dt like a pacing sleep. Returns: float – The perf_counter() reading the next frame starts at. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 1717 1718 1719 1720 1721 1722 1723 1724 1725 1726 1727 1728 1729 1730 1731 1732 1733 1734 1735 1736 1737 1738 1739 1740 1741 1742 1743 1744 1745 1746 1747 1748 1749 1750 1751 1752 1753 1754 1755 1756 1757 1758 1759 1760 1761 1762 1763 1764 1765 1766 1767 1768 1769 def run_frame_step ( self : Self , * , frame_start_seconds : float , paced : bool = True ) -> float : """Run one step of the frame loop: one frame, or a held frame presented again. Args: frame_start_seconds: The perf_counter() reading this frame starts at (the previous step's return value, or ``begin_frames``'). paced: True (``start``) paces the frame as always: the timer backend's deadline, else the pygame clock, or the doors' pacing. False (an outer driver that waits for its own tick, ``GameHost.run_async``) never waits or calibrates a timer: the wait for the next tick is the pacing, and is measured into the next frame's start-to-start dt like a pacing sleep. Returns: The perf_counter() reading the next frame starts at. """ # The doors may hold the loop between frames (a paused watched replay): no frame # runs, the last one is presented again with the doors' overlay self . last_step_was_held = active_sources () . hold_frame () if self . last_step_was_held : # Unless the hold ended the run (the viewer quit): nothing more to show if not active_sources () . stop_requested : self . _present_held_frame () # The hold is not part of the next frame's measured time return clock . raw_counter_seconds () # Frame pacing using timer backend when available # None without an engine (a bare SceneManager) or before the engine made its timer game_engine = self . game_engine timer = game_engine . timer if game_engine is not None and paced else None # The doors may pace the frame themselves (0.0: not at all, in a headless replay); # an unpaced step is never paced here paced_seconds = active_sources () . paced_frame_seconds () if paced else 0.0 period_ns = 0 if timer is not None : period_ns = ( timer . start_frame ( self . target_fps ) if paced_seconds is None else round ( paced_seconds * 1_000_000_000 ) ) self . _run_frame () # The frame's processing time: its work, without the pacing sleep that follows processing_seconds = clock . raw_counter_seconds () - frame_start_seconds return self . _finish_frame ( frame_start_seconds = frame_start_seconds , timer = timer , period_ns = period_ns , paced_seconds = paced_seconds , processing_seconds = processing_seconds , )

docs.text: Start the scene manager. Each frame starts at the previous frame's closing perf_counter() reading and ends in _finish_frame, which sets self.dt once, to that frame's start-to-start period, so logic in frame N receives the time frame N-1 took (engine audit #15). The blocking frame loop: begin_frames , then run_frame_step while should_run_frames , then end_frames . An outer driver that must give control back between frames (a browser; glitchygames/host.py GameHost.run_async ) runs the same steps itself, one per tick, unpaced. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 1672 1673 1674 1675 1676 1677 1678 1679 1680 1681 1682 1683 1684 1685 1686 1687 def start ( self : Self ) -> None : """Start the scene manager. Each frame starts at the previous frame's closing perf_counter() reading and ends in _finish_frame, which sets ``self.dt`` once, to that frame's start-to-start period, so logic in frame N receives the time frame N-1 took (engine audit #15). The blocking frame loop: ``begin_frames``, then ``run_frame_step`` while ``should_run_frames``, then ``end_frames``. An outer driver that must give control back between frames (a browser; glitchygames/host.py ``GameHost.run_async``) runs the same steps itself, one per tick, unpaced. """ frame_start_seconds = self . begin_frames () while self . should_run_frames (): frame_start_seconds = self . run_frame_step ( frame_start_seconds = frame_start_seconds ) self . end_frames ()
