LayeredDirty [ Any ], ) -> None : """Put the player on the maze's start, heading left. Args: maze: The maze. geometry: Where the maze is on screen. layer: The sprite layer it draws on. groups: The sprite group to add it to. """ super () . __init__ ( maze = maze , geometry = geometry , start = maze . player_start , layer = layer , groups = groups , ) # The way the player last asked to go: taken at the first tile centre where it is open self . wanted_direction : Direction | None = Direction . LEFT # The way the mouth faces (kept while standing still) self . facing = Direction . LEFT # Tiles travelled, for the mouth's chomping self . travelled = CHOMP_CYCLE_TILES / 2 # While dying: 0.0 (caught) to 1.0 (gone); None while alive self . dying_progress : float | None = None self . reset () def reset ( self : Self ) -> None : """Back to the start for a new life, already heading left (as in the arcade). A way asked for before play starts is taken at the first junction where it is open; until then the player goes left. """ self . place_at ( position = self . start ) self . direction = Direction . LEFT self . wanted_direction = Direction . LEFT self . facing = Direction . LEFT self . travelled = CHOMP_CYCLE_TILES / 2 self . dying_progress = None self . hidden = False self . pose () def travel ( self : Self , * , distance : float ) -> None : """Move for one step of play: reverse at once if asked, else turn at tile centres. Args: distance: How far the player can go, in tiles. """ if ( self . direction is not None and self . wanted_direction is self . direction . opposite and not self . is_at_tile_centre ): self . direction = self . wanted_direction self . travelled += self . advance ( distance = distance , choose_direction = self . _choose_direction ) if self . direction is not None : self . facing = self . direction def _choose_direction ( self : Self ) -> Direction | None : """Return the way on from a tile centre: the wanted way if open, else straight on. Returns: The direction, or None to stop (against a wall, with no open wanted way). """ if self . wanted_direction is not None and self . is_direction_open ( self . wanted_direction ): return self . wanted_direction if self . direction is not None and self . is_direction_open ( self . direction ): return self . direction return None def pose ( self : Self ) -> None : """Draw the player's picture for this moment: chomping, standing, or dying.""" if self . dying_progress is not None : step = min ( DYING_STEPS , math . floor ( self . dying_progress * DYING_STEPS )) self . image = drawing . player_dying_picture ( size = self . picture_size , progress = step / DYING_STEPS ) return cycle = ( self . travelled % CHOMP_CYCLE_TILES ) / CHOMP_CYCLE_TILES # A triangle wave: shut at the cycle's start, wide open half way, shut again opening = 1.0 - abs ( 2.0 * cycle - 1.0 ) mouth_step = min ( CHOMP_STEPS - 1 , math . floor ( opening * CHOMP_STEPS )) self . image = drawing . player_picture ( size = self . picture_size , looking = self . facing , mouth_fraction = mouth_step / ( CHOMP_STEPS - 1 ), )

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool ( bool ) – True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object. subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 1425 1426 1427 1428 1429 1430 1431 1432 1433 1434 1435 1436 1437 1438 1439 1440 1441 1442 1443 1444 1445 1446 1447 1448 1449 1450 1451 1452 1453 1454 1455 1456 1457 1458 1459 1460 1461 1462 1463 1464 1465 1466 1467 1468 1469 @classmethod @override def __subclasshook__ ( cls , subclass : type [ Any ]) -> bool : """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented

docs.text: Walk a distance along the corridors, choosing a direction at every tile centre. On each centre it reaches (or starts on), choose_direction decides which way to go on, or None to stop there. The walk ends at the distance or at such a stop. Parameters: distance ( float ) – How far to walk, in tiles. choose_direction ( Callable [[], Direction | None] ) – Called on each tile centre; returns the way on, or None to stop. Returns: float – The distance actually walked. Source code in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/actors.py 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 247 248 249 250 251 252 253 254 255 256 257 258 259 260 261 262 263 264 265 266 267 268 269 270 271 def advance ( self : Self , * , distance : float , choose_direction : Callable [[], Direction | None ] ) -> float : """Walk a distance along the corridors, choosing a direction at every tile centre. On each centre it reaches (or starts on), ``choose_direction`` decides which way to go on, or None to stop there. The walk ends at the distance or at such a stop. Args: distance: How far to walk, in tiles. choose_direction: Called on each tile centre; returns the way on, or None to stop. Returns: The distance actually walked. """ walked = 0.0 while walked < distance : if self . is_at_tile_centre : self . direction = choose_direction () if self . direction is None : break to_centre = self . _distance_to_next_centre ( self . direction ) step = min ( distance - walked , to_centre ) if step == to_centre : # Land exactly on the centre, so the turn test above sees whole numbers if self . direction . step_x : self . tile_x = float ( round ( self . tile_x + self . direction . step_x * step )) else : self . tile_y = float ( round ( self . tile_y + self . direction . step_y * step )) else : self . tile_x += self . direction . step_x * step self . tile_y += self . direction . step_y * step self . tile_x = self . maze . wrap_x ( self . tile_x ) walked += step return walked

docs.text: Return the tile whose centre is nearest a position (halves round up), column wrapped. Parameters: tile_x ( float ) – The position's x, in tiles. tile_y ( float ) – The position's y, in tiles. maze ( Maze ) – The maze (for its width). Returns: tuple [ int , int ] – The tile's (column, row). Source code in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/actors.py 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 def nearest_cell ( * , tile_x : float , tile_y : float , maze : Maze ) -> tuple [ int , int ]: """Return the tile whose centre is nearest a position (halves round up), column wrapped. Args: tile_x: The position's x, in tiles. tile_y: The position's y, in tiles. maze: The maze (for its width). Returns: The tile's (column, row). """ return ( math . floor ( tile_x + 0.5 ) % maze . columns , math . floor ( tile_y + 0.5 )) A simple Mr. Muncher player: it eats sprockets, keeps away from munchers and hunts blue ones. The golden replay's input script (scripts/golden_inputs.py: mr_muncher_script ) steers the player with it, pressing the arrow key it asks for, and the tests use it to play whole levels. It reads the scene (as a person reads the screen) and never changes it. Each frame it decides at the tile the player reaches next ( MazeActor.next_cell_ahead ). For each way on from there it works out the player's territory: the corridor tiles the player would reach at least SAFETY_MARGIN_TILES before any dangerous muncher could. A way whose territory is smaller than SMALL_TERRITORY_TILES is a trap and is taken only when every way is (then the biggest wins). Among the others it takes the shortest path, through its territory, to the most wanted goal: a frightened muncher it can catch in time, the bonus, a snack when a muncher is close, a sprocket. Asked to ( seek_capture_after_seconds ), it walks into a muncher once, so a recording loses a life.

Args: scene: The game. Returns: The direction to ask for (None only on a tile with no way on). """ maze = scene . maze start , arriving = decision_point ( scene = scene ) dangerous = [ muncher . next_cell_ahead () for muncher in scene . munchers if muncher . can_touch_player and not muncher . frightened ] danger = corridor_distances ( maze = maze , sources = dangerous ) ways = [ way_on ( maze = maze , direction = direction , first = neighbour , danger = danger ) for direction , neighbour in _neighbours ( maze = maze , cell = start ) ] if not ways : return None if self . _is_seeking_capture ( scene = scene ) and dangerous : return shortest_way ( ways = ways , goals = set ( dangerous ), safely = False ) backwards = arriving . opposite if arriving is not None else None roomy = [ way for way in ways if len ( way . territory ) >= SMALL_TERRITORY_TILES ] if not roomy : # Every way is a trap: the roomiest, but turning back must be much roomier (turning # back and forth between two traps is the surest way to be caught) return max ( ways , key = lambda way : ( len ( way . territory ) * ( BACKWARDS_TRAP_DISCOUNT if way . direction is backwards else 1.0 ) ), ) . direction # Going on beats turning back: turn back only when no roomy way on leads to anything onwards = [ way for way in roomy if way . direction is not backwards ] goals_in_order = goal_sets ( scene = scene , start = start , danger = danger ) for candidates in ( onwards , roomy ): for goals in goals_in_order : direction = shortest_way ( ways = candidates , goals = goals , safely = True ) if direction is not None : return direction return max ( roomy , key = lambda way : len ( way . territory )) . direction def _is_seeking_capture ( self : Self , * , scene : MrMuncherScene ) -> bool : """Whether it is time to walk into a muncher (until the first catch). Args: scene: The game. Returns: True while it should seek capture. """ if self . seek_capture_after_seconds is None or self . has_been_caught : return False if scene . phase is Phase . DYING : self . has_been_caught = True return False return scene . game_time >= self . seek_capture_after_seconds

You are Mr. Muncher, a popcorn bucket with an appetite. Eat every sprocket (they look like a film strip's sprocket holes) to finish the reel; four munchers, spiky fuzzballs, hunt you. Eat a snack (a wrapped candy) for a sugar rush: for a few seconds the munchers turn dull blue and run, and you can catch them for 200, 400, 800 and 1600 points. Twice a reel a bonus film reel appears under their house. You have three lives (each new one is the next take), and an extra one at 10,000 points. Each reel is faster than the last. Controls (every key by its position, ActionMap scancodes): the arrow keys or WASD steer, or a gamepad's D-pad, hat or left stick; a direction pressed before a junction is remembered and taken there. ESC or P (or the gamepad's Start) pauses; Q quits. The game pauses itself when its window loses focus. The munchers ( actors.py ) take turns retreating to their corners and chasing, each in its own way: Chomper (purple) heads straight for you, Snapper (green) for the tiles in front of you, Gnasher (orange) for the far side of you from Chomper, and Nibbles (magenta) chases from afar but loses its nerve up close. --debug-overlay (or F3) marks each muncher's target tile. A new game counts down like a film leader (3, 2, 1, ACTION!); each later life starts with its take number and each reel with its number. A cleared reel is a CUT!, and the last life ends with THE END. Everything is deterministic: positions, timers and the frightened munchers' random turns run on the scene's game time and the engine's seeded random streams, so --record-trace recordings replay exactly. High scores are kept with the engine's saves ( open_saves ).

Capped by MAX_FRAME_SECONDS where set, and it does not advance while the scene is not running (paused, or switched away), so cooldowns and timers measured with it pause with the game and replay exactly. Use it for gameplay timing instead of the wall clock.

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool ( bool ) – True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object. subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 1425 1426 1427 1428 1429 1430 1431 1432 1433 1434 1435 1436 1437 1438 1439 1440 1441 1442 1443 1444 1445 1446 1447 1448 1449 1450 1451 1452 1453 1454 1455 1456 1457 1458 1459 1460 1461 1462 1463 1464 1465 1466 1467 1468 1469 @classmethod @override def __subclasshook__ ( cls , subclass : type [ Any ]) -> bool : """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented
docs.title: __subclasshook__

docs.text: The world point the engine aims the camera at this frame, or None (manual camera). Override to aim the camera anywhere (a point between two players, a cutscene focus). The default returns the camera's follow target position (Camera2D.follow()). The engine applies the camera's follow axes to whatever point this returns. Returns: tuple [ float , float ] | None – tuple[float, float] | None: The target's (world_x, world_y), or None when the camera follows nothing. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 3218 3219 3220 3221 3222 3223 3224 3225 3226 3227 3228 3229 3230 3231 3232 3233 3234 def camera_target ( self : Self ) -> tuple [ float , float ] | None : """The world point the engine aims the camera at this frame, or None (manual camera). Override to aim the camera anywhere (a point between two players, a cutscene focus). The default returns the camera's follow target position (Camera2D.follow()). The engine applies the camera's follow axes to whatever point this returns. Returns: tuple[float, float] | None: The target's (world_x, world_y), or None when the camera follows nothing. """ target = self . camera . follow_target if target is None : return None # Camera2D.follow() checked that the target has world_x and world_y return ( float ( target . world_x ), float ( target . world_y ))

docs.text: Forget every key press recorded by record_key_press. SceneManager calls this whenever the scene becomes active (switched to, resumed, or the target of a transition), before setup(). A press whose release went to another scene would otherwise stay recorded, and a later release of that key (whose press was discarded during a transition) would quit. Games never call it; it is public only because the scene manager calls it. docs.text: Pause the current scene. Default implementation requests a PauseScene for the end of this frame. Scenes can override this method to provide custom pause behavior. The switch happens after this frame renders (via next_scene), not immediately: pause() usually runs during event processing, after sprites have moved this frame, so an immediate switch would freeze the previous frame's picture one frame behind the game. Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 4192 4193 4194 4195 4196 4197 4198 4199 4200 4201 4202 4203 4204 4205 4206 4207 4208 @override def pause ( self : Self ) -> None : """Pause the current scene. Default implementation requests a PauseScene for the end of this frame. Scenes can override this method to provide custom pause behavior. The switch happens after this frame renders (via next_scene), not immediately: pause() usually runs during event processing, after sprites have moved this frame, so an immediate switch would freeze the previous frame's picture one frame behind the game. """ from .builtin_scenes.pause_scene import PauseScene self . next_scene = PauseScene ( options = self . options ) self . log . info ( 'Scene pause requested' )

docs.text: Start a shake on the world (camera), the whole screen, or both. Rumble, if the shake has it, is sent automatically by the scene manager. Parameters: shake ( Shake ) – The shake to start. targets ( ShakeTarget , default: WORLD ) – ShakeTarget.WORLD, ShakeTarget.SCREEN, or both combined with |. Raises: RuntimeError – If WORLD is requested on a scene that is not active (for example from a transition cue, which runs after the scene was cleaned up). Source code in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py 3167 3168 3169 3170 3171 3172 3173 3174 3175 3176 3177 3178 3179 3180 3181 3182 3183 3184 3185 3186 3187 3188 3189 3190 3191 3192 3193 3194 def shake ( self : Self , shake : Shake , * , targets : ShakeTarget = ShakeTarget . Args: shake: The shake to start. targets: ShakeTarget.WORLD, ShakeTarget.SCREEN, or both combined with |. Raises: RuntimeError: If WORLD is requested on a scene that is not active (for example from a transition cue, which runs after the scene was cleaned up). """ if ShakeTarget . WORLD in targets : if self . scene_manager . active_scene is not self : message = f ' { self . NAME } is not the active scene; use ShakeTarget.SCREEN' raise RuntimeError ( message ) self . camera . shake_effect . add ( shake ) if not self . _world_shake_warning_logged and not self . _world_shake_moves_anything (): LOG . warning ( 'WORLD shake on %s has no effect: no sprites are positioned through its ' 'camera; use ShakeTarget.SCREEN' , self . NAME , ) self . _world_shake_warning_logged = True if ShakeTarget . SCREEN in targets : self . scene_manager . screen_shake . add ( shake )

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool ( bool ) – True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object. subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented

docs.text: Forget every key press recorded by record_key_press. SceneManager calls this whenever the scene becomes active (switched to, resumed, or the target of a transition), before setup(). A press whose release went to another scene would otherwise stay recorded, and a later release of that key (whose press was discarded during a transition) would quit. Games never call it; it is public only because the scene manager calls it. docs.text: Whether frightened munchers flash white now (they are about to recover). They flash for the last FRIGHTENED_FLASH_SECONDS (all of a shorter frightened time), alternating blue and white every quarter second, white first. Parameters: remaining_seconds ( float ) – Frightened time left. frightened_seconds ( float ) – The full frightened time of this level. Returns: bool – True while they show white. Source code in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/levels.py 181 182 183 184 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 def frightened_is_flashing ( * , remaining_seconds : float , frightened_seconds : float ) -> bool : """Whether frightened munchers flash white now (they are about to recover). They flash for the last FRIGHTENED_FLASH_SECONDS (all of a shorter frightened time), alternating blue and white every quarter second, white first. Args: remaining_seconds: Frightened time left. frightened_seconds: The full frightened time of this level. Returns: True while they show white. """ flash_window = min ( FRIGHTENED_FLASH_SECONDS , frightened_seconds ) if remaining_seconds > flash_window : return False flash_quarter_seconds = 4 return math . floor ( remaining_seconds * flash_quarter_seconds ) % 2 == 1

docs.text: Return how a level plays. Parameters: level ( int ) – The level number, 1 or more. Returns: LevelSettings – The level's settings. Raises: ValueError – If the level is below 1. Source code in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/levels.py 98 99 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 def settings_for_level ( level : int ) -> LevelSettings : """Return how a level plays. Args: level: The level number, 1 or more. Returns: The level's settings. Raises: ValueError: If the level is below 1. """ if level < 1 : message = f 'levels start at 1, got { level } ' raise ValueError ( message ) steps = min ( level , LAST_RAMP_LEVEL ) - 1 player_speed = PLAYER_SPEED_LEVEL_ONE + PLAYER_SPEED_STEP_PER_LEVEL * steps muncher_speed = player_speed * min ( MUNCHER_SPEED_FRACTION_MOST , MUNCHER_SPEED_FRACTION_LEVEL_ONE + MUNCHER_SPEED_FRACTION_STEP_PER_LEVEL * steps , ) is_level_one = level == 1 return LevelSettings ( level = level , player_speed = player_speed , sugar_rush_speed = player_speed * SUGAR_RUSH_SPEED_FACTOR , muncher_speed = muncher_speed , frightened_speed = player_speed * FRIGHTENED_SPEED_FRACTION , tunnel_speed = player_speed * TUNNEL_SPEED_FRACTION , house_speed = player_speed * HOUSE_SPEED_FRACTION , eyes_speed = player_speed * EYES_SPEED_FRACTION , hurry_speed = muncher_speed * HURRY_SPEED_FACTOR , hurry_sprockets = HURRY_SPROCKETS_LEVEL_ONE + HURRY_SPROCKETS_STEP_PER_LEVEL * steps , frightened_seconds = max ( FRIGHTENED_SECONDS_SHORTEST , FRIGHTENED_SECONDS_LEVEL_ONE - FRIGHTENED_SECONDS_STEP_PER_LEVEL * steps , ), mode_schedule = LEVEL_ONE_MODE_SCHEDULE if is_level_one else LATER_MODE_SCHEDULE , release_seconds = LEVEL_ONE_RELEASE_SECONDS if is_level_one else LATER_RELEASE_SECONDS , bonus_points = BONUS_POINTS_BY_LEVEL [ min ( level , len ( BONUS_POINTS_BY_LEVEL )) - 1 ], ) Mr. Muncher's maze: a hand-designed layout of walls, corridors, sprockets and a house. The layout is text, one string per row of tiles ( MAZE_LAYOUT ). It is symmetric left to right, every corridor is one tile wide, there are no dead ends, and every open tile can be reached from every other (the member's tests/test_mr_muncher_maze_and_actors.py checks all four). The long corridors at the top and bottom are tunnels: leaving one side enters the other. Positions are in tile units: the centre of the tile in column c, row r is (c, r), so an actor standing on a tile centre has whole-number coordinates. The maze knows nothing of pixels; the game scales tiles to the screen ( MazeGeometry ).

Source code in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/maze.py 98 99 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 143 144 145 146 147 148 149 150 151 152 153 154 155 156 157 158 159 160 161 162 163 164 165 166 167 168 169 170 171 172 173 174 175 176 177 178 179 180 181 182 183 184 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 200 201 202 203 204 205 206 207 208 209 210 211 212 213 214 215 216 217 218 219 220 221 222 223 224 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 247 248 249 250 251 252 253 254 255 256 257 258 259 260 class Maze ( BaseModel ): """A maze layout and the questions the game asks of it. Attributes: layout: One string per row of tiles, all the same width (characters as above). """ model_config = ConfigDict ( frozen = True , extra = 'forbid' ) layout : tuple [ str , ... ] @model_validator ( mode = 'after' ) def _check_layout ( self : Self ) -> Self : """Refuse a layout whose rows differ in width, or without exactly one player start. Returns: The maze. Raises: ValueError: If the layout is not a rectangle or has no single player start. """ widths = { len ( row ) for row in self . layout } if len ( widths ) != 1 : message = f 'every row of a maze layout must have the same width, got { sorted ( widths ) } ' raise ValueError ( message ) player_starts = sum ( row . count ( PLAYER_START ) for row in self . layout ) if player_starts != 1 : message = f 'a maze layout needs exactly one player start, got { player_starts } ' raise ValueError ( message ) return self @property def columns ( self : Self ) -> int : """The maze's width in tiles.""" return len ( self . layout [ 0 ]) @property def rows ( self : Self ) -> int : """The maze's height in tiles.""" return len ( self . layout ) def tile ( self : Self , * , column : int , row : int ) -> str : """Return the layout character of a tile; columns wrap, rows outside are wall. Columns wrap so the tunnel row joins its two ends; every other row has walls at both edges, where wrapping changes nothing. Args: column: The tile's column (any integer: it wraps). row: The tile's row. Returns: The tile's character. """ if not 0 <= row < self . rows : return WALL return self . layout [ row ][ column % self . columns ] def is_open_for_player ( self : Self , * , column : int , row : int ) -> bool : """Whether the player may stand on a tile (not a wall, the house or its door). Args: column: The tile's column. row: The tile's row. Returns: True for a corridor tile. """ return self . tile ( column = column , row = row ) in PLAYER_OPEN_TILES def is_tunnel ( self : Self , * , column : int , row : int ) -> bool : """Whether a tile is part of the wrapping tunnel. Args: column: The tile's column. row: The tile's row. Returns: True for a tunnel tile. """ return self . tile ( column = column , row = row ) == TUNNEL def cells_holding ( self : Self , * , character : str ) -> list [ tuple [ int , int ]]: """Return every tile holding a layout character, row by row. Args: character: The character (SPROCKET, SNACK, ...). Returns: Each tile's (column, row). """ return [ ( column , row ) for row , row_text in enumerate ( self . layout ) for column , tile in enumerate ( row_text ) if tile == character ] @property def player_start ( self : Self ) -> tuple [ int , int ]: """The player's start tile (column, row).""" (( column , row ),) = self . cells_holding ( character = PLAYER_START ) return ( column , row ) @property def door ( self : Self ) -> tuple [ int , int ]: """The house door's tile (column, row).""" (( column , row ),) = self . cells_holding ( character = DOOR ) return ( column , row ) @property def house_entrance ( self : Self ) -> tuple [ int , int ]: """The corridor tile just above the door, where munchers leave and enter the house.""" door_column , door_row = self . door return ( door_column , door_row - 1 ) @property def house_centre ( self : Self ) -> tuple [ int , int ]: """The house tile two below the door: the middle of its three rows.""" door_column , door_row = self . door return ( door_column , door_row + 2 ) def wrap_x ( self : Self , x : float ) -> float : """Wrap an x position (in tiles) that went more than half a tile past either edge. Args: x: The position. Returns: The same place inside the maze's width. """ if x < - HALF_TILE : return x + self . columns if x >= self . columns - HALF_TILE : return x - self . columns return x def tile_distance ( self : Self , * , first : tuple [ float , float ], second : tuple [ float , float ] ) -> float : """Return the straight-line distance between two positions, the short way round. Two positions near opposite ends of the tunnel are close: the distance across the wrap counts. Args: first: One position, in tiles. second: The other position, in tiles. Returns: The distance, in tiles. """ across = abs ( first [ 0 ] - second [ 0 ]) across = min ( across , self . columns - across ) return math . hypot ( across , first [ 1 ] - second [ 1 ])

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool ( bool ) – True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object. subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 1425 1426 1427 1428 1429 1430 1431 1432 1433 1434 1435 1436 1437 1438 1439 1440 1441 1442 1443 1444 1445 1446 1447 1448 1449 1450 1451 1452 1453 1454 1455 1456 1457 1458 1459 1460 1461 1462 1463 1464 1465 1466 1467 1468 1469 @classmethod @override def __subclasshook__ ( cls , subclass : type [ Any ]) -> bool : """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented

docs.text: Override the default subclasshook to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool ( bool ) – True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object. subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 1425 1426 1427 1428 1429 1430 1431 1432 1433 1434 1435 1436 1437 1438 1439 1440 1441 1442 1443 1444 1445 1446 1447 1448 1449 1450 1451 1452 1453 1454 1455 1456 1457 1458 1459 1460 1461 1462 1463 1464 1465 1466 1467 1468 1469 @classmethod @override def __subclasshook__ ( cls , subclass : type [ Any ]) -> bool : """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface. A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it). Returns: bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides. """ # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods. interface_attributes = set ( cls . __abstractmethods__ ) abstract_methods = getattr ( subclass , '__abstractmethods__' , frozenset [ str ]()) subclass_attributes : set [ str ] = set ( abstract_methods ) interface_is_implemented = False methods : list [ bool ] = [] for attribute in sorted ( interface_attributes ): if hasattr ( subclass , attribute ) and attribute not in subclass_attributes : if callable ( getattr ( subclass , attribute )): cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (callable)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> implemented (attribute)' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( True ) else : cls . log . debug ( ' %s . %s -> unimplemented' , subclass . __name__ , attribute ) methods . append ( False ) # all([]) returns True, so mask it # # This protects against an empty attribute list # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface if len ( methods ) > 0 and all ( methods ): interface_is_implemented = all ( methods ) if interface_is_implemented : return True return NotImplemented

""" return font . render ( text , antialias = True , color = color ) Mr. Muncher's sound effects and jingles, as synth recipes (glitchygames/audio/recipes.py). All original, and all cinema: eating a sprocket is a popcorn crunch (two slightly different ones, alternating, so a run of them never repeats exactly), a snack is a clapperboard's clack and a rising shimmer, a new game counts down like a film leader (a beep a number), and every take starts with the clapperboard and a bright chord ("ACTION!"). Catching a muncher is a camera flash, being caught snaps the film and slides down a sad trombone, and THE END is a falling minor phrase. Values are starting points tuned by ear; edit them freely.

docs.text: Driver Comparison # The test suite draws in software on SDL's dummy video driver, which has no window. The platform's own driver (macOS cocoa , Windows windows , Linux wayland or x11 ) draws through the same code, and the engine presents opaque frames, so every test should show the same pixels on both. When they differ, the engine depends on the driver: on macOS a display with per-pixel alpha once showed black frames (BUGS.md #142) and a black box around the player during Clockwork Keep's elevator ride (BUGS.md #189), neither visible on dummy . Every local run compares # Outside CI, uv run pytest (and nox -s test ) runs the suite twice at once: on dummy , in the pytest process and its xdist workers, with coverage and the 99% gate as always; on the native driver, as a child pytest run with the same arguments. The usual workers are split between the two runs (the native run gets two thirds: it is slower per test), so the machine is no busier than for one run. Both runs record a fingerprint (size and SHA-256 of the RGB bytes, as the window shows them) of every frame each test presents ( src/glitchygames/testing/frame_fingerprints.py ). When both have finished, the frames are compared ( src/glitchygames/testing/frame_comparison.py ; its command line is scripts/compare_driver_frames.py ). Any difference, or a failure in the native run, fails the run; the differing tests are re-run on both drivers to save the differing frames as PNG files with a difference image (the baseline dimmed to grey, differing pixels magenta) under test-results/driver-comparison/pytest/ . The terminal summary names every file and the native run's log. The comparison is off, and the summary says why, in CI ( CI=true ), with --dummy-only (fast iteration), when SDL_VIDEODRIVER or SDL_AUDIODRIVER is set (that driver runs alone), and on a Linux machine without a display. Tests whose frames vary # A test whose frames are not expected to match between runs or drivers is marked @pytest.mark.frames_vary(reason=...) : it is listed with its reason and not compared. Today these are a session recorded through the real frame loop (each frame moves by its measured frame time), watched replays of a live session (the overlay shows the live window's mouse focus, which dummy always reports and a background window does not have) and a test that switches the display back to the run's driver part way through. On demand: nox -s compare-drivers # The session compares every driver configuration available on this machine with every other, an N-way matrix ( scripts/driver_configurations.py lists them and finds which run here): Configuration What runs Needs dummy SDL's windowless driver, run twice (a test whose frames differ between those runs is nondeterministic: it should be marked) nothing; always the baseline cocoa ( windows , wayland , x11 ) the platform's own driver its platform (Linux: WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY ) x11-macos x11 on this Mac, drawing on XQuartz, through SDL built with x11 macOS, XQuartz, a C compiler and make x11-linux x11 in the Linux container of nox -s test-linux-x11 , forwarded to XQuartz over TCP macOS, XQuartz (TCP enabled), Docker The runs go one after another with four workers each (the container's too), so the machine stays usable. nox -s compare-drivers -- --drivers dummy,cocoa,x11-macos chooses configurations ( dummy is always added: it is the baseline; one that cannot run here is refused with the reason), and other arguments select tests ( -- tests/scenes ). The tests that differ anywhere are re-run on every configuration saving their differing frames, and every differing pair gets both PNG files and a difference image under test-results/driver-comparison/nox/differences/<first>-vs-<second>/ . The report, test-results/driver-comparison/nox/matrix.md (and matrix.json ), holds each run's time, a summary row per pair (tests compared, how many differ, by kind: pixels, size, present count, display, outcome), the patterns of agreement ("cocoa differs from all others", "x11-macos and x11-linux differ from dummy and cocoa"), a table per test file and, folded per file, a row per test with a cell per pair: agree , n/a (not recorded by both) or the first differing frame's index and kind with the differing pixel count linked to the difference image. The session prints the pair summary and the patterns at the end. It reports; it never fails on a difference. It fails when a run recorded no test, naming the run: arguments that make pytest run nothing and exit 0 ( -- --help , -- --collect-only ) reach every run, and a report of empty runs would say every configuration agrees. It fails too when a pytest run cannot run at all. A comparison that fails or is interrupted never replaces the last complete one: while a comparison runs, the last complete one waits in test-results/driver-comparison/nox-previous/ , and it goes back to test-results/driver-comparison/nox/ when the comparison fails; the failed comparison's runs are kept in test-results/driver-comparison/nox-failed/ . x11 on macOS: SDL built with x11 # pygame-ce's macOS wheel bundles an SDL without x11. SDL's dynamic API loads another SDL at run time instead: with SDL_DYNAMIC_API=/path/libSDL2-2.0.0.dylib the wheel's SDL fills its jump table from that library, and every SDL call (pygame's, SDL_image's, SDL_mixer's, SDL_ttf's) runs it. nox -s build-sdl-x11 (run by compare-drivers when needed) builds the very version the wheel reports ( pygame.get_sdl_version() ) from its GitHub release tarball, its SHA-256 pinned per version in scripts/build_sdl_x11.py , with SDL's autotools build (SDL 2's CMake build never enables x11 on Apple platforms) and x11 against XQuartz's /opt/X11 . Smallest window : XQuartz's window manager widens a window narrower than 72 pixels (a 64x48 window becomes 72x48), so pygame warns "Requested window was forcibly resized by the OS" (an error in this suite). Tests open windows at least 96 pixels wide. Late resizes : resizing an existing window is asynchronous on x11. SDL waits 100 ms for the window manager, then keeps the old size (pygame warns as above) and the new size arrives on a later pump. On a loaded machine every resize came late (over TCP from the container, 8 processes resizing at once: 0.8-3.4 s), so a window changed from 800x600 to 800x480 reported the old size. The engine and the tests set the display mode through glitchygames.display_mode.set_display_mode , which pumps until the size changes and warns only if the window ends at another size than the requested one. Real window events : the X server sends focus, exposure and move events for the real window; a recording made on x11 holds them, and tests that assume only the dummy driver's window events see them. Its raw messages (pygame's SYSWMEVENT ) stay blocked unless a game opts in ( NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES ); before 2026-10-23 the engine's allow-all enabled them, filling queues, recordings and instant-replay journals. No OpenGL ( x11-macos ): with OpenGL, SDL on macOS marks every window OpenGL, loading XQuartz's libGL and Apple's Xplugin into the process, and draws window surfaces through an OpenGL texture. Under load that ended pytest workers without a traceback ( GLXBadContext in X_GLXMakeCurrent through Xlib's default error handler; a crash in SkyLight on Xplugin's event thread). The build leaves OpenGL out ( --disable-video-opengl ), so window surfaces are drawn in software, as in the container, which has no libGL. Root in the container ( x11-linux ): the container runs as root, who can read a file without read permission, so tests/templates/test_template_errors.py 's permission test is skipped there (an outcome difference, not a failure). It runs with an init process ( docker run --init ) that reaps orphaned processes, as on a real system. Pixels : no passing test drew different pixels on x11 than on dummy or cocoa; every x11 difference was a window size or a test's outcome (the two x11 configurations' pixels differed only in the final frames of tests that had already failed on the widened window). Linux in Docker: nox -s test-linux-x11 # The suite runs on Linux in a container ( scripts/linux_x11/Dockerfile ) with real X11 windows on the Mac's XQuartz (TCP enabled: defaults write org.xquartz.X11 nolisten_tcp -bool false , then restart XQuartz) and its sound on the Mac's PulseAudio ( brew install pulseaudio ; the project's .envrc installs it). The session starts XQuartz and, when it is not running, the PulseAudio server with TCP on port 4713, accepting connections without a cookie only from loopback and Docker's private ranges ( 127.0.0.1;192.168.0.0/16;172.16.0.0/12 ); both are left running afterwards ( pulseaudio --kill stops PulseAudio). The container plays through it with SDL_AUDIODRIVER=pulseaudio and PULSE_SERVER=tcp:host.docker.internal:4713 . Without PulseAudio, or when it will not start, one line says so and the container uses dummy audio. compare-drivers ' x11-linux runs use dummy audio (frames do not depend on sound); --sound plays theirs through PulseAudio too. Linux as CI runs it: nox -s test-linux-ci # nox -s test-linux-x11 runs the suite on Linux for its drivers; nox -s test-linux-ci runs it the way CircleCI's Linux job does, to reproduce that job's failures here. It reads the job ( build-and-test-linux ) from .circleci/config.yml : its image ( cimg/python at PYTHON_LATEST_VERSION ), its resource class's memory and CPUs ( small : 2 GB, no swap, and one CPU, given to docker run as --memory , --memory-swap and --cpus ) and its environment ( PYTEST_WORKERS=0 : one serial process; GLITCHYGAMES_TEST_RSS_LIMIT_MB=1600 : tests/memory_guard.py stops the run past it, naming the test), with CI=true and CIRCLECI=true . The container gets what git would commit from this checkout: tracked files and untracked ones that are not ignored, uncommitted changes included, never an ignored file (the host's caches, Hypothesis's database) and no submodule's contents (CircleCI's checkout has none). Its .git is cloned from the repository's git directory, mounted read-only at its own path, so the session runs from a worktree too; HEAD is this checkout's, on its branch, and the remote branches are this checkout's, as fresh as its last fetch. It installs fontconfig, uv and Python at the job's versions, then nox as a uv tool, and runs nox -s test as the job does. Its test-results/ (junit.xml) come back to test-results/linux-ci/ . The memory guard's summary line names the peak it saw (the container's memory less its page cache, what the kernel's 2 GB kill counts), and the last line the container's raw peak (the page cache included, so near 2 GB even on a healthy run). It takes as long as the job (a serial run) or longer: the image is amd64, as CircleCI's machines are (the same wheels: taplo has no arm64 Linux wheel, and building it ran out of the 2 GB), emulated on Apple silicon. Made on macOS; on a Linux host the results are made writable for any user.

docs.text: Replay Performance # How long the engine takes to process each frame of the recorded sessions (the golden replays in each game's tests/fixtures/replays/ and the demos bundled with the games), commit by commit. Every measurement replays a recording headless and unpaced on one machine ( --rebaseline , which times each frame's work without the pacing sleep), so a line moves only when the code got faster or slower, or the machine changed. Times compare only on one machine: each machine (its CPU model) and kind of run is its own line. What the graphs show # Processing time per frame : the median (p50), the 99 th percentile (p99) and the slowest frame (max) of one replay, in milliseconds, by commit (oldest on the left, labelled with the short hash). A frame's budget at 60 FPS is 16.7 ms. Frames over budget : frames whose processing alone took longer than the budget. Live frame time : for the runs that recorded a session live (paced, in a window), how long each frame really took, start to start: how steady pacing was. Replays have none. FPS by commit : the same runs as frames per second. A live run's line (solid) is the FPS it achieved (1 / its frame time); it is paced, so it never passes the target (the dotted line, 1 / the frame budget). A replay's line (dashed) is its headroom (1 / its processing time): how fast the work alone could run. Each point is the average, with a bar from the "5% low" to the "5% high": the mean of the slowest and of the fastest 5% of frames (at least one frame; pause frames count; a live run's first frame, timed from the clock's start, does not). The axis is logarithmic, as headroom runs to thousands. Paced and unpaced numbers do not compare: the processor slows down between paced frames. Machines : each machine's latest replay, as a bar of its average headroom FPS with the same 5% low and high, so platforms compare at a glance for the same recording. Replays only; machines marked (CI) measured on continuous integration's virtual runners, which are noisy. The figures are stored in seconds and turned into FPS only for display. Measurements from before them (2026-10-28) have no FPS point. glitchygames measure and glitchygames report print the same FPS beside the milliseconds. Slowest frame across the recording, by commit : a heatmap per machine. Each column is a stretch of the recording (about 1% of it, start to end) and each row a commit; the color is the slowest frame of that stretch. Hover a cell for its frames, its scene and the time. It shows time only: whether the work itself changed (frames whose content hash differs) is what glitchygames report shows. Measurements from before per-frame profiles have no row. Hover a point for the commit's date and when it was measured. Measurements made on a checkout with uncommitted changes (a trial: nox -s replay-metrics -- --allow-dirty ) are never published: the published site leaves them out, while a local build ( mkdocs build , mkdocs serve , nox -s docs-serve ) shows them, labelled "uncommitted changes". They stay in the pending file after a deploy, so they remain visible locally only. Where the numbers come from # Every commit carries the measurements of its code. A pre-commit hook ( scripts/measure_staged_replays.py , installed by .envrc ) works out the code tree of what is being committed ( src/glitchygames/code_tree.py : only what can change how the replays run, the engine, games, demos, apps, recordings, uv.lock and pyproject.toml ). When this machine has not measured that code yet, it measures every golden replay and bundled demo on it and adds one small file per recording to the commit, under quality/replay-ledger/ . A docs commit after a measured one is instant; code that arrived by a merge from main or a rebase is measured by the next commit (or by hand: uv run python -m scripts.measure_staged_replays , then commit). SKIP=replay-metrics git commit ... skips it. The site shows what landed on main . Every docs build reads the repository's row files and keeps those whose code tree is the code tree of a commit that added rows: on main , the squash merge, so each is shown under the commit its code landed in. Rows of a branch's intermediate commits match none and are left out. A local build shows a branch's rows before it merges; only main is ever published ( nox -s docs-deploy refuses anything else). After each merge to main , CircleCI deploys the site with them; CI never measures (its machines vary). The history measured before this (rows naming their commit) was moved into the repository too ( scripts/import_published_ledger.py ). nox -s replay-metrics still measures by hand ( glitchygames measure ) into the local pending file ( test-results/replay-metrics/pending.jsonl ), which a local build shows. The measuring and the pages are the engine's tools, so any game can keep its own ledger the same way ( Tools for any game ), with the paths in its [tool.glitchygames] (ours: ledger-directory , pending-ledger , published-ledger , measured-paths ): uv run glitchygames unmeasured --game <game> # what is not measured yet on this machine uv run glitchygames measure --game <game> # measure it into the pending ledger uv run glitchygames performance-pages <directory> # the ledger and one graph page per recording ( <game> --measure , --unmeasured and --performance-pages <directory> are the same tools as the game's own flags.) Our docs build makes these pages through scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py and scripts/generate_performance_graphs.py , which only add our docs paths and the snippet below. A recording holds its own last ten runs too; uv run glitchygames report PATH (or <game> --report PATH ) prints them, which frames got slower or faster between runs (only frames that did the same work, by their content hash), and where behavior changed (the frames whose content hash differs, with both runs' commits). Design: plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics.md (Parts 1 and 2). What logging costs # A benchmark rebaselines every golden replay and bundled demo headless three times, through the same child command glitchygames measure runs: at --log-level warning (the replay tools' level and a game's default: logging off), at --log-level info (what a bug report asks a player to run with) and at --log-level debug (everything on). It is not part of the test run ( nox -s test ; it takes under a minute), but CI runs it with the other benchmarks in the macOS job's nox -s performance-test , where a failed rebaseline fails the job. Run it alone with uv run pytest tests/benchmarks/test_logging_cost.py -o addopts = -p no:xdist --benchmark-only --dummy-only or with every other benchmark in nox -s performance-test . It prints two tables and writes them to test-results/logging-cost.md : Top loggers by volume at debug , per recording : each recording's five chattiest loggers, with their records per frame, record count and share of all the records. A logger far ahead of the others (tens of records a frame) is where logging needs cleaning up: a log.debug inside a per-frame or per-sprite loop. Logging cost : per recording, the mean processing time per frame at each level and the change of info and of debug against warning , the medians, each run's peak resident memory, the records per frame at each level and how much output info and debug wrote. The processing times are the engine's own per-frame measurements (what the performance graphs above plot), so the change is the time logging adds to each frame's work. Times compare only on one machine and between runs of the same table. The peak memory is the replaying child's ( n/a on Windows), and its output goes to a file, so a large difference there means the game keeps records in memory. On one Mac (2026-10-28) info cost every recording within 1% of warning (0.08 to 0.33 records a frame), while debug doubled PaddleSlap's processing time per frame (about 10 records a frame) and added 15% to Brave Adventurer's papyrus golden (about 33). At warning no recording should emit an INFO or DEBUG record (the startup options block is one CRITICAL record a run): a logger that does has a level set behind the command line's back (BUGS.md #236), which tests/replay/test_replays_log_quietly.py and tests/test_logger_levels_at_import.py fail on in the ordinary test run. docs.title: Replay Performance

docs.text: How long the engine takes to process each frame of the recorded sessions (the golden replays in each game's tests/fixtures/replays/ and the demos bundled with the games), commit by commit. Every measurement replays a recording headless and unpaced on one machine ( --rebaseline , which times each frame's work without the pacing sleep), so a line moves only when the code got faster or slower, or the machine changed. Times compare only on one machine: each machine (its CPU model) and kind of run is its own line.
docs.title: Replay Performance

docs.text: Processing time per frame : the median (p50), the 99 th percentile (p99) and the slowest frame (max) of one replay, in milliseconds, by commit (oldest on the left, labelled with the short hash). A frame's budget at 60 FPS is 16.7 ms. Frames over budget : frames whose processing alone took longer than the budget. Live frame time : for the runs that recorded a session live (paced, in a window), how long each frame really took, start to start: how steady pacing was. Replays have none. FPS by commit : the same runs as frames per second. A live run's line (solid) is the FPS it achieved (1 / its frame time); it is paced, so it never passes the target (the dotted line, 1 / the frame budget). A replay's line (dashed) is its headroom (1 / its processing time): how fast the work alone could run. Each point is the average, with a bar from the "5% low" to the "5% high": the mean of the slowest and of the fastest 5% of frames (at least one frame; pause frames count; a live run's first frame, timed from the clock's start, does not). The axis is logarithmic, as headroom runs to thousands. Paced and unpaced numbers do not compare: the processor slows down between paced frames. Machines : each machine's latest replay, as a bar of its average headroom FPS with the same 5% low and high, so platforms compare at a glance for the same recording. Replays only; machines marked (CI) measured on continuous integration's virtual runners, which are noisy. The figures are stored in seconds and turned into FPS only for display. Measurements from before them (2026-10-28) have no FPS point. glitchygames measure and glitchygames report print the same FPS beside the milliseconds. Slowest frame across the recording, by commit : a heatmap per machine. Each column is a stretch of the recording (about 1% of it, start to end) and each row a commit; the color is the slowest frame of that stretch. Hover a cell for its frames, its scene and the time. It shows time only: whether the work itself changed (frames whose content hash differs) is what glitchygames report shows. Measurements from before per-frame profiles have no row. Hover a point for the commit's date and when it was measured. Measurements made on a checkout with uncommitted changes (a trial: nox -s replay-metrics -- --allow-dirty ) are never published: the published site leaves them out, while a local build ( mkdocs build , mkdocs serve , nox -s docs-serve ) shows them, labelled "uncommitted changes". They stay in the pending file after a deploy, so they remain visible locally only.
docs.title: What the graphs show

docs.text: Every commit carries the measurements of its code. A pre-commit hook ( scripts/measure_staged_replays.py , installed by .envrc ) works out the code tree of what is being committed ( src/glitchygames/code_tree.py : only what can change how the replays run, the engine, games, demos, apps, recordings, uv.lock and pyproject.toml ). When this machine has not measured that code yet, it measures every golden replay and bundled demo on it and adds one small file per recording to the commit, under quality/replay-ledger/ . A docs commit after a measured one is instant; code that arrived by a merge from main or a rebase is measured by the next commit (or by hand: uv run python -m scripts.measure_staged_replays , then commit). SKIP=replay-metrics git commit ... skips it. The site shows what landed on main . Every docs build reads the repository's row files and keeps those whose code tree is the code tree of a commit that added rows: on main , the squash merge, so each is shown under the commit its code landed in. Rows of a branch's intermediate commits match none and are left out. A local build shows a branch's rows before it merges; only main is ever published ( nox -s docs-deploy refuses anything else). After each merge to main , CircleCI deploys the site with them; CI never measures (its machines vary). The history measured before this (rows naming their commit) was moved into the repository too ( scripts/import_published_ledger.py ). nox -s replay-metrics still measures by hand ( glitchygames measure ) into the local pending file ( test-results/replay-metrics/pending.jsonl ), which a local build shows. The measuring and the pages are the engine's tools, so any game can keep its own ledger the same way ( Tools for any game ), with the paths in its [tool.glitchygames] (ours: ledger-directory , pending-ledger , published-ledger , measured-paths ): uv run glitchygames unmeasured --game <game> # what is not measured yet on this machine uv run glitchygames measure --game <game> # measure it into the pending ledger uv run glitchygames performance-pages <directory> # the ledger and one graph page per recording ( <game> --measure , --unmeasured and --performance-pages <directory> are the same tools as the game's own flags.) Our docs build makes these pages through scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py and scripts/generate_performance_graphs.py , which only add our docs paths and the snippet below. A recording holds its own last ten runs too; uv run glitchygames report PATH (or <game> --report PATH ) prints them, which frames got slower or faster between runs (only frames that did the same work, by their content hash), and where behavior changed (the frames whose content hash differs, with both runs' commits). Design: plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics.md (Parts 1 and 2).
docs.title: Where the numbers come from

docs.text: A benchmark rebaselines every golden replay and bundled demo headless three times, through the same child command glitchygames measure runs: at --log-level warning (the replay tools' level and a game's default: logging off), at --log-level info (what a bug report asks a player to run with) and at --log-level debug (everything on). It is not part of the test run ( nox -s test ; it takes under a minute), but CI runs it with the other benchmarks in the macOS job's nox -s performance-test , where a failed rebaseline fails the job. Run it alone with uv run pytest tests/benchmarks/test_logging_cost.py -o addopts = -p no:xdist --benchmark-only --dummy-only or with every other benchmark in nox -s performance-test . It prints two tables and writes them to test-results/logging-cost.md : Top loggers by volume at debug , per recording : each recording's five chattiest loggers, with their records per frame, record count and share of all the records. A logger far ahead of the others (tens of records a frame) is where logging needs cleaning up: a log.debug inside a per-frame or per-sprite loop. Logging cost : per recording, the mean processing time per frame at each level and the change of info and of debug against warning , the medians, each run's peak resident memory, the records per frame at each level and how much output info and debug wrote. The processing times are the engine's own per-frame measurements (what the performance graphs above plot), so the change is the time logging adds to each frame's work. Times compare only on one machine and between runs of the same table. The peak memory is the replaying child's ( n/a on Windows), and its output goes to a file, so a large difference there means the game keeps records in memory. On one Mac (2026-10-28) info cost every recording within 1% of warning (0.08 to 0.33 records a frame), while debug doubled PaddleSlap's processing time per frame (about 10 records a frame) and added 15% to Brave Adventurer's papyrus golden (about 33). docs.text: Upstream Issues # Problems found in the tools this project depends on, worked around here, to be reported to their projects. Each entry holds the evidence an upstream report needs: the versions, the measurements, how the cause was found, a reproduction, and the issue text drafted for posting. None has been posted yet. When a release fixes one, upgrade, check the reproduction no longer shows it, remove the workaround and move the entry to the Fixed section. Open # mkdocs serve keeps every rebuild alive (griffe and mkdocstrings-python) # Found 2026-10-24, BUGS.md #213. A local mkdocs serve ( nox -s docs-serve ) was at 14.5 GB. Versions : griffe ( griffelib ) 2.4.1, mkdocstrings 1.0.8, mkdocstrings-python 2.0.10, mkdocs 1.6.1, Python 3.14, macOS. Both griffe and mkdocstrings-python were the latest releases on PyPI when this was measured. Measurements (resident memory after each build; the same inputs every time): Build Four builds in one process, as serve builds With the workaround mkdocs serve , with the workaround start 674 MB 0 694 MB 688 MB 1 1016 MB 685 MB 913 MB 2 1375 MB 718 MB 936 MB 3 1532 MB 647 MB 920 MB 4 905 MB 5 928 MB About 330 MB per rebuild was never freed, though gc.collect() ran after each build. In the live server (last column, rebuilds triggered by touching docs/index.md ) the first rebuild raised it to about 920 MB, and it stayed there. How the cause was found : Not the data: the graphs this project's hook generates are a few kilobytes, and its scripts load once ( sys.modules stayed at 736 modules over the builds). Counting live objects by type across one build: the growth was griffe's models ( ExprName +23,876, Alias +17,512, Parameter +9,304, Function +4,314, ...), mkdocstrings' InventoryItem and autorefs' BacklinkCrumb : a whole API tree and its handler per build. Weak references to each build's config and Python handler showed every one still alive. The old handler's referrers were all inside the build (the mkdocstrings plugin, its Markdown extension and AutoDocProcessor ), so something outside reached that group. Clearing every populated functools cache in the process freed the first build's handler (958 -> 521 MB). Clearing the suspect caches one at a time: mkdocstrings-python's _test_existing_template freed the old handler (959 MB, its tree still held), then griffe's _dataclass_parameters freed the tree (530 MB). Clearing others after those changed nothing. The two caches : griffe, griffe/_internal/extensions/dataclasses.py : @cache def _dataclass_parameters ( class_ : Class ) -> list [ Parameter ]: An unbounded cache keyed by Class objects. Each Class references its module and the whole modules collection, so one entry keeps the build's entire API tree (about 430 MB here). - mkdocstrings-python, mkdocstrings_handlers/python/_internal/rendering.py : @cache @pass_environment def _test_existing_template ( env : Environment , path : str ) -> bool : return path in env . list_templates () Keyed by the Jinja Environment , which each build makes afresh; through it the cache keeps the build's PythonHandler . Reproduction : run from a project whose mkdocs.yml uses mkdocstrings' Python handler on a package with dataclasses ( uv run python repeat_builds.py 4 ): """Build the docs several times in one process, as mkdocs serve does, printing memory after each.""" import gc import os import subprocess import sys import tempfile from mkdocs.commands.build import build from mkdocs.config import load_config def resident_megabytes () -> int : output = subprocess . run ( [ 'ps' , '-o' , 'rss=' , '-p' , str ( os . getpid ())], capture_output = True , text = True , check = True ) . stdout return int ( output ) // 1024 site_directory = tempfile . mkdtemp () for build_number in range ( int ( sys . argv [ 1 ])): # serve loads the config afresh for every rebuild (mkdocs/commands/serve.py builder()) config = load_config ( config_file = 'mkdocs.yml' , site_dir = site_directory ) config . plugins . on_startup ( command = 'serve' , dirty = False ) build ( config , serve_url = 'http://127.0.0.1:8002/' ) del config gc . collect () print ( f 'build { build_number } : resident { resident_megabytes () } MB' , flush = True ) To name the caches, after two builds clear one at a time and watch the first build's handler ( weakref.ref(config.plugins['mkdocstrings'].handlers.get_handler('python')) ) and resident memory: caches = { f ' { item . __module__ } . { item . __qualname__ } ' : item for item in gc . get_objects () if isinstance ( item , functools . _lru_cache_wrapper ) and item . cache_info () . currsize } for name in [ 'mkdocstrings_handlers.python._internal.rendering._test_existing_template' , 'griffe._internal.extensions.dataclasses._dataclass_parameters' , ]: caches [ name ] . cache_clear () gc . collect () print ( name , 'first handler alive:' , first_handler () is not None , resident_megabytes (), 'MB' ) Workaround here : on_post_build in scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py empties every module-level functools cache of the loaded griffe and mkdocstrings modules after each build ( documentation_caches() finds them by scanning the modules, so a renamed cache is still found); tested in tests/test_generate_complexity_graphs.py . The caches only speed up work within one build, so emptying them between builds costs nothing. Remove both, and their tests, when both projects have fixed theirs. Issue drafted for griffe (github.com/mkdocstrings/griffe): _dataclass_parameters cache keeps every mkdocs serve rebuild's API tree alive griffe/_internal/extensions/dataclasses.py decorates _dataclass_parameters(class_) with an unbounded functools.cache keyed by Class objects. Under mkdocs serve , each rebuild loads a new API tree, and the cache keeps the previous trees reachable (each Class references its module and the whole collection). With griffe 2.4.1 on a package of about 4,000 functions, memory grew by about 330 MB per rebuild (694 -> 1016 -> 1375 -> 1532 MB over four in-process builds, gc.collect() after each); calling _dataclass_parameters.cache_clear() after each build kept it flat (about 690 MB). Suggestion: cache on the Class instance (e.g. a private attribute), or in a weakref.WeakKeyDictionary , so the cache dies with the tree. Reproduction: load the config and call mkdocs.commands.build.build(config) several times in one process, gc.collect() between, tracking resident memory (script attached). Issue drafted for mkdocstrings-python (github.com/mkdocstrings/python): _test_existing_template cache keeps every rebuild's handler and Jinja environment alive mkdocstrings_handlers/python/_internal/rendering.py decorates _test_existing_template(env, path) with functools.cache , keyed by the Jinja Environment . Each mkdocs serve rebuild makes a new environment, so the cache keeps every previous one and, through it, the previous PythonHandler (mkdocstrings-python 2.0.10). Clearing it after each build frees the old handler. Suggestion: cache per environment (on env itself, or in a weakref.WeakKeyDictionary ). Fixed # None yet.

docs.text: glitchy.games website on AWS — Design # Date: 2026-10-27 Status: DRAFT, awaiting the owner's review. Nothing is built yet. Repo: glitchygames (this repo). The site and its AWS setup live here; no separate repo. Intent # Put the GlitchyGames Arcade on the public web. A visitor opens play.glitchy.games and gets the arcade (the gallery in the owner's mockup: a featured demo with sound on top, a grid of live silent demo tiles below, arrows / d-pad to browse, Enter / A to play). Every game runs in the visitor's own browser (Pyodide/WebAssembly; plans/2026-10-23-game-host-and-browser-runner.md , scripts/build_browser_bundle.py ), so the server only serves files. Later, a GPU instance on AWS will run AI work (e.g. Bitmappy's AI sprite generation, AI players driven through the outer GameHost layer). It is out of scope to build now, but it is scoped into the cost estimate. Goals # https://play.glitchy.games serves the browser build, over HTTPS, fast worldwide. Every push to main on GitHub publishes the site automatically. The AWS setup is code in this repo, reproducible from scratch. Launch cost stays around $1.50–2.50 / month. The owner hears about it (email) before an AWS bill surprises them. Non-goals (for now) # No servers at launch: no EC2, Lightsail, containers or databases. No GPU instance yet (later phase, below). No home page at glitchy.games yet — it redirects to play.glitchy.games . No docs site yet ( docs.glitchy.games is reserved for the MkDocs site, later). The 24 other domains the owner holds at Namecheap ( glitchygames.* , twitchplaysglitchy* ) stay untouched. Not transferring any domain registration away from Namecheap. Anti-goals # Long-lived AWS access keys stored in GitHub. A setup that only works because of hand-clicked console changes nobody can reproduce. A bill that can grow silently (runaway GPU instance, traffic spike) without an alert. Constraints and facts # AWS account: the owner's existing, long-standing account. It is past the old 12-month free tier and was created before the July 15, 2025 credit-based free plan, so only the "Always Free" allowances apply (CloudFront: 1 TB transfer and 10M requests / month; Lambda; DynamoDB). Domains: registered at Namecheap (namecheap.com). Two are in scope: glitchy.games and glitchygames.ai . Region: us-east-1 (CloudFront certificates must live there; cheapest GPU pricing later). Browser build: scripts/build_browser_bundle.py (on main ) writes build/browser/<game> : the page, the engine and our pygame-ce WebAssembly wheel. The wheel is built from the third_party/pygame-ce submodule and takes several minutes the first time. The games already build as a site: python -m scripts.build_browser_bundle all writes build/browser/site (a directory per game plus an index.html linking them). nox -s docs-deploy runs it and publishes it with the docs as play/ on GitHub Pages ( https://terrysimons.github.io/glitchygames/play/ ; scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py ). PyScript comes from a CDN: browser/index.html loads core.js / core.css from pyscript.net . The Arcade app ( plans/2026-10-23-arcade-showcase.md , feature #43) is a spec, not built. src/apps/ holds only Bitmappy today. CI is CircleCI ( .circleci/config.yml ); there is no .github/ . Its deploy-docs job runs after build-and-test-macos passes on main (macOS m4pro.medium , one at a time via serial-group ), already caches the Pyodide toolchain (~2 GB) and the pygame-ce WebAssembly wheel keyed on the submodule commit, and runs nox -s docs-deploy -- --no-measure . House style: uv, nox sessions, Python 3.14, explicit long names.
