docs.text: Sprite QuickLook preview for macOS — Design # Date: 2026-10-29 Status: BUILT on feat/sprite-quicklook (2026-10-29); the owner checked it in the real QuickLook panel and opened a PR. Plan: plans/2026-10-29-sprite-quicklook-implementation.md . How to build and install: src/quicklook/README.md . Repo / location: glitchygames (this repo), under src/quicklook/ (the owner, 2026-10-29). Intent # When the owner selects a GlitchyGames sprite .toml in Finder and presses space, QuickLook shows the sprite itself — rendered as the sprite, not the TOML text (the owner: "I want to see what the file contents are - rendered as the sprite"). Animated sprites play; static sprites show as one image. Goals # Static sprites ( [sprite] pixels = """…""" , no [[animation]] , e.g. src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/sprites/small_heart.toml ) render as a single image. Animated sprites ( [[animation]] + [[animation.frame]] , e.g. slime-jump.toml at the repo root) auto-play as soon as the preview opens (the owner, 2026-10-29), honoring each animation's frame_interval , each frame's own frame_interval override, and loop . Pixel art stays crisp : scaled up with nearest-neighbor to fill the preview, integer scale factors only, centered. Matches what the engine draws (rules below, taken from src/glitchygames/sprites/animated.py and pixel_utils.py ). If the preview and the game disagree, the preview is wrong. Transparency is visible : transparent pixels show a checkerboard behind them; partial alpha blends over it. Every frame is visible: a film strip per animation (the owner, 2026-10-29: "we need to show all of the frames of the sprite"). Any sprite with more than one frame or more than one animation previews as one row per animation, in file order: the animation's name on the left; every frame left to right, each with its number above it and its duration below it ("0.50s"), wrapping onto more lines rather than scrolling sideways (the owner chose the annotated layout, number on top and timing on the bottom); the live animation playing at the right end of the row on a checkerboard, labeled "playing", "playing (once)" for a non-looping animation, or "still" for a one-frame one; the frame on screen is outlined in blue in its strip; every row plays at once from the moment the preview opens, which replaces the old picker. Claude's calls (the owner agreed 2026-10-29): strip frames fit a 64 pt cell and the live view a 192 pt box, both at a whole-number scale unless the sprite is bigger than that; the panel scrolls vertically when the rows don't fit; a static sprite (one animation, one frame) keeps the single large view, since a one-frame strip would only repeat it. Non-sprite .toml files ( pyproject.toml , .taplo.toml , …) still preview as plain text. macOS gives every .toml the single type public.toml , so the extension is asked for all of them; it must fall back gracefully. An extension can't hand a file back to Apple's built-in text preview, so the fallback is the extension's own scrollable, monospaced, read-only text view with no highlighting. The owner accepted that it will look slightly different from Apple's (2026-10-29). No Python needed at preview time: parsing and rendering are native Swift. Finder thumbnails (the owner, 2026-10-29): icon view, column view, Get Info and the like show the sprite instead of a generic TOML icon. A QuickLook Thumbnail Extension sits in the same host app as the preview extension, and both use one shared parser/renderer. The thumbnail is the first frame of the first animation in file order (the frame that plays first in the preview). For a static sprite it is the single image. It is scaled nearest-neighbor to fit the requested size, centered, and transparent pixels stay transparent (no checkerboard), so it sits on Finder's own background. A sprite smaller than the requested size is scaled up by a whole-number factor. A sprite that doesn't divide evenly may be scaled down nearest-neighbor; it must never be smoothed. Non-sprite .toml files get no custom thumbnail. The extension fails the request, so Finder keeps the normal TOML icon. The builder must confirm that a failed thumbnail request really does fall back to the default icon (not a blank one) on this macOS. Non-goals (v1) # No editing; preview only. No hitbox / frame-anchor overlays, no [[transition]] state-machine playback. No swatch (palette-swap) variants: the [colors] palette as written is what renders. No distribution: no notarization, App Store, or Homebrew cask. It runs on the owner's Mac. Anti-goals (would make it a failure even if it works) # Rendering that disagrees with the engine (wrong colors, transparency, frame order or timing). Blurry / smoothed pixels. Breaking QuickLook for ordinary .toml files. Touching the engine or third_party/ (see the owner's "leave third_party alone" rule). The format, as the engine reads it # Source of truth: AnimatedSprite._load_toml and helpers in src/glitchygames/sprites/animated.py , plus src/glitchygames/sprites/pixel_utils.py . Is it a sprite? It is if the parsed TOML has either a non-empty animation array of tables, or sprite.pixels . Anything else → plain-text fallback. A file that is a sprite but fails to render (bad TOML, no frames) shows a short error plus the text, never a blank pane. Colors — [colors] , keyed by a one-glyph string. docs.title: Sprite QuickLook preview for macOS — Design

docs.text: When the owner selects a GlitchyGames sprite .toml in Finder and presses space, QuickLook shows the sprite itself — rendered as the sprite, not the TOML text (the owner: "I want to see what the file contents are - rendered as the sprite"). Animated sprites play; static sprites show as one image.
docs.title: Intent

docs.text: Static sprites ( [sprite] pixels = """…""" , no [[animation]] , e.g. src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/sprites/small_heart.toml ) render as a single image. Animated sprites ( [[animation]] + [[animation.frame]] , e.g. slime-jump.toml at the repo root) auto-play as soon as the preview opens (the owner, 2026-10-29), honoring each animation's frame_interval , each frame's own frame_interval override, and loop . Pixel art stays crisp : scaled up with nearest-neighbor to fill the preview, integer scale factors only, centered. Matches what the engine draws (rules below, taken from src/glitchygames/sprites/animated.py and pixel_utils.py ). If the preview and the game disagree, the preview is wrong. Transparency is visible : transparent pixels show a checkerboard behind them; partial alpha blends over it. Every frame is visible: a film strip per animation (the owner, 2026-10-29: "we need to show all of the frames of the sprite"). Any sprite with more than one frame or more than one animation previews as one row per animation, in file order: the animation's name on the left; every frame left to right, each with its number above it and its duration below it ("0.50s"), wrapping onto more lines rather than scrolling sideways (the owner chose the annotated layout, number on top and timing on the bottom); the live animation playing at the right end of the row on a checkerboard, labeled "playing", "playing (once)" for a non-looping animation, or "still" for a one-frame one; the frame on screen is outlined in blue in its strip; every row plays at once from the moment the preview opens, which replaces the old picker. Claude's calls (the owner agreed 2026-10-29): strip frames fit a 64 pt cell and the live view a 192 pt box, both at a whole-number scale unless the sprite is bigger than that; the panel scrolls vertically when the rows don't fit; a static sprite (one animation, one frame) keeps the single large view, since a one-frame strip would only repeat it. Non-sprite .toml files ( pyproject.toml , .taplo.toml , …) still preview as plain text. macOS gives every .toml the single type public.toml , so the extension is asked for all of them; it must fall back gracefully. An extension can't hand a file back to Apple's built-in text preview, so the fallback is the extension's own scrollable, monospaced, read-only text view with no highlighting. The owner accepted that it will look slightly different from Apple's (2026-10-29). No Python needed at preview time: parsing and rendering are native Swift. Finder thumbnails (the owner, 2026-10-29): icon view, column view, Get Info and the like show the sprite instead of a generic TOML icon. A QuickLook Thumbnail Extension sits in the same host app as the preview extension, and both use one shared parser/renderer. The thumbnail is the first frame of the first animation in file order (the frame that plays first in the preview). For a static sprite it is the single image. It is scaled nearest-neighbor to fit the requested size, centered, and transparent pixels stay transparent (no checkerboard), so it sits on Finder's own background. A sprite smaller than the requested size is scaled up by a whole-number factor. A sprite that doesn't divide evenly may be scaled down nearest-neighbor; it must never be smoothed. Non-sprite .toml files get no custom thumbnail. The extension fails the request, so Finder keeps the normal TOML icon. The builder must confirm that a failed thumbnail request really does fall back to the default icon (not a blank one) on this macOS.
docs.title: Goals

docs.text: No editing; preview only. No hitbox / frame-anchor overlays, no [[transition]] state-machine playback. No swatch (palette-swap) variants: the [colors] palette as written is what renders. No distribution: no notarization, App Store, or Homebrew cask. It runs on the owner's Mac.

docs.text: Rendering that disagrees with the engine (wrong colors, transparency, frame order or timing). Blurry / smoothed pixels. Breaking QuickLook for ordinary .toml files. Touching the engine or third_party/ (see the owner's "leave third_party alone" rule).
